en: *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others of the Song Dynasty.
The great masters of antiquity, having heard much regarding the profound dharmas and having beheld the traces of the noble ones, have already explained all their meanings.
Though they sought with diligent skillful means, they never obtained anything different [from what they taught].
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* has been expounded by those of great learning;
some [expositions] are extremely concise, while others are immeasurably extensive.
Such various explanations do not accord with the *Sūtras*.
Radiant, excellent, and well-conforming—this treatise alone is supreme.
Without relying on this discourse on emptiness, even the wise would not understand it.
If too concise, it is difficult to comprehend; if too extensive, it causes the intellect to recoil.

I now speak from the middle position, adorning it with the meaning of the extensive exposition (*vaibhāṣya*). "Extensive exposition" is called *vaibhāṣya* in the Sanskrit language; within the *Vaibhāṣya*, the meanings adorn the discourse of the middle position. Regarding the various masters' explanations of the meaning of Dharmatrāta’s *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, their versions differ in being either extensive or concise. That which was explained by Dharmatrāta is the most concise. Upaśānta has an explanation of eight thousand verses, and there is another master who has an explanation of twelve thousand verses; these two treatises are called "extensive. Vasubandhu explained the Dharma in six thousand verses; his work is vast, profound, and far-reaching, and because he has no attachments regarding the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), it is known as the *Anupālambha-ākāśa-śāstra* (The Treatise on Non-Attachment like Space).
I pay homage to the Venerable Dharmatrāta; what he has spoken, I receive upon my head.
I, Dharmatrāta, shall now expound that which was never before taught.
At the earnest request of all his disciples, [I shall explain] the Abhidharma-vibhāṣā.
Diligently contemplate the meaning, that which the assembly of the wise should study;
this essential core is easy to understand and comprehend, bringing liberation from affliction and saving all living beings.

Furthermore, in order to manifest the antidotes for the purification of afflictions, and because it is what ought to be relied upon according to the Abhidharma-vibhāṣā, the Venerable Dharmatrāta and I, Dhamatrāta, have together adorned the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya* to explain the true meaning, free from both excessive prolixity and brevity.
Question:
Setting aside the true meaning for a moment,
what is meant by "Abhidharma"?
What is meant by *vibhāṣā*? Answer:

Regarding the profound meaning and flavor of the various truths and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as taught by the Muni, the detailed exposition and clear elucidation of the meaning of their true nature is called *abhidharma*.

Furthermore, it can manifest the meaning of the sūtras just as a lamp provides illumination; this is the nature of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). If one grasps its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is the awakening to phenomena (*dharma*), which is Abhidharma.

If one grasps it as the collection of factors—the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and names—it is superior among all treatises and leads toward liberation; thus it is called Abhidharma.

Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* investigates and elucidates the essential truths through questions and answers regarding the meaning of the true nature as taught by the Muni; it accords with the sūtras and brings joy to the minds of the multitude.

That which explains the various meanings of infinite phenomena through manifold categories and manifold expositions—namely, nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), stages (*bhūmi*), bases (*āśraya*), conduct (*caryā*), conditions (*pratyaya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), faculties (*indriya*), concentrations (*samādhi*), mundane wholesomeness (*laukika-kuśala*), as well as the meanings of elements (*dhātu*), training (*śaikṣa*), and abandonment through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*); and how these are acquired through application (*prayoga*) or through detachment (*vairāgya*); where they first arise; their inclusion (*saṃgraha*); their association (*samprayoga*); causes (*hetu*), conditions (*pratyaya*), fruits (*phala*), and results with fruit (*saphala-phala*)—this is called the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, briefly explained two types of knowledge:

dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). The *Vibhāṣā* explains them with infinite distinctions. Regarding that which is called dharma-knowledge: it is of the nature of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā); this is its characteristic as knowledge. As for its name, because one first knows the dharmas through it, it is called dharma-knowledge.

In the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*), based on the sixteen aspects of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) as its object, the knowledge of the four truths and the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) constitutes the characteristic of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). It is associated with the three faculties (*trīṇi indriyāṇi*) and the three samādhis; the three faculties are joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The three samādhis are: with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, and without vitarka and without vicāra; they pertain to the three time periods, take the three time periods as their object, and are world-transcending. These are wholesome and take three kinds of objects—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and are non-bound, taking the desire realm and the non-bound as their objects.

These [factors] have three types of objects—namely, those that are *śaikṣa*, *aśaikṣa*, and neither-*śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*. They have three types of conditions that are not abandoned—namely, those abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those that are not abandoned (*aheya*).

These are the conditions of name and the conditions of meaning; they are acquired through skillful means and through the attainment of detachment. They are phenomena arising within the desire realm that pertain to the dharma-realm, are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and are associated with the mind-realm (*manodhātu*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness-realm (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The three causes are those produced by the three causes of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The four conditions are those produced by the four conditions of intrinsic nature.

These are the initial outflow-free (*anāsrava*) fruits of reliance (*niśraya-phala*) and fruits of functional effort (*prayoga-phala*); those that arise simultaneously are exclusively fruits of functional effort.
Regarding those with results, there are three results: namely, the two preceding ones and the result of liberation; the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*) is not mentioned.
All phenomena should be understood in this way.
Question:

Having already understood the fundamental principle of dependent origination over a long period, why is it that the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* explains its antidote by means of the "ultimate meaning" (*tattvārtha*)?
Answer: It is for the sake of knowing the ultimate meaning; if one does not analyze the various treatises, it is difficult to comprehend.

Because of this lack of knowledge, true wisdom does not arise; because true wisdom does not arise, one does not know reality; because one does not know reality, one does not see the faults and evils of afflictions and conditioned formations; and because one does not see these faults, one falls into the evil destinies.
Conversely, by being the opposite of that, one is born in the heavens or attains liberation.
Question:
You have already explained the reason for speaking; you should now explain the true meaning. Answer:
This treatise is the most preeminent among all treatises; it fully elucidates all spheres of experience and expands wisdom within the Abhidharma-śāstra.

When the five corruptions increase, life span, wisdom, and mindfulness all diminish. Observing that people feel fear and dread upon hearing and retaining this vast treatise, [the author], for the benefit of himself and others, has briefly explained the true and well-spoken teachings of the three times. Out of compassion for the teachers of heterodox and erroneous doctrines, and out of a deep longing for the former supreme masters of the True Dharma and the assembly of noble ones, he has conceived great reverence and faith toward them. In order to awaken in sentient beings mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and to manifest the true merits of the Triple Gem, he now begins the treatise and speaks these verses.
I pay homage to the Foremost One, who has transcended all afflictions and is honored for his peaceful teachings;
he whose speech is entirely complete, the Arhat who perceives the ultimate truth.
Regarding "I pay homage": it means to generate a virtuous mind that transforms the fruits of craving, prostrating with one's entire body in reverence.
"Former" means "prior. What is prior?
It refers to that which is most excellent, as it indicates the locus of worship.
What is the meaning of "supreme" (*parama*)?
It is called supreme because it subdues all afflictions (*kleśa*).
As stated in the verse:
Upaka, you should know that we Buddhas have all already abandoned all outflows (*āsrava*); for this reason, we are called "Supreme.
As for being "free from affliction," the various entanglements of the afflictions (*kleśa*) burn one's body and mind.
The World-Honored One has brought all sentient beings to peace throughout vast eons; because he has eternally extinguished their blazing afflictions, he is called "Free from Distress.
Since he speaks with ease and security, one should know that he is free from distress; therefore, he next teaches the doctrine of peace.
"Peace" (an) refers to tranquility; "teaching" (jiao) refers to verbal instruction. Because the teaching brings about peace, it is called the "teaching of peace.
Briefly stated, this involves bringing peace to oneself and bringing peace to others: being free from affliction is bringing peace to oneself, while the teaching of peace is bringing peace to others.
Because it is non-erroneous, one knows that the teaching is peaceful; therefore, it is next stated that both the speaker and the spoken are fully complete.
"Speaker" refers to verbal expression, which is precisely the peaceful teaching.

"Endowed with" means that one possesses eloquence that is correct, profound, subtle, manifest, and decisive; it refers to teaching without inversion so as to reach the ultimate reality, for this does not contradict the two truths—therefore, it is called "endowed."
Therefore, paying homage to them is called making offerings to the Dharma.
An Arhat is one who has reached the ultimate state where the characteristics of the Dharma are fully perfected; for this reason, the Arhat is discussed next.
Being a true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) worthy of receiving offerings, they are called *arhats*; this refers exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Having explained those beyond training, one next explains the trainees (*śaikṣa*) who perceive reality.

"Reality" refers to the four noble truths being non-perverted; that is, having already trained in the eight patiences and eight knowledges, one perceives those true truths, and is therefore said to "see reality."
Although one abiding in the path of seeing has not yet fully traversed the four truths, because they will certainly see them, this stage is also called "seeing reality.
Question:
For what reason is he paid homage?
Answer: The Honored Sage fully knows the two kinds of characteristics of the collection of dharmas;
having also manifested them for others, I shall now explain a small portion.
A Muni is so called because his body, speech, and mind are perfected; thus he is named Muni.
"All" refers to all the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma spoken by the Omniscient One, which have been disseminated down to the present day.
"Knowing" (jñāna) means knowing-seeing; it has the sense of awakening.
"Dharma" means to uphold; because it upholds its own nature, it is called dharma.
Because dharmas have accumulation, they are called "dharma-aggregates" (dharmaskandha).
Those wholesome dharmas and the collection of wholesome dharmas; unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas are likewise.
Second, "number" refers to names.
"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to marks or appearances.
Question:
What are the two characteristics? Answer:

There are specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Specific characteristics are unique; they belong to this [thing] alone and not to others, such as the characteristic of resistance being that of matter (*rūpa*), and so forth.
General characteristics are common; they belong to both this and other things, such as the impermanence of matter, and so forth.
Question:

If the characteristic of resistance (*pratigha*) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form (*rūpa*), it is also a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). When viewed in relation to the four aggregates (*skandha*), it is a specific characteristic; when viewed in relation to the ten kinds of form, it is a common characteristic.

Since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is thus observed as the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), both the two kinds of specific characteristics and universal characteristics would consequently fail to be established.
Answer: Because they are one and the same self-nature.
That which is obstructive is the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it is the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and constitutes the various distinctions among forms, ten types are taught.
Your claim that the self-characteristic and common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are not established because of [the need for] contemplation is incorrect.
Why is this? Because they are not subject to destruction.

It is like father and son, like a seed and its fruit, like the truths of suffering and its origin, or like a prohibition and its hearing; if one contemplates their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are not general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and if one contemplates their general characteristics, they are not specific characteristics.

It is like a single person who is called both father and son; he is called "son" by virtue of being a father, and he is called "father" by virtue of being a son. If one contemplates the father, one does not contemplate the son; if one contemplates the son, one does not contemplate the father.
If it is argued that [the reason] is unestablished, this is not so. Why?
Because it is already established.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the principle of father and son.
Whether good or evil, right view or wrong view—these are explained in detail therein—and from them, one may give rise to the karma of immediate retribution.

If the principle of the father did not exist, there would likewise be no wrong view of denying the father nor right view of acknowledging the father. If these were absent, then purity and impurity would also be absent; if purity and impurity were absent, then liberation would also be absent.

If there were no karma of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma), then cause and effect would also not exist; if cause and effect do not exist, then all phenomena (dharma) would likewise not exist—do not say that this is not a fault.
Therefore, the principle of father and son is established; that which is already established cannot be established again.

If that which is already established were to be established again, it would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, the meaning of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is established.
Question:
Should all phenomena known by the Buddha be explained?
Answer: No. Question:
What is being explained? Answer:
It is also manifested for others; I shall now explain a small portion of it.
"Manifesting" means to reveal and explain the meaning.
"Others" refers to those who are to be transformed.
If the meaning is beneficial and conforms to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), as stated in the *Śiṃśapāvana Sūtra*, I shall now speak briefly regarding the teaching of the Dharma for others therein.
The knowledge of the Tathāgata is profound, vast, and immeasurable; even those such as Śāriputra cannot fully expound it, let alone others.
Question:
What Dharma does the World-Honored One teach?
Answer: They are all thus, whether with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
All conditioned phenomena with outflows are devoid of self, pleasure, permanence, and purity.
Because one does not perceive the outflows (*āsrava*), one falsely experiences them as a self and so forth.

These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that possess outflows are devoid of a self because they lack autonomy; they are devoid of pleasure because they consist of the three types of suffering; they are devoid of permanence because they arise through the power of conditions; and they are devoid of purity because they are the locus of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question:
What are the conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*)? Answer:
The five aggregates produced by all afflictions.
Question:
If tainted formations are devoid of self, pleasure, permanence, and purity, how do sentient beings experience them therein?
Answer: Because they do not perceive the outflows (āsrava), they falsely experience [them] as a self and so forth.

Sentient beings, having failed to understand the characteristics of outflowing formations, then grasp at them as self, blissful, permanent, and pure. Being shrouded by their karma, they do not know them to be non-self; being shrouded by their deportment, they do not know them to be suffering; being shrouded by a continuous succession of similar states, they do not know them to be impermanent; and being shrouded by a thin skin, they do not know them to be impure.
Thus, because of this lack of knowledge, one experiences a self that is pleasant, permanent, and pure.
Question:
What characteristics constitute contaminated action (*sāsrava-karma*)?
Answer: That which increases the various afflictions is called "with outflows" (sāsrava) by the Noble Ones;
because of that name "outflow," the wise call them afflictions.

If, based upon or conditioned by [certain factors], the various afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) increase—as explained in the *Anuśaya-varga*—those formations (*saṃskāra*) are called "tainted phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*) because they arise from outflows (*āsrava*), give rise to outflows, and serve as the locus for outflows.
The uncontaminated (anāsrava) objects do not increase.

This is not the case for the weak, medium, and superior [levels], because they increase based on their support; thus, it is not that they do not increase. They increase based on their support, yet they do not increase with respect to their object.
Question:
Why is this? Answer:
Because they are designated by the name "outflows" (āsrava), the wise call them afflictions (kleśa).

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are called outflows (*āsrava*), because they constantly leak from all sense bases (*āyatana*) and because the mental outflows flow forth in a continuous stream; therefore, one should know that those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which increase the afflictions are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Question:
Does that [consciousness] have another name? Answer:
They are also called afflictions (*kleśa*), the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), and strife (*raṇa*);
because they give rise to affliction, sensation, and strife, so the noble ones have declared.
These very conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are termed afflictions, the aggregate of sensation, and strife.
Why is this? Because they give rise to affliction, sensation, and contention; thus it is said by all the noble sages.
The various afflictions, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), torment sentient beings; therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
Because one experiences it for oneself, it is called "feeling" (vedanā);
because it disturbs the mind, it is called "contention" (raṇa).
There are three kinds of contention:
There are three kinds of contention: the contention of afflictions, the contention of the aggregates, and the contention of strife.
The contention of afflictions refers to the one hundred and eight afflictions.
The contention of the aggregates refers to death.
"Those who engage in strife" refers to those who are mutually opposed.
It should be understood that what is discussed here is the strife of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since the various afflictions such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arise, and all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) arise from these afflictions, they are called "afflictions."
Because it arises from sensation (*vedanā*), it is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Because it arises from contention (*raṇa*), it is called contention.
Having already explained the characteristics of the aggregate of sensation, the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha-lakṣaṇa*) shall now be explained.
If one practices to leave behind afflictions and is likewise liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*),
this and the previously mentioned aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)— these are the aggregates taught by the Noble Ones.
Because one practices to leave behind afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and all outflows, it should be known that this is untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*).

These various untainted formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*) and the previously mentioned aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) are what is called the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the distinction between "aggregate" (*skandha*) and "aggregate of feeling" (*vedanā-skandha*): the combination of that which evolves (*pravartate*) and that which does not evolve (*na pravartate*) constitutes the aggregate; that which evolves is the aggregate of feeling.
Question: What is it? Answer:
What are called the aggregates of form and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
these five aggregates are taught in their sequential order according to their relative coarseness and subtlety.
These five aggregates are the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
It comprises all forms—past, future, and present—and so forth, as explained at length.
That which has arisen and ceased is called the past; that which has not yet arisen and not yet ceased is called the future; and that which has already arisen but not yet ceased is called the present.
That which pertains to one's own body is called "internal," while that which pertains to the bodies of others and to non-sentient things is called "external.
Furthermore, the meaning of internal and external is as explained in the context of the sense bases (*āyatana*).

That which is coarse is called "with resistance" (sapratigha), and that which is subtle is called "without resistance" (apratigha). If you say this is not established, it is not so, because it is observed.
That it is not established because it is observed is incorrect; for if one observes what is coarse, it is not subtle.
That which is defiled is called "ugly color" (*durvarṇa*); that which is undefiled is called "beautiful color" (*suvarṇa*).
The past and future are called "distant," while the present is called "near.
There are four meanings of "distance," as explained in the *Caryā-varga*.
All of these are collectively and briefly described as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); this is a brief designation of the name, not a brevity of the phenomena themselves.
As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding the distinctions therein: that which is experienced by one's own body is called internal, while that which is experienced by another's body is called external.
These arise through the power of internal conditions or external conditions, and through the power of skillful means or the power of objective spheres.
The coarse refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness, while the subtle refers to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
This applies likewise to the defiled and non-defiled realms and stages, and even up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
This formation is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); one should know that those external to it are reckoned as either sentient beings or non-sentient beings.
Question:
What are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

Answer: Obstructive characteristic is the characteristic of form (rūpa); the characteristic of following and experiencing is that of feeling (vedanā); the characteristic of conforming and cognizing is that of perception (saṃjñā); the characteristic of conditioning and constructing is that of formations (saṃskāra); and the characteristic of differentiation is that of consciousness (vijñāna).
Although past matter does not obstruct, it did so in the past;
although future matter does not yet obstruct, it will do so in the future.
Although each individual atom does not obstruct, when atoms aggregate, they do obstruct.
Although the unconditioned (*avijñapti*) is not obstructive, because conditioned form (*vijñaptirūpa*) is obstructive, it too is obstructive.
It is like a tree: when the tree moves, the shadow also moves.
As it is with the past and future of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with the other four aggregates.
Question:
For what reason were the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) through to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) previously taught? Answer:
These five aggregates are explained in sequence according to their relative coarseness and subtlety.

Among those five aggregates, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the coarsest because it is the basis for the five consciousnesses and the objective domain of the six consciousnesses; therefore, it is mentioned first.

Although the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is not material, it is described as being like matter because its activity is coarse; for example, when one says "my head or foot hurts," sensation follows that movement. In this way, up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), which is the most subtle; therefore, it is explained last.

Furthermore, from the unknowable beginningless limit until now, men have been attached to the forms of women and women to the forms of men; because of this attachment to such objects, it was stated previously.

Craving arises for pleasant feeling because of attachment; craving for pleasant feeling arises because of the perversion of perception; the perversion of perception arises because of afflictions; and afflictions arise based on the mind.

Furthermore, because there are two kinds of contemplation of form (*rūpa*), they serve as gateways to the nectar of the Buddha-dharma: namely, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

Since the contemplation of impurity contemplates derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) and mindfulness of breathing contemplates the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is contemplated first.

Having contemplated form, one perceives the faults of feeling; having perceived the faults of feeling, perception becomes non-perverted; when perception is non-perverted, the afflictions do not arise; when the afflictions do not arise, the mind becomes resilient. This is the sequential explanation of the five aggregates.

Now I shall explain this in reverse order. The arising of purity and impurity has the mind as its root; therefore, one first contemplates the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Once consciousness is contemplated, afflictions (*kleśa*) diminish. When afflictions have diminished, the perception of phenomena (*dharma-saṃjñā*) arises. When the perception of phenomena has arisen, craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) do not arise. Because craving and grasping do not arise, one observes form (*rūpa*); for this reason, the aggregates are explained starting from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness.
Question:
How is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) analytically explained? Answer:
The tenfold [category] refers to the sense-spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*), as well as unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*);
this is the analysis of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as taught by the Muni.
"The tenfold refers to the sense-spheres of form" means: the eye and visible forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, and the body and tangibles.
Regarding unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), it is as explained in the *Karmapada*.
Each of these forms is individually called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which is named the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is precisely the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
Within the eighteen elements (dhātus), seven kinds are also taught:

namely, that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is itself the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), and within the eighteen elements, it is spoken of as the seven mental elements (citta-dhātu).

The remaining [aggregates] consist of the three aggregates; together with the unconditioned and the three unconditioned phenomena, these constitute the entrance of the teaching on dharmas, and they also constitute the dharma-realm.
The "remaining three aggregates" refer to the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations.

The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) without activity are space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
These seven phenomena are called "dharmas," and their entry is also called the "dharma-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*).
Question:

For what reason are sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) established as separate aggregates (*skandha*), while the other mental factors are established as the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)? Answer:
One should know that these two are the roots of contention within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, feeling and perception are established as two distinct aggregates.
It is due to two factors that sentient beings revolve in birth and death: namely, craving for pleasant feeling and inverted perception.

Because of craving for pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), one gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because of attachment through inverted perception (*viparīta-saṃjñā*), one gives rise to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the two roots of contention: the bond of desire-craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā-bandhana*) arises from feeling, while the bond of view-craving (*dṛṣṭitṛṣṇā-bandhana*) arises from perception.
One cultivates the various dhyānas through feeling (vedanā) and cultivates the formless realms through perception (saṃjñā).

Furthermore, among mental factors, some are faculties (indriya) and some are not faculties; the faculty-factor is feeling, while the non-faculty-factor is perception. Therefore, they are explained according to their respective meanings.
Question:
Since all five aggregates are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), why is only one aggregate designated as the "aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāraskandha*)? Answer:

Although the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all formations (*saṃskāra*), they are designated by the single name "aggregate of formations" because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are numerous; thus, it is said that the aggregate of formations is distinct from the others.

Within the aggregate of formations, there are many conditioned formations, both associated (*saṃprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*). Those that are associated include volition (*cetanā*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and so forth; those that are dissociated refer to acquisition (*prāpti*) and the like.
Question:
Since everything is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), why does the sūtra state that only volition (*cetanā*) is the aggregate of formations and not the others? Answer:
Because it is superior, because it is predominant, and because it comes first.
The characteristic of performing is the aspect of mental formation (*saṃskāra-nimitta*); that volition (*cetanā*) is the nature of performing.
If there are other aggregates (*skandha*), they are all included within the five aggregates; this shall now be explained according to reality.
The extensive teachings on the aggregates of dharmas number eighty thousand;
the aggregate of morality and the other aggregates are all subsumed within the five aggregates.
All eighty thousand aggregates of dharma are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because the Buddha taught that their nature is speech.
Some say that what is termed "nature" (dharmatā) is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

As for the other five aggregates, such as morality (śīla), the aggregate of morality is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), while the aggregates of concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuktijñānadarśana) are all subsumed under the aggregate of formations.
If there are other names for aggregates (*skandha*), they are all included within the five aggregates.
Question:
To what extent should one speak of the aggregate of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*)?
Answer: The "aggregates of Dharma" (dharmaskandha) refer to the sūtras and śāstras;
each of these is explained individually, along with their various remedial practices—all such categories are termed "aggregates of Dharma."
Some say that each individual sutra or treatise is called a *dharmaskandha*, and that there are six thousand such sutras and treatises.
Others say that each individual aggregate (*skandha*) or sense-base (*āyatana*) is a *dharmaskandha*.
Furthermore, it is said that the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) constitute the number of dharma-skandhas.
According to this teaching, sentient beings possess eighty thousand types of conduct.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, in accordance with their respective conducts, taught the corresponding remedies; all of these constitute the number of dharma-skandhas.
Question:
It was previously stated that the ten bases (*āyatana*), namely the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What, then, are the bases?
Answer:
What are called the eye, ear, and nose, the tongue, body, and mind;
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; and the remainder are termed the spheres of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
That which is the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) is the pure matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the support for visual consciousness; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body bases.
As for the distinctions, they follow the basis of consciousness.
Regarding the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), it consists of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
One should understand the distinctions produced by those [factors]—name, object, activity, time, and designation—as they pertain to name and so forth.
As for the names: they are called "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
As for the meanings: "gathering and arising" is the meaning of mind; "deliberating" is the meaning of intellect; and "discerning" is the meaning of consciousness.
Regarding "function" (*karma*): knowing at a distance is this mind (*citta*); knowing what precedes is this thought (*manas*); that which arises in succession is this consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding "time" (*adhvan*): the past time is this thought; the future time is this mind; the present time is this consciousness.

Regarding "provisional designations" (prajñapti): the designation of the elements (dhātu) is mind; the designation of the sense-bases (āyatana) is intellect; the designation of the aggregates (skandha) is consciousness.
Furthermore, when greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth are differentiated, their objects are immeasurable.
A concentrated mind is called "undistracted"; a defiled mind contrary to this is called "distracted.
A mind associated with laziness is called "lax," while a mind associated with diligence is called "aroused."
Familiarity with a small amount of pure mind and defiled mind is called "small"; familiarity with a great deal of pure mind is called "great.
A small number of roots, easily obtained, with few counteragents and few concomitants—such defiled minds are called "minor"; wholesome minds that are the opposite of these are called "major."
Regarding that [object], there is cultivation and non-cultivation. Thus, a defiled mind is called "uncultivated," while its opposite, a wholesome mind, is called "cultivated.

Regarding intrinsic liberation (*svabhāva-vimukti*) and liberation-in-abiding (*avasthāna-vimukti*), a defiled mind is called "unliberated," while its opposite, a wholesome mind, is called "liberated."

There are some minds that are liberated by their very nature but are not currently abiding in liberation; there are some minds that are currently abiding in liberation but are not liberated by their very nature; there are some minds that are both liberated by their very nature and currently abiding in liberation; and there are some minds that are neither liberated by their very nature nor currently abiding in liberation.
That which is liberated by nature but not currently in liberation is the untainted mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
That which is currently in liberation but not liberated by nature is the tainted mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is both naturally liberated and currently in a state of liberation is the untainted mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That which is neither naturally liberated nor currently in a state of liberation is the tainted mind of one in training (śaikṣa) as well as the mind of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
The sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is of three kinds: namely, form (*rūpa*), location (*sthāna*), and both.
"Form" refers to blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth, as explained at length.
"Location" refers to bodily form (*kāyavijñapti-rūpa*).
"Both" refers to things such as the creation of paintings and the like.

There are three types of sound-entrance (*śabdāyatana*): namely, sound caused by the four great elements that are appropriated (*upātta*), sound caused by the four great elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta*), and sound caused by both.
Sound produced by the four great elements that are appropriated refers to sound generated through the conditions of the throat, lips, and tongue.
Sound produced by the four great elements that are not appropriated refers to sound generated through the conditions of wind, bells, trees, and so forth.
Regarding "sounds produced by causes," this refers to sounds generated through conditions such as striking a drum or blowing a conch.
Each of those sounds is of two kinds: agreeable and disagreeable.
The sense-base of odor (*gandhāyatana*) is of three kinds: namely, pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and odor that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant.
The sense-base of taste (*rasāyatana*) is of six kinds: namely, pungent, sour, sweet, bitter, salty, and bland.
Question:
When one tastes a flavor, does the tongue-consciousness perceive it first, or is it the body-consciousness? Answer:
If one first perceives cold or heat, then the body-consciousness precedes the tongue-consciousness.
If one first distinguishes tastes such as pungency, then the tongue-consciousness precedes the body-consciousness.
The sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) is of eleven kinds: namely, the four great elements and the seven kinds of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
The seven kinds of derived matter are: roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.

The rough is coarse and rigid; the smooth is fine and soft; the light cannot be weighed; the heavy is dense and substantial; the cold seeks warmth; the hungry desires food; and the thirsty desires drink.
Question:
By the increase of which great element do roughness, smoothness, and even hunger and thirst arise? Answer:
Some say that there is no partial increase [of the elements], and that as a result of karma, one first experiences the fruit of coarse *mahābhūta*s, up to hunger and thirst.

Others say that because water and fire increase, there is smoothness; because earth and wind increase, there is coarseness; because earth and water increase, there is heaviness; because wind and fire increase, there is lightness; because water and wind increase, there is cold; because wind increases, there is hunger; and because fire increases, there is thirst.
Question:
How many types of contact can give rise to body-consciousness? Answer:
Some say that each [sensory object], from roughness to thirst, can individually give rise [to consciousness].
Others say that five types of contact can give rise to the four great elements and roughness, and so on, up to hunger and thirst.
Still others say that eleven kinds [of objects] give rise to body-consciousness and the like; since these are the objective spheres of body-consciousness, there is no fault.
There are two kinds of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): the specific characteristic of the thing (*vastu*) and the specific characteristic of the sense-base (*āyatana*).
The specific characteristic of the thing refers to the common objective field.
The specific characteristic of the sense-base refers to its own unique objective field.
Of these eleven kinds, two are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-viprayukta*): hunger and thirst are not bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Nine kinds are bound to both the desire and form realms; although garments in the form realm cannot be weighed, the others can be weighed and can also be accumulated.
Although there is no suffering from cold or heat, there is nourishment and regulation.
Regarding hunger and thirst, some say they are "concordant fruits" (*niṣyanda-phala*), because they can be eliminated by food and drink.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that retributive matter (vipākaja-rūpa), once severed, cannot be resumed.

The Kaśmīris maintain that hunger and thirst are obstacles to wholesome and unwholesome retribution; therefore, they are not perceptible, but once food has been digested, they become perceptible again.
Therefore, for the wealthy, hunger and thirst are the result of wholesome karma; for the poor, hunger and thirst are the result of unwholesome karma.
As for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it consists of four kinds of non-manifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), as explained in the *Karmapada*.
Mental factors (*citta-dharma*) are as explained in the Chapter on Conduct (*Caryā-varga*).
Mental non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are as explained in the Chapter on Miscellaneous Topics (*Saṃkīrṇa-varga*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) shall be explained later in this chapter.

Among the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*) is mentioned first because its objective field is coarse; among the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) is mentioned first because its intrinsic nature is coarse.
They are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they are the gateways through which suffering and pleasure enter.
Furthermore, the meaning of "killing" (hana) is the meaning of "entrance" (āyatana), for it is within this that the mind and mental factors cease.
Question:
What is the distinction between an entrance (āyatana) and a contact-entrance (sparśāyatana)?
Answer: The sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) is itself a sense-base.
Alternatively, there are sense-bases that are not the sense-base of tangibility; these are the external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
If an internal sense-base (*āyatana*) is "non-part" (*aprakāra*), it means that although it is a sense-base, contact does not arise due to a deficiency in conditions; thus, it is called "non-part.
Because it is the locus where contact resides, it is called a "contact sense-base" (*sparśāyatana*).
That which touches emptiness is merely the sense base (*āyatana*),
because it is the gateway through which contact enters, just as windows and doors allow wind to enter in India;
and because it is the locus where contact abides, it is like a noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*).

One should also say that feeling (vedanā) arises because it is nourished by contact (sparśa), sustained by contact, and brought forth through the transformation of contact; it manifests through the power of contact. Therefore, it is said that one who enters the noble abode (āryavihāra) does so through contact. "Central regions" (madhyadeśa) are called the noble abodes, while "borderlands" (pratyantajanapada) are the lands where the Mlecchas dwell.
Question:
How does a single body possess the twelve bases (āyatana)? Answer:
Although within a single body, the functions performed are each distinct;
because they depend on conditions and their own nature, there are twelve kinds of discrimination.
Within a single body, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are complete, yet their functions are each different.
If a thing is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), that thing is not, up to and including, the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*);
if a thing is the dharma-base, that thing is not, up to and including, the eye-base.
Question:
What are the objects of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the objects of the mental-object-base (*dharma-āyatana*)? Answer:
The eye has seeing forms as its object; form has being the range of the eye as its object; and so on, up to the mental-object-base.
For example, it is like twelve people staying in a single room, each engaged in different activities; such is the case here as well.
Furthermore, they are spoken of as twelve based on the distinction between bases and objects: that is to say, the six groups of consciousness have six bases and six objects.
Furthermore, self-nature is explained as twelvefold: from the self-nature of the eye up to the self-nature of non-dharmas, and from the self-nature of dharmas up to the self-nature of non-eyes.
Question:
Since ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are form (*rūpa*), why is only one base specifically called the base of form (*rūpāyatana*)? Answer:
Although there are many kinds of forms, they are spoken of as a single "form base" (*rūpāyatana*);
one should know that this single form base is so called because it is the objective domain of three eyes:

the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom-eye. Within that base, that which is the objective domain of these three eyes is termed the "form base. These are the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom-eye.

Because form is coarse, twenty kinds are taught, namely: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, oblong, round, oval, high, low, smoke, cloud, dust, mist, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness.
Those eight factors, beginning with length, are divided into three types; all others are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question:
Since all twelve bases (*āyatana*) are entirely of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), why is only one called the "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*)?
Answer: Although all those phenomena are entirely included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
because there are many [subdivisions] within that dharma-sphere, it is designated as "one" dharma-sphere and not otherwise.

Although all of those are entirely included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), because many dharmas are contained within this single sphere—namely, material dharmas and non-material dharmas, associated dharmas and dissociated dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas—it is therefore designated as simply one sphere of mental objects.

Furthermore, there are three characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), and since these characteristics are not distinct from those phenomena, they are included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); therefore, only one sphere of phenomena is spoken of.
Moreover, all phenomena are manifested through names, and those names are included within the sphere of phenomena.
The Dharma is the mark of reality, namely the gate of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
Because one awakens to phenomena by means of prior phenomena, this emptiness enters into the entrance of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
It is not the case that the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) can awaken itself, for it functions through perversion (*viparyāsa*).
The Dharma is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely, quiescent *nirvāṇa*; this Dharma is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Question:
The World-Honored One has taught immeasurable spheres (*āyatana*) in the sūtras; for what reason does he speak of only twelve spheres?
Answer: Those ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana), the eight bases and the two fourfold bases,
as well as the five liberative bases, are all entirely subsumed within the twelve [bases].

Among the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the first eight totalities and the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are of the nature of the wholesome root of non-attachment; they are all included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If their attendants are taken into account, they are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and are entirely included within the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects.

Among the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the last two totalities and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are of the nature of the four aggregates; they are all included within the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
As for the two [remaining] spheres, they refer to the sphere of non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattvāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The beings in the state of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) enter into ten bases (āyatana), excluding the bases of odor and taste.
When the four formless attainments (ārūpya) are explained, the base of non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) has already been explained.
The five liberations (vimokṣa-āyatana) are of the nature of wisdom (prajñā); their attendants are of the nature of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). All of these are included within three bases:

Regarding the five bases of liberation within the sense-base of sound, the sense-base of mind, and the sense-base of mental objects: first, one attains liberation immediately upon the Buddha’s teaching; second, one attains it by reflecting after hearing [the teaching]; third, one attains it by reciting the sūtras oneself; fourth, one attains it by preaching the Dharma for others; and fifth, one attains it through conditions.
Question:
Regarding the eighteen elements (dhātus) that have been mentioned, do they exist as eighteen substances or are there merely eighteen names? Answer:
The elements (dhātu) are said to be seventeen, or they are said to be twelve;
based on their objects and supports, they are distinguished as eighteen kinds.

Regarding the eighteen elements, there are seventeen kinds or twelve kinds: if one includes the mind-element (manodhātu), the six consciousnesses are lost; if one includes the six consciousnesses, the mind-element is lost.

For example, if one takes up individual trees, the forest is lost; if one takes up the forest, the trees are lost. The analogies of the fingers and the fist are likewise: if one takes up the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the six consciousnesses are lost; if one takes up the six consciousnesses, the mind-element is lost.
Question:
If that is so, why are eighteen elements (dhātus) taught? Answer:
The bases, the possessors of the bases, and the objects—these eighteen types are distinguished.
For three reasons they are called the eighteen *dhātus*: because of the basis, the possessor of the basis, and the object.
The bases refer to the six bases: the eye-element up to the mind-element.
The supported refer to the six consciousness-elements: the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element.
The objects refer to the six external elements.

If it is argued that the final mind of an Arhat does not give rise to a subsequent consciousness because it is not the mental element (*manāyatana*), this is not so; rather, the subsequent consciousness does not continue due to the absence of other conditions, just as there is no sprout when there is no seed in the earth.

Furthermore, based on contact (*sparśa*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are established. Eye-contact arises from three causes and conditions: namely, the eye, form, and consciousness; and so it continues up to the mind.
By way of the vessel, the food, and the eater.
The vessel refers to the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*); the food refers to the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*); the eater refers to the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñāna-dhātu*).
Question:

One should say there are twenty-one elements: the two eyes, the two ears, and the two nostrils make six; the tongue element and the body element make seven; then the mind element and the six external objects.
Answer: The two eyes are said to be one element, because the two are of a single nature.
The ears and nose are also like this; these two are collectively said to constitute one element (*dhātu*).
This is for the sake of making the body beautiful, and because they are not each individual [elements].

Although there are two eyes, they are said to be one element because they possess a single self-nature, because they are both produced by the same four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and because they share a single visual perception.
It is not the case that a single [organ] possesses two faculties, because it is the support for a single consciousness.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the two eyes to be the supports for eye-consciousness, because a single consciousness relies upon a single sense-base (*āyatana*), and because both [eyes], as objects of a single sense-base, experience a single objective field simultaneously.
The two eyes together apprehend a single form; when one eye sees a form, it is not clear, but when both eyes see a form, it is clear.
The two ears and two nostrils constitute a single element (*dhātu*), as explained for the eyes.

To adorn the body, two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils arise; for if one had but a single eye, people would not hold one in affection or respect. Therefore, while the eyes and so forth arise as pairs, the body and tongue arise as single entities.

Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, although he has taught various kinds of elements (*dhātu*), they are all included within the eighteen elements; these shall now be explained in their proper order.
Whatever other elements there may be that the World-Honored One has spoken of in the sūtras, each according to its own intrinsic nature, are all included within the eighteen elements.
If the Blessed One says that all other elements are included within the eighteen elements by way of three things— namely, the basis, that which depends on the basis,
and the object— as the Blessed One said: "Kauśika!"
There are various elements (*dhātu*) in the world, namely the various views, which are designated by the term "element"; all of these are included within the *dharmadhātu*.
As for the sixty-two elements mentioned in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* and other sūtras, they are likewise subsumed therein.
When explained by way of the *dhātus*, each is included within the eighteen *dhātus* according to its respective meaning.
Question:
What is the distinction between the *dhātus*, the *āyatanas*, and the *skandhas*?

Answer: The "elements" (dhātus) designate all phenomena; these are the same as the twelve "bases" (āyatanas), with the exception of the three unconditioned phenomena. The remainder are designated as the five "aggregates" (skandhas).

All phenomena are explained as the eighteen *dhātus* because they do not depart from their bases, because they are bases themselves, and because they are conditions; those same all-encompassing phenomena are also explained as the twelve *āyatanas*.
The seven mind-elements constitute the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*); this is merely a distinction in terminology.
With the exception of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), all other dharmas are called the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) because they possess the characteristic of accumulation.
Question:
If all phenomena are explained as *dhātus*, then the *dhātus* are themselves the *āyatanas*; excluding the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, they are explained as *skandhas*.
Why did the Blessed One teach these three categories? Answer:

The Muni, observing that sentient beings differ in their inclinations and faculties, and that their natures, behaviors, and delusions vary, has therefore taught the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Sentient beings have three types of inclination: extensive, concise, and intermediate.
For those of extensive capacity, he teaches the *dhātus*; for those of middling capacity, he teaches the *āyatanas*; and for those of concise capacity, he teaches the *skandhas*.

It is the same for those of weak, middling, and superior faculties: for those who are arrogant and negligent due to their innate nature, he teaches the *dhātus*, as the meaning of "nature" (*dharma*) is the meaning of *dhātu*; for those who are arrogant and negligent due to their wealth, he teaches the *āyatanas*.

The meaning of "entrance" (*āyatana*) is the sense of "entering. For those who rely on life and are arrogant and negligent, the aggregates (*skandha*) are taught because the aggregates are subject to death. For beginners, the elements (*dhātu*) are taught; for those with limited practice, the entrances (*āyatana*) are taught.

For those who have already practiced, he explains the aggregates (skandha); for those deluded regarding form and mind, he explains the elements (dhātu); for those deluded regarding form, he explains the sense bases (āyatana); and for those deluded regarding mental phenomena, he explains the aggregates.
Question:
What is the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)? Answer:
The meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is accumulation; the meaning of "entrance" (*āyatana*) is explained as a gateway for the flow [of consciousness];
the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is explained as lineage—these are the three types of distinctions.
The eleven kinds of immeasurable forms and so forth are collectively termed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), like a storehouse or like an army.
For example, just as four distinct types of troops, though different in kind, are collectively called an "army," so too is form (*rūpa*):
although it comprises eleven categories, they share the same characteristic of form and are thus called the "aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*).

As stated in the Abhidharma, one who correctly observes the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) understands that a single atom (paramāṇu) comprises a portion of one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate.
One who does not observe correctly claims that a single atom comprises one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate.
As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
They are called "entrances" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being gateways, because they provide passage for both suffering and pleasure.

They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of lineage or nature (*gotra*), just as a single mountain may contain many different natures, such as the nature of gold, the nature of silver, and so forth.
Thus, because the various natures within a single body are each distinct, they are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
Question:
For what reason are the eighteen *dhātus*, the twelve *āyatanas*, and the five *skandhas* said to be neither more nor less?
Answer: Because they depend on objects as their basis, and because they correspond to the appropriate measures of phenomena,
the elements (dhātus), bases (āyatanas), and aggregates (skandhas) neither increase nor decrease.

Regarding that which is to be measured by the elements, there are six bases; these six bases are the six conditions. If those bases increase, they are no longer bases because there would be no basis for them; if they decrease, then that which depends on them would have nothing upon which to depend.
In this way, all that enters [into experience] is also measured by its dependence on conditions.
Why does the aggregate (skandha) cling to form?
Because it clings to pleasant feeling.
For what reason is there attachment to pleasant feeling?
Because of the perversion of perception.
For what reason is there the perversion of perception?
Because it is associated with afflictions (*kleśa*).
Afflictions depend upon the mind (*manas*), and the mind itself depends upon the mind.
As it is said: "Conditioned by the mind and dharmas, mental consciousness arises. Apart from this basis, there is no other basis.
The intrinsic nature and causal conditions of the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) have already been explained;
now the elements shall be explained in detail. Among the elements, one is visible;
furthermore, it is said that all elements are indeterminate (avyākṛta) in eight types, while the remainder are either wholesome (kuśala) or unwholesome (akuśala).
Regarding "one [element] among the elements is visible": among the eighteen elements, the form element (*rūpa-dhātu*) is visible and observable; because it exists here and there, it is visible.
Furthermore, it is visible because it demonstrates the mental activities of people.
Furthermore, because they manifest themselves, they are said to be the domain of the eye.
It should be understood that seventeen [elements] are invisible, as they lack the characteristic of being an object of visual perception.
Moreover, it is said that all elements are visible, for they are the objects of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
As it is said in the verse:
"The wise perceive all those phenomena as being without self.
As stated in the Abhidharma, one who is in training (śaikṣa) is called a "trace-seer" because they have seen the traces of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, all eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are visible.

Regarding the statement that "eight kinds are indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*): these eight elements are indeterminate, namely the five sense faculties, odor, taste, and the tangible; they are called indeterminate because they cannot be designated as having either desirable or undesirable fruits.

The remaining ten elements can be designated as either wholesome or unwholesome, because they are either virtuous or non-virtuous; namely, the elements of visible form, sound, mental objects, and the seven mind-elements.
Wholesome bodily movement is wholesome form; unwholesome bodily movement is unwholesome form; all other forms are indeterminate.

Thus, sound, the vocal faculty, the active mind, and the seven consciousness-elements are wholesome when associated with a pure mind; they are unwholesome when associated with a mind characterized by lack of shame and lack of dread; otherwise, they are the neutral dharma-element.
If they are associated with the mind, they are explained as in the section on the mind; if they are dissociated from the mind, they are explained as in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
There are four kinds of wholesomeness: by intrinsic nature, by association, by co-arising, and in the ultimate sense.
That which is wholesome by intrinsic nature consists of shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness.
That which is wholesome through association refers to the mind and mental factors associated with those.
That which is wholesome through co-arising refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The ultimate truth refers to nirvāṇa.
These are the four kinds of wholesomeness.
Wholesomeness by intrinsic nature consists of shamelessness, lack of dread, and the three unwholesome roots.
"Associated" refers to those mental states and mental factors that are associated with it.
"Arising together" refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, as well as the formations dissociated from mind.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the perilous cycle of saṃsāra.
That which is diametrically opposed to both is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question:
All phenomena are the twelve bases (*āyatana*), which are precisely what the World-Honored One has declared; for what reason, then, are they called "undeclared" (*avyākṛta*)? Answer:

They are not called "undeclared" because they are not spoken of at all. Rather, that which is wholesome is declared to be wholesome, and that which is unwholesome is declared to be unwholesome; because it is neither declared to be wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called "undeclared."
If cause and effect are simultaneous, they are determinate; if cause and effect are distinct, they are indeterminate.
Alternatively, that which is not spoken of is called indeterminate, as stated in the *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
"All must die"—this is a categorical declaration (*ekāṃsavyākaraṇa*).
"All die and are reborn"—this is called an analytical exposition (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*).
If one asks about a superior rebirth, this is called an interrogative exposition (*paripṛcchāvyākaraṇa*).
The five aggregates of sentient beings differ; this is called the "thesis to be set aside" (sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa).
As for the "thesis to be answered categorically" (ekāṃśika-vyākaraṇa), it is as if someone were to ask:
"Will all sentient beings inevitably die?"
One should answer categorically:
"All sentient beings must die.
As for those who employ analytical discourse, if someone asks:
"Will all who die be born again? One should answer by making a distinction:
"Those with afflictions (*kleśa*) will die and be born again; those without afflictions, having died, will not be born again."
Regarding the *Prakaraṇapāda* (or *Vibhaṅga*), if someone asks:
"Is human birth superior? one should answer with a counter-question:
To which realm do you belong that you ask this?
If you say: "I belong to the heavenly realm."
One should answer:
"Inferior.
If one says:
Regarding the evil destinies,
one should answer:
"Superior."
Regarding the method of setting aside a question (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*):
if someone asks, "Are the aggregates (*skandha*) different from the sentient being, or are they the same?
one should set it aside.
Why is this? Because it is untenable.
It is like asking whether the son of a barren woman is well-mannered and respectful.
A barren woman has no child; how could she answer whether one is respectful or disrespectful?
Likewise, where there are aggregates (skandhas) but no sentient beings, how could there be identity or difference?
It was not answered because it was inappropriate.
The Abhidharmikas say that regarding a categorical (ekāṃśika) discourse, if someone were to ask:
"Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha? [the answer would be given directly].
Is the teaching well-expounded?
Are the disciples of the Blessed One well-directed?
Is form impermanent, and are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness impermanent?
"Are you skilled in discerning suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
To this, one should answer categorically:
"Yes," because it is for the sake of benefit and welfare.
If a Vibhajyavādin says, "I shall preach the Dharma for you," one should ask him:
Dharmas are manifold: whether past, future, or present.
Which dharma do you wish to speak of? If one says:
If one asks me to explain past phenomena, one should ask: "Past phenomena are also manifold;
they consist either of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) or the aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna)."
What is being explained? If one says:
"The aggregate of form."
One should ask:
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is also manifold—being sometimes wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Which of these is being described?
If one says:
"Wholesome form," one should ask:
There are seven kinds of wholesome bodily actions: abstaining from killing, up to abstaining from frivolous speech.
To explain which these are, if one says:
Regarding non-killing,
one should ask:
there are three kinds of non-killing— non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
What is it that he teaches? If one says:
non-attachment.
One should ask:
"Non-greed is of two kinds: manifest (kṛta) and unmanifest (avijñapti).
Which one are you referring to?"
Discourses such as these are called *vibhajya-vyākaraṇa* (analytical exposition).
Regarding *paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa* (interrogative exposition): if someone asks about a phenomenon (*dharma*), one should counter-interrogate them, saying:
"Phenomena are manifold."
"What do you ask? [is the response].
One does not engage in discrimination regarding whether it is past, future, or present, nor even regarding action or non-action.

If the person has a gentle mind, one explains by means of discrimination; if the person is deceitful and crooked, one instead returns the question to them, causing them to answer for themselves. This is called the *vitandā-vāda* (the dialectic of cavil).
Regarding the "thesis of non-communication":
if someone were to ask, "Is the world finite? Is the world infinite?
and so forth—just as one cannot communicate whether a garland of flowers in the sky is fragrant or not—this is called the thesis of non-communication.
Having already explained the determinate and the indeterminate, the twelve obstructive elements shall now be discussed:
Twelve elements are obstructive; one element is said to be partially so;
ten elements and seven [of the remaining] are obstructive, and one is likewise partially so.
It is said that there is resistance (*sapratigha*) regarding the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), as well as regarding obstruction and conditions.
The twelve elements—the elements of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the seven mental elements—are said to possess resistance.
A small portion of the dharma-dhātu is also said to be resistant, namely the mental factors (*caitta*).
Furthermore, the ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) are said to be resistant; likewise, seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*) and a small portion of the dharma-dhātu are also said to be resistant.
Question:
What is meant here by "possessing resistance" (sāpakṣāla)? Answer:
It is said that there are three kinds of resistance (*pratighāta*): resistance as an object (*viṣaya-pratighāta*),
resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), and resistance as a condition (*ālambana-pratighāta*).

Regarding "resistance through objective sphere" (*viṣayapratighāta*), it is as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: the eye is in resistance with visible forms, and so on, up to the mind being in resistance with mental objects (*dharma*).
Since the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has already been explained, one should know that the seven mind-elements and a portion of the dharma-element have also been explained.

Therefore, one should know that among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), one base and a portion of another base are with resistance (*sapratigha*); the five external bases and a portion of the dharma-base (*dharmadhātu*) are without resistance (*apratigha*).
As stated in those sūtras and other texts: "If one contemplates the land, one does not contemplate the water," and so forth, as explained at length.
Obstruction by resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*) refers to mutual opposition and mutual obstruction in their respective locations.
If one [atom] is present, a second cannot abide there, because it is an aggregation of atoms, because it possesses resistance, because it is divisible, and because it occupies a specific location.
It should be known that eight [factors] are non-obstructive; this should be explained in detail herein.
Regarding those with objective obstruction (*sapratigha*), the mind and mental factors operate upon their objects; thus one should ask:
"If a dharma has objective obstruction, does that dharma also have obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇapratigha*)?"
One should formulate four propositions:

either there is resistance by way of object (*ālambana-pratighāta*) but not resistance by way of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), which refers to the seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*) and the mental concomitant dharma-element (*citta-samprayukta-dharma-dhātu*);
or there is resistance by way of obstruction but not resistance by way of object, which refers to the five external elements (*bāhya-dhātu*).
Those that are both objects and possess resistance through obstruction are the five internal elements (*dhātus*).

Those that are neither objects nor possess resistance through obstruction are the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
If a phenomenon is resistant with respect to its objective sphere (*ālambana-pratighāta*), is it also resistant with respect to its object (*ālambana-pratighāta*)?

That is to say, that which is resistant with respect to its object is necessarily resistant with respect to its objective sphere. However, there may be that which is resistant with respect to its objective sphere but not resistant with respect to its object; namely, the five internal elements (*pañca-adhyātma-dhātu*).
There are fifteen [realms] that are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*); the remaining two, three, and three belong to existence;
four are within the desire-existence (*kāmadhātu*); eleven reside in two existences.
Fifteen realms are invariably with outflows:

The five internal bases, the five external bases, and the five consciousness bases are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because they are produced by outflows, because they give rise to outflows, and because they are the locus of outflows;
outflows arise within them, and thus they are said to be with outflows, just as there was previously fear.
Furthermore, they are said to be with outflows because they coexist with outflows, just like food mixed with poison.

As for the remaining two—the mind element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—these three elements are of two kinds: either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
If they are produced by outflows, they are with outflows; if they are the opposite, they are without outflows.

Regarding the "three [realms] within the three existences," the mind-element (manodhātu), the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) are found within the three existences:
the existence of desire (kāmadhātu), the existence of form (rūpadhātu), and the existence of formlessness (ārūpyadhātu).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is unconditioned (*aniyata*); although it is attained within a body belonging to the three realms, it is not attained through their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four [objects]: the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), the taste-element (*rasadhātu*), and the consciousnesses that take these as their objects.
It is not the case that [contact] does not exist in the form and formless realms, for they are free from the desire for edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Since the first three bases (*āyatana*) have the nature of edible food, it would follow that contact (*spraṣṭavya*) should also be absent there; however, this is not so.
The nature of the sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) is of two kinds: either of the nature of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) or not of the nature of non-edible food.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it does not possess the nature of edible food, because the body there is subtle.

Odors and tastes are invariably of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); therefore, they do not exist there. Since their objects are absent, their corresponding consciousnesses are also absent.
Question:
If odors and tastes are absent and their consciousnesses are also absent, then the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) and the tongue-element (*jihvādhātu*) should likewise be absent.
Answer: Because they possess all the faculties (*indriya*), and because the faculties mutually support one another.
Regarding the eleven [faculties] existing in two realms of existence: these are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The five internal bases, the bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles, along with the consciousnesses that take these as their objects—these eleven are not of the formless realm, because they are devoid of the nature of matter.
Five possess both vitarka and vicāra; three are of three types; the remainder are without them.
One should know that seven have an object; the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) is said to include only a portion [of those].

Regarding "with vitarka and with vicāra," there are five [realms]: the five consciousness-elements (pañca-vijñāna-dhātu) possess vitarka and vicāra because they are coarse; this extends up to the Brahma-world, but not to the higher stages.
Regarding "three types of activity" (trayaḥ saṃskārāḥ), there are three kinds within the three realms:
the mind-element (mano-dhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (mano-vijñāna-dhātu), and the element of mental factors associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma-dhātu).

The desire realm and the first dhyāna possess both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); the intermediate dhyāna possesses no vitarka but has vicāra; the higher stages and all dissociated phenomena possess neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Question:
Regarding the factors of the stage characterized by both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), there are four types:
