This refers to the acquisition at six times: namely, during the abandonment of the suffering truth (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm, and during the abandonment of the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation in the form and formless realms; specifically, at the time of the respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), at the time of the four fruits of the śramaṇa, and at the time of the enhancement of the faculties (*indriya-vardhana*).

The five [attainments] abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the form and formless realms are acquired at five times, excluding their own specific antidote (*svabhūmi-pratipakṣa*), because they are first acquired through the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Regarding the five types abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm:
they are acquired at five times, excluding the three types belonging to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
In four moments, there is the "soft-soft" type;
in three moments, there are the eight types of the seven stages of the form and formless realms as well as the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
in three moments, there are those excluding the first three fruits of śrāmaṇya and the soft-soft type.
At two times: [the attainment of] the fruit of arhatship and the enhancement of the faculties.
Question:
How are the various afflictions abandoned?
Answer: It refers to the awakening regarding those conditions, as well as the teaching on the severance of those conditions,
the teaching on the attainment of the antidote, and furthermore, the cessation of those conditions.

There are four ways in which afflictions are abandoned: namely, knowing the object-condition (*ālambana*), the severance of the object-condition, the attainment of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), and the cessation of that object-condition.

Regarding "knowing the object-condition": through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin, one abandons those [afflictions] whose object-conditions belong to one's own realm as well as those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava*).
Those whose conditions are severed are those with outflow-objects that are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
Those who have attained the antidote are those abandoned by the path of cultivation.
Those whose objects are extinguished are those with objects belonging to other realms.

Furthermore, there are five matters by which afflictions are abandoned: namely, the permanent extinction of the cause, attainment of abandonment, transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), knowledge of conditions, and attainment of the antidote.
Having already explained the establishment of the causes and conditions for abandoning afflictions, the knowledge of abandonment shall now be discussed.
Regarding liberation within the desire realm, the Noble Ones speak of four types of abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*);
apart from the form and formless realms, one should know there are five types of abandonment-knowledge.

The nine abandonment-knowledges are established based on the abandonment of afflictions in the desire realm; the four abandonment-knowledges are established based on the abandonment of afflictions in the form and formless realms. Although these five abandonment-knowledges involve knowing through wisdom, they are nonetheless [designated as] abandonment.
Because it is the fruit of knowledge, it is called "abandonment-knowledge" (*prahāṇa-jñāna*); just as the fruit of an action is also called an "action.
The exhaustion of afflictions regarding suffering and its origin is collectively termed one abandonment-knowledge;
for cessation and the path, there is one each, as there are three for the desire realm and the higher realms respectively.

Regarding those afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), one single knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) is established; for those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), two; and for those to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), three.

As it is with the desire realm, so it is with the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*): one is established for those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, two for those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, and three for those to be abandoned through the vision of the path.
This will be explained in detail later in this chapter.
One should know that what is abandoned through the path of cultivation is abandoned realm by realm; each such abandonment is said to be one [fruit].
Three types of abandonment are the fruit of knowledge (*jñāna*); the remainder are said to be the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*).

There is one *prahāṇa-parijñā* for what is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), two for what is abandoned in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and three for what is abandoned in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it should be known that these are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna-phala*).
Question:

For what reason is there established as one *prahāṇa-parijñā* for what is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the form and formless realms, while two are established for what is abandoned through the path of cultivation?
Answer: Because those abandoned by the path of seeing share the same antidote, whereas those abandoned by the path of cultivation do not.
Question:
What is the fruit of the remaining types of abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇajñāna*)? Answer:
The remaining ones are said to be the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the six knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*) that exhaust what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are said to be the fruits of the patiences (*kṣānti*), because the patiences act as their antidotes.

If it were claimed that these abandonments exhausted by the path of seeing are not knowledges of abandonment but rather fruits of the patiences, this would be incorrect; for the patiences are the retinue of knowledge (*jñāna-parivāra*) and share the same fruit as that knowledge.
Therefore, that which is abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation both receive the name "fruit of knowledge.

Having already explained that abandonment is the fruit of knowledge—referring to whether it pertains to a specific stage or path, or to dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—I shall now explain the fruits that are of the same category as those.
The first stage is said to include all; The dhyānas have five and also eight;
The formless attainments are said to have one fruit; The same applies to their associated fruits.
Regarding "the first stage is said to include all": the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) possesses nine fruits of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), because it serves as the antidote to all three realms.
Regarding the statement "the five dhyānas and likewise the eight," the Abhidharma masters explain:

the five fruits of abandonment through knowledge (*prahāṇajñāna*) pertain to the fundamental dhyānas; that is, the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form and formless realms, as previously described.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
There are eight knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) that exhaust the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), because they are the fruits based on the *anāgamya* [concentration].
He intends to show that the exhaustion of what is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm is the fruit of dhyāna.
Regarding the intermediate dhyāna, it is as explained for the dhyānas.

As for the statement that there is one fruit in the formless realm: among the three formless attainments, one is said to have the abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) as its fruit, which is the total exhaustion of all fetters.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit of the retinue is likewise," it is as follows: in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the retinue is also said to have a single fruit of abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-jñāna-phala*), which is the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga-ksaya*).

Although the abandonment-knowledge is established based on the complete exhaustion of what is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) across four stages, it is only when the most subtle of the subtle seeds (*mṛdu-mṛdu-bīja*) in the fourth dhyāna are exhausted that it receives the name "abandonment-knowledge. Therefore, it is described as the fruit of the retinue of the sphere of infinite space.
The fruits of the mundane path are two; the noble [fruits] are nine; those of dharma-knowledge are three;
and those of subsequent knowledge are said to be two. Regarding the fruits of their respective categories, there are six and five.

As for "the fruits of the mundane path are two": the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) are the fruits of the mundane path; this is because noble ones (*ārya*) sever the fetters of the two realms by means of the mundane path.
Regarding the nine noble [knowledges]: all nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) are the fruits of the noble path, because the noble path serves as the antidote to all afflictions.
Regarding the three dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*): three knowledges of abandonment are the fruits of dharma-knowledge.

The exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the exhaustion of attachment to the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*), and the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana*) constitute the two types of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*). This is because the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) within the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) abandons the fetters of the three realms;
thus, the two types of knowledge of abandonment are said to be the fruit of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

The exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga*) and the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana*) constitute the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the realms of form and formlessness.

Regarding the statement "the fruits of those categories are six and five": there are six knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*) that are the fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*):
the three abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm, and the three previously mentioned as the fruits of dharma-knowledge.

The category of the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*) consists of five fruits of abandonment: three abandoned by the path of vision regarding the form and formless realms, and two previously mentioned as the fruits of the knowledge of the unknown.
Question:
Who possesses how many abandonments through knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*)?
Answer: There may be certain noble ones who have not yet accomplished the knowledge of abandonment,
or who have accomplished one, two, or three, four, five, or six.

During the five moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one does not yet possess the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*): first, during the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudayadharmajñānakṣānti*); second, during the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*) and the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñānakṣānti*); third, during the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) and the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*); fourth, during the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) and the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñānakṣānti*); fifth, during the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) and the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*); and sixth, at the stage of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Regarding those progressing toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*: if they transcend and rise above birth by exhausting double the [remaining] desires as previously described, or if they proceed sequentially, they accomplish six [faculties].
For the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* itself, there are likewise six.

Regarding the candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*: if one transcends and rises above through the exhaustion of sensual desire as previously described, or if one achieves it through the sequential path, six factors are accomplished.
The attainment of the fruit of *anāgāmin* is one; this is the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Regarding those who are heading toward the fruit of arhatship: if craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is not yet exhausted, they are of one type; if craving for the realm of form is exhausted, they are of two types.
Regarding the fruit of arhatship itself, there is one type: the full knowledge of the exhaustion and abandonment of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana*).
Question:
Who abandons how many knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*)? Answer:
One, two, five, or six are abandoned; as with abandoning, so it is with attaining.
Upon attaining a fruit or crossing over a realm, one realizes the abandonment and knowledge of the two [aspects].
Regarding "one, two, five, or six are abandoned": when an Arhat falls back from the fruit, one abandons one type of abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
An Anāgāmin who has exhausted craving for the form realm but falls away due to the fetters of the form realm loses one.
If one who has not yet exhausted craving for the form realm falls away due to the fetters of the desire realm, they lose one.
An Anāgāmin who has exhausted craving for the form realm but falls away due to the fetters of the desire realm loses two.
Upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one abandons two.
If one transcends the stage of Anāgāmin through the exhaustion of sensual desire, one abandons five;
in the sequential case, one abandons six.
Question:
Who attains how many types of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*)? Answer:
As with relinquishment, so it is with acquisition.
There may be the acquisition of one *prahāṇaparijñā* (full knowledge of abandonment) at the sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, or fourteenth moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Thus, for each instance of the mind of the "knowledge of the unknown regarding the path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there is the acquisition of one [parijñā] in succession.
The fruit of *anāgāmin* is one [attainment]; the exhaustion of the five lower fetters is the noble one’s exhaustion of desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), which is one.
The exhaustion of desire for the realm of form is the fruit of *arhat*, which is one; the exhaustion of all fetters is the attainment of two.

Regarding the statement that an Arhat who falls away due to the fetters of the formless realm attains six [attainments]: whether it be an Arhat or an Anāgāmin who falls away due to the fetters of the desire realm, there is no case of attaining five; therefore, this is not mentioned in the Sūtra.
Question:
Where does this knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-jñāna) arise? Answer:
Regarding the attainment of the fruit and the crossing of the realm, in these two instances there is the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

This knowledge of abandonment occurs in two instances: the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*). Because one attains the fruit in that very place and crosses over the realm in that very place, when the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are abandoned, the path and the subsequent knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*) arise.

Although the six kinds of abandonment result in the attainment of fruits, they do not constitute crossing over the realms; although the exhaustion of craving for the form realm constitutes crossing over the realms, it does not constitute the attainment of a fruit; and as for the remaining cases, they neither constitute crossing over the realms nor the attainment of a fruit. Therefore, these various points of abandonment and knowledge are not designated as "aggregates."

Having already explained the establishment of the nature of abandonment, attainment, and the accumulation of the fruition, I shall now explain the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) that is attained when those causes and conditions are severed.

That is to say: through the cessation of those two causes, through dissociation (*visamyoga*), through transcending a realm (*dhātusamatikrama*), through the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*), and through the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Due to four causes and conditions—or five—the abandonment is attained; this abandonment is known as the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The four causes and conditions are: the cessation of the common cause (*sahabhūhetu*), the separation from common fetters (*sahajānusaṃyoga*), the attainment of the acquisition of untainted liberation (*anāsravavimuktiprāpti*), and the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

When that dharma-patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti), dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), and subsequent patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti) arise, the causes [of the afflictions] are not extinguished simultaneously.
Although the causes to be abandoned by seeing suffering (duḥkha-darśana-heya) are extinguished, those to be abandoned by seeing the origin (samudaya-darśana-heya) are not.
For this reason, there is neither simultaneous bondage nor liberation; although one has attained the attainment of untainted liberation, the first existence (bhavāgra) has not yet been severed.
Thus, while these three conditions are met, the other three conditions are not.

When the dharma-patience regarding the unknown suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*) and the origin (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) arise, although one attains untainted liberation and the attainment of the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the other two causes are not yet complete; therefore, the "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) is not established at this stage.

The arising of the knowledge of the origin (samudaya-dharma-jñāna) is the simultaneous cessation of its causes; that is to say, while previously the causes to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) were ceased, now the causes to be abandoned by the vision of the origin are ceased. It should be understood that this is also the attainment of the severance of simultaneous fetters and the attainment of untainted liberation (anāsrava-vimukti).
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering arises, the first existence has already been severed; therefore, the knowledge of abandonment is established at this stage.
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding the origin arises, all causal conditions are complete; therefore, the knowledge of abandonment is established at this stage.

Thus, the third is the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation, the fourth is the subsequent knowledge of cessation, the fifth is the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path, and the sixth is the subsequent knowledge of the path; these are said to constitute the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) abandons five causal conditions: the first four, plus the permanent abandonment of the realms (dhātu), making five in total.

The nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are bound to one another in succession; this is likewise true for all stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

In that desire realm, from the abandonment of one type up to eight types, two conditions are fully present: namely, the attainment of the acquisition of untainted liberation, and the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Three conditions are not fully present.
The ninth type of cessation possesses five causal conditions; therefore, the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) is established in this context.
From the single type of abandonment in the first dhyāna up to the eighth type, two causal conditions are present and no others, as previously explained.
The ninth type of abandonment possesses four causal conditions; if one causal condition is lacking, it is called "crossing over the realm.
The same applies to the second and third dhyānas as well as the three formless attainments.
From the stage of the fourth dhyāna up to the eight types of abandonment, two causes and conditions are present and no others.
For the ninth type of abandonment, five causes and conditions are present; therefore, the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) is established at this point.
The same applies to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

For this reason, the abandonment and knowledge (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) of an ordinary person who has abandoned desire is not established, because such a person has not attained untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*), nor have they attained the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Having already explained the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), the three types of objects and the five ways in which craving arises shall now be explained:
"When a pleasant object is either accompanied or unaccompanied [by its opposite], two kinds of craving arise;
it is the same for the two [types of] unpleasant objects; and one [type of craving] is said to be equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
Regarding "desire arises in two ways toward pleasant objects, whether they are present or absent": "pleasant" refers to desirable and agreeable objects.
If one has obtained such an object, desire arises that does not let it go, thinking:
"How can I ensure that I do not part from this thing?"
If one has not yet attained [a state], the thought of attaining it gives rise to craving:
"How might I attain it?
The same applies to the two [types of] unwholesome objects.
Ill-repute is an unlovely object; it is also of two kinds:
that which arises from the perception of what is associated with craving, and that which arises from the perception of what is not so associated.
The first is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Equanimity refers to an object that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, toward which a one-sided deluded attachment arises.
Question:
Is that underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) or dissociated from the mind (*viprayukta*)?
What is the source of this doubt?
It is because the two masters hold divergent views.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain that [the mental factors] are dissociated.
Yuktavādin wishes to bring [the two] into correspondence,
yet harbors doubt regarding this.
The answer is:
With what are they associated?
They are the latent afflictions that reside within the mind;
they obstruct it yet do not contradict the pure, sublime, and wholesome mind, for they are not dissociated from it.
There are two reasons why the latent dispositions (anuśaya) afflict the mind:
their object (ālambana) and their association (samprayoga).
If the latent dispositions were not associated with the mind, they would not afflict the mind within the context of an object, because they would lack such an object.

All mental factors dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-dharma*) are neither objective conditions (*anālambana*) nor associated with the mind, because they are not factors that can be associated with it.
The mind is afflicted by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); as it has been said: "Because the mind is afflicted by sensual desire, the mind is not liberated."
From this explanation, it is known that the *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) are associated with the mind.
Regarding "obstruction": if the *anuśayas* were dissociated from the mind, they would not constitute an obstruction when the Path arises, because they would not contradict the continuity of the mind.
Because they act as obstructions, they are not dissociated [from the mind].

As for their non-contradiction with the pure [mind]: if these were dissociated from the mind, they would not be contradictory to a wholesome mind; thus, it would be improper for them to arise simultaneously with a wholesome mind and cause an offense.
Because they constitute transgressions, they are therefore not dissociated [from the mind].
Furthermore, wholesome and sublime minds can be found; because these [defilements] are contrary to such virtues, they are called *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
If the *anuśayas* were dissociated from the mind, they would function constantly, and thus there would be no occasion for a wholesome mind to arise.
Because wholesome states of mind arise, one should know that they are not dissociated [from them].
Furthermore, it is because the characteristics such as "attachment" (rāga) are explained.
What is the latent tendency of attachment (rāgānuśaya)?
This refers to the characteristic of defiled attachment.
What is the latent tendency of aversion?
It refers to the affliction of the mental factors.
What is the latent tendency of pride?
It refers to the inflation of the mental factors.
It is to be understood in this manner.
Therefore, it is not the case that the mind is not dissociated [from them].
If it were argued that the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions) are contrary to the wholesome mind but are not *anuvartakas* (concomitants), this is not so. Why?
Because they possess the characteristics of being driven [by afflictions], that which is bound by the obsession of sensual desire is called "bound by the obsession of sensual desire," and so forth.
Since no specific cause for distinction is stated, both are simply sensual desire.

To claim that the *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts) are associated with the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) while being dissociated from them is merely empty talk; ultimately, no specific causal conditions for such a distinction are stated.

If one asserts that the *paryavasthānas* have the *anuśayas* as their seeds, what is said is untenable. This is because there would be the fault of the cause being dissociated while the effect is associated; therefore, these *anuśayas* are not dissociated [from the mind].
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others.
Chapter Five: On the Noble Ones (Āryavarga). Having already explained the various afflictions, the practice shall now be explained.
The first is called the beginner’s practice; the second is that of one who has already practiced;
as for the one who has transcended through reflection, know this to be the third type.
These three modes of cultivation are: the beginner’s practice, the practice of one who has already trained, and the transcendence through reflection.
The beginner practices the transformation of impurity, yet has not yet attained the stage of mental comprehension and reflection regarding the object.

The practitioner who has already trained practices the transformation of the foundations of mindfulness according to their specific characteristics, yet has not yet attained the roots of goodness of the stage of certainty.
One should know that above this, one has already transcended through reflection, by virtue of this aforementioned path of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Furthermore, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) also consists of three types of practice: namely, beginning from the toes up to the crown of the head, one removes the skin, flesh, and blood through mental resolve and reflection; this is called the "beginner's stage" (*ādikarmika*).

Regarding this skeleton, one does not form a conceptualization of it as arising to pervade the entire earth; furthermore, observing the skeleton without forming such a conceptualization, those skeletons strike against one another until, driven by a great wind, they are dispersed and dissolved into a mass of snow. This is called "having practiced the cultivation."

Briefly observing the skeletal remains until they return to one's own body, one contemplates only a single color within that object of focus—pure and tranquil; this is called "having transcended through contemplation.
In this way, even as the objective field is further condensed, one should know that the roots of virtue gradually increase.
One should know that all other skillful roots of merit resulting from expedient means are likewise so.
Having already explained the practice, the remainder shall now be discussed:
"If one fears these afflictions, one remains far removed from the noble ones."
"Truly and correctly endowed with skillful means, one should listen well.
"If" refers to the seed, the skillful means, or the differentiation.
"This" refers to the sequential explanation and demonstration of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Afflictions" (kleśa) are so called because they cause burning distress.
Furthermore, one is detached from all outflows (āsrava), yet the fault of afflictions is like poisoned food; therefore, it is said that one is detached from afflictions.
The root of all terrors gives rise to various karmas and various births.
To be far removed from them means to extinguish them through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The noble ones (*ārya*) are those in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), namely the seven types of persons and the true ordinary beings (*bhūta-pṛthagjana*).
"One who is truly and perfectly endowed" refers to one who abides in the path of reality.
"The skillful means should be listened to well" means that the path of skillful means should be heard with a single-minded focus.

As for "skillful means," it refers to the application of all wholesome dharmas directed toward the practice of liberation; it arises from giving and so forth, and is not merely the [noble] path itself.
Oppressed by the three types of suffering, the world is unable to awaken;
therefore, to cause them to cultivate meditative concentration, one first binds the mind to its own physical parts to bring it to stillness.
Desiring to bind the foot of consciousness, one acts thus to exhaust the enemy that is ignorance.
"Beginning" means first.
"A portion of one's own body" refers to a single location within one's own body, such as the space between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, or the toes.
"Binding" means establishing [the mind] upon an object so that it does not scatter.
What is established?
It is that wisdom arises through the power of the concentration of one's own mind.
Question:
Why is this? Answer:

Because desire binds the consciousness at its feet, the mind flows on without staying still; therefore, by binding it within a single object, one knows the truth with a unified mind and without distraction.
Question:
For what reason are they bound within a single object? Answer:
It is for the sake of exhausting the enemies of wisdom.
The enemies of wisdom refer to the various afflictions (*kleśa*), which ought to be severed.
Although one contemplates the bodies of others as if they were corpses, [one does so for this purpose].
The sūtra states:
"Because that is the remote cause.
This refers to the contemplation of the proximate cause.
Furthermore, because it accords with all gates of deliverance (*nairyāṇika-mukha*): that is to say, contemplating the parts of the body as white bones accords with three gates of deliverance;
contemplating a corpse accords solely with the single gate of deliverance of impurity (*aśubhā*).

Regarding the three gates of deliverance: these are the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), and the analytical observation of the elements (*dhātu-prakāra-parīkṣā*).

Those with a temperament of sensual desire are delivered by the contemplation of impurity; those with a temperament of discursive thought are delivered by mindfulness of breathing; and those with a temperament of speculative views are delivered by the analytical observation of the elements. One should practice according to one's inclination, following what has been taught by the teacher.

The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) have been explained extensively in the *Sūtra* section. Now, the contemplation of the skillful means regarding the elements (*dhātu-upāya-bhāvanā*) shall be explained.

Herein, ordinary people, their eye of wisdom obscured by improper reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), do not contemplate the true nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Due to the seeds of past karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), which are immeasurable phenomena, they accumulate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and give rise to the perception of a "heap."
Due to delusion and confusion, one is bound by various false views, such as the notion of a self-actor, regarding the functioning of dependent origination.

At times, however, by practicing in the proximity of virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, and giving rise to correct reflection, one is able to skillfully contemplate the various intrinsic natures, various activities, and various characteristics within the elements of one's own body—namely, the six elements, such as earth and so forth.

Because the earth element is moistened by the water element, they do not separate; because the water element is supported by the earth element, it does not flow away; because of the maturation of the fire element, it does not become stagnant or decayed; because of the movement of the wind element, growth is achieved; because of the emptiness of the space element, food and so forth enter and exit; and because of the conjunction of the consciousness element, there is volitional activity.
Furthermore, one contemplates this body from the feet to the crown of the head, seeing it as filled with various kinds of impurities and foulness.

One observes this form as being like a heap of sand scattered by a violent wind; one observes the formless phenomena in their sequential continuity and distinct divisions. One who contemplates in this way obtains the seed of the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*);
through weariness and detachment toward that cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one obtains the seed of the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Having become disenchanted with birth and death, one turns directly toward nirvāṇa and attains the seeds of the signless door of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

Once one has attained the realization that there is nothing to be done regarding these, and observes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are entirely subject to disintegration, this is called the fulfillment of the skillful means regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
Question:
Having observed in this manner, what then? Answer:
This skillful means regarding the body is the determination of its true characteristic;
one should likewise observe sensations, one's own mind, and phenomena in this same way.

After that practitioner has dwelt individually in the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and the skillful means of observing the elements, they contemplate the reality of each—the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena—separately.
Reality is that which is non-erroneous.
Characteristics are of two kinds:
namely, specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is the specific characteristic of the body, consisting of the four primary elements and their derivatives;
the characteristic of perception (*vedanā*) is the specific characteristic of feeling; and the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the specific characteristic of the mind (*citta*).

In the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are various phenomena with various distinct characteristics; the cognition that conforms to them is the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*), and the mental engagement that acts upon them is the characteristic of volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
The common characteristics will be explained later.
Question:

Since these foundations of mindfulness are established like the great earth, they should be spoken of as one; yet, because of the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), they should be spoken of [as two].

Second, there should be three distinctions based on the categories of weak, medium, and superior; six distinctions based on the distinction between that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*);
eight distinctions based on the distinction between the body and so forth as being with outflows or without outflows; nine distinctions based on the nine grades (*navavidha*);
and twelve distinctions based on whether the body and so forth are internal, external, or both internal and external. Thus, there are nine [categories].
If one were to distinguish between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), there would be eighteen categories;
if one were to distinguish the body and so forth by way of the weak, medium, and superior grades, as well as the contaminated and the uncontaminated, there would be twenty-four;

if one were to distinguish the body and so forth by way of internal, external, or both internal and external, as well as by way of revulsion, lack of delight, and investigation, there would be thirty-six; and if one were to distinguish the nine grades of the body and so forth... [the text continues].
If distinguished by way of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), they should be said to be seventy-two; if distinguished moment by moment, they should be said to be immeasurable.
For what reason, then, are only the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) taught?

Answer: Because the four inversions, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four stations of consciousness, and the aggregates are to be remedied through four modes of cultivation, four modes of cultivation that correspond to them are taught.

Since they remedy the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is taught; since they remedy the inversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, the foundation of mindfulness of feeling is taught; since they remedy the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind is taught; and since they remedy the inversion of perceiving the non-self as self, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is taught.
In this manner, the remaining types [of mindfulness] should be explained as appropriate.
Question:
How is this application of mindfulness fulfilled?
Answer: It is fulfilled by two causes and conditions, namely, the destruction of the objective field (*viṣaya*) and the increase of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Regarding the destruction of the objective field, it refers to the destruction of the objective field at the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*), according to their respective meanings.
The increase of roots of goodness refers to the increase from the weak roots of goodness to the middling ones.
This is called fulfillment.
Question:
Why was the mindfulness of the body taught first, followed by the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth?
Answer: Because it arises in accordance with the sequence of practice.
The Blessed One taught three kinds of conformity:
conformity of arising, conformity of teaching, and conformity of realization.
Conformity of arising refers to the foundations of mindfulness and the dhyānas.

For practitioners of the formless realm, the application of mindfulness of the body arises first, followed by the applications of mindfulness up to the application of mindfulness of phenomena; therefore, the World-Honored One taught the application of mindfulness of the body first, followed by the applications of mindfulness up to the application of mindfulness of phenomena.
It should be understood that the same applies to the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Regarding the statement "conducive," this refers to the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*). At the moment of arising, one exerts diligence and possesses all four right abandonments; this is stated for the sake of simplicity.

"Having arisen, one applies skillful means to abandon unwholesome and unvirtuous states," and so on, up to "having arisen, one applies skillful means to maintain wholesome states"; thus it is explained in detail.
These right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) are called the four right efforts because they consist of what is performed, not because of their intrinsic nature.

Regarding "conformity with the immediate realization" (*abhisamaya-anuloma*): this refers to the teaching of the Truths. Because the practitioner first enters the immediate realization of suffering, it is explained first; the detailed exposition is as follows.
Question:
For what reason does the practitioner first cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body, up to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena? Answer:
Because they are coarse.
What are the five aggregates that are coarse?
They are the four primary elements and their derivatives; therefore, one contemplates them first.
Although feeling (*vedanā*) is not form (*rūpa*), it is explained next because its activity is coarse; that is to say, when pain occurs in the hands, feet, and so forth, feeling follows accordingly.

Although the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are coarser than consciousness (*vijñāna*), they are established as the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) in conjunction with *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are the most subtle. For this reason, one contemplates the mind first and then contemplates phenomena.

Although everything is indeed the Dharma, this [foundation of mindfulness] is established because it fulfills the conceptualization of the Dharma; therefore, it is said that there is only one foundation of mindfulness of phenomena and no others.

Just as the "Dharmāyatana" was explained in the *Dhātuvarga*, so it is here: for one whose conceptualization is fulfilled, the sound is the "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*) and the meaning is the "fulfillment of the name" (*nāma-pūraṇa*).
Question:
How many kinds of foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are there? Answer:

The three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* are taught as being both intrinsic (*svabhāva*) and concomitant (*sahagata*), and they are also said to be designated by their objects (*ālambana*). The same applies to the wisdom derived from hearing and so forth.

Regarding the statement that the three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* are taught as being both intrinsic and concomitant, and also designated by their objects: the three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* refer to the intrinsic *smṛtyupasthāna*, the concomitant *smṛtyupasthāna*, and the objective *smṛtyupasthāna*.
Regarding the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), it is explained as non-erroneous wisdom (*aviparīta-prajñā*). Why?

As it is said, "contemplating the body in accordance with the body," this contemplation is the activity performed by wisdom and mindfulness, because it does not forget the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Because they eliminate inherent faults, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
As for the shared foundations of mindfulness, they are dharmas that share a single fruit with right wisdom (*samyakprajñā*).
As the Blessed One said:
"Monks! The accumulation of wholesome qualities refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; this is the correct teaching.
All phenomena have the foundations of mindfulness as their object."
As it has been said: "O Bhikṣus!
To speak of all phenomena as the four foundations of mindfulness—this is the correct teaching."
Because they encompass the complete [factors] and because their objects are concise,
it is through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) taken together that afflictions are abandoned,

and not by others. Although the application of mindfulness in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*) possesses concise objects, because its complete factors are insufficient, it is the application of mindfulness that encompasses the complete path which abandons the afflictions.

Although the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) encompass all requisite conditions, because their objects are widely dispersed, one briefly severs afflictions through the path of those objects.
Question:
Are these three types of foundations of mindfulness the only ones, or is it the same for the others as well?
Answer: Wisdom arising from hearing and so forth is likewise.
The others are also of three kinds, namely: wisdom arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
"Listening" (śruta) always arises in relation to names; it consists of receiving the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma from a teacher.
"Reflection" (cintā) arises either in relation to places or independently of reflection.
As for cultivation, it arises by being consistently detached from names.
It is like three people learning to swim: the first is a beginner, the second is a partial learner, and the third is one who has mastered the skill.
The beginner stays near the shore; the partial learner is sometimes near and sometimes away; the master is far from the shore.
The first person is analogous to wisdom derived from hearing; the second is analogous to wisdom derived from reflection; and the third is analogous to wisdom derived from cultivation.
Wisdom derived from cultivation is able to sever the afflictions because it is characterized by permanent detachment and right concentration.
To say that there are two kinds of non-meaningful [objects] is not correct.
Why? Because they lead toward the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
One who cultivates wisdom possesses the four foundations of mindfulness:
body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.

Among these, it is the foundation of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that abandons the afflictions, and not the others; this is because it has a comprehensive range as its object, whereas the others do not.
Because it takes phenomena as its objective sphere, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) arises; therefore, it is not without purpose.
There are two kinds of application of mindfulness to phenomena: that which analyzes conditions (*bhajyamānapratyaya*) and that which does not analyze conditions (*abhajyamānapratyaya*).

If wisdom takes form as its object, it is the foundation of mindfulness of the body; if it takes feeling as its object, it is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling; if it takes mind as its object, it is the foundation of mindfulness of mind; if it takes perception, formations, and the unconditioned as its object, it is the undecaying object.
The remaining foundations of mindfulness regarding phenomena shall now be explained.
Entering into phenomena and contemplating them as a whole, one attains the true characteristic of phenomena:
these four are impermanent, empty, non-self, and not pleasant.

Regarding "entering into the Dharma and comprehensively observing to attain the true characteristic of phenomena": the practitioner enters the application of mindfulness of non-disintegrating objects (*avipariṇāmadhamma-satipaṭṭhāna*), cultivates each individual application of mindfulness, and after universally observing the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, enters the application of mindfulness of disintegrating objects (*vipariṇāmadhamma-satipaṭṭhāna*).

The foundation of mindfulness conditioned by form-feeling, the foundation of mindfulness conditioned by form-perception, the foundation of mindfulness conditioned by form-formations, and the foundation of mindfulness conditioned by form-consciousness—likewise for the four, five, or all five aggregates.

This is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna), which accomplishes all foundations of mindfulness of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, crossing over through the single awakening of universal contemplation.

What is this? These four are impermanent, empty, non-self, and not pleasant. One contemplates all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) collectively through the aspects of impermanence and so forth:

they are impermanent because they perish moment by moment; they are empty because they are devoid of permanence and so forth; they are non-self because they lack autonomy; and they are suffering because they are truly oppressive.
From this it is called "Heat" (uṣmagata), arising from awakening to the Dharma;
the sixteen aspects and so forth arise, observing the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the line "From this it is called Heat, arising from awakening to the Dharma": for that practitioner, through the application of mindfulness on phenomena as the disintegration of conditions, the roots of goodness arise in succession, which is called "Heat."
Question:
How many modes of activity are there, and what is their objective sphere? Answer:
One observes the Four Noble Truths through the arising of the sixteen aspects.

Those aspects of the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) consist of the sixteen aspects beginning with the aspect of suffering within the Truth of Suffering, up to the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering, and so on, up to the four aspects of the Truth of the Path.
The practice of the meaning [of these factors] shall be explained extensively in the Chapter on Wisdom (*jñāna-varga*).

When that stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) arises, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present with respect to the three Truths, and four are cultivated in the future; one aspect is cultivated in the present, and four are cultivated in the future. These belong to their own category (*svabhāga*), not to a non-own category.

When one practices the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) directed toward the Truth of Cessation in the present, that same practice is cultivated in the future; it is not the case that one first attains cultivation by observing the path conditioned by the aggregates (*skandha*). One aspect is cultivated in the present, and four aspects are cultivated in the future.

Based on the three truths, one advances in the four foundations of mindfulness: for each foundation of mindfulness, one currently cultivates one and will cultivate four in the future; for one aspect, one currently cultivates one and will cultivate sixteen in the future.

Conditioned by the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one cultivates the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*): in the present, one cultivates one; in the future, four. In one mode of practice, one cultivates in the present and sixteen in the future.
One cultivates the roots of goodness not yet increased, and cultivates the roots of goodness previously cultivated that constitute one's own level of practice.
Cultivation at the present moment consists of cultivating that which pertains to oneself, not that which pertains to others.
The stage of Heat (*ūṣmagata*) has wisdom as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while the concomitant factors have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature.
It is called "Heat" because it generates the fire of noble wisdom; it is termed the "stage of Heat" because it serves as the seed.

When this dharma has increased, it gives rise to the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*), and one attains the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), all based upon a single moment.

Regarding the statement, "When this dharma has increased, it gives rise to the Summits and Patience": as the practitioner’s right application (*samyak-prayoga*) and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) increase, they obtain the various requisites for conforming wholesome karma; thus, the Dharma of Heat (*uṣmagata*) attains further growth, and subsequently, the root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) named "Summit" arises.

Practicing the sixteen aspects based on the Four Noble Truths, those Peak Factors (mūrdhan) take the Four Truths as their object; taking the Truth of Cessation as their object, they advance in the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), which is cultivated in the present, while four are cultivated in the future. One aspect is cultivated in the present, and sixteen are cultivated in the future.

Based on the three truths, one advances in the four foundations of mindfulness: for each [truth], one practices one in the present and four in the future; for one aspect, one practices one in the present and sixteen in the future.
These roots of goodness are also of the nature of wisdom, and the concomitant dharmas are of the nature of the five aggregates.
As for the "Summits" (mūrdhan), they are called "summits" because they are above the "Heat" (uṣmagata); being inferior to "Patience" (kṣānti), they are termed "lower."
At times the World-Honored One speaks of faith, as when he spoke to Pāṭikāputra;
at other times he speaks of wisdom, as when he spoke to the young bhikṣus.
To fall back from this summit after having attained it is called "falling from the summit" (mūrdha-pratyāgama) and "falling from the summit" (mūrdha-patana).
The stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) should also involve falling away, yet it is not mentioned.
Falling away from the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) occurs because of abundant sorrow and affliction.

One gives rise to great sorrow and affliction in three instances, as if losing a great treasure: namely, the falling away from the detachment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
One who falls away from detachment from the desires of the desire realm or from the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage is said to lack the nature of accomplishment.

That practitioner, having achieved the wholesome roots of the Summit through this correct means, advances to produce the "patience in conformity with the truths" (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*), taking the four truths as objects and practicing the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).

Regarding the initial patience (*kṣānti*) and the further development of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): one cultivates it in the present and four in the future; for the single practice, one cultivates it in the present and sixteen in the future.
Patience (*kṣānti*) refers to the endurance and aspiration toward the Four Noble Truths.

If it were claimed that the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Peak (*mūrdhan*) are also capable of endurance (*kṣānti*), this would not be correct. Because Endurance is non-retrogressive, because it opposes the evil destinies, and because it is proximate to the Noble Path, it is said that the "conformity-to-truth endurance" (*satyānulomikī kṣāntiḥ*) is neither Heat nor Peak.
Question:
What roots of goodness are produced by the increase of patience? Answer:

The attainment of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) occurs in a single moment; that is to say, it is the most excellent root of goodness attained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), arising through the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) following the stage of Superior Patience (*adhimātrakṣānti*). This is also of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Because they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are called "mundane" (*laukika*); because they are superior to [the stages of] heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they are said to be "supreme" (*agra*).

These are also the most excellent qualities cultivated by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*): because they do not abide for even a single moment, because they resemble the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because they consist of the continuous succession of the stages of heat, summits (*mūrdhan*), and patience (*kṣānti*).

Some say that through the cultivation of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as a universal contemplation, there arises in succession the mundane roots of goodness belonging to the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). These are established in nine grades: the soft-soft, soft-middle, and soft-superior are called the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma;
the middle-soft and middle-middle are called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) dharma;
and the middle-superior...
The superior-soft is [the stage of] Heat; the superior-middle is named the Dharma of Patience;
the superior-superior is named the Supreme Mundane Dharma.

If one contemplates the impermanence of the aggregates and other such roots of goodness, it is called the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata); contemplating the merits of the Triple Gem is called the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan); observing the Noble Truths is called the stage of "Patience" (kṣānti); and contemplating the Noble Truth of Suffering in sequence up to the Noble Path is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).

Once he has attained the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), even if he loses it through regression, through death, or by transcending to another realm or stage, and even if he commits an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma), severs his roots of goodness, or is born into the evil destinies, he will nonetheless attain nirvāṇa by virtue of this merit.
The same applies to falling back from the *mūrdhāna* (Summits) stage, with the sole exception that one does not sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

As for the *kṣānti* (Patience) stage, there is no falling back; however, there is relinquishment at the end of life and relinquishment upon transcending a realm or level. One does not commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), does not sever the roots of goodness, and does not fall into the miserable destinies (*durgati*), due to the great power of *kṣānti*.
Just as the king of lions causes the various beasts to flee far away, so too is the power of patience.
All malevolent minds are not merely suppressed by analytical cessation; furthermore, just like the dwelling place of a great king, the evil deeds and minds of humans and devas all become supple.
Question:
What are the conditions and how many aspects (ākāra) does the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) possess? Answer:
The lower suffering has four aspects; it is said to be comprised within six stages.
The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is likewise; others say it may depend on seven.
Regarding "the lower suffering has four aspects": the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "lower."

The object of that supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) proceeds by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and not otherwise, because it resembles the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
There are two types of practitioners: those who act out of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*) and those who act out of views (*dṛṣṭi-carita*).
There are two types of conduct characterized by craving:
the conduct of self-conceit and the increase of indolence.
Conduct characterized by views is likewise of two types.
Attachment to "I" and "mine," as well as the conceit of "I am," leads one to practice the mundane supreme dharma of impermanence;
for those in whom indolence increases, one practices the cultivation of suffering.
For one who is attached to the notion of "I," they should practice the cultivation of non-self.
For one who is attached to the notion of "mine," they should practice the cultivation of emptiness.
Question:
By how many stages (bhūmi) is it subsumed? Answer:
It is subsumed by six stages: the preliminary stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas.
It is not the desire realm, because there is no meditative concentration there;
it is not the formless realm, because there is no path of seeing there.
Question:
By how many stages are the remaining roots of goodness conducive to penetration subsumed?
Answer: The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is also like this.
This means that patience (*kṣānti*) is subsumed within six stages, just like the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
As for the statement that "the others may depend on seven," this refers to the levels of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), which likewise consist of six stages;
however, the Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that they also exist within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question:
The sequential arising of the *niyāmāvakrānti* (the stage of certainty) has already been explained; how, then, does the sequential arising of the noble path (*āryamārga*) occur? Answer:
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is followed by the arising of the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*);
following that Patience, Knowledge (*jñāna*) arises; both observe the suffering of the lower realm.

Regarding "the Supreme Mundane Dharma is followed by the arising of the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering": the Supreme Mundane Dharma gives rise in succession to the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering. This is the antidote to the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the Desire Realm; it is the first untainted path of non-obstruction (*anāsrava-ānantarya-mārga*).

Furthermore, immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one does not act, does not incline toward, and does not practice; one abandons wrong action, wrong destination, and wrong view.

Wrong action refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*); wrong destination refers to the evil realms (*durgati*); and wrong view refers to the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) establishes fivefold certainty for the subsequent patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti); namely, certainty of the stage (bhūmi), certainty of the practice (carita), certainty of the object (ālambana), certainty of the moment (kṣaṇa), and certainty of the immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Regarding the determination of the stage (*bhūmi*): if this stage is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), then it is the same stage as the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Regarding the determination of the practice (*carita*): if this practice is the supreme mundane dharma, then it is the same practice as the patience regarding the dharma of suffering.
Regarding the determination of object (*ālambana-niyama*): because they must share the same object.
Regarding the determination of moment (*kṣaṇa-niyama*): if this moment is averted, then that very moment arises.

Regarding the determination of sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya-niyama*): immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) necessarily arises.
The stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) is established as three types of meditative concentration, excluding the momentary and the sequential conditions.

For this reason, following the patience that takes suffering as its object, one subsequently attains transcendence and departure from the state of ordinary birth. When one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm as well as the suffering of the form and formless realms, up to the antidote for the formations of the form and formless realms, this is called "inferior patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).

He further contemplates the suffering of the desire realm up to the antidote for the formations of the desire realm, while relinquishing the antidote for the formations of the form and formless realms; this is "patience" (*kṣānti*).

He observes each truth individually and returns to it, practicing until he reaches the continuity of the characteristics of suffering in the desire realm; thereafter, he again relinquishes that continuity and contemplates even a single moment of the suffering of the desire realm—this is "supreme patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Following this, the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) arises.

Regarding the statement that "following the patience, knowledge arises": immediately after the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the Dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises, which is the intrinsic nature of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question: What is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this patience and knowledge?
Answer: Both contemplate the suffering of the lower realm.
The suffering of the lower realm is the suffering of the desire realm; they both contemplate that suffering.
That is to say, the suffering of the form and formless realms, as well as their origin, cessation, and path, are likewise;
these dharmas of uninterrupted realization are called the sixteen moments of mind.

Regarding "the suffering of the form and formless realms," the suffering of the form and formless realms is also like this: the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*) is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

The same applies to the truths of origination, cessation, and the path: for these truths as well, two types of patience (*kṣānti*) constitute the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*), and two types of knowledge (*jñāna*) constitute the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that "this realization of the dharma through immediate succession (*dharmābhisamaya*) refers to the sixteen moments of mind": during these sixteen moments of mind, there occurs the realization of the dharma through immediate succession; "immediate succession" (*anantara*) has the meaning of "seeing" (*darśana*).
These fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the final moment of mind constitutes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Question:

Why are the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the three truths included within the path of seeing, whereas the final moment of mind regarding the truth of the path is included within the path of cultivation?
Answer: Because one cultivates the sixteen aspects of the path.

It is the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) that is associated with the cultivation of the sixteen aspects, not the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that cultivates the sixteen aspects.
Because the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is a continuous succession, it is subsumed under the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).

As for the objection that this is not the case: it is not so; for just as when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is accomplished, this [subsequent knowledge] is also accomplished, if this were not part of one's lot, then the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) would likewise not be part of one's lot.
Briefly stated, there are three stages:
the stage of seeing, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of no-more-learning; it is upon these stages that persons are established.
This meaning shall now be explained.
Those of sharp faculties who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin) exist within these fifteen moments of mind;
those of dull faculties who practice in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin) should be known to be likewise therein.

Regarding "those of sharp faculties who practice in accordance with the Dharma exist within these fifteen moments of mind": among persons on the path of seeing (darśanamārga), those of sharp faculties are called *dharmānusārin*.
One is called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārin) because they practice in accordance with the Dharma, rather than out of faith in another.
It should be understood that those of dull faculties among these fifteen moments of mind are called "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin), for they attain deliverance through faith in others.
The follower by faith has little observation, while the follower by dharma has much observation.
Whether following by faith or by dharma, if they possess the fetters of afflictions up to the fivefold abandonment, one should know they are heading toward the first fruit.

These practitioners who follow by faith or follow by dharma, if they possess the fetters of afflictions or have severed one, two, three, four, or five types thereof, are called those "heading toward the fruit of stream-entry."
The afflictions are established as nine grades based on the distinctions of "superior-superior" and so forth.
If, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has not yet abandoned even a single grade, one is said to be "bound by all fetters.
If one has abandoned one grade, one is said to be "not bound by all fetters. If one has abandoned five grades, one transcends and rises above the state of being an ordinary person (*viśeṣādhigama*).

When the five categories [of afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm are abandoned, one attains the realization of liberation through the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

This continues up until, when the five categories to be abandoned through the vision of the path are abandoned, one attains the realization of liberation through the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
When five categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm are abandoned through the path of cultivation, one attains the realization of liberation as the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
When six through eight categories are abandoned, one is a candidate for the second fruit;
having become free from desire up to the eighth stage, one is then a candidate for the third fruit.

Regarding the statement that "having exhausted six up to eight [categories of afflictions] constitutes one who is heading toward the second fruit": this refers to those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) or follow by dharma (dharmānusārin); if they have already abandoned six, seven, or eight categories [of afflictions], they are said to be heading toward the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin.

Regarding "from the abandonment of desire up to the eighth stage, this is the third candidate": these practitioners who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), if they abandon desire up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), they both proceed toward the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is called abiding in the fruit.
One with dull vision is called "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta); one with sharp vision is called "attained to vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

Regarding the statement, "If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is called abiding in the fruit": the sixteenth moment of mind is named the "subsequent knowledge of the path" (mārgānvayajñāna), and when it arises, both are said to abide in the fruit—whether as a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, or an anāgāmin.

Regarding those with weak vision who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*): if one with weak vision enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are called a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); when that person abides in the three fruits, they are called liberated through faith. Regarding those with sharp vision who are "attained to vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*):
if one with sharp faculties enters the path of seeing, they are called a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*); when that person abides in the three fruits, they are called attained to vision.
One who has seen through the faculty of faith and possesses superior conviction and liberation is called "one who has seen" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) because they are impregnated with wisdom.
When all those various afflictions have been exhausted,
yet one has not yet proceeded further, this is called a *srotāpanna*.
If one has exhausted the eighty-eight fetters abandoned through the path of seeing, this is the fruit of srotāpanna.
As long as one has not yet accumulated [the further] practices, this is called abiding in the fruit of srotāpanna.
If one abandons the superior and most superior seeds through skillful means, this is called "one heading toward the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

When these seeds—up to five categories—are abandoned, one transcends and rises above the state of ordinary birth; when the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path arises, one is named a *srotāpanna*, not one heading toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. This is because the path leading toward that fruit has not yet manifested for even a single moment.
Question:
Since many defilements are abandoned, why did the Blessed One speak of the exhaustion of the three fetters? Answer:
The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the roots:
the five views, doubt, craving, aversion, pride, and ignorance.
Among these, six are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*): the five views and doubt.
In him, the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing are forever exhausted.

Therein, there are three turnings and three subsequent turnings: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the turning, and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the subsequent turning; attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the turning, and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the subsequent turning; doubt (*vicikitsā*) is the turning, and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the subsequent turning.
Having explained the transformation, one should know that the subsequent transformation has also been explained.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The destruction of the three fetters constitutes a stream-enterer."
Furthermore, these afflictions consist of either one, two, or four types.

Since the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has already been explained, it should be understood that the first type has been explained. Since the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) has already been explained, it should be understood that the second type has been explained.
Having already explained doubt, one should know that the four types have been explained.
In this same manner, all pervasive and non-pervasive factors, as well as those with outflow-objects and those without outflow-objects, should be understood to be fully accounted for.

These fetters are already exhausted and known; even up to the stage of Arhat, because there still remains a semblance that continues to follow, they have not yet exhausted the seeds of the path of cultivation.
Receiving birth and death for seven more times—this which has been taught should be understood as the fully perfected Srotāpanna.
That stream-enterer has not yet exhausted the seeds for the cultivation of the path; it should be known that when these are fully completed, there will be seven existences at most.

These consist of seven births among humans—both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*)—as well as births among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This is stated collectively as "seven existences" because they do not exceed seven, just like the *saptaparṇa* tree.
Question:
For what reason is it said that there are seven existences (bhava), neither more nor less? Answer:
Just as one bitten by a seven-step snake travels seven paces due to the power of its four limbs, yet fails to reach the eighth due to the power of the venom;
so too, due to the power of karma, there are seven births, but due to the power of the Path, one does not reach an eighth.

When he dwells in the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), with the exception of seven births in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all other births attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) such that they never again manifest.

If he transcends birth in the human realm, he completes seven full lifetimes there; if in the heavenly realms, he likewise completes seven full lifetimes there. Although the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests during these intervals, by the sustaining power of karma (*karmabala*), he does not enter parinirvāṇa.
Question:
If seven births are completed and a Buddha has not appeared in the world, how can one attain the fruit of arhatship?
Answer:
Some say that one may attain the fruit of arhatship while remaining a householder, but having attained that fruit, one no longer dwells at home.

Others say that such a person immediately leaves the household life in their current form because they have accomplished the invincible purities (*aveccappasāda*), because their aspirations are fulfilled, and because they perceive the faults of evil conduct; therefore, the dharma of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) does not lead to rebirth in the miserable realms.

Furthermore, because they are born into the lineage of the Buddha, because the fire of their wisdom is bright and pure, because they perceive the faults of the objective realm, because they are fully endowed with śamatha and vipaśyanā, and because they are permeated by the medicine of the noble path, they are like a crown prince, like a person whose internal fire has increased, or like a skillful fisherman; therefore, the srotāpanna does not fall into the evil destinies.

Although ordinary beings do not fall into the evil destinies, they are not so described because this is only partial and uncertain; because they abide in the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they are said to be "fixed"; and because they will certainly attain nirvana, they are said to be "destined for perfect enlightenment."
Regarding the "seven existences," they are as previously explained.
"Abiding" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and "arising" refers to the state of birth (*upapattibhava*); thus, they are called "abiding and arising.
Because one no longer undergoes further rebirths, it is called "abiding at the limit of suffering."
It is not necessary that all *srotāpannas* undergo seven more existences.
If one has abandoned three or four categories [of afflictions] and has accomplished their antidotes,
such that only two or three births remain, this is called a *kulaṃkula*.
The "Family-to-Family" (kulaṃkula) stage is established based on three causes and conditions: the abandonment of afflictions, the perfection of faculties, and the manner of rebirth.

Regarding the abandonment of afflictions: it refers to the abandonment of the third or fourth categories of afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm; there is no case of abandoning five categories, which is termed "Family-to-Family."
