If one is able to sever five grades [of afflictions], by the force of that power one will necessarily sever the sixth grade as well, thereby becoming a Sakṛdāgāmin; it is not the case that the power of the sixth grade is capable of obstructing one from reaching this fruit.
Regarding the "attainment of faculties," it refers to obtaining those untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties that serve as their antidote.
Regarding "rebirth," it means either taking birth again in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or undergoing two or three more births.
If any one of these three causes and conditions is not complete, one is not a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.
There are two types of family-to-family practitioners:
those who are gods and those who are humans.

Regarding "family-to-family among the gods" (*deva-kulaṃkula*): this refers to those among the gods of the desire realm who undergo two or three births, or who take birth in one celestial abode for two or three times within that same class of beings.
"From family to family" (*kulaṃkula*) refers to a human body, whether in one world-system, two, or three; or within one household, two, or three.
Question:
What is the meaning of "from family to family"?
Answer: Because one attains parinirvāṇa after going from family to family, it is called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
A superior srotāpanna is named "family-to-family."
When six grades of afflictions are abandoned, and all those to be abandoned by the path of seeing have been abandoned,
this is called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner), provided that one has not yet progressed further. If,

among the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, the upper three grades and the middle three grades— as well as all those to be abandoned by the path of seeing— have been completely exhausted, and one abides in the fruit without having progressed further, one is named a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Question:
What is the meaning of "sakṛdāgāmin"? Answer:
Dying here, they are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm; returning once more to the human world, they attain parinirvāṇa.
If seven or eight grades [of defilements] are abandoned, and they have perfected the faculties that serve as antidotes, with only one birth remaining, they are called "One-Seed" (ekabījika).

If one has abandoned seven or eight grades [of afflictions] through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the desire realm, or has completely abandoned all [afflictions] through the path of seeing (darśanamārga), and has attained the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya) that serve as their antidotes, while having only one remaining birth in the desire realm, such a person is called "One-seeded" (ekabījika).
If any one of the three causes and conditions is lacking, it is not a single-seed being (*ekabījaka*).
If one is a single-seed being destined for heaven, they will experience one heavenly body and then enter parinirvāṇa;
the same applies to those in the human realm.
Because one birth-germ remains, they are called "one-germ" (ekabījika).
Question:
For what reason is the abandonment of the eight grades [of afflictions] termed "one-germ"?
If one has abandoned five grades [of defilements], is this not called *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family)? Answer:

Even if one has abandoned six grades and is thus a *kulaṃkula*, they still take birth in the desire realm; therefore, the karma and afflictions of the desire realm do not constitute an obstacle for them.

One type of seed, comprising all nine grades, is born entirely within the form realm; therefore, the karma and afflictions of the desire realm act as extreme obstacles. For this reason, it is said that the karma of sentient beings in these three places acts as an extreme source of disturbance.
The three locations shall be explained later.
One who has exhausted nine grades [of defilements] is a non-returner (anāgāmin); one should know that there are many such types.
Whether five, seven, or eight, or even said to be many;

when the nine grades [of fetters] are exhausted for one who is a non-returner (anāgāmin)—having abandoned everything through the path of seeing and having exhausted the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm—one should know him to be an anāgāmin.
Question:
Since there are so many abandonments of afflictions, why did the Blessed One state that the exhaustion of the five lower fetters constitutes an *anāgāmin*? Answer:
The four types and the five types— since all such [categories] are fully subsumed within the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni*)—
"despicable" (*heya*) and "lowly" (*hīna*) have the same meaning.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of "lower":
"Below in terms of realms and below in terms of persons.
"Below in terms of realms" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); "below in terms of persons" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they are bound by greed and hatred.
The lower realm is difficult to transcend because it is bound by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Regarding "the masses of beings below," it is because they act like gatekeepers or patrols.
A noble person may first sever two or three fetters; however, because [the text] speaks of their collective abandonment, five are mentioned.
One who does not return to the desire realm is called an Anāgāmin.
This is also of many kinds; it is either fivefold, sevenfold, eightfold, or even said to be manifold.

Regarding the explanation of the five types of *anāgāmin*: these are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who attain parinirvāṇa by ascending the stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Seventh, there are three types of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). As the sūtras state regarding the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state: first, like a small spark of fire; second, like a tiny spark from heated iron; and third, like a glowing iron ball being cast forth.
This refers to what is taught in the Sūtras; four are as previously explained.
Regarding the eight, five kinds are as previously explained.

Furthermore, for those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) in the formless realm, and those who are not fixed [in their destiny], there are fifteen when established according to the five types of faculties in the form realm.
Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, there are superior, middling, and inferior faculties; this applies likewise up to those who go upstream.
As for the establishment by way of stages (*bhūmi*), there are twenty:
there are five in the first dhyāna, and likewise five up to the fourth dhyāna.
The establishment of the spiritual lineages (gotra) consists of thirty types.

There are six kinds of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), namely: the lineage of those subject to regression (parihāṇadharman), the lineage of those who contemplate the Dharma (cetayitadharman), the lineage of those who protect the Dharma (anurakṣaṇādharman), the lineage of those who abide in their state (sthitākampya-dharman), the lineage of those who advance (prativedhanādharman), and the lineage of those who are immovable (akopyadharman).
In this manner, it continues up to the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards),
which is likewise established in eighty locations:
five in the Brahmakāyika heavens, and so on, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The establishment by way of lineage (*gotra*) and faculty (*indriya*) is ninety;
the establishment by way of stage (*bhūmi*) and lineage is one hundred and twenty;
the establishment by way of stage, lineage, and faculty is three hundred and sixty.
Established by way of the spiritual lineage (gotra), there are four hundred and eighty;
established by way of the faculties (indriya) within the spiritual lineage, there are one thousand four hundred and forty.
The record states:
Fifteen, twenty, thirty, eighty, ninety, one hundred and twenty, three hundred and sixty,
four hundred and eighty types, and one thousand four hundred and forty.
Thus, having been explained both extensively and concisely, the summary of the Anāgāmin—

regarding their faculties, stages, and lineages, as well as the extensive establishment of their abodes and the abandonment of their afflictions according to those types— shall now be explained in due order.
Furthermore, regarding one *anāgāmin*, namely the one who attains *parinirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*):

there are three [categories] established by faculties (*indriya*), four by stages (*bhūmi*), six by spiritual lineages (*gotra*), sixteen by locations (*sthāna*). There are eighteen by lineage and faculty; twenty-four by stage and lineage; thirty-six by stage and freedom from desire (*vairāgya*); seventy-two by stage, lineage, and faculty; ninety-six by location and lineage; two hundred and sixteen by stage, lineage, and freedom from desire; two hundred and eighty-eight by location, lineage, and faculty; six hundred and forty-eight by stage, lineage, faculty, and freedom from desire; eight hundred and sixty-four by location, lineage, freedom from desire, and faculty; and two thousand five hundred and ninety-two established by location, lineage, freedom from desire, and faculty.
It should be known that among these, the number of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is as follows;
this applies likewise up to those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).
All of these together comprise twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty.
The Record states:
One, three, four, and six; sixteen and eighteen—these are said to be twenty-four, and further, thirty-six.
Seventy-two kinds, ninety-six kinds, two hundred and sixteen,
two hundred and eighty-eight, six hundred and forty-eight, eight hundred and sixty-four.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two thousand five hundred and ninety-two.
Such Anāgāmins, when multiplied by five, total twenty-five hundred and ninety-two; multiplying this by five again results in twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty.
Having already explained all *anāgāmins*, the characteristics of the five types of *anāgāmin* shall now be explained:
One with sharp faculties and mild afflictions, Abiding in a single [birth] karma, attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; These are distinguished into six types of natures.

Regarding one who possesses sharp faculties and mild afflictions and abides in a single type of karma, attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*): this person, having sharp faculties and mild afflictions, performs and increases karma for the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), but does not perform karma for the rebirth existence (*upapattibhava*). Having passed away from the desire realm, they abide in the intermediate existence of the form realm and attain the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*). By means of this path, they abandon the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attain parinirvāṇa; this is called parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Because it is difficult to transcend the desire realm, one does not attain parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.

If one were to attain parinirvāṇa therein, one would have to sever both types of fetters—the unwholesome and the neutral—and attain two or three fruits of the śramaṇa, thereby transcending the three realms;
however, the intermediate state of the desire realm lacks such capacity.
If one passes away from the form realm (rūpadhātu), they are included among those of the "Upstreaming" (ūrdhvasrotas) category.
Question: How many types of spiritual dispositions (gotra) does such a person possess?
Answer: One should distinguish six types of lineages.

It should be known that those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) comprise six types of lineage, from the one subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) up to the immovable one (akopyadharman).
If it is said that those of sharp faculties do not regress from their spiritual lineage, this is not so, for they too are established as having nine grades of faculties.
Through diligent application of effort and the cultivation of the path of swift progress, one attains parinirvāṇa upon birth; regarding this, there are likewise two explanations.

One who practices with diligence and skillful means, swiftly progressing on the path, is one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin). Such a person who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth performs karma for both the intermediate state (antarābhava) and the state of rebirth; at the end of life, they experience the intermediate state and the state of rebirth within the heavens of the form realm (rūpadhātu).

He gives rise to the path of practice upon being born, namely the path of diligent application and the path of swift progress; he swiftly severs the remaining fetters and attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon birth. Therefore, he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin).

Regarding that, there are also two explanations. One explanation says: if it were the case that one attains parinirvāṇa by severing the afflictions immediately upon birth, that is not so, because there would be no relinquishing of the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*).
There is no practice of relinquishing the life-span; rather, one should remain until the end of that lifespan—this meaning is superior.
Third, regarding diligent application: it is to be free from the path of excessive haste.
The fourth is "not diligent in seeking"; for all three [types], six kinds are taught.

Regarding the third, "one who is diligent in application but lacks the path of swift progress": if one distinguishes their *abhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin* (attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion), they do not practice the path of swift progress; the rest is as previously explained.

As for "name": one who gives rise to the path with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-mārga*), abandons the remaining afflictions, and attains parinirvāṇa is one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (*abhisamskāra-parinirvāyī*).
Furthermore, one who relies on conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) and samādhi to abandon the afflictions and attain parinirvāṇa is likewise one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion.

Regarding the fourth, the one who does not strive: this refers to the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion; they neither strive nor practice the path of rapid progress. The rest is as previously explained.
As for "name": one who gives rise to the path of non-action (*anabhisamskāra-mārga*) to sever remaining afflictions and attains *parinirvāṇa* is one who attains *parinirvāṇa through non-action*.

Furthermore, one who relies on the samādhi of the unconditioned object (*asaṃskṛtālambana-samādhi*) to sever afflictions and attains *parinirvāṇa* is also one who attains *parinirvāṇa through non-action*.

Regarding the statement that all three [types] possess six kinds: it should be understood that both those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), as well as those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), are each said to possess six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Although these three are all forms of *upapadya-parinirvāyin*, there is no error in speaking of them as three, because they differ in their specific meanings.
"Skipping, half-skipping, and going to every place—these are called 'those who go upstream' (ūrdhva-srotas).
These also consist of six types of natures; one should know [the distinction between] those who progress and those who do not.
Regarding "skipping, half-skipping, and going to every place—these are called 'those who go upstream': there are two kinds of those who go upstream."
Some have previously attained the refined dhyāna, while others have not.

Regarding those who have previously attained it: having first cultivated the third dhyāna with refinement and subsequently regressing to abide in the first dhyāna, they die while in a state associated with the relish of the first dhyāna and are reborn among the Brahmā gods.
That [attainment] is also of three kinds: the leaper (*pluta*), the half-leaper (*ardhapluta*), and the one who passes away from every stage (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

As for the leaper: having been born in the first dhyāna and so forth, up to becoming free from desire for the third dhyāna, they cultivate and perfect the leap to the fourth dhyāna; at the end of that life, they are born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Regarding those who transcend halfway: having passed away from the Brahma heavens, they are born in one, two, or three places, and subsequently take birth in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Regarding those who pass away from all places: they are born in each and every place up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

Those who have not previously attained the merit [of the pure abodes] will not be reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, but will instead be reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); the rest is as explained before.
Question:
How many types of lineage (gotra) are there?
Answer: This also consists of six types of lineage.
The "one who goes upstream" likewise consists of six types of lineage, from the "one liable to fall back" up to the "immovable."

This is not the case for those of the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) at the first stage; rather, it refers to those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharman*) who, after regressing from cultivated meditation, attain the stage of seeing (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

One should know that regarding those who progress or do not progress: as for those who "flow upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), one should know there are cases of both progressing and not progressing, which should be formulated as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
"Those who are progressing but not non-progressing" refers to those dwelling in the desire realm and the Brahma heavens.
"Those who are non-progressing but not progressing" refers to those dwelling in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
"Both progressing and not progressing" refers to those dwelling in other heavens.
"Neither progressing nor not progressing" does not exist.
As for those heading toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is not through cultivated practice; therefore, it is said that they are born in the formless realm.
Question:
The Blessed One has spoken of seven destinations for persons (*pudgala-gati*).
How are those seven destinations for persons established?
Answer: It is said that there are three types of those who produce roots of goodness and afflictions;
likewise for those who do not produce them, as well as the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* and the one [who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state].

There is one type of non-returner (anāgāmin) who is established in seven ways due to four causes and conditions: namely, establishment by way of faculties (indriya), establishment by way of afflictions (kleśa), establishment by way of birth and non-birth, and establishment by way of further progress (abhyudgama).
Regarding those born [in this way]: the first has sharp faculties and mild afflictions;
the second has medium faculties and middling afflictions;
the third has dull faculties and intense afflictions.
As there are three types of those who are born [in the form realm], there are likewise three types of those who are not born [there].
Regarding the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), they are said to be those who progress upward; because ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) revert [to lower realms], they are not Upstreamers.

There are five matters in which the Upstreamer of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) is superior: namely, superiority of realm, superiority of stage, superiority of meditative attainment (samāpatti), reduction of the aggregates (skandha), and abandonment of afflictions (kleśa).
Although there are five superiorities, because one cannot achieve meritorious cultivation, the destiny of a *puruṣa* (spiritual hero) is not established therein.
Thus, these nine afflictions reside within the eight higher stages;
it is said by the World-Honored One that they are extinguished by the twofold path.

Regarding these nine afflictions existing in the upper eight stages: just as the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm consist of nine grades, ranging from the soft-soft (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) up to the strong-strong (*adhimātra-adhimātra*).

The same applies to the eight higher stages, namely the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments; when the path of vision first arises therein, one abandons the nine grades of afflictions by means of a single grade of the path.
Question:
If the afflictions of the form and formless realms are also of nine types, why is it that those [afflictions] do not establish a person who has attained detachment? Answer:
Because it is impossible for two births to occur within a single location.

In the desire realm, there are such heavens, such directions, and such families where a noble one may undergo two births; however, this does not apply to the two births of noble ones in the form or formless realms.
If there were two types of birth, there would be no such things as one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) up to one who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Regarding what the Blessed One said—that these afflictions of the three realms are extinguished by the "pair of paths"—it should be understood that they are extinguished by the path of unimpeded liberation (*anantarya-vimukti-mārga*). The path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to sever the afflictions, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is attained upon the realization of liberation.

The path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) abandons the afflictions (kleśa), while the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) does not lose what has been accomplished; therefore, it is said that both paths effect cessation.
If one were to say that the path of liberation abandons the afflictions, how would that be?
Does it arise, or has it not yet arisen?
If it has already arisen, then at the moment that initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, there would still be afflictions (*kleśa*); in that case, it would not be ultimate.
If it has not yet arisen, how could future paths (*anāgata-mārga*) not sever the afflictions?
Question:
By which path are the afflictions abandoned? Answer:
The defiled and the undefiled paths, both are able to transcend the eight stages;
abiding therein, one is said to be a "body-witness," meaning one has attained the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding "the defiled and the undefiled paths, both are able to transcend the eight stages": the defiled refers to the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), while the undefiled refers to the noble path (*ārya-mārga*).

When one becomes free from desire for the remaining stages, excluding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it should be known that both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths are involved.
However, becoming free from the Peak of Existence involves only the uncontaminated path, because the contaminated path is not applicable there.
Because the mundane path ascends to a higher stage, it abandons the afflictions of the lower stage like a *śālākī* insect [climbing up and leaving behind its cast-off skin].

In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no higher stage to which one can ascend to abandon those fetters; since one is bound by the ties of one's own stage, one cannot abandon the fetters of that very stage.
Just as a person who is bound cannot free themselves,
so too there are three modes of the mundane path of non-obstruction (*laukikānantaryamārga*): namely,
the coarse (*audārika*), the painful (*duḥkha*), and the coarse obstacle (*audārikādīnava*).

They are called "coarse" because they manifest; they are called "suffering" because they consist of the three types of suffering; and they are called "coarse obstacles" because they are easy to observe.
The path of liberation also has three aspects:
namely, tranquility (*śamatha*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*); each of these corresponds to an uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The lower object is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), while the upper object is the noble practice (*āryacaryā*), which shall be explained later.

Abiding therein, one is said to be a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*); that is, one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Abiding in the abandonment of the eight stages through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and abiding within the abandonment of one stage through the path of seeing, one attains the meditative absorption of cessation and is thus called a body-witness.
Therefore, a practitioner, within the detachment from each stage up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Such a person may attain the meditative attainment of cessation while still bound by all fetters (*saṃyojana*), or they may attain it upon the exhaustion of eight categories [of defilements].

Because the World-Honored One has transcended all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he speaks of transcending everything up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having realized the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) through bodily witness and dwelling therein fully, because Nirvana is conjoined with the body, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*).
The meditative attainment of cessation shall be explained in detail in the chapter on concentration (*samādhi*).
Following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) necessarily arises;
having given rise to the thought, "Birth for me is exhausted," he becomes an Arhat, free from all outflows (*āsrava*).

Regarding the statement that "the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is immediately followed by the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)": the ninth path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) for the abandonment of desire in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is called the diamond-like samādhi (*vajra-samādhi*).
Because there is nothing that cannot be destroyed, it is called "vajra" (diamond).
This meaning shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga* (Chapter on Analysis).

Following the sequence of the vajra-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) must necessarily arise. These first two knowledges are either the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudayānvayajñāna*). That is to say, once that knowledge of exhaustion has arisen, it gives rise to its own activity, producing the thought: "Birth for me is exhausted."

Because that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes the four aggregates as its causal condition for existence, the Arhat who has abandoned all outflows gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), whereby all outflows are completely exhausted; thus he is called an Arhat (*arhan*). He is so named because he is worthy of all offerings, because he has destroyed all afflictions, and because he no longer plants the seeds of consciousness within the field of existence.

In the case of an Immovable Arhat, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna). That knowledge of exhaustion lasts for one moment; the knowledge of non-arising may also last for one moment, or, if right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) subsequently presents itself, it lasts for one moment; however, if the knowledge of non-arising presents itself, it continues in a succession.

At that time, for one liberated through wisdom, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) lasts for either a single moment; or, if right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) subsequently manifests, it lasts for one moment; or, if the knowledge of exhaustion again manifests, it continues as a succession.
Question:
How many types of arhats are there? Answer:
There are six types of arhats; five arise from those who follow by faith.
They attain two knowledges; one should know them as "liberated by time. Regarding the "six types of arhats," these are:

the one subject to regression (parihāṇadharman), the one intent on reflection (cetana-dharman), the one intent on guarding (anurakṣaṇā-dharman), the one established in his state (sthitākampya-dharman), the one destined for advancement (prativedhanādharman), and the one immovable (akopyadharman).
If one at the stage of a beginner does not employ constant application nor sudden application, this is called the "dharma of regression" (parihāṇadharman).
The same applies to the "dharma of reflection" (cetana-dharman), who is capable of reflecting and making vows.
As for the "dharma of protection" (anurakṣaṇādharman), because they employ constant application rather than sudden application, they do not regress due to their protective cultivation.
One who abides in the Dharma employs sudden skillful means rather than gradual skillful means; they neither regress nor advance.
One who necessarily progresses employs both gradual and sudden skillful means; such a person has dull faculties yet is able to attain immovability.
One of immovable dharma always employs sudden means; such a person possesses sharp faculties.

Some say that one who is of the nature to fall back will necessarily fall back, and so on, up to: one who attains the state of "necessarily advancing" will necessarily advance, and one who is of the nature of "necessarily advancing" will necessarily advance.
He explains that there are six types of Arhats in the desire realm.
In the form and formless realms, there are two types: those who abide in their state (*dharmasthita*) and those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*).
Some say that those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) do not necessarily fall away; if they do fall away, it is only those of this specific lineage and no others.
He asserts that all three realms possess six types of arhats.

Regarding the statement that "five arise from those who follow by faith": among these six types of arhats, the first five belong to the lineage of faith (*śraddhā-gotra*). They accomplish two knowledges, namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Because he may at times regress, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) is not mentioned.
Since the Blessed One will no longer undergo rebirth, all sūtras state that he knows, as it truly is, that he will not again receive a future existence.

One should know that regarding those who are liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*), they are known as "liberated by occasion" because they depend upon the suitability of clothing, food, bedding, dwellings, the teaching of the Dharma, and other persons.
Because their roots of goodness increase such that they cannot advance at all times according to their desire, they are called "liberated by time" (*samaya-vimukta*).
Those of immovable dharma (*akopya-dharman*) possess sharp faculties; these are "liberated independent of time" (*asamaya-vimukta*).
They attain three knowledges (*jñāna*) and achieve liberation for themselves.

The one of immovable dharma with sharp faculties is one liberated at any time. If one is of immovable dharma and possesses exclusively sharp faculties, they are able at all times to advance and cultivate wholesome deeds according to their desire, without depending on external requisites.
Regarding those who attain the three knowledges through occasional liberation, they accomplish three knowledges:

the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*); these constitute the state of non-retrogression.
Regarding the one who has achieved liberation through oneself, it should be known that because they are similar to themselves, this is called "achievement of liberation.
As for "liberation by time," it is so called because it depends upon time.
At that time, one who has attained liberation through wisdom and accomplished the state of immovability is so called because they are immovable;
they are said to be immovable because they cannot be moved by afflictions, which signifies non-retrogression.
Question:
For what reason is temporary liberation of mind (*samayavimukti*) called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), and not "immovability" (*akopya*)? Answer:
Because he protects himself most rigorously, like a person with only one eye; because he lacks self-mastery and fears falling back;
and because those associated roots of goodness are not his own, being like borrowed goods.

The immovable liberation possesses associated wholesome roots because it includes other samādhis; therefore, it is not called "emptiness-of-emptiness," "wishlessness-of-wishlessness," or "signlessness-of-signlessness. This is because the abandonment of concentration is designated as being "associated" with concentration.
One should know that the one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
If one attains the meditative absorption of cessation, one should know them to be one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).

Regarding "one should know that the one liberated by wisdom does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation": among these six types of arhats, those who do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation are called "liberated by wisdom. Because they are liberated from the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) through the power of wisdom, they are named "liberated by wisdom."

Regarding the statement, "If one attains the attainment of cessation, know that they are 'liberated in both ways'": this refers to those among the six types of arhats who have attained the attainment of cessation and are called "liberated in both ways. Because they have abandoned the hindrance of afflictions through the power of wisdom, their minds attain liberation; because they have abandoned the hindrance to liberation through the power of the meditative absorption of cessation, they attain liberation. For this reason, they are named "liberated in both ways."
Furthermore, regarding those of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*) who are liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
One who is of the receding type but not liberated in both ways refers to one of the receding type who has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Those who are both liberated and not subject to falling away are the five types of arhats who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Those who are both subject to falling away and both liberated are those of the "falling away" type who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation.

Nor are they those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), nor are they those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). This refers to the five types of *arhat*s who do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The same applies up to those with immovable liberation (*akopyavimukti*).
The faculties are said to be of nine kinds, and likewise nine kinds of persons are taught:
the seven types of śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Tathāgata.
These are said to be the nine kinds of faculties, ranging from the soft-soft up to the superior-superior.

Arhats are also of nine types: namely, the aforementioned five types, plus two types of immovable liberation—either those who attain immovability through occasional liberation, or those who initially attain immovability.
These seven types of śrāvakas, along with the pratyekabuddhas and the tathāgatas, are called the nine types of persons.
Having already explained the classification of persons by way of their faculties (indriya), I shall now explain the persons according to the possession of those faculties.
The person of the lowest-of-the-low faculties is the first type; up to the highest-of-the-high, one should know that this is the ninth type.
Among them, the one subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) possesses the lowest-of-the-low faculties;

the one intent on reflection (cetayitṛdharman) possesses the low-middle; the one subject to guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman) possesses the low-high; the one established in the dharma (sthitākampya) possesses the middle-low; and the one progressing upward (prativedhanādharman) possesses the middle-middle.

Among those of the lineage of liberation through causes and the immovable dharma, the former is superior; within the immovable liberation, the superior-soft is the highest; the pratyekabuddha is superior-middle; and the Tathāgata is superior-superior.
That is to say, by means of the lineage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), one attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
this may be through that very same lineage, or through advancing to the stage of non-retrogression.
Regarding the six types of arhats: some attain arhatship from the stage of a learner with such a lineage, and thus they are arhats of that very lineage.
Alternatively, one may enhance the faculties and attain non-retrogression by cultivating the faculties of that specific lineage.
There are three matters regarding those of the "subject to retrogression" (parihāṇadharman) which will be explained later;
for those of the "immovable nature" (akopyadharman), there is only one matter: namely, abiding in that state and attaining parinirvāṇa.
There are two further matters concerning the Arhats.
Having already explained the Arhats of the fundamental lineage (*mūla-gotra*), the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) shall now be discussed.
That is to say: three, four, five, six, and seven increase in succession.
These various types, such as those subject to regression (parihāṇadharman) and so forth, are said to be the five kinds of arhats and others.
Among them, the one subject to regression has three factors: namely, regression, abiding, and the faculty of being subject to regression (parihāṇadharmin-indriya).

If one abides in that parinirvāṇa, or if one further increases one's faculties (indriya), there are four matters regarding the practitioner who contemplates the Dharma (cintāmayī): namely, falling back and abiding in the learner’s faculties (śaikṣendriya), and falling back and thus abiding in the faculty of the one subject to falling back (parihāṇadharmin).
If they were different, there would be progress and no regression, because it was previously stated that those of that lineage do not regress.
One who abides in the faculty of the "dharma of regression" (parihāṇadharman) is one who abides in that very state of parinirvāṇa while subsequently cultivating superior faculties.

There are five matters regarding the protection of the Dharma: namely, protecting those who abide in the faculty of training from falling away; protecting those who abide in the faculty of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharmin) so that they may abide in the faculty of the nature of reflection (cetana-dharmin); and protecting those who abide in the faculty of the nature of reflection so that they may abide in the faculty of higher progress toward parinirvāṇa.
The six modes of abiding in the dharmas necessarily lead to the seven stages of progress; this is explained according to their respective meanings.
Having already explained the establishment of the characteristics of noble persons (*āryapudgala*), the establishment of the dharmas shall now be explained.
That is to say, the dharma of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the dharma of the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*),
and the path of seeing reality (*darśanamārga*)— these are all of one and the same characteristic.
These three types of dharma— the dharma of the follower by faith, the dharma of the follower by dharma, and the path of seeing reality— are entirely identical in their single characteristic.
As for the distinction: those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) have dull faculties, while those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) have sharp faculties.
Among these, the dharmas pertaining to the faculties are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
as for the remaining dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the Buddha taught them as the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).

Regarding the statement, "Among these, those faculties (indriya) that are dharmas are called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (ājñāsyāmīndriya)": there are nine factors comprised within the faculties subsumed under the vision of the truths (satyadarśana), namely, the mental faculty (manendriya), the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhādi-pañcendriya); these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
These faculties are accomplished by those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow through dharma (dharmānusārin).
As for the name: because one has yet to know what is not yet known, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Question:

When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) arises, one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm; subsequently, the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises. Is it not the case that these five aggregates have already been known or are to be known?
If you say they are "yet to be known," that is not so.
Answer: Patience (kṣānti) is neither knowledge (jñāna) nor of the nature of knowledge; therefore, there is no fault.
This is because patience is a form of vision (darśana), not of the nature of knowledge.
Because it is known through wisdom, it is not the case that it is not so.

That is to say, regarding the "faculty of having already known" (*ājñātendriya*) which the Buddha taught as referring to other dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*): excluding the dharmas of training belonging to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the remaining dharmas of training—namely these nine factors enumerated here—are called the faculty of having already known.
This faculty is accomplished by those who are liberated through faith, those who have attained vision, and those who are bodily witnesses.

Although the subsequent knowledge of the path arises upon the contemplation of the subsequent patience regarding the path, it is called "the unknown that is yet to be known"; however, because it is so slight, it is not mentioned—like a single drop in the great ocean, a single speck of dust on Mount Sumeru, or the space occupied by a mosquito.
One should know that the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) are called the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Attaining the fruit, one abandons the previous path; this is what the Unobstructed Wisdom has taught.

Regarding "one should know that the dharmas of one beyond training are called the faculty of 'I have known'": one should know that the dharmas of one beyond training consist of these nine factors enumerated as faculties, which are called the faculty of "I have known. This faculty is accomplished by those who are liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and those who are liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
The path of seeing belongs to six stages:

the four dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgāmya), and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara); it does not belong to the preparatory roots of goodness of the higher stages, because those are not its constituent parts and do not have such an extensive object.
The nine stages of training in the path of cultivation consist of these six stages, as well as the five aggregates of the three formless realms.

Regarding the statement that "upon attaining the fruit, one abandons the preceding path through the knowledge of non-obstruction," it should be understood that at the time of attaining the fruit, one abandons the preceding untainted (*anāsrava*) path.
Upon attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna*, one abandons the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
If one has previously exhausted double the [afflictions] of desire, one likewise abandons the path of vision.
If it is a gradual process, one abandons both the fruit of *srotāpanna* and the path of progress toward *srotāpanna*.
Upon attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*, if one has previously exhausted sensual desire, one also abandons the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
If one follows the sequential order, one abandons the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* as well as the path of progress toward *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, one abandons the fruit of anāgāmin as well as the path of progress toward the fruit of anāgāmin.
Question:
The World-Honored One has spoken of seven types of persons, beginning with those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin).
How is it established? Answer:
Through skillful means and the faculties, together with meditative absorption and liberation.
One should know that while there are seven noble ones (ārya), in terms of their actual entities (vastu), they are said to be six.

Regarding "the means, the faculties, the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and liberation—know that there are seven noble ones": it is on account of five causes and conditions that seven persons are spoken of; these are called the "seven [noble ones]" in name, but not seven in terms of their actual entities.
The five causal conditions are: means (upāya), faculties (indriya), right attainment (samāpatti), liberation (vimukti), and right attainment and liberation (samāpattivimukti).
As for "means," they refer to those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
The follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) is so called because of the predominance of faith;
he is said to follow by faith because he previously performed various karmas out of reliance on others. Once he has subsequently attained the Path, he is still designated by his original name.
One who follows the Dharma by practice first contemplates and undertakes various karmic actions, and after attaining the Way, speaks using their original name.
As for the faculties, they are those of liberation through faith and those of vision.
Those of dull faculties are said to be "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta); those of sharp faculties are said to be "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
One who possesses "right attainment" (samyaksamāpatti) is a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
One who possesses "liberation" (vimukti) is one "liberated through wisdom" (prajñāvimukta).
Those who have attained right realization and liberation are those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

Regarding the statement that there are six types of persons: among these noble ones (*ārya*), there are six; in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two, namely the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*);
in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are two, namely the one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
The path of no-more-learning is of two kinds: namely, liberation by occasion and unconditioned liberation.
For the follower by faith, it should be stated as one, because of the seven types of persons based on their faculties.
One should say there are three, namely, because of the soft, medium, and superior lineages (*gotra*).
One should say there are five, namely, from those of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*) up to those who will certainly advance on the path (*prativedhanādharman*).

One should say there are fifteen, from those abiding in the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*).

For one who is free from desire, seventy-three [types of abandonment] should be stated: ten for freedom from desire in the desire realm—namely, from being bound by all fetters up to the exhaustion of the nine grades—and nine for the first dhyāna, continuing thus up to the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, the establishment of the increase based on the faculties, lineages, paths, and supports should also be explained in detail.
Thus, there are one hundred forty-seven thousand eight hundred and twenty-five followers by way of faith (*śraddhānusārin*), who are included therein.
One, three, five, and fifteen, as well as seven and thirty;
these refer to the faculties, lineages, and paths. One should know that regarding the abandonment of afflictions, there are threefold, fivefold, fifteenfold, and ninefold increases respectively.
Thus, although there are many such types, only the "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin) has been mentioned;
it should be understood that for the other noble ones (ārya), they should likewise be described according to their respective meanings.
Question:
As stated in the Sūtra, there are eight types of persons, beginning with those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*).
What does this mean? Answer:
Because there are five matters, eight types of persons are spoken of:
one matter each for the preceding and succeeding stages, and three in the middle.
These refer to the four candidates and four fruits; thus, while eight types of persons are named, the underlying matters are five.
The candidate for stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) and the arhat—these are called one matter and one [person].
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the candidate for once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka)—these are called two matters and one [person].
The same applies to the Sakṛdāgāmin and the candidate for Anāgāmin, as well as the Anāgāmin and the candidate for Arhat.

Those first four individuals accomplish the noble path of a single stage; it is precisely these who are also described as "those who go from family to family" (kulaṃkula) and "those with only one more birth" (ekavīcika).
The candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) is in either the first stage (bhūmi) up to the sixth stage.
The fruit of non-returning is in either the third stage up to the sixth stage.
The candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka) is in either the third stage up to the ninth stage.
An Arhat accomplishes nine stages.
Regarding the destruction of the path and the destruction of the stage in those fruits of śramaṇaship, four permutations should be established.
That which is the destruction of the path but not the destruction of the stage is the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
When the ground is destroyed but the path is not, this refers to the fruit of arhatship.
When both the path and the ground are destroyed, this refers to the fruit of anāgāmin.

When neither the path nor the ground is destroyed, this refers to the fruit of srotāpanna. That which is mixed with both outflow (sāsrava) and non-outflow (anāsrava) is called the destruction of the path; that which is mixed with reliance upon the various dhyānas is called the destruction of the ground.
"Exhaustion is liberation; one attains reliance upon a single fruit;
the ninth is undefiled; cessation should be explained. Regarding "exhaustion is liberation;

one attains reliance upon a single fruit": when one attains liberation and the fruit during the various paths of liberation within the path of progress (*pratipannaka-mārga*), all that is to be abandoned by the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) is exhausted, and thus one attains a single liberation.

Having attained that which is abandoned by the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one fully attains the two liberations; because the attainment of the Path is indestructible, it is said that there is a single attainment of the fruit.

At this time, five causes and conditions are taught: attaining the unprecedented path while relinquishing the previous path, suddenly attaining the eight knowledges, simultaneously cultivating the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), and attaining the fruit of the liberation of a single flavor.
Question:
The abandonment of defiled [phenomena] has already been explained; how are non-defiled [phenomena] abandoned? Answer:
The non-defiled [afflictions] of the ninth stage of cessation should now be explained.

It has already been stated that the nine grades of the afflictions and their attendants are abandoned; as for the non-defiled ones, they are abandoned instantaneously upon abiding in the ninth unimpeded path, not gradually.
That which is non-defiled consists of mundane wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states.
The defiled form among the five aggregates is also severed by the ninth unimpeded path; however, it is not mentioned because it is so minor.
Question:
Why is it that the nine grades of afflictions are abandoned through the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), whereas the non-defiled [afflictions] are not? Answer:

Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are incompatible with the noble path (*āryamārga*), the noble path is incompatible with the afflictions; it is not incompatible with that which is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

Therefore, it is as follows: when such a path arises, the afflictions to be abandoned accordingly are abandoned. When the weakest-weak (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) path arises, the strongest-strong (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) afflictions are abandoned, continuing in this manner until the strongest-strong path arises and the weakest-weak afflictions are abandoned.
Just as a small light extinguishes coarse darkness and a great light extinguishes subtle darkness, so it is with this case.
That which is defiled is not established because its intrinsic nature is severed; that which is undefiled abandons the faults of affliction like discarding mixed poison.
Those who possess names similar to the Unattached (Anāgāmin) can attain the Immovable (Akopya);
those of the lineage of liberation through faith (śraddhādhimukta) likewise advance and increase the Path.

Regarding "those who possess names similar to the Unattached can attain the Immovable": it is not the case that all Arhats can attain the Immovable; only those whose names are similar in their qualities [to the Unattached] attain it.

This means that those who necessarily advance among these five types attain it by increasing their faculties; specifically, one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman) progresses to the "nature of reflection" (cetayitṛdharman), and so on through the sequence until the end. One should understand this accordingly.
Furthermore, one attains nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation regarding the immovable [attainment], just as in the case of attaining arhatship.

During the eight paths of liberation among these nine paths of non-obstruction, one is categorized as "liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta); during the ninth path of liberation, one is categorized as "not liberated by occasion" (asamaya-vimukta). All of these are subsumed under the category of the path of fruition.
Regarding that path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), if it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is subsumed under the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*); if it is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is not so subsumed.

As for the lineage of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who progresses and increases the path: if that one liberated through faith necessarily progresses toward a higher lineage, they are able to attain the lineage of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and no other; therefore, the five types within the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*) also increase their faculties (*indriya*).
The advancement of the path refers to the faculty of ardor (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
The advancement of the faculties occurs among human beings and not in other realms of existence; it pertains to the noble path (*āryamārga*) and not to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Those in training (śaikṣa) rely on dhyāna; those beyond training (aśaikṣa) rely on both dhyāna and the formless attainments (ārūpya).
Srotāpannas and Sakṛdāgāmins rely on the future stage to advance their faculties (indriya), whereby they relinquish one stage and acquire another.

An Anāgāmin who, having previously relied upon the first dhyāna and its attendants, has transcended to the state beyond birth (vitarāga) either by leaping over or by gradual succession, but has not yet attained the second dhyāna—if such a person further develops their faculties (indriya-vivardhana), they relinquish the fruit of three stages and attain the fruit of three stages.

If one attains the second dhyāna but not the third, and subsequently develops the faculties based on the first dhyāna, they relinquish the fruits of three stages as well as the path of superior fruit of the fourth stage, and immediately attain the fruits of three stages.

In this manner, up until one attains the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one abandons the fruits of three stages and the paths of superior fruit belonging to nine stages, and attains the fruits of three stages.
If it is argued that one would fall back because one abandons many paths to obtain few paths, this is not so.
Why is this? Because they have attained the superior path;
because their minds have achieved understanding.
Question:
When one abandons the path, does one also abandon the abandonment [of defilements]? Answer:
Those abandoned by the mundane path are not relinquished.

When one abandons each type of affliction of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and attains the stage of vision, those [afflictions] abandoned through the path of cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are relinquished; furthermore, the acquisition of the afflictions is no longer established, as in the case of an ordinary person being born into a higher realm.

Furthermore, if one first transcends the state of ordinary birth by relying on the first dhyāna, and later progresses by refining the faculties (indriya) by relying on the second dhyāna, one relinquishes the fruits of three stages as well as the path of superior fruit belonging to four stages, and attains the fruit of the fourth stage.
In this manner, all the stages (*bhūmi*) should be explained in detail.

If one who abides in a fruit further develops their faculties (*indriya*), that skillful means (*upāya*) is comprised within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

If one who dwells in the path of the superior fruit sharpens their faculties (*indriya-vivardhana*), then that which is subsumed under the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of superior fruit, as well as that subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and its fruit, consists of one preparatory path, one path of non-obstruction, and one path of liberation.

In this way, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) also consists of six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), yet it lacks the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) because it is a swift path (*kṣipramārga*).
Likewise, the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) also consist of six types of spiritual lineage.

The practitioner’s faculties advance progressively; however, the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) alone does not involve such advancement of faculties, because it lasts for only a single moment.
Having explained the fulfillment of the faculties, I shall now explain which trainees (*śaikṣa*) have fulfilled them and which have not.
Some have fulfilled the fruit of training, some the faculties, or the meditative attainments;
or again, all three may be fulfilled. It is likewise for the two cases of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Those in training (*śaikṣa*) have fulfillment in three matters: either fulfillment of the fruit, fulfillment of the faculties, or fulfillment of the meditative attainments.

If a faith-liberated non-returner does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation, they possess fulfillment of the fruit alone but not fulfillment of the faculties, because their faculties are dull;
nor do they possess fulfillment of meditative attainment, because they have not attained the absorption of cessation.

The Dṛṣṭiprāpta, Srotāpanna, and Sakṛdāgāmin possess fulfillment of the faculties (indriya-paripūri), but not fulfillment of the fruits (phala-paripūri) nor fulfillment of meditative attainments (samāpatti-paripūri).

The Śraddhādhimukta and Anāgāmin who has attained the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) possess fulfillment of the fruits and fulfillment of meditative attainments, but not fulfillment of the faculties.

Regarding those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) but have not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they possess fulfillment of the fruit (*phalapūrṇa*) and fulfillment of the faculties (*indriyapūrṇa*), but not fulfillment of meditative attainment (*samāpattipūrṇa*).
Regarding those who have attained vision and have attained the meditative absorption of cessation, all three matters are fulfilled.
The same applies to the two types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): because all those beyond training have fulfilled the fruit and lack the nature of the two [inferior] fruits.
For one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) with dull faculties, the fruit is fulfilled but the faculties are not fulfilled.
Those of sharp faculties possess fulfillment of the fruit and fulfillment of the faculties, but neither is fulfillment of meditative attainment.
Those of weak faculties who are liberated both ways possess fulfillment of the fruit and fulfillment of meditative attainment, but not fulfillment of the faculties.
Those of sharp faculties fulfill three matters.
Question:
Regarding the "threefold fulfillment" which refers to skillfully contemplating the truths, how does one contemplate the truths?
Is it sudden, or is it gradual? Answer:
By establishing merit and [avoiding] evil, one gradually perceives the True Reality.
Attained through the power of the path of non-obstruction, there are conditioned and unconditioned fruits.

Regarding the establishment of merits and faults, for one who gradually perceives the truths, the truths of suffering and its origin are established because they perceive the faults within these truths.
Because one perceives their merits, the truths of cessation and the path are established.
Therefore, it is not that one perceives merits at the time of perceiving faults, nor is it that one perceives faults at the time of perceiving merits, for their essential natures are distinct.
Nor is it the case that seeing the truths as they truly are is called the "subsequent realization of the truths" (satyābhisamaya).
Nor is it the case that a single cognition perceives the truths collectively, because the truths possess a manifold nature; therefore, one realizes the true truths progressively.
Some say that the practice of the markless (animitta) proceeds through immediate realization (abhisamaya) all at once. They state as follows:
"The practice of the markless takes all phenomena as its object; therefore, it should proceed through immediate realization all at once. This is not so.

Why is this? Because inversions (*viparyāsa*) are manifold; because [the self] is not the object of the dharmas that are associated with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and co-existent; and because the characteristics of the truths (*satya*) are distinct.
Regarding these truths, there are many gates such as non-self (*anātman*), and thus inversions are not singular.
Because the arising of selflessness eliminates numerous inherent afflictions, it is not singular.
This realization occurs gradually; the details regarding this sequential realization will be explained extensively in the section on discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
Question:
Regarding the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya through the realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya), how is this so?
Are these fruits conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?
Answer: The power of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) brings about both conditioned and unconditioned fruits.

Both the analytical cessation of afflictions (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are acquired through the power of the path of non-obstruction; therefore, both are described as fruits of śrāmaṇya.

The cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) is both the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) and the fruit of effort (*prayoga-phala*); the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is both the fruit of effort and the fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Question:
How many types of this immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and so forth are there?

Answer: Regarding the three types of direct realization (*abhisamaya*), one should know that there are three kinds based on the object (*ālambana*) and the realization (*darśana*); alternatively, there may be two or even one.

There are three kinds of clear realization (*abhisamaya*): namely, clear realization by way of object (*ālambana-abhisamaya*), clear realization by way of thing (*vastu-abhisamaya*), and clear realization by way of vision (*darśana-abhisamaya*). Wisdom consists of these three kinds of clear realization.
"Equanimity regarding objects" (ālambana-yathābhūta-parijñā) exists because there are objects;
"equanimity regarding phenomena" (vastu-yathābhūta-parijñā) exists because it can accomplish the task;
"equanimity regarding views" (dṛṣṭi-yathābhūta-parijñā) exists because it is the nature of vision.
The factors associated with wisdom have two kinds of clear realization (*abhisamaya*):
clear realization by way of object (*ālambana-abhisamaya*) and clear realization by way of substance (*vastu-abhisamaya*);
their concomitant factors have only one, namely, clear realization by way of substance.

That patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) constitute threefold direct realization (*abhisamaya*) with respect to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and direct realization of the facts (*vastv-abhisamaya*) with respect to the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*).

It should be understood that patience regarding origination (*samudaya-kṣānti*) and knowledge regarding origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) are likewise with respect to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

The patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) constitute three moments of immediate realization (*anantarya-samāpatti*) with respect to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), while they constitute immediate realization of the facts (*vastu-anantarya-samāpatti*) with respect to the truths of suffering, origin, and the path.

The patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*) constitute three moments of immediate realization with respect to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), while they constitute immediate realization of the facts with respect to the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.
The path of cultivation follows its respective meaning; it should be understood in this way.
Since the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths occurs without interval, by this causal condition one should know that the clear realization is gradual and without interval.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Six: On Knowledge (Jñāna-varga) The establishment of the noble and holy persons has already been explained; knowledge shall now be discussed.
If the nature of knowledge can clearly discern, illuminating all that exists—both existence and non-existence, as well as nirvāṇa—I shall now explain its various characteristics.
"Yadi" (if) means "regarding that matter.
"Jña" (knowing) has the sense of "ascertainment.
"Vijñāna" (discernment) means "differentiation."
"Brilliant illumination" refers to observation.
"All that exists" refers to the limits of the three realms of existence (*bhava*), namely the truths of suffering and its origin.
"Existence" refers to the nature of existence.
"Existence and non-existence" refers to the exhaustion of existence.
"Nirvāṇa" is the cessation of all afflictions; this explains the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
As for the indication of the characteristics of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) within those [preceding truths], it is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and spontaneous nature (*prakṛti*).
The present exposition reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Question:
What is wisdom (*jñāna*)?
Answer: The Buddha has taught three types of knowledge, the supreme and foremost awakening:
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
These three knowledges encompass all knowledge.

Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): it is the untainted knowledge whose objective domain consists of the suffering, origin, cessation, and path within the desire realm; because this is the first apprehension of the characteristics of phenomena, it is called the knowledge of phenomena.

Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) regarding the suffering, origin, cessation, and path within the form and formless realms that serves as the object of wisdom. If this dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) proceeds in a certain manner, then this inferential knowledge proceeds accordingly; it is called inferential knowledge because it knows by means of analogy.
Regarding "knowledge of conventions" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*): if knowledge has all phenomena as its object, it is impure knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*).

"Convention" (*saṃvṛti*) refers mostly to worldly designations, such as male and female, long and short, and so forth; therefore, "conventional knowledge" is so called. Furthermore, "convention" (*saṃvṛti*) carries the meaning of the gathering of many things.
Regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, two knowledges arise from the truths;
these, together with the four [other] knowledges, are what the Muni taught according to the truths.

These—dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge—proceed in accordance with the truths. The World-Honored One spoke of them using the terminology of those truths: when their object is the truth of suffering, they are called "knowledge of suffering"; when their objects are the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, they are called "knowledge of the path."
If wisdom observes the minds of others, it is said among these three;
the two—knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising—have the four doors as their objects.

Regarding "if wisdom observes the minds of others, it is said among these three": three types of wisdom observe the minds of others. When observing with the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), it is called dharma-knowledge; when observing with the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), it is called subsequent knowledge; and when observing with impure mind and mental factors, it is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the two knowledges of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*):

these two knowledges refer to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). When the activity of these two has reached its culmination and proceeds with certainty—that nothing more remains to be done—it is the knowledge of exhaustion;
when it proceeds with certainty that nothing further will arise, it is the knowledge of non-arising.
Question:
What is the objective sphere of the truths? Answer:
Their objective spheres reside in the four gates, meaning they take the Four Noble Truths as their objects.
Question:
If the Blessed One speaks of three knowledges, why does he speak of ten?
Answer: Antidote and skillful means, Intrinsic nature, practice, and conditions;
That which has been performed, causes, and nourishment— For these reasons, ten knowledges are taught.

The ten knowledges are taught by way of seven causal conditions: namely, antidote, means, intrinsic nature, activity, objective condition for activity, that which has been accomplished, and nourishment by causes.

Regarding their antidotes: dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*); dharma-knowledge is said to be the antidote for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while subsequent knowledge is said to be the antidote for the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
Although the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is an antidote to the form and formless realms, it is neither universal nor complete in all its aspects; therefore, it is not mentioned here.

As for the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) also cognizes both the mind and mental factors, yet that preparatory application is intended specifically to know that [other] mind.

Regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) mostly takes conventional designations as its object, as previously explained. Regarding their activity (*carita*):

the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)—these two knowledges have unbroken activity because they share a single object, though that object is broken [into aspects].

These two knowledges share a single object; therefore, when they operate upon that object through the mode of impermanence, the knowledge of suffering should also be said to be [the knowledge of] impermanence.
However, because this knowledge produces an extreme degree of revulsion toward suffering, it is specifically called the "knowledge of suffering."
Furthermore, because it is unique [to the practitioner], ascetic practice (duṣkara-caryā) exclusively has outflowing (sāsrava) objects.

As for the practice of impermanence (anitya-carita), if it is outflowing, it has the three truths as its objects; if it is outflow-free (anāsrava), it has both outflowing and outflow-free things as its objects.

For one who practices the contemplation of emptiness and non-self, if they take all contaminated phenomena as their object, or if they take uncontaminated phenomena that have contaminated objects as their object—
therefore, regarding the knowledge of suffering and the practice of suffering, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
There are cases where there is knowledge of suffering but not the mental application of suffering: this refers to the knowledge of suffering when it is associated with other mental applications.
There are cases where there is the mental application of suffering but not the knowledge of suffering: this refers to those phenomena associated with the knowledge of suffering.
That which is both knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the practice of suffering refers to the knowledge of suffering that practices the mode of suffering.
That which is neither knowledge of suffering nor the practice of suffering refers to the knowledge of suffering that practices other modes and their associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
As it is with the practice, so it is with what has been practiced and what is yet to be practiced.
As it is with the practice of suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self, so it is likewise.
As it is with the knowledge of suffering in twelve ways, so it is likewise up to the knowledge of the path.

Regarding "conditioned by formations" (*saṃskārapratyaya*), this refers to the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); for by means of those knowledges, the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is not destroyed, and the formations are likewise not destroyed.
Regarding "that which has been done" (*kṛta*), this refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because that which was to be done has already been accomplished.

That which is nourished by causes refers to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), because it is based on all untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*) and because it abides in the immovable body (*aniñjyakāya*).
Having explained the establishment of the ten knowledges according to their causal conditions, the classification of them as wholesome and so forth shall now be discussed.
Nine knowledges are said to be exclusively wholesome; one knowledge is analyzed into three parts;
one is vision and two are non-vision; the remainder are of two kinds.

Regarding "nine knowledges are said to be exclusively wholesome": with the exception of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the remaining nine knowledges are said to be wholesome because they result in desirable fruits.
Regarding "one is knowledge of three kinds of discrimination": conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Regarding "one is vision": it is the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), because it is a discrimination by way of being vision.
Regarding "the two are not views": the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not views, because they are not of a discriminative nature.
Regarding "the others are of two kinds": the remaining seven knowledges are either views or not views.

Those factors not included within dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, are views; those that are so included are not views.
Conventional knowledge (samvṛti-jñāna) is either view (dṛṣṭi) or non-view.
The five views and mundane right view (laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi) are views because they are swift and incisive.
Wisdom associated with doubt, craving, hatred, pride, and ignorance is not view.
Why is this? Because it is obscured by the two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Although wisdom associated with ignorance lacks these two latent tendencies, ignorance alone is capable of utterly obscuring it, more so than any other affliction.
