Why is this? Because it is not an investigative skillful means (*upāya*).
Wisdom that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is not a vision (*darśana*), because it is not swift.
The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), because it lacks the nature of deliberation (*tarka*).
Six [types of wisdom] belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); two types of wisdom are said to belong to those beyond training;
one type belongs to neither those in training nor those beyond training; and it should be known that one type consists of three kinds.

Regarding the six [knowledges] that are either of the learner (*śaikṣa*) or of the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*): these are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. They are either of the learner or of the one beyond learning;
if they are attained by a person who is still training, they are of the learner; if they are attained by a person who is no longer training, they are of the one beyond learning.

Regarding the statement that two knowledges belong to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are those beyond training, because they abide free from afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the one that is neither for training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*): this refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), which is neither for training nor beyond training because it is with outflows (*sāsrava*).

It should be understood that the three types consist of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which may be either *śaikṣa*, *aśaikṣa*, or neither-*śaikṣa*-nor-*aśaikṣa*. If it takes only the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) of one in training as its object, it is *śaikṣa*; if it takes the mind and mental factors of one beyond training as its object, it is *aśaikṣa*; and if it takes only contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors as its object, it is neither-*śaikṣa*-nor-*aśaikṣa*.
The nature of the eight knowledges is uninterrupted; two knowledges are said to be of two kinds;
one is both with-outflow and without-outflow; one is said to be with-outflow alone.

Regarding "the nature of the eight knowledges is uninterrupted": with the exception of the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the remaining eight knowledges are uninterrupted because they are free from defilement.

Regarding the statement that the two knowledges are of two types: the knowledge of others' minds, if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is not abandoned.

As for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), if its antidote is patience (*kṣānti*), it is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*); if its antidote is knowledge (*jñāna*), it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the oneness of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*): the knowledge of others' minds is either tainted or untainted. It is tainted when it takes tainted minds and mental factors as its object; it is untainted when it takes untainted minds and mental factors as its object.

First, regarding the statement that [certain] knowledges are with-outflows (*sāsrava*): conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) is exclusively with-outflows, because it is the locus where afflictions (*kleśa*) reside.
It should be understood that the eight knowledges which are not abandoned are said to be without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Four knowledges have conditioned objects; One has a constant object;
Five knowledges have two spheres— This is what the Wise One has taught. Regarding "four knowledges have conditioned objects":
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path, which have conditioned objects because they take the aggregates (*skandhas*) as their sphere.

Regarding "having one [type of] object when there is a constant object": this refers to the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), which has the unconditioned as its object because it takes *nirvāṇa* as its cognitive sphere.

Regarding "five knowledges having two types of objects": this refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). When these take the three truths as their objects, they have conditioned objects; when they take the truth of cessation as their object, they have unconditioned objects.

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) takes the three truths as its object, thus having conditioned things as its domain; it takes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*) as its object, thus having unconditioned things as its domain.
One should know that dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) arises from six stages, while subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) pertains to nine stages;
knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) resides within the dhyānas.

Regarding the statement that "Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) should be known to arise from six stages": Dharma-knowledge is obtainable in six stages by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), namely the four dhyānas, the preliminary stage (*anāgāmya*), and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*). It is not present in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), because those in the formless realms do not take the desire realm as their cognitive object.

Regarding "comparative knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) pertains to nine stages": comparative knowledge can be obtained in nine stages, namely the preliminary stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).

Regarding "the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) exists in the dhyānas": this means that the knowledge of others' minds exists in the fundamental dhyānas, because it is the fruit of the four- or five-limbed meditative concentration (samādhi).
One should know that conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) resides in eleven stages;
as for the other various types of knowledge, they are categorized stage by stage as previously explained.

Regarding the statement "one should know that conventional knowledge resides in eleven stages": conventional knowledge exists in eleven stages, namely: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Regarding the other categories of knowledge mentioned previously—namely, the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising: if they belong to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), they reside in six stages just like dharma-knowledge; if they belong to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), they reside in nine stages just like subsequent knowledge.
Regarding the statement that among the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one should know that after [the first] there is one wisdom,
and that three are said to be one wisdom, while the remaining four are explained by the Wise One:

as for "among the foundations of mindfulness, one should know that after [the first] there is one wisdom," this means that the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), because it takes the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as its object.

Regarding "the third is said to be one wisdom": this refers to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); because it takes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others as its object, it consists of three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), excluding the application of mindfulness to the body.

Regarding "the remaining four are said by the Wise One to be clear knowledge": this means that the remaining eight knowledges constitute all four applications of mindfulness, because they take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their objects.
One wisdom has its basis in the desire realm; one wisdom has its basis in two realms;
two wisdoms have their basis in all three realms; and for the remaining six, it is either one or three.

Regarding "one wisdom has its basis in the desire realm": the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has its basis solely in the desire realm, because dharma-knowledge arises in accordance with [the body], or because it is produced by the four great elements of the desire realm.
Regarding the one that has two realms as its basis: the knowledge of others' minds is based on the desire and form realms, because it depends upon matter.
Regarding the two knowledges that have all three realms as their basis: inferential knowledge and conventional knowledge are based on all three realms.

Regarding "the remaining six, or one, or three": these refer to the six knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). If they belong to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-pakṣa*), they rely on the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); if they belong to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*), they rely on the three realms. "Rely" (*niśraya*) is another name for the body (*kāya*).
In name, there are sixteen aspects; in substance, some speak of sixteen.
Apart from these sixteen aspects, the removal of darkness is not untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding "in name, there are sixteen aspects": this refers to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; cause, origin, existence, and condition; cessation, stillness, excellence, and renunciation; and path, correctness, track, and vehicle.

It is impermanent because it is sustained by various conditions; it is suffering because it is oppressive; it is empty because it is the antidote to the view of "mine"; and it is non-self because it is the antidote to the view of "self. It is the cause because it is the nature of a seed;
it is the origin because it is the basis for arising; it is existence because it is a continuity; and it is the condition because it is the maturation of characteristics.

Because all aggregates (*skandha*) have ceased, it is extinction; because the three fires have subsided, it is stillness; because internal afflictions are abandoned, it is sublime; because external afflictions are abandoned, it is transcendence. Because it leads toward [liberation], it is the path (*mārga*);
because it is skillful means, it is right (*samyak*); because it proceeds equally, it is the track (*padavyañjana*); because it reaches the ultimate, it is the vehicle (*yāna*).

Furthermore, it is impermanent because it is not ultimate; it is suffering because it is a heavy burden; it is empty because it is internally devoid of a person; and it is non-self because it lacks sovereignty. It is a cause because it is the means for coming into being;
it is an origination because it is the means for production; it is existence because it causes growth; and it is a condition because it provides support.

It is cessation because it is non-continuous and free from continuity; it is stillness because it is free from the three characteristics of the conditioned; it is sublime because it is virtuous and eternal; and it is detachment because it is the supreme rest.

It is the "path" (*mārga*) because it is the antidote to deviant tracks; it is "right" (*samyak*) because it is the antidote to what is not right; it is "feet" (*pāda*) because one ascends by them to the city of Nirvāṇa; it is a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because it is the antidote to all existence (*bhava*).
Question:
How many types of practice (*caryā*) are there?
Answer: Regarding the objects (*vastu*), some say there are sixteen; these are called the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
Others say there are seven objects: namely, four aspects of suffering (*duḥkhākāra*) and four objects, because they serve as the antidotes to the perversions (*viparyāsa*).
The "compendium of practices" consists of four names for one reality;
the same applies to cessation and the path.
To speak in this way is called the sixteen realities, and it is also excellent that there are sixteen.
Question:
Is there any untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the sixteen aspects? Answer:
Apart from the sixteen aspects, there is no other darkness that is not untainted (anāsrava).
Apart from the sixteen aspects, there is no untainted wisdom.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"My births are exhausted"—this too is suffering; it is the exhaustion of birth through even-minded practice.
It is like saying, "I am cutting wood": for whom is it cut?
It is said, "by the axe. This is also like that.
Question:
How many aspects (ākāra) does each of these knowledges (jñāna) possess? Answer:
The two knowledges have sixteen aspects; the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) possess these aspects or their opposites.
This is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Regarding "the two knowledges have sixteen aspects:

the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge," it means that all instances of the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge proceed according to the sixteen aspects as they have been described.
Regarding such practice or what is called "equal wisdom" (*samatājñāna*): equal wisdom functions through sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), yet it is not limited to those sixteen aspects.
The sixteen aspects refer to the wholesome roots of *ūṣmagata* and so forth, as well as other indeterminate wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*).
Furthermore, as for "not [the path]," practices such as viewing things as a disease or an abscess are called "not [the path].
Question:

If conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) consists of these sixteen aspects, why is it not referred to by names such as "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhajñāna*) up to "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: Because they destroy their objects.
Untainted (anāsrava) formations do not destroy their objects, because they take individual truths as their conditions.

The contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations have the destruction of objects as their aspect; the contaminated [knowledges] have the three truths as their objects and are impermanent in their aspect; the empty and non-self [knowledges] have all phenomena as their objects.
These four knowledges possess four aspects, as definitively explained regarding the nature of their practice.
When a knowledge knows another's mind, its aspects may be either such [as described above] or otherwise.

Regarding the statement that "the four knowledges have four aspects determined by their mode of operation": the knowledge of suffering has four aspects, and this applies likewise up to the knowledge of the path.

If a knowledge knows another's mind as having such aspects or otherwise, then if it is untainted knowledge of others' minds, it consists of the four aspects of the path; if it is tainted knowledge, it does not take specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), being free from the aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*), are said to possess fourteen aspects; this is because they are proximate to the [knowledge of] equality (*samatā*).

Regarding "the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, being free from the aspects of emptiness and selflessness, are said to possess fourteen aspects": the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising each possess fourteen aspects, excluding the aspects of emptiness and selflessness.
Question:
Why is it not the practice of emptiness and non-self? Answer:
This means they are proximate to the state of equality.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are proximate to equality in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
the practices of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*) are proximate to the foremost [state] in terms of the ultimate truth.
Question:
By whom are those formations performed?
Are they also performed by another?
What is its nature? Answer: It is the practice of wisdom, that which is capable of being practiced, and that which is also practiced by others.
The remaining [factors] have two kinds of dependence; those that do not depend on others are the objects of activity.

That is to say, when wisdom is both an activity and an object of activity for others, the intrinsic nature of wisdom is itself an activity, capable of performing activities such as impermanence within those objective spheres (*ālambana*); those [spheres] are likewise the objects of activity for activities such as impermanence.

Regarding the remaining two types that have a basis (*sāśraya*): with the exception of wisdom (*prajñā*), the other associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) and so forth are also capable of performing [the activity of] mental application (*manasikāra*), because they possess an object (*sālambana*);
furthermore, they are also objects of performance for others, because they serve as the objects of others' cognition and because their nature is neither that of performance nor of wisdom.

Regarding "that which does not have the other-dependent as its object": those factors that are dissociated from it—namely, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)—have the other-dependent as their object, because they do not have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is not that which performs the practice, because it lacks an object.
Having already explained the establishment of practice, the establishment of attainment shall now be explained.
That is to say, regarding the first untainted mind, some may possess one [attainment].
Two, or three, are accomplished; at each of the four stages, one is added.

That is to say, regarding the first untainted mind, there may be cases where one is accomplished: namely, the mind associated with the initial *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*. If one has not yet abandoned desire, one accomplishes one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); if one has abandoned desire, one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Regarding "two or three are accomplished": the second mind associated with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) accomplishes three knowledges—namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of dharma, and conventional knowledge—if one has not yet abandoned desire; if one has abandoned desire, it accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding "each of the four periods increases by one": in each of the aforementioned four periods, one increases the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
If one has not yet abandoned desire, there are four knowledges:

dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). If one has abandoned desire, one acquires the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). In the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), one increases the knowledge of origin; in the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), one increases the knowledge of cessation; and in the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), one increases the knowledge of the path.
Within the patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is not attained, because it does not have the nature of knowledge.

The subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding origination, cessation, and the path do not increase knowledge, as they derive their designation from the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
Having explained the attainment of knowledge, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) shall now be discussed.

If one attains the cultivation of knowledge (*jñāna*), which occurs during the Noble Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), then that very [knowledge] will be cultivated in the future; the same applies to all the Patiences (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the statement "if one attains the cultivation of knowledge, which occurs during the Noble Path of Seeing, then that very [knowledge] will be cultivated in the future": when the various knowledges of the Path of Seeing are cultivated in the present, they are simultaneously cultivated in the future.

This means that when the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is being cultivated in the present, one cultivates the future dharma-knowledge of suffering; it is not the [dharma-]patience (*kṣānti*), nor is it any other knowledge.
This continues in the same manner up to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).

Regarding all the patiences as well: when the dharma-patience of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is being cultivated in the present, that very same patience is cultivated in the future; it is not a knowledge, nor is it any other patience.
All forms of patience (*kṣānti*) are likewise so.
Question:

Why is it that in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) one cultivates only its own category (*svabhāga*), whereas in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) one cultivates both its own category and those that are not its own category (*asvabhāga*)?

Answer: Because they have first attained the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), and because they first perceive the truths (*satya*) at the beginning of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), they cultivate only their own respective [factors] and no others.
Furthermore, it is because the path is unmixed, because it is swift, and because the path is not yet fully realized.
Within those three moments of mind, one attains the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
It should be known that in the final moment of mind, one either cultivates seven or six [knowledges].

Regarding the statement "within those three moments of mind one attains the cultivation of conventional knowledge": during the three moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), at the limit of immediate succession (*anantara*), one cultivates conventional knowledge; that is to say, the subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation.

If one, relying on the preliminary stage of dhyāna (anāgamyadhyāna), transcends and leaves behind birth, they cultivate the path of seeing in one stage and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) in two stages—namely, the preliminary stage of dhyāna and the desire realm.
If one transcends and rises above the state of birth by relying on the first dhyāna, one cultivates the path of seeing in two stages and conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) in three stages.
Up to the fourth dhyāna, one cultivates the path of seeing in six stages and conventional knowledge in seven stages.
Question:
Why is it that the path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) do not cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)? Answer:
Because it is not a partial aspect (*koṭi-apakṣa*).
Since it is the cultivation of the limit (*koṭi*) of the immediate realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), it is called the "limit of immediate realization" (*abhisamayakoṭi*).
There is no one capable of cultivating the limit of all paths and Buddhas, yet [this knowledge] knows all suffering, its origin, and its cessation.

Furthermore, because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has never previously attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding those truths, and because it is cultivated as an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);

since the knowledge of the limit of direct realization (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*) is an attendant of the path of seeing and the subsequent inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is not cultivated in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as the path of seeing does not exist there.
Question:
Why is dharma-knowledge not cultivated? Answer:
Because [the path] is not ultimate immediately following the truths.
If it were cultivated, it should be mentioned among the "immediate realizations" (ānantarya-samāpatti).
If it belongs to the desire realm, its nature consists of the four aggregates, because it is indeterminate.

If it pertains to the form realm (rūpadhātu), its nature consists of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). Because it is characterized by meditative concentration (samādhi), concentration exists; and because concentration exists, there is matter concomitant with concentration (samādhisaṃprayukta-rūpa).
Since the aggregate of matter exists, there are thus five aggregates. Furthermore, because wisdom (prajñā) increases, it is said that one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).

If there are four matters regarding the limit of the immediate realization of suffering— namely, the desire realm taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object, and the form realm taking the suffering of the form and formless realms as its object—
the same applies to the limits of the immediate realization of the origin and cessation [of suffering].
This is a dharma that is non-arising, because it relies upon and follows those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who practice through the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
Those practices of following through faith and following through the Dharma are accomplished, yet they do not manifest before one.

Regarding the statement "one should know that either seven or six [knowledges] are cultivated in the final mind": if one attains the path through the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) while free from desire, one will cultivate seven knowledges in the future, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
If one has not yet abandoned desire, one cultivates six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds.

One cultivates the path of counteraction for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated because it is not a counteraction to that sphere.

Regarding the seventeen untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) on that higher path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one should know that seven [knowledges] are cultivated, or six when increasing the faculties (*indriya*).

As for "regarding the seventeen untainted minds on that higher path of cultivation, one should know that seven [knowledges] are cultivated": if one has not yet abandoned the six types of desire, then proceeding from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) through the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates seven knowledges; this is because these paths are subsumed within the *dhyānāntara* and the *anāgāmya* concentrations.

The knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not cultivated because they belong to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); the remaining seven knowledges must necessarily be cultivated.
If conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is free from desire, one cultivates one kind of knowledge—the conventional knowledge—in the present, and seven kinds in the future.
If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), one cultivates each of the four *dharmajñānas* in the present and seven in the future.

Regarding the increase of faculties (*indriya-vardhana*) where there may be six: this refers to one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) seeking to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). In that case, during the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), one cultivates six knowledges; it is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because it is incompatible with the path of non-obstruction;
nor is it conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it resembles the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
It is not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), because these belong to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If one has not yet abandoned desire, one cultivates these six knowledges in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*);
if one has abandoned desire, one cultivates seven knowledges.
Therefore, it is said that those who progress and attain immovability cultivate seven knowledges during the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
These do not include the knowledge of others' minds, because that is incompatible with the nature of the path of non-obstruction;
nor do they include conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because it is not the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
It is not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), because it has not yet been attained.
In the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates eight knowledges, as one also attains the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
In the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates ten knowledges; therefore, the word "or" is used.

When attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and when departing from the upper seven stages, one cultivates the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and practices the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Upon attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*, one necessarily attains the fundamental dhyānas; therefore, one cultivates eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Regarding the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments—when one becomes free from desire in these seven stages, one cultivates eight knowledges (*jñāna*) during the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
If one becomes free from desire via the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated in the present and eight [knowledges] in the future.

If one becomes free from desire via the supramundane path (*anāsrava-mārga*), each of the six knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is cultivated in the present and eight [knowledges] in the future.
Regarding the six knowledges: these are the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path.
When practicing the one path of liberation through the cultivation of dhyāna, a learner (śaikṣa) cultivates eight knowledges, while one beyond learning (aśaikṣa) cultivates ten knowledges.

In the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the supernormal powers of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the recollection of past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*), one also cultivates eight knowledges (*jñāna*), because they are subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*).

Because the paths of liberation for the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*), these three higher supernormal powers are not cultivated [in their preparatory stages]. At the time of their acquisition and during subsequent application, all are paths of liberation, and all paths of liberation are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

Because the supernormal power of the bases (*ṛddhipāda*) subdues sentient beings, while the other two [powers] perceive only what is subtle or distant, and because the eyes and ears lack this capacity, they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

These paths of non-obstruction (*anantaryamārga*), as well as the cessation of the "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*), are precisely those eight liberations (*vimokṣa*); one should know that seven of them are cultivated.

Regarding the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for detachment from the desires of the seventh stage, as well as the two paths of non-obstruction for the cultivation of dhyāna: for the training in the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are five paths of non-obstruction. For detachment from the desires of the seventh stage and for cultivation, one employs one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and one untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) as the path of non-obstruction; because they involve two moments of mindfulness, they are said to be "two. Since each of the five supernormal powers has its own single path of non-obstruction, they are said to be "five. In cultivating these, seven knowledges are involved, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), because it is incompatible with the nature of the path of non-obstruction.
In the eight paths of liberation for the detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates seven knowledges, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
because it is not an antidote [to that level]. Regarding the detachment from the Peak of Existence,
one should know that in the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) of the higher vehicle, one cultivates the knowledges of the lower stages.

Regarding "the six [knowledges] cultivated in the path of non-obstruction for the detachment from the Peak of Existence": in the nine paths of non-obstruction for the detachment from the Peak of Existence, one cultivates six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
On all paths of skillful means, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), one cultivates the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).

It should be understood that in the Higher Vehicle (*uttarayāna*), one cultivates the qualities of lower stages. When one becomes free from desire for a particular stage, one cultivates the uncontaminated knowledge of that stage as well as those of the lower stages; that is to say, when one becomes free from desire for the First Dhyāna, one cultivates the merits of the First Dhyāna and the *anāgāmya* (preparatory stage). This continues in this manner until, by becoming free from desire for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates the uncontaminated merits of all stages.
The superior counteragent is called the "superior vehicle" (*uttarayāna*).
Within the first moment of mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one cultivates [the path] across all stages;
this is a cultivation similar to that of one beyond training, or it consists of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*).

Regarding "the first mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates [virtues] of all stages": the first mind of one beyond training, which is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), cultivates the merits of the nine stages.
Question:
What kinds of virtues beyond training are cultivated?
Answer: It refers to the practice resembling that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

For one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*), it consists of cultivating the lowest-of-the-low virtues of the nine stages, up to the cultivation of the highest-of-the-high virtues of the stage of the Tathāgata.
Question:
What is the knowledge of the first moment of the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)? Answer:
Whether it be the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin, or the subsequent knowledge of suffering, or the subsequent knowledge of its origin,
because birth has been conditioned, one forms this thought:
"My births are exhausted."
Because this is the final exhaustion of the conditions for the arising of the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having already explained the cultivation of untainted merit, the tainted shall now be explained.
The mind associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) cultivates wholesome, outflow-tainted (sāsrava) merits.
From the nine stages down to the first stage, they are cultivated sequentially and also diminished.
At the time of attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one may cultivate the wholesome, outflow-tainted merits of up to nine stages, or even those of a single stage.
Question:
Why [are there] nine stages down to one stage? Answer:

This refers to one born in the desire realm cultivating the out-flowing [dharmas] of nine stages; if born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), then cultivating those of one stage; or if born in the desire realm and attaining the fruit of arhatship.

One attains the roots of goodness cultivated in the nine stages through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); if one is born in the first dhyāna, one cultivates those of eight stages, excluding the desire realm.
In this manner, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one cultivates the roots of goodness of that respective stage.
Question:
For what reason does one cultivate the roots of goodness of the three realms at this stage? Answer:
Because all bonds are severed and there is eternal rest, it is like the threefold liberation from bondage.
It is like the subduing of the Malla of afflictions, where the multitude all cry out "Excellent!
It is like a king ascending the throne and receiving the empowerment of liberation, wherein everyone presents him with rare and wondrous treasures.

Although one previously attained the virtues of the lower stages, because of the afflictions of the higher stages, the light of wisdom was not clear; upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, all virtues increase and shine with clarity.
The meaning of cultivation shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis).
Question:
Does the Blessed One teach that vision and wisdom are one and the same, or are they different?
Answer: All patiences (kṣānti) are not knowledge (jñāna); cessation-knowledge and non-arising-knowledge are not views (dṛṣṭi).
It should be known that all other noble wisdoms possess these three natures.

The various types of patience (*kṣānti*) are not knowledge (*jñāna*); the patiences associated with the eight stages of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) are not knowledge because they are not yet definitive, because they are bound by the doubt that opposes their own category, and because the meaning of "definitive" is the meaning of "knowledge."
Furthermore, patience (*kṣānti*) involves aspiration and seeking, whereas wisdom (*jñāna*) involves the cessation of aspiration.
Furthermore, patience is a form of vision (*darśana*), while wisdom is not of the nature of vision.

Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*): these two knowledges are not vision because they have ceased all seeking, because they are characterized by equanimity (*madhyastha*), and because they turn their backs on birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Regarding the statement that all other noble wisdoms should be known as being of three natures: with the exception of patience (*kṣānti*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the remaining types of wisdom are called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because they are capable of seeking, and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because they are determinate.
Question: What is it? Answer:
The eight knowledges of one in training, as well as the right view of one beyond training;
if it is wholesome contaminated knowledge, when it resides in the mind it is "view," whereas when it is a defiled view it is "knowledge. These and others are said to be "wisdom."
Wholesome, out-flowing knowledge on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because it is capable of seeking.

Some say that not all wholesome, out-flowing knowledge associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is of the nature of view; that is to say, because it arises from a group of cognitions that do not involve discursive deliberation (*anabhyūha*), it is not view. For instance, the mental consciousness that arises immediately after the five sensory consciousnesses is not view.
The mind at the moment of death is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), because it is weak and feeble.
The mind that initiates action is not "view," because it is directed outward.
Such is "thus" (*evam*); that is to say, when the initial statement and the subsequent explanation accord with reason, it is called "thus-spoken" (*evam-vādin*).

The wise one perceives these afflictions as views; if one perceives their intrinsic nature—such as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth—they are called "views" because they arise from deliberation, and they are also called "knowledge" because they involve certainty.

Regarding "this and other [factors] said to be wisdom": this refers to what has been stated as either knowledge (*jñāna*) or vision (*darśana*), as well as other factors not yet mentioned—namely, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), excluding the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), along with all defiled states on the level of the mental consciousness and all those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses. It should be understood that all these are wisdom.
Regarding what has been said and what has not yet been said: if indeterminate wisdom (*avyākṛta-prajñā*) were not insight (*dṛṣṭi*), it would be because it is not swift.
Although the wisdom of arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika-prajñā*) is swift, it is not insight because it is obstructed by the pursuit of livelihood.
The defiled [factors] have already been explained previously.

The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), because it does not involve conceptual discrimination, because it is not swift, and because it is directed only toward a single object.
Question:
How many knowledges do each of these knowledges take as their objects? Answer:
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge observe nine knowledges.
Causal knowledge and resultant knowledge have both types of knowledge as their objects.
Regarding the observation of the nine knowledges by dharma-knowledge and inference-knowledge: dharma-knowledge takes the nine knowledges as its object, excluding inference-knowledge.
Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) also takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
Question:
Why do they not take each other as objects?
Answer: Because their objects are lower and higher respectively.
Dharma-knowledge takes the lower as its object, while subsequent knowledge takes the higher as its object; therefore, they do not take one another as objects.
It is like two people dwelling together, one looking downward and the other looking upward; because their observations of the earth and the sky differ, they do not see one another's faces.
If it is argued that [the mind] does not take itself as its object—just as one does not see one's own face—that is not so, because there is continuous observation.

Regarding the statement that "the objects of causal knowledge and resultant knowledge pertain to two types of knowledge": knowledge of suffering and its origin takes contaminated phenomena as its object; this is because the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge are subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin.
Path-knowledge takes nine knowledges as its object; Liberation-knowledge has no object;
The rest have all things as their sphere— This is what the Knowledge of Certainty has taught.

Regarding "path-knowledge takes nine knowledges as its object": path-knowledge takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*); it takes the other nine knowledges as its object because they are subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Regarding "the knowledge of liberation has no object": the knowledge of cessation does not take knowledge as its object, because it takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.

Regarding "all other spheres are said to be the objects of determinate knowledge": the remaining four knowledges—the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising—take the ten knowledges as their objects.
Question:

As previously stated, if the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is neither the antidote to all [afflictions] of the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), nor is it the antidote to them in their entirety. Which dharma-knowledge serves as the antidote to the form and formless realms?
Answer: It refers to that cessation and the path, which are the domain of dharma-knowledge;
they are the antidotes to the three realms, not the subsequent knowledge of the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that "the range of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path is the antidote to the three realms": there is dharma-knowledge of the cessation [of defilements] and dharma-knowledge of the path belonging to the path of cultivation; these are the antidotes for what is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the three realms.

He perceives the faults of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to their utmost extent, contemplates the cessation of the formations of the desire realm and their antidotes, and thereby attains detachment from the desires of the three realms.
Question: Why is this not the "knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering and its origin" (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: Because the lower is inferior and the higher is superior, one cannot abandon desire for a superior state by contemplating an inferior one.
Since both Cessation and the Path are superior, one contemplates these two to extinguish desire for the three realms.

Furthermore, if one were to take the desire realm as an object while being detached from the form and formless realms, this would constitute a different kind of revulsion, a different kind of non-delight, and a different kind of liberation; however, this is not the case.
Question:
Is there any subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is free from the desire realm?
Answer: Yes.

It is not the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the desire realm, nor is it the subsequent knowledge [of higher realms], because its own task—the antidote to the desire realm—is not yet completed.
It is like a king who, having first subdued the enemies within his own domain, subsequently subdues those of others.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is likewise; there is no instance where subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) first extinguishes [defilements] of the form and formless realms and subsequently extinguishes those of the desire realm.
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena is an extremely sharp wisdom; it can even extinguish unwholesome states, let alone neutral ones.
Question:
Of how many types of knowledge (jñāna) is supernormal power (abhijñā) of the nature? Answer:
The bases of psychic power, the divine eye, and the divine ear—these are said to be one type of knowledge (*ekavidyā*).
Alternatively, six knowledges are the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), and five are said to be the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Regarding "the bases of psychic power, the divine eye, and the divine ear—these are said to be one type of knowledge": the bases of psychic power, the divine eye, and the divine ear constitute one type of knowledge; untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) does not proceed by way of these.

The bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) consist of various manifestations; the divine ear superknowledge (divyaśrotra-abhijñā) is the wisdom associated with the consciousness of the divine ear, and the knowledge of birth and death (cyutyupapādābhijñā) is the wisdom associated with the consciousness of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
The supernormal power of the bases of psychic power will be explained in other chapters.

Regarding the application of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), one contemplates great sounds; as that application gradually increases, one attains the pure divine ear composed of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), by which one hears all sounds, whether distant or near.

By means of the skillful application of contemplating the sign of light for the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), that skillful application gradually increases until one attains the pure divine eye produced by the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) within the circumference of the eyes. Standing in one place, one perceives all ten directions; though everything is seen, it is not all at once.
Regarding the statement that "six knowledges [constitute] the knowledge of past lives," the Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
these six knowledges are not the knowledge of others' minds, because they take the present as their object;
nor are they the knowledge of cessation, because they take the unconditioned as their object.
It is not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), because it does not perceive the nature [of phenomena].
The Abhidharmikas say: first, it is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) because it takes the names, surnames, and so forth of sentient beings as its object.

Regarding skillful means (*upāya*): whether with respect to one's own person or another's person, that which is the skillful means in a particular instance is also the culmination in that very instance, or it may be elsewhere.
From their previous lives until their ultimate attainment, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can recollect according to their own wishes;
however, only the Tathāgata possesses sovereign mastery over his will, such that he can remember everything he has heard or seen, whether in the past or the future.

Regarding the fifth [type of] knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds: five knowledges cognize the minds of others. Specifically, the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) cognizes the minds and mental factors belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge in others, because it takes its own sphere as its object.
Subsequent knowledge is also like this.
Knowledge of the path knows the other's uncontaminated mind and mental factors;
conventional knowledge knows the other's mundane mind and mental factors.
The knowledge of others' minds is the fifth. Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*):

one takes up the characteristics either from one's own body or from one's own mind, such that "a body with such-and-such characteristics possesses a mind with such-and-such characteristics. By these skillful means, the roots of goodness gradually increase until one knows the minds and mental factors of others; this is called accomplishing the skillful means regarding form. Furthermore, from the initial arising within one's own mind until the time of accomplishment, one does not take form or one's own mind as an object; rather, being free from the objects of conditioned formations, one knows the faculties, stages, and lands of the knowledge of others' minds.

Regarding "a person who knows the degrees but does not know the faculties": this refers to one who does not know the soft, medium, or superior faculties; that is to say, up to the soft faculty of the fourth dhyāna stage, they know the soft untainted (anāsrava) faculty of the lower stages, but nothing else.
Regarding those with outflows (*sāsrava*), one who knows those with outflows does not know those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the degree of stages (*bhūmi-pāra*): one in the first dhyāna does not know the second dhyāna.
Regarding the degree of persons (*pudgala-pāra*): one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*) does not know one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Therefore, the Buddha’s mind and mental factors are not the objective domain of all other-mind-knowledges (*paracittajñāna*). They are the objective domain of all other-mind-knowledge in its functional aspect, its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), its aspects of mind and mental factors, its present aspect, and its aspect of others. With the exception of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), these are acquired through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, they are dissociated from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*), are not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and are distinct from the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*).
Question:
How do the supernormal powers arise as described? Are they different [from that description]? Answer:
Some say they arise according to how they were taught.
For example, as the Blessed One first taught the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), they arose first;
and so on, until he last taught the knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), which therefore arose last.

The Venerable Ghoṣaka says: The arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) occurs as previously described; however, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is otherwise.

When a practitioner hears mention of the gods of the realm of form but does not see them, they develop the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) because they wish to see them. Because they can see them but cannot go there, they develop the power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Because they can go there but do not hear the teachings being spoken, they develop the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*). Although they hear them, because they do not know how the minds [of others] function, they develop the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Because they know the minds of others but do not know their own previous origins, they develop the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).

According to this teaching, there is no sequential meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) among the supernormal powers, nor is there any skipping attainment, nor any forward attainment, nor any reverse attainment.
It should be understood that these are subsumed within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), not the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Question:
Of how many types of knowledge (*jñāna*) are each of the powers (*bala*) and grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) constituted?
Answer:
The power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible, and the first fearlessness—these constitute the ten knowledges of a Buddha; the others are variations within these.

Regarding the power of knowledge of what is possible and impossible and the first fearlessness—these constitute the ten knowledges of a Buddha: because the power of knowledge of what is possible and impossible and the first fearlessness are of the nature of these ten knowledges, as their objective sphere is universal.
Question:
Of what nature of wisdom are the remaining powers and fearlessnesses? Answer:
There are further distinctions within this context:

there are other powers distinct from the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*), and there are other fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) distinct from the first fearlessness. The Blessed One established these various types because he observes the aspirations of those to be converted.
Question:
For what reason did the Blessed One himself proclaim his own virtues? Answer:
It is for the sake of those seeking the Buddha-way who practice the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
Furthermore, it is because he manifests distinctions within equal liberation;

because of his eloquence in joyful exposition (*pratibhāna*), which is inexhaustible, unimpeded, and flawless; and because, even when taming the intoxicated elephant and other such acts, those with doubts do not know by whose power this is done, so as to manifest his own power for their sake.
Furthermore, for the sake of those to be converted, the true merits are explained because they are not exaggerated and because they are free from the conduct of those who are not great beings.
"Pure karma has desirable fruits; impure karma has undesirable fruits"—this is called the possible (*sthāna*).
To say otherwise is called the impossible (*asthāna*).
One should understand it thus: this is the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).

To say that pure karma has pleasant results and impure karma has unpleasant results is what is called "the possible. This refers to the certainty of cause and effect; the unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) knows that this is the definitive cause for that—namely, that pure karma has pleasant results and impure karma has unpleasant results—just as external seeds produce fruits according to their respective types.
Regarding "if it is otherwise, it is called an impossibility" (*asthāna*): that which is contrary to this is termed an impossibility.

One should understand the power of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) as follows: the meaning of "possible" (*sthāna*) is the sense of being appropriate or admissible; that which is contrary to this is the meaning of "impossible" (*asthāna*).
Because they are neither submissive nor yielding, and because they are unsurpassed and immovable, they are called "powers.
These ten knowledges (*jñāna*) constitute their intrinsic nature; they abide in eleven stages.
It is definitively taught that the Tathāgata is the one who relies upon Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those ten knowledges, it is as previously explained because they have universal objects.

The ten knowledges take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as their objective conditions; they consist of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), or are dissociated from those aspects, and are associated with the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the three right absorptions (*samyaksamādhi*), and the three faculties (*indriya*).
"Abiding in the eleven stages" refers to the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the preliminary stage (*anāgāmya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four formless realms.
"Definitively speaking of the Tathāgata" means that this explains the establishment of the powers of a Tathāgata, not those of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Because the Tathāgata has eliminated two kinds of ignorance—namely, the defiled and the non-defiled—the Buddha’s wisdom is not overcome by what is non-wisdom; it is neither that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) nor that which is neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), but it is not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas eliminate defiled [doubt], they do not eliminate non-defiled [doubt].
The Tathāgata eliminates two kinds of doubt:
doubt regarding the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and doubt regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna).
This means that those who rely on Jambudvīpa are those whose bodies are present in Jambudvīpa and not elsewhere, because Buddhas do not appear in other regions.
The people of Jambudvīpa possess sharp faculties and are easily awakened; therefore, Buddhas appear in Jambudvīpa and not elsewhere.
The second power consists of eight knowledges; it operates with respect to those karmic actions, as well as the acceptance of dharmas and afflictions. The remainder is as previously explained.

Regarding "the second power consists of eight knowledges": the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma consists of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, because [those two] take the untainted as their object; therefore, eight are mentioned.
Whether in practice or detached from practice, it is associated with emptiness and wishlessness.
Question:
By what cause?
Answer: It refers to the engagement in those activities and the afflictions associated with the acceptance of phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Those activities" are the fruits of karma; bodily and vocal actions, as well as volition (*cetanā*), constitute karma.

Regarding the acquisition of dharmas, there are four types of acquisition of dharmas; there is the acquisition of dharmas that brings happiness in the present life and happiness in future lives, and so forth.
Afflictions are the cause of karma; they evolve from this and arise conditioned by this.
"Others are as previously explained" means that the others are as described under the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).
Regarding the various dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and samādhis:
the third power revolves through them; it consists of nine knowledges, and the rest is as previously stated.
Regarding "the various dhyānas, the liberations (vimokṣa), the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and the samādhis, which revolve by means of the third power": "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas;
"liberation" refers to the eight liberations.

"Right attainment" (*samyaksamāpatti*) refers to the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
"Samādhi" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Regarding the third power, it functions by taking these dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), right attainments, and samādhis as its objective support.
Question:
What is the nature of this power? Answer:
It consists of nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it excludes the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) associated with the four aspects of cessation, because its object is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The remainder is as previously stated; the rest is as explained in the context of the power of knowledge regarding the results of one's own actions (*karma-vipāka-jñānabala*).
Regarding the superior and inferior faculties, the fourth power revolves;
the fifth is said to be the power of resolve, and the sixth concerns the objective field of the elements (*dhātu*).
Regarding "the superior and inferior faculties": "superior" means excellent, "inferior" means base, and "faculties" (*indriya*) means sovereign.
The fourth power is the power of the higher and lower faculties (*indriya*).
"Revolving" refers to the conditions (*pratyaya*), meaning it takes the three truths as its objects.

Because it arises from the skillful means of the faculties based on those conditions, it is called the power of the higher and lower faculties, just like the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Regarding the fifth, the explanation of the power of resolve (*adhimukti-bala*): "resolve" refers to aspiration (*chanda*). This is also of two kinds: superior and inferior. The superior is wholesome aspiration; the inferior is unwholesome aspiration.
Furthermore, those who seek the path and its fruit are superior, while those who desire birth and death are inferior; this also takes the three truths as its object.
Because it arises from the skillful means of desire, it is called the power of desire.
Sixth, regarding the objective condition (ālambana) of the realms (dhātu): "Realm" refers to intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which is of two kinds as previously explained.
Regarding those various destinies (gati), the seventh power revolves [therein];
it should be known that four have already been explained, and the remainder are all as previously stated.
Regarding the seventh power, the turning of various destinies (*gati*): "destinies" refers to paths; these are also various, ranging from the hells up to nirvāṇa.
Because it takes those destinies (*gati*) and their requisite conditions as its object, it is called the power of destiny (*gatibala*).

Regarding the statement, "It should be known that the four [powers] have already been explained, and the rest are all as previously stated": the powers of faculties (*indriya*), inclinations (*adhimukti*), elements (*dhātu*), and destinies (*gati*) have already been explained; it should be understood that the remaining causal conditions are as described in the explanations of the dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and samādhis.
Some say that the power of knowing the paths leading to [rebirth] consists of ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
Knowing the conduct of past lives is said to be the eighth power;
this refers to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) along with their afflictions (*kleśa*). The rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the statement that "knowing past lives and their formations is called the eighth power": through the power of knowing past lives, one fully knows all the various things experienced in past lives, as well as the actions performed and the experiences undergone therein.

That which is practiced by them is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); that which is experienced is called the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*). Because one experiences [the fruits] through the prior existence—whether as a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa—all such things are fully known.
This power of past lives speaks of a single knowledge, namely, the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), which is of two kinds: that previously attained and that now attained.
It is described as three stages according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior, and is established as fourfold.

Regarding the soft, medium, and superior [levels], those previously attained and now attained are said to comprise six stages; those previously attained and now attained are said to comprise eight; from the lowest-lowest to the highest-highest, they are said to comprise nine stages; when distinguished as low-low, low-medium, and low-superior, they are said to comprise twelve; when the low-low and others are considered both previously attained and now attained, they are said to comprise eighteen stages; when the low-medium and others are considered previously attained and now attained, they are said to comprise twenty-four stages; when the low-low and others are distinguished, they are said to comprise thirty-six stages; and when the low-low and others are considered both previously attained and now attained, they are said to comprise seventy-two. This is the general explanation of the single knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).

Regarding "meditative absorption" (dhyāna): it refers to the fundamental dhyānas and not their preparatory stages (sāmantaka), because these are the samādhis that serve as the basis for the formless attainments (ārūpya) and the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
The samādhis subsumed under the four and five factors are the bases for the supernormal powers; they exist only in the dhyānas and nowhere else.
If one attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsābhijñā) based on a particular dhyāna, one knows that dhyāna and the lower stages.
If one attains the supernormal powers based on the first dhyāna, one knows the first dhyāna and the intermediate stage, because they belong to the same level.

Regarding those with afflictions (*sāsrava*), it has already been stated that these constitute conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); therefore, there is no untainted (*anāsrava*) matter [in this case], which constitutes the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
As for "the rest is as previously explained," it is as described in the section on the power of the knowledge of inclinations (*āśayajñānabala*).
The ninth power should be known as being free from objects of perception;
it pertains to the passing away and rebirth of beings among the classes of sentient beings.

Regarding "the ninth power should be known as being free from objects of perception": the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-bala*) is devoid of objective conditions; the rest is as explained for the power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
A śrāvaka who lacks skillful means sees a thousand-world system;
one with skillful means sees two thousand-world systems.
A pratyekabuddha who lacks skillful means sees two thousand-world systems; [one with skillful means sees three thousand-world systems].
Through skillful means, one sees three thousandfold world systems;
without skillful means, a Buddha does not see three thousandfold world systems;
through skillful means, one sees immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands of three thousandfold world systems.
Question:
For what reason? Answer:
Regarding the process of death and rebirth among the class of sentient beings, they take form as their object.
As it has been said, the knowledge of phenomena as they truly are—according to the karma one receives—should be understood as referring to its associated factors;
the knowledge of birth and death, however, pertains to internal phenomena.

The tenth power consists of ten knowledges, or six; it exists in all stages and is manifested as power, clarity, and supernormal knowledge. The rest are as previously explained. Regarding "the tenth power consists of ten knowledges, or six":

if one speaks of the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) as that which is attained by one who has destroyed the outflows, then it is said to have the nature of the ten knowledges.

If one considers the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) by way of its condition of the destruction of the outflows, it is said to consist of six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path.
Regarding "all stages" (*sarvabhūmika*): the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows exists in eleven stages, because it encompasses rebirth.

Regarding the manifestation of power, clarity, and penetration: the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) is called "manifestation," meaning the manifestation through instruction, which causes others to rejoice and remain unshakable; it is called "power" because it is eternally free from ignorance; it is called "clarity" because it is luminous; and it is called "penetration" because it penetrates the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*) and the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*) are said to be the powers of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñābala*) that communicate [to others], not those that manifest [directly].
Question:
Are these not neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Why is this? For the Sūtra states:
"The three types of clear knowledge (vidyā) belong exclusively to those beyond training (aśaikṣa)."
Answer: Because it is attained within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and because it leads to the illumination of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Question:
Question: For what reason are three of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*), and not the others?
Answer: Because they serve as antidotes to three types of delusion (*moha*).

The first [vidyā] eliminates ignorance regarding the past; the second eliminates ignorance regarding the future; and the third eliminates ignorance regarding the Truths, as they lead to the three doors of liberation.

Among the six supernormal powers (abhijñās), two are manifestations rather than vidyās, namely the power of psychic transformation (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
The second is that which clarifies what is not a manifestation, namely the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).
Both are present in the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), while both are absent in the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*).
As for the statement "the rest are all as previously explained," this means that regarding the remaining points not yet mentioned, their causes and conditions are as previously explained.
The powers have already been explained; the fearlessnesses shall now be discussed.
The first is like the first power; the second is like the tenth;
the remaining two are like the second and seventh. These are called the assurances.

"The first is like the first power" means that this first fearlessness of mine, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is precisely the power regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).
"The second is like the tenth" means that my outflows are exhausted; this is the power regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-bala*).

Regarding the phrase "the other two are as in the case of the two sevens; this is called 'fearless assurance'": it means that when I preach the factors that obstruct the path to my disciples, they might say those factors do not obstruct the path; I have no fear of such a claim.
This is precisely the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma.
When I declare to my disciples that this is the path of the noble ones leading to deliverance, I have no fear that it does not lead to deliverance.
One should know that this is precisely the power of the destination (*gati*).
Question:
For what reason did the Blessed One speak this sūtra?
Answer: This sūtra was spoken in order to restrain Sunakṣatra and to refute the slanders of Brahmaputra.
Sunakṣatra said:
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses no superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma).
It is for the sake of refuting him that the first two fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) were spoken. Vāḷavā said:
"I fully know and see the Dharma of the Śramaṇas and the sons of the Śākyas.
It is for the sake of restraining them that the latter two fearlessnesses are taught.
Furthermore, the first two fearlessnesses concern proclaiming one's own peace, while the latter two fearlessnesses concern bringing peace to others.
The meaning of being unsubdued is the meaning of fearlessness, because it is free from terror.
Question:
What is the difference between the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)?
Answer: Some say there is no distinction between them.
Others say that wisdom is the power (*bala*), while the universal illumination of the light of wisdom is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
Abiding securely is power; valor is fearlessness.
Inexhaustible wisdom is power; inexhaustible eloquence is fearlessness, and so forth.
Furthermore, each of the powers subsumes the four fearlessnesses, and each of the fearlessnesses subsumes the ten powers; these constitute fourteen dharmas.

Furthermore, the three unique applications of mindfulness and great compassion constitute the Buddha’s eighteen unique qualities; they are called "unique" because they are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The foundations of mindfulness and great compassion are of the nature of wisdom.
Question: In which stage is the absence of conflict (araṇā) located?
What is its practice?
In what state does it manifest?
What is its object-condition?
What kind of person gives rise [to this],
and what is its intrinsic nature? Answer:
The fourth dhyāna has impurity; the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) relies on three directions;
it takes as its object a desire that has not yet produced affliction, and relies on the wisdom of the immovable.

Regarding the fourth dhyāna: the absence of conflict exists only in the fourth dhyāna and not elsewhere, because its sphere is universal, because it is supreme among all bases, and because it possesses impurity while being free from noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*).
"Non-contentious" (*araṇā*) refers to its being contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Dependent on three directions" means that it manifests only in the three directions and not elsewhere, because it is said to be produced by power.

"Taking as object an unarisen affliction in the desire realm" means taking as its object future afflictions of the desire realm—namely, the specific-characteristic afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—and not the general-characteristic [afflictions].

The universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is the universal object; therefore, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding "relying on the immovable," this is because it is attained by relying on a body free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This can be aroused only by those of immovable dharma, and not by others.
"Wisdom" refers to the intrinsic nature of wisdom.

Because that Arhat does not engage in five causal conditions, he is able to prevent the arising of afflictions; these are: proper deportment, proper speech, discerning what should and should not be accepted, observing one's dwelling place, and observing persons.

Regarding one who maintains right deportment: sitting upright with the body aligned in one direction, if someone approaches, he immediately observes that person’s mind, examining what kind of deportment will prevent the arising of fetters in their mind.
If this deportment prevents another from arising [in a state of agitation], he immediately remains in such deportment.

Regarding "speaking correctly": if someone approaches, he observes their mind; if speaking would cause their fetters to arise, he does not speak to them; if not speaking would cause them to arise, he then speaks to them.

Regarding the discernment of what should and should not be accepted: when others offer various requisites, one should examine them; if accepting the gift would give rise to fetters, one should not accept it even if it is needed;
if not accepting it would give rise to fetters, one should accept it even if it is not needed.
Regarding the observation of the dwelling place: if, by staying in this location, those fetters arise, then even if provisions are abundant, one should abandon it and depart.

Regarding the observation of persons: first observe the people before entering the village; if there are those who give rise to fetters in a house or an alleyway, do not enter. How could one again create conditions for evil toward them?
In order to gather others, one reflects as follows:
"In the past, when I possessed a body of afflictions, those beings gave rise to afflictions toward me and consequently experienced unpleasant results."
How much more so now that he is free from desire; he should employ skillful means to ensure that they certainly do not give rise to affliction toward him.

Although the Buddha and his śrāvakas who have attained the perfection of *araṇā* (freedom from conflict) do not frequently enter it, they sometimes do not enter the *araṇā-samādhi* for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation through affliction.
That which is called the wondrous knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) is far removed from those [lower] realms;
it is attained at the very end therein, as the nature of mastery over the six knowledges.

Regarding the phrase "the wondrous knowledge of aspiration is far removed from its realm": the wondrous knowledge of aspiration likewise resides in the fourth dhyāna; it is a support for outflows (sāsrava) and is attained by those who are immovable in the three directions.
