This is the nature of wisdom, for it takes all phenomena as its object and has them as its universal sphere. Regarding the "basis of the formless" (*ārūpyāśraya*):

as for the term "basis of the formless" mentioned above, this "basis" (*āśraya*) carries the sense of "moisture" or "sustenance. This means that because the desire and form realms are the "vapor" or "extension" of the formless realm, they are called its basis. This explains the causal basis of the Knowledge of Aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), which results in the knowledge of the formless realm. The distinctions in contemplative practice are like those of a farmer; therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are taught.
It is said that he knows according to his wish; the meaning of this is that through the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), he knows whatever he desires to know.

Regarding "attaining it at the very end": when that knowledge arises—meaning when a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is followed by the manifestation of the first dhyāna, and so on in sequence up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and then in reverse order back down to a wholesome mind of the desire realm, and again in forward order up to the manifestation of the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, having progressed from the weak to the medium and from the medium to the superior within the fourth dhyāna, he subsequently gives rise to the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) within that superior fourth dhyāna.

Regarding "the nature of mastery over the six knowledges," this knowledge has sixfold intrinsic natures, namely the three unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), excluding the unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, there is the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*), the knowledge of the final limit (*paryanta-jñāna*), and the sublime knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).

This knowledge arises due to three causes and conditions: for the sake of gathering others, for the sake of gathering the teachings, and for the sake of awakening to the security and insecurity of the world.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratibhāna) is both with-outflow (sāsrava) and without-outflow (anāsrava), and it exists in all stages;
the Buddha taught this as a skillful means (upāya). The rest is as previously explained.

Regarding "the analytical knowledge of meaning is both with-outflow and without-outflow": this analytical knowledge has the nature of the ten knowledges (daśajñāna), because it pertains to the ultimate truth (paramārtha) of all phenomena.

Some say that it consists of six types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path; because the Truth of Cessation is the supreme ultimate meaning, it is therefore said to have the application of mindfulness as its object and samādhi as its basis.
Regarding "existing in all stages," this analysis exists in eleven stages because it is acquired through its own nature (*svabhāva*).

As for the Buddha’s statement that it is "expedient means" (*upāya*), this refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*); it takes what the Buddha has taught as its expedient means. If there were no prior teaching by the Buddha, there would be no one capable of giving rise to it, for they would not know the meaning.
"Others are as previously explained" means that those not yet mentioned are as explained in the context of the Knowledge of Vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).
That is to say: for the sake of debate, regarding the object, the path, and the teaching;
the skillful means of the treatise on logic (*hetuvidyā-śāstra*); or the three [remaining categories] are as previously stated.

Regarding what is called "the path of the object to be analyzed" and "the speaker," one should analyze the path of conditions and verbal expression; therefore, the nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), possess twelve aspects (*ākāra*).

Regarding the means of the *hetuvidyā-śāstra*: if this debate were not conducted by means of the *hetuvidyā-śāstra*, there would be no one capable of initiating it, because they would not know what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.

Therefore, it is said that the Abhidharma serves as the skillful means (*upāya*), for there is no treatise on logic (*hetuvidyā*) equal to the Abhidharma, because it is fully endowed with wisdom (*jñāna*).

As for "or three," this distinguishes the nature of three types of wisdom: namely, analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the final wisdom (*paryantajñāna*).
Some say that knowing the ultimate meaning of all phenomena is also analytical eloquence regarding meaning.
The rest is as previously stated; what has not yet been mentioned here is to be explained as in the case of analytical eloquence regarding meaning.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) has its object in designations;
it exists within the five stages and takes numerical calculation as its skillful means. The rest is as explained regarding the absence of conflict (araṇā).
As for "the analytical knowledge of phenomena having designations as its object," this means that the analytical knowledge of phenomena has names and their delimitations as its objects.

Regarding those who abide in the five stages: this refers to the desire realm and the four dhyānas, but not the higher stages; for in the formless realm, one does not take names as an object, nor does one take lower stages as objects, because they are not part of its sphere.
Regarding "using number as a means": the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) uses numerical discourse as its means.
As for "the rest is as explained in the section on non-contention": the remainder that has not yet been mentioned is as previously explained in the section on non-contention.
Skill in the treatises on grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) constitutes eloquence (*pratibhāna*);
its sphere is verbal expression. The remaining [details] for the second stage are as previously stated.

Regarding "skill in the treatises on grammar constitutes eloquence": eloquence takes the treatises on grammar as its skillful means (*upāya*). This is because if one has not previously practiced the treatises on grammar, one cannot give rise to [eloquence], which is free from seeds.

Regarding "the sphere of verbal expression," this refers to the discernment that takes verbal expression as its object; therefore, it is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

As for "the two stages," these are the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna, but not the higher stages, because [those stages] are free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
"Other matters are as previously explained" means they are to be analyzed according to the Dharma.
Question:
How are they analyzed?
As it is asked: "Is 'arising' (jāti) different [from the dharma]?
The answer is:

Some say it is as described regarding arising; that is to say, one first gives rise to the skillful means (*kauśalya*) of naming a dharma, whereby one knows the name but not yet its meaning, and thus subsequently gives rise to the eloquence (*pratibhāna*) regarding the meaning.
Although one may know the meaning, one may not know the phrasing; therefore, the eloquence of phrasing (*nirukti-pratibhāna*) arises next.
Having known the eloquence of phrasing, one may still be unable to explain with continuous flow;

therefore, the eloquence of response (*pratibhāna*) arises next. Furthermore, it is said that first the eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*) arises; because one knows the meaning but not the names, the eloquence of phenomena (*dharma-pratibhāna*) arises next; because one knows the names but not the phrasing, the eloquence of phrasing arises next; because one knows the phrasing but cannot explain with continuous flow, the eloquence of response arises next. The eloquence of response is as previously explained.

It is also called "turning according to expression"; therefore, one first gives rise to the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and subsequently gives rise to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
Meaning turns in dependence upon names; therefore, one next gives rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
These three types of analytical exposition (pratibhāna) should now be explained.
Question:
What is this analytical exposition?
Is it attained one by one? Answer: Not so.
If one is attained, then all four are possessed, just as the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are attained simultaneously;
this case is likewise. *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Six;
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta;
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others.
Chapter Seven: On Concentration (Samādhi). Having already explained wisdom (*jñāna*), concentration shall now be explained.
Wisdom relies upon the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*); it proceeds with stability and immovability.
Therefore, one should contemplate concentration and diligently seek to see reality.
The meaning of "certainty" is wisdom; the continuous succession of that virtuous mind’s right nature is concentration; and the meaning of "establishment" is reliance.
There are two kinds of dependence:
simultaneous arising and sequential conditions; these two are designated as "dependence.
They are called dependence because they are established based upon them.
The knowledges of the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) are of eight kinds:
the four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).
Regarding "abiding in the imperturbable" (*āneñja*), it is called "imperturbable" because it does not waver or shake.
"Transforming" (*parāvṛtti*) has the meaning of taking up conditions (*ālambana*).

Just as a lamp relying on pure oil and a wick in a place sheltered from the wind has a light and flame that are extremely bright, so too does wisdom, relying on various meditative concentrations and being free from the winds of distraction, transform while remaining unmoving.
The phrase "therefore" explains the causal conditions.
"Concentration" (samādhi) is that upon which wisdom relies; this will be explained later.
"Volition" (cetanā) has the meaning of knowing and seeing.
"Vigorously seeking" refers to the time of seeking and desiring.
"Reality" means being non-erroneous; it refers to the Four Noble Truths.
"Seeing" refers to immediate realization (*abhisamaya*).
This is called the vision of reality, because true wisdom arises without departing from meditative concentration.
Question:
How many kinds of samādhi are there?
Answer: It is definitively taught that there are four dhyānas, as well as the formless attainments;
each of these is explained as being of three types: with relish, pure, and untainted.
Regarding the definitive teaching on the four dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), it means that the one of definitive wisdom briefly explains eight kinds.

These samādhis encompass all samādhis; that is to say, the World-Honored One knows the various samādhis and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the names of which are unknown even to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as explained at length in the sūtras.
Regarding the statement that each of these is of three types—savoring (*āsvādana*), pure (*śuddha*), and outflow-free (*anāsrava*)—each meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is said to be of three kinds:
savoring, pure, and outflow-free.
Wholesome states with outflows are "pure"; those without outflows are free from the burning heat [of defilements].
Taste is associated with craving; the supreme is the untainted (anāsrava).
Regarding "the wholesome tainted is pure": if it is wholesome and tainted, one should know that it is pure.
Question:
Since wholesome states with outflows are defiled, why are they said to be pure? Answer:
Because it is contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*), because it is unmixed with the afflictions, and because it leads toward the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding "the untainted is free from burning": one should know that being free from the burning of the afflictions constitutes the untainted.
Although they are eternally free from afflictions, it should be understood that the designation "supremely pure" is established for the sake of distinction.
Regarding "associated with relishing": if a meditative absorption is associated with craving, it should be understood as being associated with relishing.
Question:
For what reason is dhyāna said to be associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and not with other afflictions (*kleśa*)? Answer:
Because they are similar.
It is exclusively attachment that takes this samādhi as its object; no other affliction has such an object of attachment as craving does.
Furthermore, since craving has already been explained, it should be understood that the other afflictions have also been explained, for these [afflictions] are sufficient to represent them all.
Regarding the statement that "the supreme [attainment] is without the outflow-free," this is said because it is a general description; thus, it is stated that each [of the first two] has three types.
One should know that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has only two types, as it lacks the outflow-free, because it is not swift.
There are two extremes, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); the noble path that transcends these two extremes is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
The transcendence of the root of the two existences is likewise so.

If one is attached to the flavor [of meditative experience], it is called "attainment with flavor" (*āsvādana-samāpatti*); if one is not attached to the flavor, it is called "pure attainment" (*śuddha-samāpatti*); and if one contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent and so forth without outflows (*anāsrava*), it should be known as "outflow-free attainment" (*anāsrava-samāpatti*).
Question:
How many kinds of purity are there? Answer:
Purity has four parts: the part conducive to decline, the part conducive to maintenance, the part conducive to progress, and the part conducive to certainty;
these accord with various virtues. The part conducive to decline accords with afflictions;
the part conducive to maintenance accords with its own level; the part conducive to progress accords with higher levels; and the part conducive to certainty accords with the noble path.

Furthermore, regarding the stage of decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*): if one dwells therein, one declines. Regarding the stage of maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*): if one dwells therein, one neither progresses nor declines. Regarding the stage of distinction (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*): if one dwells therein, one is able to excel and progress. Regarding the stage of certainty (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*): if one dwells therein, one is able to successively transcend and emerge from the state of ordinary birth.

Furthermore, as for the stage of decline (*hānabhāgīya*), it is overwhelmed and intermingled with afflictions (*kleśa*); from the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), afflictions manifest in succession, and from afflictions, the meditative absorption manifests in succession.
Regarding the stage of abiding: one is able to cultivate the contemplation of the coarseness and other defects of the lower stage, and experience the tranquility and other virtues of one's own stage.
Regarding the stage of excellence: one is able to cultivate the contemplation of the faults of one's own stage and experience the merits of the higher stage.
The factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
As it is with the dhyānas, so it is with the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), with the sole exception of the qualities such as heat and the rest.
Question:
What is the nature of dhyāna? Answer:
Having five factors, with vitarka and vicāra, And likewise possessing three feelings,
various [mental states], and four minds— This is called the first dhyāna.
"Five factors" means that which is constituted by five factors.
The meaning of "division" (bhāga) is the meaning of "limb" (aṅga), as a chariot has many parts.
The meaning of "requisite" (sādhana) is the meaning of "limb," as a king has generals and soldiers.
As for these limbs, they may be either different from or identical to [the whole].
If they were different, it would be as in the six branches of the Vedas and the four Vedas:
first, the Ṛgveda; second, the Atharvaveda; third, the Yajurveda; and fourth, the Sāmaveda.
Veda means knowledge; it is composed of six branches:

first, study (śikṣā); second, ritual desire (kalpa); third, phonology (vyākaraṇa); fourth, etymology (nirukta); fifth, prosody (chandas); and sixth, astronomy (jyotiṣa). A bhikṣu is composed of five superior branches:
first, faith (śraddhā); second, lack of deceit (aśāṭhya); third, freedom from illness (aroga); fourth, diligence (vīrya); and fifth, wisdom (prajñā).
If they were identical, it would be like the sixteen factors of the breath-meditation or the eightfold noble path.
Those factors are: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
At the time of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the initial perception of coarse mental factors is called *vitarka* (applied thought).
The continuous succession and following along of those coarse mental factors is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).
At the time of meditative absorption, the joy of the mind is called *prīti* (rapture).
Because body and mind are free from evil, this happiness is called "pleasure" (*sukha*); it is the pleasure of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*), not the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*).
The non-diffusion of the mind and mental factors with respect to their objects is called "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*).
"With applied thought and sustained thought" refers to the first dhyāna having applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Question:
Since the five factors have already been mentioned, why are "having applied thought and sustained thought" stated separately?
Answer: "Factors" (*aṅga*) refers to the wholesome; they are mentioned separately because the defiled states also possess initial and sustained application (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Furthermore, there are three feelings (*vedanā*): those [states] possess three feelings, namely, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the three groups of consciousness, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in the mental stage, and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in the four groups of consciousness.

"Various kinds" means that the Brahmā heavens possess various bodies, some superior and some inferior, because they are produced by the power of vitarka and vicāra; thus, there exist places for elders and their retinues.
Regarding "and the four minds," there are four minds therein:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
These are called the first dhyāna; these dharmas are designated as the first dhyāna because they surpass all afflictions.
Because one correctly contemplates all objects of experience, it is called dhyāna.
The second has four factors: various [mental states] and two types of feeling.
The third is said to have five factors; this dhyāna also possesses two types of feeling.
The second [dhyāna] has four factors: inner serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
As for "various," it means that there are no various bodies therein, because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are not part of its nature.

There are various states of mind; that is to say, when the fundamental joy faculty (*somanassindriya*) is present, once the joy has subsided, the associated equanimity faculty (*upekkhindriya*) manifests; and once the equanimity has subsided, one enters again into the joy faculty.
Regarding the "two feelings," these refer to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
These factors are said to constitute the second dhyāna. As for the third [dhyāna], it is said to have five factors:

mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*samprajanya*), bliss (*sukha*), equanimity of formation (*saṃskāropekṣā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). This "equanimity of formation" refers to the state of being equanimous, acting with equanimity, and behaving with equanimity; it is this equanimity of formation, not the faculty of equanimity. One-pointedness of mind is as previously explained.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetfulness of the object of focus.
Clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) is the discerning awareness at the times of settling, uplifting, and equanimity.
Pleasure (*sukha*) is the feeling that accords with the object of focus.
Regarding the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one delights in pleasure, one does not seek other acquisitions.
Regarding one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*), it is the non-distraction from the object of focus.
This dhyāna also possesses two feelings; those [feelings] are also two: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
These dharmas are called the third dhyāna.
It is free from inhalation and exhalation; the fourth [dhyāna] has four branches (*aṅga*).
"Branches" refers to what is called wholesome; they follow the respective matters as previously explained.

Regarding "the fourth [dhyāna] has four factors, being free from inhalation and exhalation": in the fourth dhyāna, there is no inhalation or exhalation because the pores of the body in that meditative attainment are closed, as the four great elements are extremely dense.
The four factors are: neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity regarding formations, pure mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
"Neither-pain-nor-pleasure" means that one has already transcended both pain and pleasure.
Equanimity of practice (*upekṣā*) is so called because one does not seek other matters.
Pure mindfulness (*śuddhasmṛti*) is mindfulness that protects the roots of goodness; it is pure because it is free from the eight higher afflictions.

These eight higher afflictions refer to the four faculties, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and inhalation and exhalation; it is so called because it is free from internal and external disturbances.
The meaning of distraction shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga* (Chapter on Analysis).
As for "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*), it is the non-diffusion of the mind toward its object.
Question:
Why are right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and other factors not established as factors (*aṅga*) in the first and second dhyānas? Answer:

Because they are disturbed by joy (*prīti*) and applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), these [factors] are not established as constituent types; for this reason, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is likewise not established.

Furthermore, equanimity (upekṣā) as a mental formation is not established [as a separate factor], because it is contrary to the pleasure of tranquility (praśrabdhi-sukha); pleasure is mobile, whereas equanimity is serene.
Question:
Why is "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" (aduḥkhāsukha) not established in the third dhyāna?
Answer: Because it conforms to the category of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance are mutually exclusive, for this reason right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is not established in the fourth dhyāna.
Question:
Are all three types of dhyāna—those associated with relish (*āsvādana*), and so forth—fully endowed with their constituent factors (*aṅga*)? Answer:
The factors (*aṅga*) are said to be exclusively wholesome.
It should be understood that wholesome dhyāna is associated with these factors, whereas defiled dhyāna is not.
Question:
What is absent in the defiled [first dhyāna]? Answer:
It lacks the joy and bliss born of seclusion, because it is associated with afflictions.
In the second dhyāna, there is no [internal serenity], because it is turbid and disturbed by the affliction of internal impurity.
In the third dhyāna, there is no [mindfulness and clear comprehension], because one is deluded by the pleasure that constitutes an affliction.
In the fourth dhyāna, there is no [pure mindfulness and equanimity], because they are incompatible with the affliction of equanimity.
Furthermore, in the first and second dhyānas there is no bliss of non-attachment (*anāśrita-sukha*), because they are exclusively wholesome;
likewise, in the third and fourth dhyānas there is no equanimity of formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).

Regarding the statement that "matters are as previously explained": if a matter has already been explained for a particular dhyāna and is then mentioned again for another dhyāna, it is not an addition of something never before mentioned.

Just as joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are explained in the case of the first and second dhyānas, one should know that these two factors (*aṅga*) are not four; this applies to all stages (*bhūmi*).
Question:
How many such dhyāna-factors are there?
Answer: The factors of dhyāna are eighteen in name, but in substance there are eleven;
in the formless realms there are no such factors, and the same applies to the attendants of dhyāna.
Regarding the statement that "the factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga) are eighteen in name," there are eighteen names for these factors:
the first dhyāna has five factors, and the third dhyāna is likewise; the second dhyāna has four factors, and the fourth dhyāna is likewise.
The branches have already been explained previously.

As for the "eleven matters," there are five branches in the first dhyāna, which are named five and constitute five matters; in the second, inner serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) is added; in the third, equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), bliss (*sukha*), and correct wisdom (*saṃprajanya*) are added; and in the fourth, neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*) is added.
Regarding the fourfold permutation of the factors of the first dhyāna that are not factors of the second dhyāna:
those that are factors of the first dhyāna but not of the second are *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
Those that are of the second but not of the first are *adhyātmasaṃprasāda* (inner serenity).
"Both the first and the second" refers to joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).
"Neither the first nor the second" excludes those previously mentioned.
In this manner, it is explained progressively up to the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding the statement that "the formless [attainments] lack factors, and the same applies to the retinue of dhyānas": the four formless attainments and their retinues of dhyānas do not establish constituent factors (*aṅga*) because they constitute a practice of austerity (*duḥkhacara*).

Dhyāna as comprised by factors is a practice of ease (*sukhacara*); therefore, those stages are described as the path of suffering. If those stages were to establish factors, then all stages would have to be called the path of ease.
"With both vitarka and vicāra, this is called the preliminary dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna);
the intermediate dhyāna has vicāra—this is what the wise have declared.

Regarding "with both vitarka and vicāra, this is called the preliminary dhyāna": it refers to the state with vitarka and vicāra that serves as the basis for the preliminary stage; "preliminary" (anāgamya) is a subordinate member (parivāra) of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the statement that "there is insight within the intermediate dhyāna as explained by the Wise": there is insight within the intermediate dhyāna but no initial application of thought (*vitarka*), because the practitioner has transitioned into a state of profound tranquility.
Question:
Why are the intermediate supports established for the first and second dhyānas, but not for the higher stages?
Answer: Because their ascent and descent can be discerned.

In the first dhyāna there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); in the second dhyāna, these are absent; and in that intermediate state, there is vicāra but no vitarka. Therefore, it is established as a separate basis.
Because the higher stages lack this ascending and descending, they are not established [as such].
The *anāgāmya* (preparatory stage) may be of two kinds, namely excluding that which is associated with tasting (*āsvādana-samprayukta*).
The intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is of three kinds; these are all likewise said to possess a single feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding the future [dhyānas], there are two types, namely those dissociated from attachment (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*). Some say that the future dhyānas possess two natures—pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*)—and are not associated with attachment.

Although he is bound by the chain of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the power of that craving causes him to experience the future dhyāna and be born among the Brahmā devas; thus, birth and death remain linked by the fetter of craving for the first dhyāna. If this is excluded, there are two [fetters]; if this is included, there are three. He lacks craving for meditative attainment (*samāpatti-tṛṣṇā*), yet there is no fault in not excluding the craving for rebirth (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding this statement that it is associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*):
as for the three types of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there are three natures within the intermediate dhyāna—
associated with relishing, pure (*śuddha*), and untainted (*anāsrava*)— and it is also associated with relishing, just as in other stages.

Regarding the statement that there is also "one feeling" in both [the intermediate state and the future existence]: in both the future existence and the intermediate state, there is only one feeling, namely, the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the future existence, because there is fear, there is no feeling of pleasure; this is because it is close to the desire realm.
Because the practitioner has fear, pleasant feeling does not arise, for the task is not yet complete.

Because the practitioner is tending toward detachment from desire but has not yet attained it, pleasant feeling does not arise; sorrow arises instead, as there remain residual bonds of the desire realm.
Just as when a person is bound, even if they have been released, there remains something left undone and they still give rise to doubt and fear, such that they do not experience pleasant feeling;
so it is with that [state], because its tranquility is inferior.
As it is with the future [state], so it is with the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*); it should be explained according to its meaning.
The stages have already been explained; the virtues that arise from them shall now be discussed.
Concentration, the supernormal powers, the immeasurables, the spheres of totality, the spheres of mastery, the various knowledges, and the liberations arise therein.
Regarding that samādhi, there are three samādhis:
emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apraṇihita)—which should be called "realitylessness" (aniḥsaraṇa)—and signlessness (animitta).
Because that wholesome mind is balanced and upright, it is called samādhi.
That emptiness is of two kinds: namely, with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
That which is with outflows takes all phenomena as its object; that which is without outflows takes phenomena with outflows as its object.

This, moreover, is of nine kinds: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, conditioned-unconditioned emptiness, non-substantiality emptiness, ultimate emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness.
Internal emptiness refers to contemplating the internal sense bases as empty and devoid of self.
External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, and the emptiness of both the conditioned and the unconditioned are likewise.
Emptiness of non-existence refers to the absence of this or that thing.

Emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā) refers to the fact that when the eye arises, it comes from nowhere, and when it ceases, it goes nowhere; it is explained in this manner and so forth.

Regarding "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā): it refers to the contemplation of emptiness as empty with respect to contaminated emptiness (sāsrava-śūnyatā) by means of uncontaminated emptiness (anāsrava-śūnyatā).
"Wishlessness" (apraṇihita) is likewise of two kinds: namely, contaminated and uncontaminated.
Both possess two kinds of conditions, as explained according to their respective meanings.

These further comprise five types: namely, the three beginning with the internal, as well as the conditioned wishlessness (*saṃskṛta-apraṇihita*) and the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*).

Regarding the wishless (apraṇihita) with respect to conditioned phenomena: one contemplates conditioned dharmas through the wishless—whether tainted or untainted—by means of mental applications such as impermanence and so forth.
The rest is as explained for emptiness.
Regarding signlessness (*animitta*), there are two kinds of signlessness: namely, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

These are further divided into four types: that is, contemplating the cessation (*nirodha*) of the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) through the contaminated and uncontaminated as cessation, tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*)—this constitutes signless contemplation. Likewise, the external, the internal-external, and the signless itself are also signless.
The signless samādhi will be explained in detail in the *Sūtra* chapter;
the repeated samādhi will be explained in detail in the *Miscellaneous* chapter;
as for the supernormal powers, they have already been discussed in the *Knowledge of the Six Supernormal Powers* chapter.
Question:

If the cultivation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) means the manifestation of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*), such that when what is to be done is not lost, then what is to be done is manifested—when those supernormal powers are accomplished, do they arise or do they not arise?
Answer: If liberation were indeterminate (avyākṛta), then its arising would be called "arising from meditative absorption" (vyutthāna).
If liberation were indeterminate, one would be emerging from samādhi; if it were wholesome (kuśala), it would be samādhi itself, and if it were wholesome, there would be no such thing as "arising."
Regarding the immeasurables:
two are immeasurable and free from ill-will; the last is said to be non-attachment, and the third is said to be the faculty of joy. These are said to have their basis in the desire realm.
The two immeasurables that are non-ill will are loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
These have the nature of the wholesome root of non-ill will, as they are the antidotes to malice (*vyāpāda*).
Loving-kindness serves as the antidote for ill will toward those who are its proper objects; compassion serves as the antidote for ill will toward those who are not its proper objects.

Furthermore, for those who give rise to anger toward the lives of sentient beings, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the antidote; for those who give rise to anger toward the infliction of punishments upon sentient beings, compassion (*karuṇā*) serves as the antidote.

Therefore, one who seeks merit can give rise to the immeasurable [brahmavihāras] rather than seeking out faults; such a person seeks merit even in those who have severed their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), perceiving their originally pure karma.
Those who seek out faults do so even toward an Arhat, namely by perceiving his original impure karma.
The final mention of non-attachment refers to the relinquishing of the immeasurable, which is the nature of the wholesome root of non-attachment.
To claim that non-attachment (*alobha*) is not the antidote to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is incorrect. Why?
Because it does not sever ill-will.
Question:
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is an antidote to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and the meditation on the foul (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is also an antidote to sensual desire.
Which specific type of sensual desire is countered by equanimity?
What kind of greed is countered by the contemplation of impurity? Answer:
Greed for physical form is countered by the contemplation of impurity; greed for sexual desire is countered by equanimity.

Regarding the third explanation of the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*): the immeasurable joy (*muditā*) is of the nature of the faculty of joy, while the phenomena that arise in accordance with it are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

As for their characteristics: benefiting others through tranquility is the characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); removing what is not tranquil is the characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*); sympathetic rejoicing is the characteristic of joy (*muditā*); and equanimity toward all is the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This refers to the "basis" (āśraya) of that desire realm, which is the body of the basis; it manifests in the desire realm and not elsewhere.
Why is this? Because it functions for the sake of providing benefit and pleasure.
This means that one perceives the suffering of sentient beings in the desire realm and desires to bring them benefit by providing happiness, thereby removing their suffering.
There is no suffering in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, because it is the antidote to ill will, the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the remedy for the fault of ill will.

As it has been said: the cultivation and repeated practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) removes ill-will; compassion (*karuṇā*) removes harmfulness; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) removes discontent; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) removes sensual desire and ill-will. These various faults do not exist in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are three directions in the desire realm, excluding Uttarakuru.
Question:
What kind of mental application (*manasikāra*) is involved in the immeasurable meditative attainments (*apramāṇa-samāpatti*)?

Answer: Sentient beings experience pleasure, pain, and joy; for sentient beings who have no other perceptions, [the mind] turns according to what is appropriate toward immeasurable objects of focus consisting of sentient beings.
Desiring to bring happiness to those sentient beings, one enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) with such reflection.
Sighing "Alas, how painful! for sentient beings who suffer and desiring to liberate them from suffering, one enters the meditative absorption of compassion (*karuṇā-samāpatti*) with such reflection.
Rejoicing in those sentient beings, he reflects in this way and enters the meditative attainment of joy (*muditā-samāpatti*).
Contemplating those sentient beings alone, without any other perceptions, he reflects in this way and enters the meditative attainment of equanimity (*upekṣā-samāpatti*).
Question:
Since the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cannot cause suffering sentient beings to obtain happiness, why is it not a misconception (*viparyāsa*)? Answer:
Because it is wholesome, because it arises from a peaceful aspiration, because it is associated with right reflection, and because it is contrary to ill-will.
As for the object consisting of sentient beings, it takes sentient beings of the desire realm as its object.
As it has been said, regarding the statement that "if one dwells having accomplished the contemplation of filling one direction," this refers to both the receptacle world and the beings within it.
For this reason, one should know that the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*), because they take sentient beings as their object.
It universally takes all sentient beings as its object—namely, those born from the four modes of birth—for there are no other sentient beings apart from these.

Regarding "attainment through detachment" and "attainment through application": attainment through detachment is acquired at the time of becoming free from desire, after which the application becomes manifest.
Question:
What is skillful means (upāya)? Answer:

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arises from one's kin. This means that when wishing to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, one establishes all sentient beings into three categories: friends, enemies, and neutral parties.
Furthermore, friends are distinguished into three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.

First, one should generate a genuine aspiration toward those previously mentioned in the "Chapter on Relatives"—namely, parents and other respected elders—thinking that because they have long habituated themselves to harmful aspirations, their minds do not incline toward benefiting others; therefore, one should again collect the mind and cultivate the perception of their benefit.

When one abides in equanimity toward those who are superior friends and even toward superior enemies, this is called the accomplishment of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise.
Equanimity arises from the intermediate category; thus it is explained in detail.
As for their names, because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their objects, they are said to be "immeasurable.

Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), there are eight; the first three are the liberations of form (*rūpavimokṣa*), and together with the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), they have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their wholesome root-nature.
These roots of goodness should be understood as having the nature of non-attachment, because they are the antidote to attachment.
They are with outflows (*sāsrava*), because they consist of mental engagement through resolute reflection (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
Question:
This is not of the nature of the wholesome root of non-attachment. Why?
Because it is described as contemplation and described as perception.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms," and so forth in detail.

This "perceiver" (vipaśyanā) is wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are of the nature of wisdom. The *Abhidharma-vimukti-sthāna* states that they are "superior knowledge and superior vision" (*abhibhu-jñāna-darśana*), and "vision" (*darśana*) is precisely wisdom.
The liberations (vimokṣa) are also described as contemplations of form; since form is the first liberation, the first three liberations are therefore of the nature of wisdom (prajñā).
Likewise, all the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are described as the single perception of earth; therefore, all spheres of totality are of the nature of perception (saṃjñā).
To say that they have the nature of non-attachment is not correct. Answer:
These roots of goodness have the nature of non-attachment because wisdom and perception are predominant.

That [text] speaks of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "perception" (*saṃjñā*) as being like the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the perception of superior forms (*varṇasaṃjñā*); therefore, there is no fault.

Just as the wisdom of recollecting a place where one previously dwelt is designated as "recollection" because of the predominance of mindfulness (*smṛti*), so too when it is said that one recollects immeasurable things previously experienced, that is also wisdom (*jñāna*).
Just as the perception of superior form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called the "perception of superior form" because perception is predominant therein.
Furthermore, it is called "perception" because perception is proximate [to it]. Thus, it is designated by the term "perception.

Wisdom that is without fault and without craving is not dissociated from perception; they share the same basis (*āśraya*), the same activity (*ākāra*), the same object (*ālambana*), and the same fruit (*phala*). They share the same "basis-fruit" (*āśraya-phala*) and "fruit-of-basis" (*niśraya-phala*); this "basis" also carries the meaning of "moistening" (*sneha*).
Fruitions that are both defiled and unwholesome are of three kinds:

first, those arising from pervasive causes; second, those arising from homogeneous causes; and third, those arising from the residual force of retributive causes—such as obtaining a short lifespan as a result of killing. For this reason, it is said to be one.
One should know that the rest are explained accordingly.
How is it known that its nature is non-greed?
Because it is the antidote to greed.
This root of goodness should be understood as the antidote to greed.
If it were of the nature of non-delusion, it should be said to be the antidote to delusion.
Although wisdom is the antidote to all afflictions, because delusion is the most proximate [affliction], it is not [the antidote] to greed.
If this were the intrinsic nature of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) in all instances, it would not be an antidote to the afflictions, because it would lack definitiveness.
Therefore, one should know that this root of goodness has the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*).
If one speaks of their retinues, these are of the nature of the five aggregates;
this teaching concerns the support of the three directions, with the sphere being the form of the desire realm.
Regarding "if one speaks of their retinues, these are of the nature of the five aggregates," one should know that these roots of goodness and their retinues are of the nature of the five aggregates.

Regarding this statement that [the roots] depend on three directions: these various roots of goodness arise within the bodies of those in three directions, excluding Uttarakuru, and not in any others. Why is this so?
Because these roots of goodness are the antidotes to sensual desire, they do not exist in the form or formless realms where sensual desire is present.
Although there is sensual desire in Uttarakuru, because the power of wisdom is inferior, one cannot give rise to these roots of goodness there.
Although the devas of the desire realm possess sensual desire, because they are attached to pleasure, they likewise cannot give rise to these roots of goodness.
Regarding "objects that are the forms of the desire realm," these roots of goodness take the forms of the desire realm as their objects.

The first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) involve the practice of [contemplating] the livid corpse and so forth; because they operate within the sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) by way of the practice of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), while the remaining ones operate by way of purity (*śubha-bhāvanā*), they are therefore established as the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Question:
For what reason does that practitioner perceive the sign of purity in relation to feeling? Answer:
It is for the purpose of testing whether [the practice] is impure; is it accomplished or not?
One who contemplates impurity may give rise to a mind of indolence, and thus [this teaching] is intended to cause them to maintain focused application.
Furthermore, wishing to observe for oneself what one is capable of, one forms this thought:
"It is not remarkable that afflictions do not arise through the contemplation of impurity; rather, it is truly extraordinary that they do not arise through the contemplation of purity."
Furthermore, because manifest roots of goodness possess functional capacity, they appear at the very end of the stage of renunciation (*prahāṇa*).
These formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) are said to rely upon two realms; first, they arise from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the last among the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*): the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) is by nature a dissociated formation.
Question:
Since all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) have ceased, why is it specifically called the "cessation of perception and feeling"?
Answer: Due to these two powers, the practitioner experiences extreme fatigue regarding the two realms: due to the power of sensation (*vedanā*), one becomes fatigued with the dhyānas;
due to the power of perception (*saṃjñā*), one becomes fatigued with the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The meanings of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are as explained in the section on the aggregates (*skandha*).

Regarding the statement that these two elements (*dhātu*) depend upon [a physical body]: it is when the bodies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are present, not those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this?
Because it is not mind.
In the desire and form realms there is form; therefore, when that mind and its mental factors cease, the life-faculty continues to function based upon form.

In the formless realm there is no form; if, at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), the mind and its mental factors were to cease, the life-faculty would have to be severed, as there would be nothing upon which it could depend.
It is not the case that one who is destined to die cannot enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

This matter is not so. For one who first arises from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—that is, one who first enters the attainment of cessation from the desire realm—having passed away there and been reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this attainment manifests again after they have abandoned the desires of that realm.
Question:
For what reason do those in the form and formless realms first attain the dhyānas, yet not the attainment of cessation? Answer:
Dhyāna arises due to three factors: namely, the power of the cause, the power of karma, and the power of skillful means regarding the Dharma.
As for the power of the cause, it refers to the fact that one has previously cultivated and brought forth dhyāna.

Regarding the power of karma: it refers to the four factors by which karma already performed is nurtured. As for the power of skillful means, it is like the time of the formation and destruction of a kalpa.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), two factors arise: the power of causes (*hetubala*) and the power of karma (*karmabala*). There is no power of skillful means (*upāyabala*), because in that realm there is neither accomplishment nor failure.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) arises from the power of teaching (*deśanābala*); "teaching" refers here to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), meaning the teachings of the Buddha, the *pāramitās*, and the *śrāvakas*. Therefore, it can first arise within a body of the desire realm and nowhere else.

In the desire realm, one who has entered meditative absorption does not remain for more than seven days; because their body is sustained by solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), if they were to exceed this period, they would dissolve upon emerging from the state.
In the form realm, one who has entered meditative absorption may remain for as long as an eon (*kalpa*).
The remainder consists of the nature of the four aggregates; they are said to be based on the three realms, or to have the formless realm as their object, as well as the untainted as their object.

Regarding "the remainder consists of the nature of the four aggregates": the remaining qualities refer to the four liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the two bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); they consist of the four aggregates because the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is excluded, as those [liberations and bases] are formless.
Regarding the statement that these are the supports for those three realms: it is because these virtues manifest within the three realms.

As for the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*) and the totality of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*), one first arises from the desire realm and the form realm in order to relinquish form; thus, they initially arise from the sphere of form.

Alternatively, regarding those with formless objects and those conditioned by the untainted (anāsrava): for the sphere of infinite space and all pervasive bases of the sphere of infinite space, they have the four aggregates as their object.
For the sphere of infinite consciousness and all pervasive bases of the sphere of infinite consciousness, they have the four aggregates as their object.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space takes as its object the four formless attainments, their causes, their cessation, and all categories of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness takes as its object the three remaining formless attainments; the rest is as explained above.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness takes as its object two formless spheres; the rest is as explained above.
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its object that very stage, its cause, its cessation, and all categories of subsequent knowledge.
The intrinsic nature of the roots of goodness has already been explained; now their accomplishment of merit shall be discussed.
It should be known that some say one accomplishes four immeasurables, or perhaps three; it is not otherwise for those who possess fewer.
If one is born in the desire realm and has abandoned the desires of the desire realm, or is born in the first or second dhyāna, one accomplishes the four immeasurables;
if one is born in the third or fourth dhyāna, one accomplishes three immeasurables, excluding sympathetic joy.
The faculty of joy (sukhendriya) exists in the second dhyāna, but not in the higher stages;
there is nothing below this that possesses it.
Whether one or up to eight, these are accomplished through the liberations (vimokṣa).
"Either four or again eight, one achieves the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
Whether it be one up to eight, one achieves the liberations (vimokṣa): some achieve one liberation, while others achieve up to eight."
Regarding the "attainment of one": if one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, craving for that realm is exhausted, but craving for the Bṛhatphala Heaven is not yet exhausted;
or if one is born in the Bṛhatphala Heaven, craving for that realm is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana), craving for it is not yet exhausted.

One who accomplishes both [the first and second dhyānas] is one who, having been born in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) or having been born in the First or Second Dhyāna, has exhausted craving for those levels but has not yet exhausted craving for the Sphere of Universal Purity (śubhakṛtsnāyatana).
If one is born in the third or fourth dhyāna, craving for the form realm is exhausted, but craving for the sphere of infinite space is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of infinite space, craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted, but craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) therein is not yet exhausted.

Regarding the accomplishment of three [factors]: if one is born in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the First or Second Dhyāna, craving for the *Śubhakṛtsna* heaven is exhausted, while craving for the *Bṛhatphala* heaven is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens, craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.

If one is born in the sphere of infinite space or the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the untainted state (*anāsrava*) arises in the higher realms and is not lost in the lower; therefore, being born in the sphere of infinite consciousness, one accomplishes the liberation (*vimokṣa*) from the sphere of infinite space, and so it is in all such cases. When craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted...
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), that craving for it is not yet exhausted.

Regarding the accomplishment of four [fetters]: if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first or second dhyāna, craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) is exhausted, but craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the third or fourth dhyāna, craving for the sphere of consciousness is exhausted, while craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, craving for the sphere of nothingness is exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one does not attain the samādhi of cessation.

As for the accomplishment of five [factors]: if one is born in the desire realm or the first or second dhyāna, craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted, while craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is not yet exhausted.

If one is born among the Śubhakṛtsna devas or the Bṛhatphala devas and has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), yet has not attained the samādhi of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
or if one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and attains the samādhi of cessation.

Regarding the accomplishment of the six [factors]: if one is born in the desire realm or in the first or second dhyānas, craving for the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) is exhausted, while craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted;
or if one is born in the *śubhakṛtsna* or *bṛhatphala* heavens, one attains the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Regarding the accomplishment of seven [factors]: if one is born in the desire realm or in the first or second dhyāna, and has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), yet has not attained the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding the accomplishment of eight [factors]: if one is born in the desire realm or in the first or second dhyāna, and has attained the samādhi of cessation.
This is the general explanation.
Regarding those who possess the mundane (sāsrava) abandonments, they are all accomplished when one has become detached from a lower stage but has not yet been born into a higher stage.
Regarding those who possess the supramundane (anāsrava) abandonments, they are also accomplished upon being born into a higher stage.
"Or one may achieve four, or likewise eight, of the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana). This means that some achieve either four or eight.

Those who achieve four are those born in the desire realm or the first and second dhyānas, for whom craving for those [lower realms] has been exhausted, but craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, one has exhausted craving for that realm and is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
Regarding the accomplishment of eight [attainments]: if one is born in the desire realm or in the first or second dhyānas, one has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
Whether one, or likewise two, eight, nine, or ten—
know that such practitioners achieve all the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (bases of totality).
Some achieve one *kṛtsnāyatana*, some two, some eight, some nine, or some ten.

As for the accomplishment of one [element], it occurs if one is born in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), where craving for that very state is not yet exhausted, or if one is born in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
As for the accomplishment of two [elements], it occurs if one is born in the sphere of infinite space and has exhausted craving for that state.

Regarding the accomplishment of eight [fetters]: if one is born in the desire or form realms, having exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven but not yet exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven.

Regarding the accomplishment of nine [fetters]: if one is born in the desire or form realms, having exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven but not yet exhausted craving for the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven.
Regarding the "attainment of ten": if one is born in the realm of desire or the realm of form, and has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space.
Having already explained attainment, I shall now explain the qualities associated with each respective stage.
The five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) reside in the four fundamental dhyānas, not in other stages;
the various knowledges (jñāna) are as previously explained, and there are either three or six immeasurables (apramāṇa).

Regarding "the five supernormal powers reside in the four fundamental dhyānas, not in other stages": one accomplishes the five supernormal powers within the four fundamental dhyānas, but not in other stages, with the exception of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā).
Why is this? Because it comprises the samādhi of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

Regarding "all knowledges as previously explained," this refers to what was stated in the previous Chapter on Knowledge (*Jñāna-varga*), according to what is attained in each respective stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the three or six immeasurables: excluding sympathetic joy (*muditā*), the remaining immeasurables exist in six stages:
the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*).
Some, however, do not wish for them to exist in the preparatory stage.
Alternatively, it is said that compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) do not arise in the first and second dhyānas because their mental faculties (*indriya*) are contradictory.

The faculty of sympathetic joy functions as an experience of joy by its very nature (*svabhāva*), whereas compassion functions as an experience of sorrow; therefore, they are not compatible with one another in those stages.
As for the claim that the knowledge of the patience regarding the origin of suffering is not so, why is this?
Because it proceeds as the practice of reality.

If it is claimed that the patience and knowledge regarding the origin of suffering involve extreme aversion yet are associated with the faculty of joy, and that the practice of compassion is likewise, such a statement is erroneous, because [compassion] is based on genuine reflection.
Regarding the statement that "arousing compassion from joy involves conceptualization and reflection, and is therefore faulty":
if it is said thus because it leads toward true contemplation, then there is no fault.

Although compassion is not itself true contemplation, it can lead to true contemplation; therefore, there is no fault in delighting in the removal of suffering, and thus compassion and sympathetic joy coexist.
Question:
What is the difference between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)? Answer:
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is characterized by the absence of hatred; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is characterized by the absence of delusion.
Furthermore, compassion is shared with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whereas great compassion is not shared.
Moreover, one who possesses compassion can feel pity but cannot deliver others, while one who possesses great compassion can both feel pity and deliver others.

Furthermore, compassion takes as its object sentient beings who experience the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who experience all three types of suffering.
Compassion takes as its object physical suffering; great compassion takes as its object both physical and mental suffering.
Question:
Why is it called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā)? Answer:

It is called Great Compassion because it delivers sentient beings from great suffering; it is called Great Compassion because the Great Merchant has attained it; it is called Great Compassion because it gathers in and sustains a vast multitude of sentient beings; and it is called Great Compassion because the Great Being enters into great perils and difficulties.
The first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), as well as the immeasurable joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*) and the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*), reside in the first and second dhyānas.
The first four spheres of mastery, the immeasurable joy, and so forth, along with the first two liberations, exist within the first and second dhyānas, and not elsewhere.

Although the third and fourth dhyānas possess roots of goodness similar to the first two liberations (vimokṣa), they are not established [as such]; for this reason, they likewise possess roots of goodness similar to the first four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).

As stated in the Sūtras: loving-kindness reaches its limit in the Sphere of Total Purity; compassion reaches its limit in the Sphere of Infinite Space; sympathetic joy reaches its limit in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; and equanimity reaches its limit in the Sphere of Nothingness.
Some say that this sutra explains the Noble Path by means of immeasurable names, because those who are to be converted enter the Noble Path through these immeasurable names.

Furthermore, its remedial factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are explained by means of immeasurable names; that is to say, the remedial factor of enlightenment of the third dhyāna is explained by the name "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), and so on, up until the remedial factor of enlightenment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which is explained by the name "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, regarding the explanation by way of analogous names: "Loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) refers to the practice of bliss and the experience of pleasure up to the third dhyāna; "compassion" (*karuṇā*) refers to the practice of suffering, the sphere of empty space, and the turning away from and revulsion toward form; "sympathetic joy" (*muditā*) refers to the practice of delight and the dwelling in consciousness within the sphere of infinite consciousness; and "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) refers to the practice of relinquishment and the state of relinquishment in the sphere of nothingness.
There are four further spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), as well as one liberation (*vimokṣa*), and also eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); these are said to exist in the highest dhyāna.
The latter four spheres of mastery, the pure liberation, and the first eight bases of totality reside in the fourth dhyāna, and not in any lower stages.
There are also roots of goodness similar to the pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*) that are not established, because they are corrupted by the impure.

For this reason, there are also roots of goodness similar to the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), which are described as the meditative attainments of earth (*pṛthivī-samāpatti*) and the universal bases of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*). Those meditative attainments of earth exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas.
The earth-kasiṇa exists in the fourth dhyāna and nowhere else.
Why? Because it is free from the eight kinds of disturbances.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are two kinds of desire for form: bodily desire and mental desire;

the first dhyāna establishes two liberations (*vimokṣa*) and four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) as their antidotes, because the desire for form in the first dhyāna likewise consists of these two kinds.
Two types of liberation (*vimokṣa*) are established in the second dhyāna because, in that stage, there are no two kinds of desire for form.
No liberation is established in the third dhyāna because its bliss is so superior that one cannot give rise to these roots of goodness.
Furthermore, one enters the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) by means of those liberations (*vimokṣa*), and enters the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) by means of the spheres of mastery.

One enters the first two spheres of mastery by means of the first liberation; one enters the third and fourth spheres of mastery by means of the second liberation; one enters the latter four spheres of mastery by means of the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*); and one again enters the spheres of totality by means of those latter four spheres of mastery.
The rest are called "reversals" (*prātikūlya-vimokṣa*); the same applies to the two "all-encompassing" (*sarvatraga*) attainments.
The "extinction" (*nirodha*) is last; the rest are untainted (*anāsrava*) and belong to nine stages.

Regarding "the rest are called reversals": with the exception of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the mind at the moment of death, all other wholesome states are fully described as the reversal of the sphere of infinite space.
In the path of non-obstruction directed toward the fourth dhyāna, the mind at the moment of death is directed toward rebirth; therefore, the "liberations" (vimokṣa) are not established therein.
One should know that the same applies to the remaining formless attainments.

Regarding the phrase "the other two are likewise," this refers to the designations for the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Question:
Why is the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) not established as a "sphere" (*āyatana*) above the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness?
Answer:

The practitioner first enters the contemplation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*) but is unable to master them; subsequently, they enter the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) but are unable to achieve the contemplation of the boundless mental resolve; thereafter, they enter the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), achieving the contemplation of the boundless blue mental resolve.
The same applies to yellow, red, and white.

Contemplating what these colors depend upon, one observes that they depend on the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*), and subsequently enters the mental resolve of the contemplation of infinite earth (*ananta-pṛthivī-manasikāra-vipaśyanā*).
The other great elements are also like this.
He further reflects in this way:
"How does one progress?"
This refers to cognitive awareness.
Specifically, when one has previously entered the sphere of infinite space in its entirety,
upon what does that cognitive awareness depend?
Contemplating based on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) as the universal base.
Since this basis has no further basis upon which to rely, no higher universal bases are established above it.
Regarding the statement that "cessation occurs last": the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is subsumed within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Why is this?
Because it accords with the mind of cessation, and because it is easily extinguished as it gradually becomes more subtle through successive stages.
Question:
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) should not be subsumed under the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). Why is this?
As it was said: "Having attained the cessation of perception and feeling through the transcendence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells therein.
Answer: It is subsumed within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

The Blessed One spoke thus because he has transcended both meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and sensual desires; he spoke thus because those in training (*śaikṣa*) have transcended meditative attainments and abide [in them]; and he spoke thus because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have transcended sensual desires.
Furthermore, "transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to what is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
"The cessation of perception and feeling" refers to what is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

In this way, one should understand that there are those previously practiced and those not yet practiced, those shared and those unshared, and those obtained through the abandonment of desire as well as those obtained through effort; these are distinguished because they are superior, because they are unshared, and because they are ultimate within their respective realms and stages.

Regarding the two types of liberation (*vimokṣa*), it is said that one realizes them through bodily witness (*kāyena sākṣātkaroti*) and enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of consciousness (*vijñānanirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, the mind that enters this concentration is still with-outflows (*sāsrava*), because it accords with the mind of cessation.

The mind upon emerging from concentration may be either with-outflows or without-outflows (*anāsrava*); this attainment is acquired through skillful means (*upāya*), not through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*).
If one regresses and then arises again, one attains what was never before attained, rather than what had already been attained.

As for the remaining untainted [attainments] of the nine stages: if there are other untainted merits—namely, the three samādhis and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows—they reside in nine stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the three formless attainments, the preliminary stage (*anāgāmya*), and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*).
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) samādhis exist in eleven stages—namely, these nine, as well as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
It should be known that the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
those regarding meditative concentration, knowledge, and supernormal powers have already been explained, while all the remaining ones are exclusively contaminated.

Regarding the three liberations that should be known as both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*): the liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness should be known as being both with-outflows and without-outflows.

Regarding the statement that "the concentrations, knowledges, and supernormal powers have already been explained": the concentrations were explained previously; the various knowledges and supernormal powers are as explained in the *Jñāna-varga* (Chapter on Knowledge).

As for the rest being entirely with outflows (*sāsrava*): the other three supernormal powers are similar to the arts and crafts (*śilpa*); the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) take sentient beings as their object; the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of transcendence (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the attainment of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃvid*) are all with outflows; the meditative attainments of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) lack swiftness; and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) is contrary to the nature of the mind—all of these are therefore entirely with outflows.
Question:
What is the distinction between the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana)? Answer:
That which is by nature turned away from [its object], capable of overcoming the sphere of its focal point,
free from darkness and universally pervasive, is called "as it is measured" (yathāpramita). Because it does not turn toward [the object],
it is said to be "turned away from" (vairāgya/vipaśyana).
They are called "mastery bases" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because one masters those objects; it is because they are mastery bases that the Blessed One taught them as such.
Although not every practitioner is able to master those objects, when afflictions do not arise toward the objective conditions, this too is termed a "mastery base."
They are called "all-bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) because of their boundless mental comprehension.

Furthermore, those with weak roots of goodness are said to possess the "releases" (*vimokṣa*), those with middling [roots] are said to possess the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*), and those with superior [roots] are said to possess the "all-bases."

Furthermore, the *vimokṣas* (liberations) were explained by way of their causes, the *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) by way of their fruits, and the *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery) by way of both cause and fruit.

Having already explained the intrinsic nature of these various qualities and the stages in which they are accomplished—whether they are *sāsrava* (with outflows) or *anāsrava* (without outflows)—namely, the three types of accomplishment regarding the *dhyānas* and *ārūpyas*, we shall now explain them.
One who has not yet abandoned desire should be known to accomplish those meditative attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*);
one who has abandoned the lower but not yet reached the higher accomplishes the pure (*śuddha*) meditative attainments.

Regarding "one who has not yet abandoned desire should be known to accomplish those associated with relishing": if one has not yet abandoned desire for a particular level, one accomplishes the meditative attainments associated with relishing belonging to that level.

Regarding "having departed from the lower [realm] but not yet reached the upper, one accomplishes the pure [attainments]": this refers to one who has abandoned the desires of the desire realm but has not yet reached the Brahma-heaven; such a person accomplishes the pure first dhyāna as well as the remaining qualities belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Ordinary persons accomplish those associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and the pure (*śuddhaka*); noble ones accomplish all three types.
One should know that while abiding in a higher [stage], one accomplishes the untainted (*anāsrava*) of a lower stage;
this is a merit produced through skillful means, and it should be known that this does not constitute freedom from desire.

Regarding the statement "one should know that abiding in the higher [stages], one accomplishes the lower untainted [states]": when a noble being is born in the Brahma heavens, they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna as well as other untainted qualities such as samādhis and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
