All conditioned wholesome qualities (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) are bound by their place of origin; those that are unconditioned (*anāsrava*) are not so bound. Therefore, when one abandons them upon leaving their place of origin, it is the conditioned wholesome qualities that are abandoned, not the unconditioned ones.

One should know that the wholesome qualities produced through skillful means (*upāya*) do not belong to one who has not yet attained detachment from desire. It has already been stated that when one achieves various wholesome qualities by becoming detached from the desires of a lower stage, one should know that what is attained is not of the present.

Those that appear before one are not obtained through the means of detachment from desire; namely, the knowledge of the divine eye and the divine ear. Because these are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they do not enter into the pure (*śuddha*), the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), or those associated with relish (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*).
Therefore, when those three types of dhyāna are attained, they do not manifest until after one has applied the necessary means.
Of the six supernormal powers (abhijñā), two are indeterminate (avyākṛta) because they are subsumed within the path of liberation (vimuktimārga); the remaining four are wholesome (kuśala).
Question:
Among the merits obtained through these various skillful means, which ones sever the afflictions,
and which ones do not sever the afflictions?
Answer: The fundamental pure first dhyāna is likewise bound by the same fetter;
it cannot sever the afflictions, and the same is true for the immeasurable states.

Regarding the statement that "the fundamental pure first dhyāna is likewise bound by the same fetter and cannot sever the afflictions": because the fundamental pure first dhyāna is itself bound by the single fetter of the afflictions belonging to its own stage, it cannot sever those afflictions; it is only when a mundane path belonging to another stage manifests that one is able to abandon them.
Just as a person who has been bound cannot free themselves, so it is with him:
because he relishes the flavor of his own stage, he is unable to relinquish it.
It is like a person who does not abandon a friend, even if that friend is inferior.

It is likewise in this case: if the fundamental dhyānas serve as the antidote for the various afflictions (*kleśa*), those [afflictions] are abandoned; if they are not abandoned, they are not the antidote. Therefore, the untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna is the antidote to the afflictions, whereas the tainted (*sāsrava*) one abandons them through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Thus it continues up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for "the immeasurable is likewise," the immeasurable does not sever afflictions because it takes sentient beings as its object; the characteristic of dharmas, however, severs afflictions.
Furthermore, because it is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), that which is subsumed under the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) abandons the afflictions.
Furthermore, because it takes the present as its object, that which takes the three times as its object abandons the afflictions, since it acts as an antidote for a brief moment.
The World-Honored One stated in the sūtras that loving-kindness cuts off ill will.
As for "temporary treatment," it means that the various fetters are briefly stilled, like a debt being granted a grace period.
One should know that this applies to the five liberations (*pañca-vimokṣa*) and the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv-abhibhvāyatana*).
Furthermore, the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, all the universal bases, and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these phenomena are subsumed under the fundamental [categories] and do not sever the afflictions, as previously explained.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling does not sever the afflictions because it is contrary to the nature of the mind.
The liberations regarding form, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality also do not sever the afflictions, as they take specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects;
it is the path that takes general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that severs the afflictions, not those that take specific characteristics.

Furthermore, because it is contemplation through conceptual understanding (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), it is contemplation of reality (*tattva-manasikāra*) that abandons the afflictions, not conceptual understanding.
Furthermore, because it is contemplation through mental construction (*parikalpa-manasikāra*), it is contemplation without mental construction that abandons the afflictions.
Furthermore, because it concerns the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), it is not by means of contemplation on the non-substantial that afflictions are abandoned.

Furthermore, because it is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it is by means of what is subsumed under the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) that afflictions are abandoned.
There are twenty-three kinds of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*):
eight associated with the flavor of existence (*sāsrava*), eight pure (*śuddha*), and seven untainted (*anāsrava*).
Question:
How many kinds of causes are there for each of these samādhis? Answer:
What is called untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi) has seven kinds of causes for each.
The cause associated with flavor is one; it is said that the pure [attainments] are likewise.

Regarding the statement that each of the untainted absorptions has seven types of causes: the untainted first dhyāna is the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the untainted first dhyāna.
Regarding the three untainted dhyānas and the three formless attainments, they are causes by way of their own nature (*sabhāga-hetu*).
This continues in this manner up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This is the general explanation.
The path subsumed under the first dhyāna is of six types:

those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin), those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), those liberated by time (samayavimukta), and those liberated independent of time (asamayavimukta).

The path of those who follow by faith has six causes; the path of those who follow by dharma has three causes; the path of those liberated through faith has four causes; the path of those who have attained vision has two causes; the path of those liberated by time also has two causes; and the path of those not liberated by time is itself the cause of being not liberated by time.
Regarding the "associated-with-taste cause" (āsvādana-saṃprayukta-hetu), there is one: the first dhyāna associated with taste is the cause of the first dhyāna associated with taste, and nothing else.
This is because the causes of the first dhyāna are not analogous [to other stages]; it is not the cause of another stage, as the cause and effect would be severed.

Those associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) are of five kinds: those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), up to those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*). Those abandoned through the vision of suffering have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;

all cases are likewise. As for the statement "the pure [dhyāna] is also like that": the pure first dhyāna has as its cause the pure first dhyāna, but it does not have the associated-with-relishing or the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its cause, because they are dissimilar.
It is not the cause of purity for other stages, because it is bound to its own stage.
There are four types of pure first dhyāna:

the part conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*), the part conducive to maintenance (*sthityaṃśabhāgīya*), the part conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), and the part conducive to penetration (*niyāmāvakrāntibhāgīya*).

The four causes for the stage of decline, the samādhi of the stage of maintenance, and two for the stage of excellence [are as previously described]; the stage of penetration is exclusively the stage of penetration and nothing else, because it is inferior to the others.
One should know that it is likewise for the remaining stages.
Question:
How many types arise in each successive stage?
Answer:
The untainted dhyānas and formless attainments, whether practiced in reverse, forward, or by skipping stages, produce six kinds of births in sequence: seven, eight, nine, and ten.
The untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna successively gives rise to six types:
those of its own level (svabhūmika), the pure (śuddhaka), and the untainted second and third dhyānas. The same applies to the untainted second and third dhyānas.
The untainted sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) successively gives rise to seven: two of its own level, one of a higher level, and four of lower levels.
From the untainted second dhyāna, eight states arise in succession: two from its own level, two from the lower levels, and four from the higher levels.
From the untainted sphere of infinite consciousness, nine states arise in succession: two from its own level, three from the higher levels, and four from the lower levels.
The remaining ten types of untainted [knowledge] arise in succession; these are subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
When the dhyānas and formless attainments manifest in succession, they are not subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).

Regarding the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*): because it relies upon a lower stage and takes a lower stage as its object, the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) do not manifest in immediate succession.
From the sixth up to the eleventh—namely, the pure (*śuddhaka*) arise in succession;
next, from two up to ten arise; those associated with relish (*sāsvāda*) do not arise from three.

Regarding "from the sixth to the eleventh, it is said that the pure arises in succession": the pure state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises in succession from six types—namely, the flavor-associated and the pure states of its own level, and the four pure states of the lower levels, as well as the untainted state that is not flavor-associated, because of the abandonment of desire.
From the pure first dhyāna, seven states arise in succession: three from its own level and four from higher levels.
From the pure and untainted (anāsrava) sphere of nothingness, eight states arise in succession: three from its own level, one from a higher level, and four from lower levels.
The pure second dhyāna gives rise to nine [attainments] in succession; the pure consciousness-sphere (vijñānāyatana) gives rise to ten in succession; the remaining [realms] give rise to eleven.

This explanation refers to attainment through application (prayoga-pratilambhika) and attainment through detachment from desire (vairāgya-pratilambhika), not innate attainment (upapatti-pratilambhika); therefore, the innate attainment associated with the "savor" (āsvādana) of higher or lower stages is not mentioned.
At the time of the conclusion of the pure life, there arises in succession that which is associated with the flavor of all stages (*sarva-bhūmi-rasa*).
Question:
What kind of pure first dhyāna gives rise in succession to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*)?
Answer: It refers to the stage of "decisive distinction" (nirvedhabhāgīya).
If it were otherwise, the fourfold classification could not be established.
Next, two up to ten arise in association with the flavor (*āsvādana*), but not three.
Regarding the first dhyāna associated with flavor, two types arise in succession: that which is associated with flavor of its own level and the pure (*śuddha*);
it is not the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), because it is contrary to the defilements (*kleśa*).
It is not of a higher stage, because one has not yet abandoned desire for that stage.
It is not of three types, because those [of the higher stages] do not arise; if one were to speak of three types, it would be incorrect.
From the second dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*), four states arise in succession: two of its own stage, excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*); [and two from the first dhyāna].

The two [types of concentration] belonging to the lower stages are those associated with attachment (*āsvādana*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), which are pure (*śuddhaka*). This is because one fears the craving for the second dhyāna; thus, relying on the pure first dhyāna, one protects oneself.

As stated in the Sūtra: "It is better to rely on the first dhyāna through meditative attainment accompanied by the thought of renunciation, than to rely on the second dhyāna through inferior thought."
The third dhyāna gives rise to five: two from its own level, two from the second dhyāna, and one from the first dhyāna.

The fourth dhyāna associated with relishing gives rise to six; the sphere of infinite space gives rise to seven; the sphere of infinite consciousness gives rise to eight; and the sphere of nothingness gives rise to nine.

In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are ten: two from its own level, two from the sphere of nothingness, and six associated with the relishing of lower levels—these being the afflictions pertaining to rebirth.
Question:
How many kinds of objects does each one take as its condition? Answer:
Pure and untainted dhyānas take all stages as their objects;
the tainted phenomena of their own stage are the objects of those associated with relishing.
Regarding "pure and untainted dhyānas take all stages as their objects": pure and untainted dhyānas take all stages and all types [of phenomena] as their objects because their scope is vast.

The category of that untainted subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes the eight stages as its object; the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) takes one stage as its object; and the roots of goodness consisting of skillful means take the four truths as their objects.

Regarding those objects associated with the savoring of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-rasa-saṃprayukta*) within one’s own stage: the savoring first dhyāna takes as its object the savoring and the pure [states] of its own stage, and nothing else. This point has already been explained in detail in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*; it does not take untainted phenomena or other stages as its objects.
The formless [attainments] do not take as their object the tainted seeds of the lower stages;
that is to say, they are fundamental wholesome states, while the defiled ones are like the dhyānas of relish.

Regarding "the formless do not take as their object the tainted seeds of the lower stages, namely the fundamental wholesome states": the pure and untainted fundamental formless attainments do not take tainted phenomena of the lower stages as their objects, because they are free from the characteristics of form (*rūpa*).
Because it takes as its objects both its own stage and the stages above, it is said not to be "lower.
Because the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the lower stages, it is said not to be of the nature of outflows (*sāsrava*).

Since the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), when subsumed under the preparatory application (*prayoga*), takes the lower stages as its object, it is said that the fundamental mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) severs the fetters; therein, the path of non-obstruction has the lower as its object, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) has the upper as its object.
Because the dhyānas associated with relish take their own stage as an object, they are said to be wholesome.

As for the defiled being like the dhyāna associated with relish: just as the dhyāna associated with relish takes the dhyāna associated with relish of its own stage as an object, so it is for the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
It is said that there are other immeasurable virtues within the form realm;
these take the desire realm as their object—this is what the Most Victorious One has taught.

It was previously stated that the four immeasurables and other such virtues take the desire realm as their object; since supernormal powers are excluded, the phrase "immeasurable virtues and so forth" is used here.

Those five supernormal powers take the desire realm and the form realm as their objects; that is to say, those in the first dhyāna take the first dhyāna and the desire realm as their objects, but not the higher stages, and the same applies to the others according to their respective meanings.
There are three types of pure dhyāna:
first, that permeated by afflictions; second, that permeated by the path; and third, that which is unpermeated.

Regarding "permeated by afflictions": it belongs to the category of retrogression and is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); because it possesses the residual influence of afflictions, it is called "permeated by afflictions."
"Merit of the Path" (*mārga-puṇya*) refers to that which is meritorious by virtue of the Path; it means the cultivation of merit.
Other [types of merit] are not "merit of the Path.
Question: Which meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are capable of constituting such merit?
Answer: If one can perfume the various dhyānas, this relies upon the fourth dhyāna;
because craving for the three stages has been exhausted, the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) are exclusively the fruition of the ultimate fruit.
The first dhyāna is eclipsed by the fourth dhyāna. Why?
Because it is free from the eight disturbances and because it is the most excellent among all bases.
There are five grades of cultivation— mild, medium, superior, superior-medium, and superior-superior— which give rise to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Although there are likewise five grades of cultivation in the lower stages, because craving for the third dhyāna has been exhausted, the Pure Abodes do not arise from those lower stages.

Regarding the basis of that [meditation], whether it arises or does not arise, and its cultivation or non-cultivation, refers to emerging from or not emerging from meditative absorption. As for the preparatory method (*upāya*): one enters the full attainment (*samāpatti*) by means of the continuous flow of the untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna; subsequently, there is the tainted (*sāsrava*), followed again by the untainted. Within that flow, one gradually abbreviates the duration until two moments of the untainted are present, followed immediately by two moments of the tainted becoming manifest. In this way, the preparatory method for the intermingled dhyāna (*miśra-dhyāna*) of the tainted and untainted is accomplished.

If there is one moment of outflow-free (anāsrava), one moment of with-outflow (sāsrava), and again one moment of outflow-free, this is called the accomplishment of the mixed dhyāna (miśra-dhyāna). It consists of fifteen moments of mind:
five with-outflow minds and ten outflow-free minds.
Question:
For what reason is it called "perfumed dhyāna" (khuṇa-dhyāna)? Answer:
Some contemplate meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), some fear the various afflictions (*kleśa*), and others take pleasure in rebirth;
these are each explained according to their respective meanings.
There are three causes and conditions for the perfumed dhyāna (*vāsita-dhyāna*).
"Mindfulness of meditative absorption" means that the practitioner cherishes meditative absorption for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
"Fear of afflictions" means fearing regression from it.
Those who delight in rebirth do so because they take pleasure in being born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Those liberated through faith possess right attainment (samāpatti) due to three causes and conditions.
Those who have attained vision possess two; they do not fear the afflictions (kleśa) because they are of a nature that does not regress.
Those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) are also of two types: those who do not delight in birth, because they turn their backs on all rebirth;

and those who are liberated at any time (asamayavimukta), who are solely devoted to meditative absorption (samāpatti), because they do not fear the afflictions and are of a nature that does not regress.
It is not delighting in birth, because it turns its back on all birth.

The nature of the five aggregates of the "perfuming dhyāna" (khuṇa-dhyāna) consists of both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava). Taking the four truths as its object, it scatters the non-out-flowing upon the out-flowing; this meaning of scattering is like flowers being scattered over a caitya, which is why it is called "perfuming" (khuṇa). Thus it is explained in detail.
The untainted mind perfumes the tainted mind, like flowers scattered upon a caitya.
Question:
The three types of meditative attainments have already been explained; how are they acquired?
Answer: Through the abandonment of desire and through rebirth, one attains pure dhyāna;
through defilement, retrogression, and rebirth, one loses it; the untainted [dhyāna] is attained solely through the abandonment of desire.

Regarding the attainment of pure dhyāna through the abandonment of desire and through rebirth: pure first dhyāna is attained at two times—namely, upon abandoning the desires of the desire realm, and upon dying in a higher plane and being reborn in the Brahma-heaven.
Question:

It is also obtained at the time of falling away; that is to say, when one falls away from the detachment of the first dhyāna, one obtains the wholesome roots of the "partaking of decline" (hānabhāgīya) of the first dhyāna.
Why is this not mentioned?
Answer: Here, "attaining all that was previously unattained" refers to the attainment of the wholesome roots conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*) at the time of falling away;

although these were previously unattained, they are now attained. However, regarding the other three types [of wholesome roots], one had previously accomplished them and lost only one while attaining three, whereas now one loses three and attains only one. Since it is not the case that these were entirely non-existent before, this does not constitute "attaining all that was previously unattained. Therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Is it the case that just as the pure first dhyāna is attained through the abandonment of desire, it is likewise abandoned through the abandonment of desire, through falling away, or through rebirth?

Answer: There is a "partaking of decline" (hānabhāgīya) first dhyāna which is attained at the time of abandoning desire for the desire realm; it is abandoned at the time of abandoning desire for the Brahma-heaven. Furthermore, one attains the "partaking of excellence" (viśeṣabhāgīya) and other types at the time of abandoning desire for the Brahma-heaven; therefore, one abandons the partaking of decline.
It is acquired when one falls away from detachment from the Brahma realm; it is relinquished when one falls away from detachment from the desire realm.
It is acquired when one dies in a higher plane and is reborn in the Brahma realm; it is relinquished when one dies in the Brahma realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
The same applies up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is acquired through the transcendence of desire (*vairāgya*), not by birth, because there is no higher stage.

Regarding the defiled [attainment], it is acquired by one who falls away from the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*); that is, when one falls away from the transcendence of desire for the first dhyāna due to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm or of the Brahma-world.

Regarding those acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*): this refers to one who dies in a higher realm and is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world; and so on, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), where [the attainment] is acquired solely through retrogression (*parihāṇi-lābhika*) in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

The untainted [attainment] belongs exclusively to those who are free from desire; the untainted first dhyāna is obtained through the departure from desire, meaning that a noble one (ārya) departs from the desires of the desire realm—this refers to one who follows the gradual path.
It may also be obtained by one who, relying on the first dhyāna, transcends and ascends beyond the stage of ordinary birth, and so it is for all stages up to the highest.
Question:
Among these various merits, which ones abandon the afflictions? Answer:
The untainted (*anāsrava*) removes the afflictions (*kleśa*), as does that which is between the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
All that is between the concentrations is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Regarding "the untainted removes the afflictions": this refers to the untainted fundamental first dhyāna, which is the antidote to the afflictions of eight stages, up to the untainted state that is the antidote to the afflictions of two stages within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Regarding "and that which is between the meditative attainments" (*samāpatti*): "between the meditative attainments" refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), meaning the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages.
As long as one has not yet abandoned the desire of the lower stage, one does not obtain the fundamental meditative attainment (*maula-samāpatti*).
The others are not antidotes.

All intermediate states of meditative concentration (*dhyānāntara*) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); all paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) are associated with the faculty of equanimity because, as they have not yet attained [the fruit], joy does not arise.
Question:
As it has been stated that there is no body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) in the higher realms,
when those in the higher realms wish to see with the eye, hear with the ear, or feel with the body, how do they see, hear, and touch?
Answer: The consciousness of the Brahma-world manifests before one.
Question:
Why do the higher stages lack this consciousness? Answer:
As previously stated, because vitarka and vicāra are not present in the higher stages, these three groups of consciousness do not exist there.

When one in a higher stage desires to see, hear, or touch, the consciousness of the first dhyāna manifests and one sees, hears, and touches; this is because it is neither of the desire realm nor a fruit of cultivation.
Question:
When is it accomplished?
Answer: According to whichever consciousness manifests before one, the higher stages are then accomplished;
if that consciousness is abandoned, they are no longer accomplished, because the power of the mind is weak and inferior.

As long as this consciousness is present—whether it be visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, or tactile consciousness—at that time it is accomplished, because the mind is weak and is of a non-obscured neutral nature.
Therefore, they are accomplished for a single moment; having arisen from that state, they do not continue to follow.
Question:
It has already been understood when wholesome and defiled attainments (*samāpatti*) are acquired and when the various consciousnesses are accomplished.
How is that transformative mind (nirmāṇacitta) attained?
How many minds are attained at one time? Answer:
Through rebirth and through detachment from desire, one attains these various minds of transformation—
two, three, four, and likewise five, all at once. There are two causes and conditions for attaining the mind of transformation:

Regarding rebirth and the departure from desire, one may suddenly attain two, three, four, or five [minds] of rebirth. When one dies in a higher realm and is born in the Brahma Heaven, at that time one attains two minds that are the fruit of the first dhyāna:
one belonging to the desire realm and one belonging to the first dhyāna.
If one is born in the second dhyāna, one attains three minds:
first, that of the desire realm; second, that of the first dhyāna; and third, that of its own level.
If one is born in the third dhyāna, one attains four minds:
Three from the lower stages and one from its own stage.
If one is born in the fourth dhyāna, one obtains five minds:
four from the lower stages and one from its own stage.
This explains acquisition through rebirth. Regarding those who become free from desire: one who becomes free from the desires of the desire realm acquires two minds, as previously described.

One who becomes free from the desires of the first dhyāna acquires three minds; one who becomes free from the desires of the second dhyāna acquires four minds; and one who becomes free from the desires of the third dhyāna acquires five minds. Therefore, it is said that one may acquire the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) in a single moment without interruption.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the final path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) at the time of becoming free from desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):

that which is acquired but not abandoned refers to the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) belonging to the fruit of the first dhyāna, which is acquired when one becomes free from desire for the desire realm. This mind is not abandoned because it is bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the first dhyāna.

Regarding "those that are severed but not attained": this refers to the transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) resulting from the second, third, and fourth dhyānas of the desire realm. Because these transformation-minds of the three stages belong to the dharma of the desire realm, they are bound by the afflictions of the desire realm. Although the bonds of desire for the desire realm have been severed, they are not attained because the first dhyāna has not yet abandoned desire.
"Both obtained and abandoned" refers to the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) that is the fruit of the first dhyāna within the desire realm.
"Neither not obtained nor abandoned" refers to the remaining transformation-minds.
This should be explained according to the same principle up to the detachment from the third dhyāna.
Regarding these fourteen types of transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*), there are four belonging to the desire realm and ten belonging to the form realm.

Those transformative minds of the desire realm produce transformations of the desire realm, while those of the form realm produce transformations of the form realm, because they transform according to their own respective levels.
That transformation is of eight kinds:

one born in the desire realm manifests in the desire realm, manifesting both one's own body and the bodies of others; likewise, for one born in the form realm who manifests in the form realm, it is also thus.
The transformations of the desire realm consist of four bases (*āyatana*), while the transformations of the form realm consist of two bases.
Why is this? Because they do not transform the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, transformations are without mind; a single mind may produce one transformation or many, yet they belong to only one stage (*bhūmi*).
One who dwells in the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is able to cause them to endure.

Although a transformation ceases upon entering *nirvāṇa*, it may continue to function; for example, after the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta had entered *nirvāṇa*, his transformation caused fire to burn his body, and the entire body of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa remained preserved for a long time.
Because the World-Honored One has completed his Buddha-work of transforming those who are not yet ready for transformation, he enters parinirvāṇa without leaving behind a transformed body.
Question:
Does the transformation produced by cultivated wisdom also give rise to wisdom?

Answer: It is also because one gives rise to wisdom and subsequently attains the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*). Therefore, it is the wisdom acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) obtained by one who has previously abandoned desire.
The mind of transformation belonging to the Māra-heaven is [an example of] wisdom born of birth (*upapattilābhikī-prajñā*).
It is like when Māra transforms himself into the body of a Buddha, or when a celestial maiden of Māra transforms herself and approaches the Buddha, or as food consumed by a transformed person.
If the original transformer intended to nourish his own body, then that food, being present, is digested within the body of the transformer.
If one originally has no desire to nourish the body, then that food merely accumulates at the place where the emanated person resides.
Question:
How many kinds of emanation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) are accomplished?
Answer: There may be two, three, or four; five, seven, and nine;
increasing by three or even five—thus the transformative mind is established.

If one is born in the desire realm and has exhausted craving for the desire realm but not yet exhausted craving for the Brahma heavens, or if one is born in the Brahma heavens and has not yet exhausted craving for them, one possesses two.
If one is born in the second dhyāna and has not yet exhausted craving for it, one possesses three.
If one is born in the third dhyāna and has not yet exhausted craving for it, one possesses four [factors].
If one is born in the fourth dhyāna, one possesses five.
If one is born in the desire realm or in the Brahma-world, and has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but has not yet exhausted craving for the second dhyāna, one likewise possesses five.
If one is born in the second dhyāna, having exhausted craving for the second dhyāna but not yet exhausted craving for the third dhyāna, one accomplishes seven [factors].

Thus, it should be explained in detail that there are nine [factors]; furthermore, when craving for the fourth dhyāna is exhausted, being born in the third dhyāna increases three [factors], and being born in the first dhyāna increases five [factors].
Question:

What is the difference between a transformation [body] of the desire realm that is the fruit of the first dhyāna, and a transformation [body] of the first dhyāna stage that is the fruit of the first dhyāna? Answer:
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is superior because its sphere is superior.

Furthermore, while it is the fruit of the second dhyāna in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the fruit of the first dhyāna in the realm of form, it is said to be "superior in range" because the capacity to reach the second dhyāna from the desire realm is superior; thus, the realm of form is superior by virtue of its sphere.

All transformations are explained in this way: the transformative mind obtained through detachment from desire and the transformative mind obtained through skillful means each have fourteen types. When one is born into a lower stage from a higher stage, one obtains the fourteen types previously acquired through detachment from desire.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven;
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others.
Chapter Eight: Sūtra. Having already explained meditative concentration (samādhi), the sūtras shall now be explained.
The sublime meaning of the sūtras spoken by the Omniscient One, I shall now briefly explain; you who practice should listen well.
Because he knows all things, he is called the Omniscient One.
"All" refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*); one thoroughly knows all their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"That which is taught" refers to what has been personally expounded by the Omniscient One.
"Sublime meaning" refers to the profound and subtle significance of the nature and characteristics [of phenomena].
Since this subtle and sublime meaning is taught in the sūtras, it is called the "sublime meaning of the sūtras."
"Presently" refers to this treatise.
"Briefly explained" means that because what was spoken by the Muni is immeasurable and boundless, it is called a brief explanation.
Regarding the *sūtra*, there are generally five meanings:
First is "giving birth," because it gives birth to all meanings.
Second is "fountain-springing," because its flavor of meaning is inexhaustible.
Third is "manifestation," because it manifests all meanings.
The fourth is called "the plumb line," because it distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox.
The fifth is called "the stringing of garlands," because it threads together all dharmas.
These five meanings constitute the meaning of *sūtra*.

Although the meaning does not reside in the words, it is manifested through them; therefore, regarding the meaning of speech: it is said that names arise dependent on speech, and meanings are manifested dependent on names.
Those who listen well should unify their minds and listen with firm resolve.
Question:
The World-Honored One has spoken of giving, morality, and cultivation.
How many types are there for each of these?
Answer: Generosity and the observance of pure precepts each have four kinds;
meditative cultivation has two; these are designated as "meritorious qualities."
Fearing the three kinds of fear, and wishing to employ skillful means to enable others to transcend these three fears, the World-Honored One briefly explained these three kinds of merit.
Regarding those who fear poverty, he employs skillful means to enable them to transcend it; therefore, he speaks of giving.
For those who fear the terrors of the evil realms, one employs skillful means to enable them to cross over; therefore, the precepts are taught.
For those who fear the terrors of birth and death, one employs skillful means to enable them to cross over; therefore, cultivation is taught.
Question:
What is the nature of giving? Answer:
Volition associated with non-greed, arising simultaneously [with it] and sharing the same fruit,
produced from the objects and locations [of giving]— this is the nature of generosity (*dāna*).

Volition associated with the wholesome root of non-greed, produced from the objects and locations of the gift, along with the bodily and vocal actions that follow it, constitutes the self-nature of this five-aggregate (*pañcaskandha*) generosity, because it is said to be complete with [the sensory qualities of] form, fragrance, taste, and so forth.
To say that intention, aspiration, and so forth are not giving is incorrect. Why?
Because the name "giving" is applied to the object [of the gift] so that the World-Honored One may inspire the mind of the donor and cause their intention and aspiration to become firm.
The designation "giving" (dāna) is applied to the object; that is, it arises from the object being given.
Question:
Regarding the four kinds of giving mentioned previously, what constitutes the types of giving?
Answer:
That which is called self-grasping, as well as grasping others, or grasping both, or grasping neither.

There is giving for the sake of gathering oneself; there is giving for the sake of gathering others; there is giving for the sake of gathering both oneself and others; and there is giving for the sake of repaying kindness that is not for the sake of gathering oneself or others—namely, when an Arhat makes offerings to a Buddha, doing so to repay kindness rather than for the sake of self or others.
Regarding those who provide for themselves:
if one who has not yet abandoned desire makes offerings at a caitya,
as does an ordinary person who has abandoned desire, this is called giving for one’s own peace.
When noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire, as well as ordinary persons who have abandoned desire, make offerings to a caitya, they thereby encompass the act of giving.
This is because the recipient of the gift receives retribution in the desire realm; that is to say, those who have not yet abandoned desire are born into the desire realm.

Although ordinary persons may be free from desire and be reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm, they later still undergo the subsequent retribution and the indeterminate retribution of the desire realm.
This is called "gathering oneself but not gathering others."
Why is this? Because a caitya is not a sentient being.
One who is free from desire is no longer an ordinary person; [for such a one], with the exception of the fruit of the present life, [there is no further rebirth].
Giving to all sentient beings is called "gathering others.

Whether it be an Arhat or an Anāgāmin, with the exception of giving that produces its fruit in the present life, any other giving performed for the sake of sentient beings is called "gathering others" rather than "gathering oneself."
The Arhat does not take birth because it is not his lot.
Although the Anāgāmin takes birth in the realms of form and formlessness, he does not receive the fruit of giving; for the realms are established based on the severance of cause and effect.
One who has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality, and an ordinary person who has already abandoned such desire—
when giving to sentient beings, it should be known that both are included. That is to say,
when a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire and an ordinary person who has abandoned desire give to sentient beings, it should be known that both are included.
Those free from desire are no longer ordinary persons; having set aside the fruit of the present life, they make offerings at a caitya—this is neither included for themselves nor for others.

Whether it be an Arhat or an Anāgāmin, setting aside the gift that produces a fruit in the present life, when they make offerings at a caitya, this is neither for their own inclusion nor for the inclusion of others.
Because Arhats are without rebirth;
although Anāgāmins do undergo rebirth, it is not their lot in the desire realm, and thus they do not take [beings] into themselves.
Since a caitya is not a sentient being, it does not take others [into itself].
Recalling their original kindness and in order to repay that debt of gratitude, they continue to make offerings at the caityas even after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore:
Some, for the sake of gathering others, make offerings at the caityas.
Immeasurable multitudes who see or hear [this] all give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Or, making offerings to a *caitya* is also for the sake of gathering others.

By offering banners, streamers, flower-canopies, burning incense, and scattering flowers to a *caitya*, one causes immeasurable sentient beings who see it to give rise to sympathetic joy, thereby creating the cause for rebirth in heaven and liberation.
Therefore, the World-Honored One stated in the Sūtras that establishing a caitya at a site where none had previously been established can generate Brahma-merit (brahmapuṇya).
Because it gathers in immeasurable sentient beings, it is called Brahma-merit.
Question:
To what extent should one speak of "Brahma-merit"? Answer:

Some say that, with the exception of Bodhisattvas on the stage proximate to Buddhahood, the karma of all other sentient beings capable of producing superior fruits such as great wealth and great power constitutes the measure of Brahma-merit.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when the world is formed, all sentient beings and the receptacle world arise; the karma capable of producing this receptacle world is called the measure of Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Furthermore, regarding this giving:
those seven types of giving, such as that which is motivated by hope and so forth, are not supreme;
the eighth, which adorns the mind, is called the most excellent gift.

The Blessed One has taught eight kinds of giving: namely, giving out of hope, giving out of fear, giving in expectation of a return, giving with the anticipation of a reward, giving as a matter of family tradition, giving for the sake of rebirth in heaven, giving for the sake of seeking fame, and giving for the purpose of adorning the mind, for the purpose of subduing the mind, for the purpose of practicing in accordance with the path, and for the purpose of attaining the supreme goal.
Regarding "giving with expectation": because the giver selects a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) in order to seek a great fruit, they give to those who come seeking.
This giving to those who come seeking is what the ancient Abhidharma calls "giving with expectation."
Giving out of fear is giving only when facing loss; that is, seeing the prospect of losing something, one gives rather than lose it.
Giving for the sake of a return is thinking, "I have previously received benefit from this person; how could I not repay them?"
Giving with expectation of recompense is giving to another while expecting a return from them.
Giving according to family custom is practicing the generosity of one's ancestors rather than giving out of one's own conviction.
Giving with the aim of rebirth in heaven is giving for the sake of seeking birth in heaven.
Giving for the sake of reputation is giving for the sake of praise and renown.
These seven kinds of giving are despised by wisdom; therefore, they are not superior.
Giving without seeking the pleasures of birth and death is called the adornment of the mind in giving.
Because this is the skillful means of the Path, it is the foremost among all material gifts; it is called the supreme gift.
Having already explained giving, the fruits of giving shall now be explained:
longevity, physical beauty, strength, happiness, and eloquence— these five kinds of rewards,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands, are what the donor obtains.
Generosity is as explained above.
There are five kinds, as taught by the Blessed One in the *Pañcaguṇadānasūtra*.
Because one’s lifespan exists through eating and not through not eating, one gives the gift of longevity.
This applies even up to eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
A similar cause produces a similar fruit; that is to say, one obtains the retribution of longevity and so forth, up to eloquence.
It is just as when planting external seeds, one harvests fruit according to their kind; this case is likewise.
"Longevity" refers to humans and devas, not those in the miserable realms; this is spoken of as the giving of longevity because it is a sustaining cause (*dhāraṇa-hetu*).
As it is said that by practicing and cultivating the abstention from taking life, one attains long life, this is spoken of as such because it is an attracting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
For example, there are two kinds of mothers: the biological mother and the foster mother.
One who abstains from taking life is like the biological mother; one who provides food is like the foster mother.
Giving to animals yields fivefold retribution and a hundredfold merit, namely, that which is obtained by those who bring them together; thus it is explained at length.
Although one does not eat during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is still able to receive offerings.
Having already explained giving and its results—namely, that the gift is itself the result—I shall now explain [the following]:
Compassion (*maitrī*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the path of seeing, and the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
"Rising from those meditative attainments, the donor obtains the immediate fruit.

This means that if one rises from the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā*), the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha*), the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), and there is a donor who makes an offering, that donor obtains the immediate fruit.

Why is this? Because giving with the characteristic of providing peace and benefit to immeasurable sentient beings is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); since the body is permeated by this loving-kindness, the donor obtains the immediate fruit upon arising from this state.

The Samādhi of Non-contention prevents the afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings from arising; because it extensively gathers meritorious qualities to perfume the body, the donor who emerges from this state attains the fruit immediately.

Because the body has been perfumed by the vast merit of the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and because it resembles *nirvāṇa*, a donor who gives after emerging from this state obtains the immediate fruit.

Because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing have been eternally exhausted and the body has been perfumed by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), a donor who gives after emerging from this state obtains the immediate fruit.

Having severed the fetters through the cultivation of the path, the mind attains mastery and dwells in the fruit of arhatship; for one who has arisen from this state, the donor obtains the immediate fruit.
Having explained the immediate fruit, the great fruit shall now be explained.
If one gives to one's parents, to those who are ill, to Dharma-preachers,
and to the Bodhisattvas who attend the Buddha, the donor attains a great fruit.
Giving to these five kinds of persons yields a great fruit.
Why is this? Because parents have the great kindness of nurturing and giving birth to one's physical body, the giver obtains a great fruit.
Because the sick have no one to rely upon, which increases one’s heart of compassion, the giver obtains a great fruit.
Because the teacher of the Dharma increases the Dharma-body and demonstrates good and evil to others, the donor obtains a great fruit.
Because those who draw near to the stage of Buddhahood accumulate merit and extensively gather in sentient beings, the donor obtains a great fruit.
Question:
Is it the excellence of the intention and aspiration that renders the gift pure, or is it the excellence of the field of merit?
If it is the excellence of the intention and aspiration, for what reason does the World-Honored One praise the field of merit?
If the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is superior, why is it that giving to a single field of merit does not result in equal fruits?
Answer: Because the intention and aspiration (*āśaya-praṇidhāna*) are superior, the giving is pure.
Due to the power of the causes of the field of merit, it is therefore said first that the volition, the aspiration, and their attendants are called the "merit of giving.
When one gives with a pure mind, free from seeking for body or wealth, and acts in accordance with wisdom, such a donor shall obtain a great fruit.
If it were otherwise, then seeking fame while giving to a superior field of merit would not constitute the generosity of a Great Being.

If the power of the field alone produced demerit or merit, then one would necessarily incur an immediate retribution (ānantarya) simply by the power of the field; yet since this does not occur, one should know that it is the power of intention and aspiration that determines the result.
The field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is capable of giving rise to superior intentions and vows; for this reason, the World-Honored One praised the field of merit.
Question:
It is already understood how giving sustains the physical body (*rūpakāya*); how, then, does giving sustain the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?
Answer: To skillfully expound the teachings of the various sūtras, to remain far removed from all inversions,
and not to slander the Muni— this is called the gift of Dharma.

To make true distinctions regarding the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; to not be attached to fame or profit; and to extensively gather in and sustain sentient beings—this is called the gift of Dharma.

Although they are free from conceptual attachment, they speak erroneously; by slandering the Tathāgata’s true causes and conditions and forming contrary conceptions, one should know that this is the cause and condition for a distracted mind.
Although one speaks without error, the mind remains defiled by attachment, just like that merchant.
Therefore, the verse says:
"One does not know that the Muni’s teaching is like a sword, fire, or poison;"
To discern this well is like consuming ambrosia.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of inversion: inversion regarding phenomena (*dharma-viparyāsa*), inversion regarding persons (*pudgala-viparyāsa*), and inversion regarding time (*kāla-viparyāsa*).
Inversion regarding phenomena (*dharma-viparyāsa*) refers, for example, to teaching that one should cultivate the perception of purity (*śubha-saṃjñā*) in order to sever sensual desire.
Inversion regarding persons (*pudgala-viparyāsa*) refers to teaching loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to those who are possessed by sensual desire.
Regarding those who are subject to inversion, for those whose faculties are not yet mature, one teaches the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is by analogy with this that what is contrary to it is called the teaching of non-inverted dharma.
The gift of Dharma has already been explained; the gift of fearlessness shall now be discussed.
By teaching through the relinquishing of equal attachment, one consoles those who are terrified;
this is called the gift of fearlessness, which is able to destroy the fear of poverty.
If one sees sentient beings who are terrified by this life, the next life, or both, and who have abandoned the undertaking of precepts, one should speak words of compassionate consolation, saying:
"Sentient beings, do not be afraid."
"I shall perform for you what is necessary to enable you to attain fearlessness.
This is called the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
Just as that terror is like poverty, providing its true remedy is called the gift of fearlessness.
Having already explained the gift of fearlessness, the great gift shall now be explained:
To all classes of sentient beings, equally receiving the restraint of the precepts,
so that the flow of merit increases and expands— this is the great gift.
The World-Honored One has declared that the five precepts constitute a great gift, because they encompass boundless sentient beings and give rise to boundless happiness.
Material giving cannot encompass all sentient beings; only the reception of the precepts can do so.

Having already received and upheld the five precepts, throughout one's entire life and in every moment of thought toward all sentient beings, one attains twelve kinds of unprecedented restraint (*saṃvara*). Through these two types of wholesome roots, one gives rise to bodily and vocal actions, both manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest (*avijñapti*), such that the flow of those precepts continues in succession without interruption.
Question:
The four kinds of giving have already been explained; what are the first four kinds of precepts? Answer:
The restraint of the desire realm and that born of dhyāna, the untainted (anāsrava) restraint, and the restraint of abandonment—these are said to be the types of restraint.
There are four kinds of restraint: namely, the restraint of individual liberation (prātimokṣa), the restraint of dhyāna, the untainted restraint, and the restraint of abandonment.
The prātimokṣa restraint refers to the precepts received by the seven classes of followers.
The dhyāna restraint refers to the outflow-tainted precepts that arise concomitantly with meditative absorption.
The untainted restraint refers to the precepts of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The restraint of abandonment refers to the precepts that arise concomitantly with the nine paths of non-obstruction for the purpose of abandoning the desires of the desire realm.
If it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is the dhyāna-precept; if it is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is the uncontaminated precept.
This restraint has already been explained in the Chapter on Karma.
Having explained the four types of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the remaining four shall now be discussed:
Some receive it out of hope, while others maintain it out of fear.
There is that which accords with the factors of enlightenment, as well as pure ethical discipline.

There are four kinds of ethical discipline: namely, ethical discipline out of hope, ethical discipline out of fear, ethical discipline that accords with the factors of enlightenment, and pure ethical discipline.
The precept for the sake of hope refers to maintaining the precepts in order to seek rebirth in the heavens or other such realms.

The precept out of fear refers to maintaining the precepts out of dread of self-reproach, dread of reproach by others, dread of punishment, dread of the miserable destinies, dread of being unable to make a living, or dread of ill repute.

The morality of the factors of enlightenment is observed for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of providing the necessary requisites for practice, and for the sake of seeking the supreme meaning.
Pure morality refers to untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*), because it is free from defilement.
Question:
How does one purely maintain the precepts? Answer:
The root is pure, the retinue is pure; it is not destroyed by discursive thoughts, it embraces right mindfulness, and it accords with parinirvāṇa.

There are five causes and conditions for the purity of ethical discipline: namely, purity of the root, purity of the retinue, not being destroyed by discursive thoughts, embracing right mindfulness, and being directed toward liberation.
Purity of the root means being free from the fundamental paths of action.
Purity of the secondary factors means being free from the preliminary means of killing and so forth.
Not being destroyed by discursive thoughts means being free from the disturbances of the three types of thought: desire, ill-will, and harm.
One who maintains right mindfulness maintains mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; for this reason, they are also free from all indeterminate states of mind.

One who is correctly oriented toward liberation upholds the precepts for the sake of liberation, not for the sake of body, wealth, or other activities; therefore, it is also said that this accords with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

Through these five causes and conditions, the precepts are purified; the World-Honored One has taught that they yield great fruit because they bring about freedom from all afflictions and disturbances.
Question:
It is already known that the precepts, which are the basis for all correct practices, are like a vessel of celestial virtue (*devakumbha*).
What are the two kinds of cultivation? Answer:
The dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the immeasurables involve both the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice.
The meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing—the meaning of these two types of cultivation is likewise so.

These various merits of the dhyānas and so forth perfume the mind, just as a garment is perfumed, as hemp is perfumed by flowers, or as gold is refined; therefore, it is said that there is "cultivation like perfuming a garment," "cultivation like perfuming hemp," and "cultivation like refining gold."

The present is cultivated through practice (*bhāvanā*), while the future is cultivated through attainment (*pratilambha*); this is because the present is currently functioning, whereas the future is yet to arise.
The present performs its activity, while the future is that which is to be performed; this is because the present has already come into being, whereas the future is yet to be attained.
The present is the portion of manifestation; the future is the portion of attainment.
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna), formless attainments (ārūpya), and immeasurables (apramāṇa) have already been explained at length in the section on concentration (samādhi).
The contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) has non-attachment as its nature, because it is the antidote to attachment.

Furthermore, in order to counteract four types of craving, another four [meditations] are taught: namely, one cultivates the contemplation of a corpse to sever craving for deportment; one cultivates the contemplation of the livid-blue and so forth to sever craving for form; one cultivates the contemplation of the skeleton by removing skin and flesh to sever craving for touch; and one cultivates the contemplation of the separation of bones and joints to sever craving for locations.
This contemplation of impurity further comprises four types: the stage of decline, the stage of maintenance, the stage of excellence, and the stage of certainty.
As for the stage of decline, one who dwells therein will regress.
The stage of abiding refers to dwelling therein without advancing or regressing.
The stage of excellence refers to dwelling therein with certain upward progression.
The stage of certainty refers to dwelling therein in accordance with the Noble Path.
As for the realms (*dhātu*), they are the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for the stages (*bhūmi*), they are the ten stages: the desire realm, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), and their four associated [stages].
The basis (*āśraya*) is the desire realm.
The practitioner does not practice [as such];
the object of focus is the desire realm;
the application of mindfulness is the application of mindfulness to the body.

The knowledge of the wise (*jñāna*) and the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) are not born from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Therefore, they are associated with the three faculties and fall within the three periods of time. That which pertains to the past takes the past as its object; that which pertains to the present takes the present as its object; and that which pertains to the future—if it is a dharma destined to arise—takes the future as its object, whereas if it is a dharma not destined to arise, it takes all three periods of time as its object.
This is wholesome, having an indeterminate object.
It is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, having a neither-learner-nor-non-learner object.
It is abandoned by the path of cultivation, having an object abandoned by the path of cultivation.
It should be said that it takes meaning as its object. Question:
Is it acquired through skillful means (*upāya*) or acquired through the transcendence of desire (*vairāgya*)?
Answer: It is obtained both through application (*prayoga*) and through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*).
If one attains the first dhyāna by abandoning the desires of the desire realm, up to attaining the fourth dhyāna by abandoning the desires of the third dhyāna, the subsequent application manifests.
Question:
What is the skillful means for the contemplation of impurity? Answer:

One who cultivates the contemplation of impurity goes to a charnel ground and thoroughly grasps that sign. Having grasped it, he returns to his seat, washes his feet, and sits down comfortably; with body relaxed and mind free from the hindrances, he takes that external object as a point of comparison for his own body.

One fixes the mind upon the bones of the feet, the shinbones, the kneecaps, the thighs, the hips, the shanks, the vertebrae, the ribs, the bones of the hands, the forearms, the shoulders, the neck, the jaw, the teeth, the gums, and the skull; or one fixes the mind between the eyebrows.
If one prefers a concise contemplation, one first proceeds from the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

If one prefers an extensive contemplation, one contemplates from the skull at the space between the eyebrows down to the bones of the feet, and then from a single sitting, a single room, a single hall, a single monastery, a single village, a single district, and finally an entire country.
If it were merely produced from thought, such a thing would be impossible.
If it pervades the entire earth up to the range of one's vision, one is able to perceive that place as filled with white bones.
If one further abbreviates the process, one returns step by step until the mind is fixed between the eyebrows.
This is called the completion of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the contemplation of impurity, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning those who take a limited object as their focus but do not possess mastery over that limited scope.
"Having few objects but not having few masteries" means that one repeatedly enters the contemplation of impurity regarding one's own body.

"Having few masteries but not having few objects" means that although one observes the impurity of the entire great earth and the four oceans all at once, one is unable to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity.
"Having few objects and having little mastery" means that at one time one contemplates the impurity of one's own body, yet is unable to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity.

"Neither having few objects nor having little mastery" means that one is able to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity even when the impurity extends throughout the four seas and the great earth.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), there is that which has an immeasurable object (*anantālambana*) but is not of immeasurable mastery (*na vaśitānantya*).

This is explained by four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). That which has an immeasurable object but is not of immeasurable mastery refers to one who perceives the entire earth and the four oceans as impure, yet is unable to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity.
"Mastery over the immeasurable while not being immeasurable in terms of the object" means that one repeatedly enters the contemplation of impurity with respect to one's own body.

"Both immeasurable in terms of the object and mastery over the immeasurable" means that one is also able to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity regarding the impurities that fill the great earth and the four oceans.

That which is neither immeasurable through conditions nor immeasurable through mastery refers to being unable to repeatedly enter the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) regarding one's own body.
Having already explained the contemplation of impurity, the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) shall now be explained.
Ānā means "bringing in"; apāna means "taking away.
It is also called āśvāsa-praśvāsa. Smṛti means "mindfulness" or "recollection."
In *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), one binds the mind with precise attention so that it is not deluded; because one cultivates that mindfulness, it is called "cultivation.

Since this mindfulness of breathing is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and because mindfulness increases within that category, it is termed "mindfulness of breathing," just as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) or the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
Regarding the initial arising: within the mother’s womb, at the site of the navel, a karmically produced wind arises, either moving downward or upward.
That which moves downward creates the lower parts of the body and all the pores of the skin.
As for "moving upward," it refers to the creation of the upper body and all its pores.
Once the pores are formed, it begins with the first exhalation and continues until the final exhalation at the end of life.

The same applies to meditative attainment (*samāpatti*): namely, emerging from the first [attainment] and entering the first [attainment], and entering the first [attainment] and emerging from the first [attainment].

One acquires six kinds of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) through six causal conditions, namely: counting (*gaṇanā*), following (*anugama*), settling (*sthāpanā*), observing (*upalakṣaṇā*), returning (*vivartana*), and purifying (*pariśuddhi*).
Regarding counting: the practitioner skillfully binds the mind to the counting of inhalations and exhalations, such that there is not a single breath that is not perceived.
If the mind becomes distracted, one may at times count too few, at times count too many, or at times count in a confused manner.
In the counting of subtraction, one treats two as one; in the counting of addition, one treats one as two; in the counting of disorder, one perceives exiting as entering and entering as exiting.
That which is not confused in mind is called "equal counting."
The five exhalations and the five inhalations are called the ten counts.
If, while counting, the practitioner’s mind becomes distracted within the ten, they should begin counting again from one.
Once the number ten has been reached, whether there is distraction or no distraction, one must return to starting from one.

Because of the fear that the mind might scatter, it does not exceed ten; because of the fear that the mind might become concentrated [and thus lose count], it does not fall below ten; and because there are no numbers beyond this that have not already been counted.
As for "following": when the inhalation and exhalation pass away, where do they go? Is it by following them that one discerns whether they are long or short?
Does it pervade the entire body, or does it reside in a single location?
Is the entry far or near? At what point does one turn back?
As for "stopping," it means to settle the mind upon a single part of the body according to one's preference, binding the mind there to cause it to abide and observe.
Whether that breath is beneficial or harmful to the body, whether it is cold or warm— observing such things as these,
through cultivation and intensive cultivation, they appear before one at will, just like recollecting one's own name.

"Returning" means that if one relies on thoughts of sensual desire, one acts with little diligence; if one relies on thoughts of renunciation, one acts with diligent effort. "Purifying" means purifying the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

That practitioner forms a single perception regarding the inhalation and exhalation; he contemplates the body as a bamboo tube and the breath as a string of pearls passing through it. As the inhalation and exhalation remain unmoving, no tactile consciousness arises within the body; this is called the accomplishment of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Some say that one may also give rise to body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) without, however, causing injury to the body.
Furthermore, when a practitioner analyzes inhalation and exhalation down to their ultimate atoms (paramāṇu), this is called the contemplation of the body (kāyānupaśyanā).
To experience the inhalation and exhalation is called "feeling" (vedanā); to contemplate that feeling is called "contemplation of feeling" (vedanānupassanā).
To cognize the inhalation and exhalation is called "consciousness" (viññāṇa); to contemplate that consciousness is called "contemplation of consciousness" (viññāṇānupassanā).

The perception of inhalation and exhalation is called "perception"; the contemplation of that perception is called "contemplation of perception. This refers to the disintegration of matter into atoms until matter is completely exhausted and extinguished; subsequently, one causes joy, perception, and consciousness to arise and become manifest. One then contemplates those three as the seeds for the skillful means of the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

It is not that the out-breath arises while the in-breath has not yet ceased, nor that the in-breath arises while the out-breath has not yet ceased; this is called crossing over by means of the practice of impermanence regarding ānāpāna.
Because the inhalation is suppressed, the exhalation ceases; this is called the perfection of ascetic practice (*duṣkaracaryā*).
This is termed obtaining the seed of the wishless liberation door (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) through skillful means.
The arising, abiding, and ceasing of inhalation and exhalation are not under one's own mastery; this is called the contemplation of the non-self (*anātman*) based on inhalation and exhalation.

Because inhalation and exhalation are free from causes such as permanence and so forth, they are empty; this practice is called obtaining the seed of the gateway to liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) through skillful means.

To give rise to a mind of revulsion toward inhalation and exhalation and to turn toward *nirvāṇa* is called obtaining the seed of the gateway to liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) through skillful means.

Based on those three mild samādhis, one progresses through the intermediate and superior stages; thus, in this sequence, one proceeds from the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) up to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Question:
The Blessed One spoke of the elements (dhātu).
What is this? The answer is:
Twenty are taught as belonging to the desire realm; those of the form realm are either sixteen or twenty.
The formless realm has four [levels], explained according to their sequential locations.

Regarding the statement that "twenty constitute the desire realm," this refers to the eight great hells, animals, hungry ghosts, the four continents, and the six heavens of the desire realm; these twenty are said to comprise the desire realm.
These sentient beings receive bodies, requisites, and a second [consciousness] through desire; therefore, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for the sixteen levels of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are: Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha. These sixteen abodes are called the Form Realm.
There are those who maintain that there are seventeen [realms], namely the sixteen as previously described plus Mahābrahmā.
Those sentient beings therein possess a physical body (*rūpakāya*), yet it is neither a collection of external requisites nor a second [body]; therefore, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The formless realm consists of four levels: namely, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because the sentient beings in these realms do not possess material bodies and are free from desire for form, they are called the formless realm.
Question:
How are the three realms established?
Is it for the sake of severing craving?
Is it for the sake of their locus?

If the abandonment of craving were to be categorized by its locus, there would be nine types: namely, the abandonment of craving for the desire realm within the desire realm, and likewise for the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If they were established by way of location, there would be forty, as previously stated. Answer:

They are spoken of in terms of the total abandonment of craving; that is to say, the abandonment of craving in the desire realm pertains to the desire realm, and likewise for the abandonment of craving in the form realm and the abandonment of craving in the formless realm.

Because the desire realm is indeterminate, it consists of one type of latent tendency (*anuśaya*); because the form and formless realms are determinate, they do not consist of a single type of latent tendency.
Question:
How are the realms established?
Answer: They are explained according to the order of their locations.
Some say they proceed from bottom to top: that is, starting from the lowest Avīci Hell, followed by the Mahāraurava Hell, and so on in succession up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Above Akaniṣṭha, there is further the Avīci Hell, continuing in succession down to Akaniṣṭha itself.

If one abandons the desires of a single desire realm, one abandons the desires of all desire realms; if one attains the supernormal power of the first dhyāna, one can reach one desire realm and one Brahma world.
Furthermore, there are those who wish to establish the realms as extending everywhere in all directions.
Question:
The World-Honored One has spoken of the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is this? Answer:
The happy realms exist in the desire realm and in three stages of the form realm.
The same applies to the three formless [realms]; these are called the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

The happy destinies of the desire realm—namely, gods and humans—the first three stages of the form realm, and the first three stages of the formless realm: these seven stages are said to be the stations of consciousness.

Those sentient beings who possess form have accomplished a physical body; those with various bodies have various shapes; those with various perceptions have perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—this is called the first station of consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding the "diverse bodies," it is as previously explained. "A single perception" refers to a defiled perception.
When those Brahmakāyika gods are first born, they form this thought:
"I have been born from Mahābrahmā."
The Great Brahmā deity forms this thought:
"I am able to produce those beings in their various high and low stations," as well as because of his possession of vitarka, vicāra, and consciousness.
Thus, the Brahmā deities possess diverse bodies; this is called the second station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
"Single body" refers to the equality of the physical form, shape, and dimensions.
"Diverse perceptions" refers to the perceptions of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

When the faculty of equanimity—which is the antidote to the weariness caused by the fundamental faculty of joy—manifests, and having abandoned that weariness, the faculty of joy manifests once again, this is called the third station of consciousness.

Regarding "a single body and a single perception": "a single body" is as previously explained; "single perception" refers to pleasure. This is called the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
As for "formless beings," they do not possess a physical body because they have transcended desire for form.

"Transcending all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*)" is said because one practices by departing from form; this is because the perception of form is associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*).

If one departs from the desire of the first dhyāna, one transcends the practice of sensual desire; if one departs from the desire of the fourth dhyāna, one transcends the practice of form. For this reason, it is said that "perceptions of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*) are extinguished," as these are associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Regarding "not attending to various perceptions": those various perceptions refer to their being universally dispersed throughout the stage of the fourth dhyāna, because they take the various sense bases (*āyatana*) as their objects.
