Regarding the statement that "two, or six, seven, or eight [faculties] are obtained at the time of initial birth, and these should be known as the retributive faculties of the desire realm": these faculties arise gradually for those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture. At the very first moment of birth, they obtain two faculties, namely, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
That momentary mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is defiled, not undefiled, because it arises as a continuation of the mind.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is likewise.
Other faculties may also be obtained [at that moment], but they are not mentioned because they are not retribution (*vipāka*).

Those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) possess six faculties without physical form—namely, the five material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Those with one gender possess seven, and those with both genders possess eight;

this refers exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding "six in the form realm and one in the formless realm": beings in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) obtain six faculties. Because they are exclusively born by transformation, they lack male and female [faculties], as has already been explained previously.
In the formless realm, there is only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Question:
At the time of death, how many faculties are finally relinquished?
Answer: One abandons four, eight, or nine, or else one abandons ten;
whether through gradual or sudden death, for each wholesome abandonment, five are increased.

Regarding the gradual or sudden death involving the relinquishing of four, eight, nine, or ten faculties: when one dies gradually with an indeterminate mind, one relinquishes four faculties, namely: the body, the mind, life, and equanimity.

If one dies simultaneously with a mind that is formless and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), one relinquishes eight faculties: namely, the five faculties beginning with the eye, the mental faculty (*manas*), the life-faculty (*jīvita*), and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣā*).
With an indeterminate mind, those of one gender relinquish nine, and those of both genders relinquish ten; the same applies to an unwholesome (*akuśala*) mind.
Question:
How many faculties (*indriya*) does a wholesome mind (*kuśalacitta*) relinquish? Answer:
The wholesome faculties each increase by five.
If one dies with a wholesome mind, the five faculties beginning with faith each increase; this refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm.

Regarding those who pass away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are reborn in a higher realm: with the exception of those without sexual organs (*avyañjana*) and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), this is because they have abandoned the categories of both [male and female] in their detachment from desire.
The same should be said for those who die at the end of life in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*); it follows the sense faculties they possess, and there is no gradual death.

This explains the relinquishing (*tyāga*) of the faculties when they are present before one, not their non-possession (*aprāpti*). Regarding the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is said that there is acquisition (*prāpti*) and relinquishing.

As for the wholesome (*kuśala*), if one dies in this very life, it is said that there is the relinquishing of the practice (*carita-tyāga*); if one is born in another place, then there is the relinquishing of the acquisition (*prāpti-tyāga*).
Question:
How many are abandoned by insight (dṛṣṭi-heya), how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and how many are not to be abandoned (aheya)? Answer:
"Two are abandoned by both [paths], four are not abandoned; the six faculties are of two kinds; three are untainted and not abandoned;
the rest are abandoned by the path of cultivation. Regarding "two are abandoned by both, four are not abandoned":

this refers to the mind faculty (*manendriya*), the pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*), the joy faculty (*saumanasyendriya*), and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*). These possess three types: they may be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not abandoned (*aheya*).
For those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), what is severed by the path is said to be severed by vision (darśana-prahātavya).
For those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), what is severed by the path is said to be severed by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
That which is untainted (anāsrava) is said to be not severed.

Regarding the six faculties being of two kinds: this refers to the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), which is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) as well as abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are abandoned through cultivation and are not abandoned (i.e., are not subject to abandonment), because they are not defiled (*akliṣṭa*). They are not abandoned through seeing.
The three untainted [faculties] are not abandoned because they are exclusively untainted.
As for the others being abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), this means that the remaining nine faculties are abandoned through the path of cultivation.

The eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are not abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) because they are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); nor are they unconditioned (*aheya*) because they fall within the cycle of birth.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), because it is associated with the five groups of consciousness, is not abandoned by insight; because it arises from afflictions, it is not non-abandonable.
Question:
If one possesses a faculty, how many faculties does that person possess?
Answer:
One may achieve three, four, five, seven, eight, eleven, or thirteen;
these are said to be the definite achievements.

If one possesses the faculty of mind (*manas*), one necessarily possesses three faculties—namely, mind, life, and equanimity (*upekṣā*); as for the others, they may or may not be possessed. Regarding the faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue:

if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one necessarily possesses them; if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has acquired them without losing them, then one possesses them; however, if one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or if one is born in the desire realm at a stage where the fetal elements have gradually thickened and the faculties are not yet complete, or if one has acquired them but lost them, then one does not possess them.

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is necessarily possessed by those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but is not possessed by those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*), it is necessarily possessed by those born in the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna-deva*), by those born in the lower heavens, and by noble ones (*ārya*) born in the higher realms; however, it is not possessed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the higher realms.
The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) is necessarily accomplished by those born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
the rest is as explained for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is necessarily accomplished by those born in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), but is not accomplished by those born in the higher realms.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is necessarily possessed by one who has not yet abandoned desire, but is not possessed by one who has abandoned desire.
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*) are necessarily possessed by one who has not severed the roots of goodness, but are not possessed by one who has severed them.

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), noble ones (*ārya*) in any given stage necessarily possess those of the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*); ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not possess them.
As it is with the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*), so it is with the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā-indriya*).

If one possesses the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*), one necessarily possesses four faculties, namely: the body, the mind (*manas*), life (*jīvitendriya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). The rest is as previously stated.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one also possesses four faculties, namely: life, the mind, pleasure, and equanimity.
If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses five faculties: namely, the body, mind, life, equanimity, and the eye faculty.
The same applies to the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
If one accomplishes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one also accomplishes five faculties, namely: joy, pleasure (*sukha*), mind (*manas*), life (*jīvita*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If one accomplishes the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily accomplishes seven faculties, namely: body (*kāya*), mind, life, and the four sensations (*vedanā*) excluding the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*).
If one possesses the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), one necessarily possesses eight faculties: namely, the aforementioned seven and one of the sexual organs.
The same applies to the female faculty (*strīndriya*).
If one possesses the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), one also possesses eight faculties: namely, the body, mind, life, and the five feelings.

If one accomplishes the faculty of faith, one also accomplishes eight faculties, namely: the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty, the life faculty, and the faculty of equanimity.
The same applies to the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

If one accomplishes the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya), one necessarily accomplishes eleven faculties: namely, the mental faculty (manas), the life faculty (jīvita), the faculty of joy (saumanasya), the faculty of pleasure (sukha), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā), the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā), and the faculty of "already known."
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is also like this.

If one possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," one necessarily possesses thirteen faculties: namely, the body, mind, life, suffering, pleasure, joy, equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Question:
How many faculties (indriya) attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya? Answer:
By means of nine faculties, one attains the first fruit; Or by means of eleven faculties, one obtains the second stage of a śramaṇa;
It is said that by means of [eleven] faculties, one ultimately realizes the fourth fruit.

Regarding "by means of nine faculties one attains the first fruit": nine faculties bring about the attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), namely: the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) pertains to the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), while the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñendriya) pertains to the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga); both possess seven faculties.

Regarding the attainment of two fruits of śrāmaṇya: if one attains the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin through the exhaustion of the double portion of desire, nine faculties are involved, as previously explained.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* through the exhaustion of sensual desire, there are likewise nine faculties: eight as previously described, with the three feelings (*vedanā*) being mentioned according to whichever is applicable.

If one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* by way of the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*) through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), there are seven: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
The untainted path consists of eight faculties: the seven preceding ones and the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*).
The sequential attainment of the fruit of *anāgāmin* is likewise.

Regarding the statement that one reaches the culmination of the fourth fruit by means of eleven faculties: one attains the fruit of *arhat* through eleven faculties, namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the three faculties of sensation (*vedanā*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the faculty of "already known," and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

The faculty of "already known" (*ājñendriya*) pertains to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), while the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) pertains to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Question: How is this so?
Is it fixed by way of category (*bhāga-niyata*) or fixed by way of function (*vṛtti-niyata*)?
If it were fixed by way of category, then the fruit of *anāgāmin* would also possess three feelings.
If it were fixed by way of function, these three functions do not exist; since even two feelings do not operate simultaneously, how much less could there be three?
Answer: Because it is attained through the body of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-kāya*) and not by means of momentary [consciousness].

That is to say, one attains the fruit of Arhatship through the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); having fallen away from that, one attains it again through the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); and having fallen away from that as well, one attains it again through the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). However, the fruit of Anāgāmin is received through this [faculty of equanimity]; if one falls away from it, one must receive it again from this very same faculty and not from any other.
Question:
The World-Honored One has taught in the sūtras the six groups of consciousness.
What objects do these various consciousnesses cognize?
Answer: If one apprehends the objects of the sense faculties, these are the five types of mental domains;
if one apprehends all phenomena, this is what is called the mental consciousness.

If one takes the objects of the sense faculties as the fivefold sphere of the mind, these are the five objects such as form, which are apprehended by the five consciousnesses: eye-consciousness apprehends form, and so on, up to body-consciousness apprehending tangibles; this is because they apprehend specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and because their objects are present.

If it is said that grasping all phenomena refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is because the mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its object, due to its engagement with general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), its nature of reflection, and its repeated recollection.
This meaning has been explained in detail as previously stated in the "Chapter on Elements" (Dhātuvarga).
The objects of consciousness and the objects of knowledge shall now be explained:
The aggregates of the desire realm and the form realm, Those of the formless realm, and those that are untainted (anāsrava).
There are eight [factors] that are both with support and without support, as well as those two unconditioned [phenomena].
There are ten factors that are associated or dissociated with the desire realm; it is the same for the form and formless realms:
conditioned phenomena, untainted phenomena (both associated and dissociated), the two kinds of unconditioned phenomena, and the wholesome and indeterminate.
Question:
These ten dharmas are known by wisdom.
For each individual wisdom, how many dharmas serve as its objective sphere?
Answer: One should know that five factors are the objective domain of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna);
seven factors serve as its conditions for the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna); and three factors are the objective domain of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).

Regarding the five dharmas that should be known as the objective domain of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*): these are the associated and dissociated [factors] of the desire realm, the associated and dissociated [factors] of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the wholesome (*kuśala*).

Regarding the seven [categories] being the conditions for subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): this refers to the associated and dissociated [factors], the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the wholesome (*kuśala*) belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the three objects of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*): this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with the desire and form realms as well as the untainted realm.
One should know that the *sāsrava* (with-outflows) consists of ten; the knowledge of cause and effect consists of six;
liberation is one, while the path consists of two; the remaining two have nine as their objects.
Regarding "one should know that the *sāsrava* consists of ten": conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) operates upon all ten factors, because its scope is extensive.

Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of cause and effect consists of six types": the knowledge of suffering and its origin knows six dharmas; namely, those associated with and dissociated from the three realms. This is because they are objects of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) realm and because they consist of both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Regarding the first, liberation: the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) takes one dharma as its object, namely the unconditioned good (*asaṃskṛta-kuśala*), because its objective sphere is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding the second, the path: the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) takes two dharmas as its objects, namely the conditioned outflow-free (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) associated and dissociated [dharmas], because its objective sphere consists of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the "other two objects, nine": the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) take nine dharmas as their objects, excluding the indeterminate unconditioned (*avyākṛtāsaṃskṛta*), because they have the four truths as their objective domain.
Question:
By what are the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) proclived?
Answer: The various afflictions of one’s own stage certainly act as fetters within that same stage;
those of their own kind and the universal ones act as fetters toward their respective kinds.

Regarding the fact that the various afflictions of a particular stage definitely act as fetters toward that same stage: the afflictions of the desire realm act upon the phenomena of the desire realm, and this applies likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because they are superior and because they act as antidotes, the lower [factors] do not cause the higher to arise;
because they involve bodily conduct free from desire, the higher do not cause the lower to arise.

Regarding those that are "universal within their own category" (*sarvatraga-svadhātu*), these are the factors of one's own category that are driven by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of their own category; those that are "universal" (*sarvatraga*) also belong to other categories, because they have five types of objects.

If dharmas are fixed within the three realms and are driven by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms, one should know that they are produced in two realms; the same applies to those fixed in one realm.

Regarding "if dharmas are fixed within the three realms and are driven by the proclivities of the three realms": these refer to the five kinds of dharmas subsumed under the three realms, which are driven by all the proclivities of those three realms.
All such phenomena should be explained according to what is appropriate.

Regarding "one should know that which arises from two realms": this refers to the phenomena subsumed within two realms, which are driven by the afflictions of those two realms as appropriate—namely, vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and chanda (desire).
The five types of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are governed by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of both the desire and form realms, namely the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The five types of the three realms are governed by all the underlying tendencies of those three realms.
In this way, all phenomena are to be understood according to their respective applications.

"The same applies to a single element" means that if a phenomenon belongs to a specific element, it is driven by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of that same element; this refers to the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The five types [of fetters] in the desire realm are all driven by the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of that same desire realm.
In this manner, all phenomena are to be understood according to their respective correspondences.
This sutra was taught by the Muni; its nature has already been analyzed.
"Consciousness, knowledge, and the latent tendencies—know that these are the three gates.

This sūtra spoken by the Buddha has been fully analyzed by me; it should be understood through these three gates, namely: the gate of consciousness, the gate of knowledge, and the gate of latent tendencies."

As with giving, the five aggregates (skandhas) whose nature is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are known by seven knowledges (jñānas), excluding subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
Because they belong to the desire realm, subsequent knowledge is excluded;
because they are tainted (sāsrava), the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are excluded.
They are cognized by three consciousnesses—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—because they are subsumed within four bases (*āyatana*).
They are all pervasive in the desire realm and are the objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
The precepts (*śīla*) are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
They are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
They are governed by all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and path-of-cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The cultivated (*bhāvita*) is the nature of non-negligence (*apramāda*); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

It is cognized by the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). It is associated with all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) throughout the three realms.
All sūtras speak in this manner according to what is appropriate. To summarize the meaning:

those who wish to understand the inclusion [of phenomena] should contemplate the establishment of the elements (*dhātu*); those who wish to understand the gateway of knowledge (*jñāna*) should contemplate the establishment of the truths (*satya*); those who wish to understand the gateway of consciousness (*vijñāna*) should contemplate the establishment of the sense bases (*āyatana*); and those who wish to understand the gateway of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) should contemplate the establishment of the categories (*prakāra*).
Thus it is said; this concludes the easily understood Sūtra Chapter.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta composed [this work],
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others;
having already analyzed all phenomena, each is established according to its specific continuity.
Regarding the various meanings explained above, I shall now briefly expound them.
Having already analyzed each phenomenon (*dharma*) as a distinct and continuous succession, I have also explained the various categories of how phenomena successively continue one another.

Regarding the various miscellaneous meanings mentioned above—those which were determined to be explained in continuous succession—the explanation of these very miscellaneous meanings has now been completed; they are discussed in this chapter, and I shall now briefly explain them.
"Having an object (sālambana) and being associated (saṃprayukta), having mental formations (sasaṃskāra) and having a basis (sāśraya)—
mind and all mental factors (citta-caittas) are spoken of as having these identical meanings.
This is the differentiation of the names for these various minds and mental factors.
Because that [condition] exists, it is said to "have an object" (*sālambana*).
Because it operates upon an objective sphere (*viṣaya*), and because the factors of time, basis, activity, and object all operate together, it is said to be "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).
That which possesses activity is wisdom (*prajñā*); this has already been explained in the section on knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because it performs activity toward conditions, it is said to have activity;
because it turns in dependence upon others, it is said to have dependence.
Arising from conditions and also having causes—thus it has causes and is also conditioned.
One should know that the locus, the path, and the fruit exist;
these are the various distinctions in the names for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because they arise from the conjunction of this or that condition, they are said to be "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
It is called a "cause" because it gives rise to other phenomena;
it is called "having a cause" by virtue of the power of that cause;
and it is called "conditioned" because it is produced by causes, conditions, and so forth.
It is called a "basis of discourse" (*vāda-sthāna*) because it is capable of generating discourse.
It is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it is subsumed under the past, future, and present paths.
It is called "having fruit" (*saphala*) because it possesses a result.
"Faulty, obscured, defiled, base, and dark;
wholesome, conditioned, called 'cultivation,' and also termed 'development.
Regarding 'faulty, obscured, defiled, base, and dark': these are synonyms for the unwholesome and the obscured-indeterminate."

It is said to be "with fault" because it coexists with faults; it is said to be "obscured" in the sense that it is loathsome and detestable, being covered by afflictions and secondary afflictions; it is said to be "defiled" in the sense that it is shrouded by outflows, being stained by the impurities of affliction; it is said to be "lowly" because it is utterly base; and it is said to be "dark" because it is shrouded in gloom.
There are two kinds of black: defiled black and disagreeable black.
Here, defiled black is being discussed, not disagreeable black, because disagreeable black also includes that which is black due to its unwholesome retribution.
Regarding the statement that "wholesome conditioned phenomena are called 'cultivation' (āsevana) and also termed 'development' (bhāvanā)," these are different names for wholesome conditioned dharmas.
They are called "wholesome" because they are subsumed under wholesome factors and result in desirable fruits; they are called "cultivation" and "development" because they increase merit and virtue.

This explains that "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and "cultivation through practice" (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*)—where "practice" (*niṣevaṇa*) has the sense of frequenting—and "seeding" (*bīja*) has the sense of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): that which is present is called "practice," while that which is future is called "cultivation"; thus, it refers to wholesome conditioned phenomena.

Regarding the cultivation of remedies (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhāvanā*), it is said that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also cultivation.
Question:
What are the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?
Answer: The two meditative attainments of non-perception, as well as the category of sentient beings,
the groups of phrases, words, and names, the life-faculty, and the acquisition of dharmas.
Regarding "non-perception" (asaṃjñin): for those non-perceiving beings, the mind and mental factors that arise at birth cease.
Some say it is the fruit of the meditative attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
Others say it is called the fruit belonging to the retinue of the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that as long as there is a mind, it is the fruit of a mind; when there is no mind, it is the fruit of no-mind.
Question:
Is the preceding mind more numerous, or is the subsequent mind more numerous?
Answer: Some say that the subsequent mind is more numerous, as the preceding mind desires to enter the state of non-conception quickly.
Those who speak thus maintain that this is not fixed; sometimes the preceding mind is more numerous, and sometimes the subsequent mind is more numerous.

If one enters the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) with such deportment, and likewise enters the state of abiding in non-conception with that same deportment, then upon arising from it, one slanders the vehicle of *nirvāṇa*. Due to the ripening of subsequent karma, one is born in the desire realm; because that ripening karma is exhausted and no further karma arises, [one remains there].
The two types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding the attainment of non-perception: when craving for the Realm of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) has been exhausted, but craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted, one first forms the perception of renunciation and contemplates the cessation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). This arises from the Desire Realm and no other, because the faculties [of those beings] are sharp.
This arises in ordinary persons, not in noble ones; no noble one possesses the perception of existence regarding that which is produced from existence.
It is attained through skillful means, not through the abandonment of desire, and is non-retrogressive.
Question:
What is the difference between the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and non-perception (*asaṃjñin*)? Answer:
The attainment of non-perception is the cause, and non-perception is the fruit.
This is wholesome; that is indeterminate.
This has retribution; that is the retribution itself.
This has activity, while that is without activity;

as for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), having first abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one brings to rest the perception of cessation and then the cessation of mind and mental factors through contemplation.
Question:
What is this right reception? Answer:

When the mind and mental factors have ceased, and during the interval of their continuity, the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), the four great elements, and the sense faculties persist; this is called the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The rest is as explained in the Chapter on Concentration (Samādhi-paṭala).
Regarding "category" (*jāti*): it refers to the similarity among sentient beings in terms of their bodies, sense faculties, limbs and joints, activities, and food and drink.

There are six such categories: namely, the category of realms (*dhātu-jāti*), the category of destinies (*gati-jāti*), the category of births (*upapatti-jāti*), the category of locations (*sthāna-jāti*), the category of individual bodies (*ātma-bhāva-jāti*), and the category of natures (*prakṛti-jāti*).
Regarding the categories of realms (*dhātu*): sentient beings of the desire realm belong to the category of sentient beings of the desire realm; the same applies to the form and formless realms.
Regarding the categories of destinies (*gati*): those born in a particular destiny belong to the category of that specific destiny.
Regarding the category of birth (*jāti-gotra*): it refers to the category of being born once and being born again.

Regarding the category of location (*sthāna-gotra*): it refers to being born in the Avīci hell and belonging to the category of the Avīci hell, and so on, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is likewise.

Regarding "one's own kind": those born together in the same realm (*dhātu*), the same destiny (*gati*), and the same birth (*yoni*)—that is, one among the four types of birth (*catur-yoni*)—may nonetheless possess various kinds of individual bodies (*ātma-bhāva*), just as with various birds; it is to be understood in this manner.
Regarding "homogeneity of nature" (*jāti-sabhāgatā*): those who possess a commonality in the nature they have received are of the same homogeneity of nature.
If there is a similarity among six types of categories, this is called "homogeneity.
A "phrase" (*pada*) is that which collects various names and expressions to ultimately manifest the meaning.

The "body of taste" (*rasakāya*) refers to the "body of syllables" (*vyañjanakāya*); "taste" here means "syllable. In the Hu language (Sanskrit), there is a sound for "taste" which refers to the method of modeling syllables; it does not refer to the current [Chinese] characters of form and color.
"Name" (nāma) refers to the naming of all phenomena; it manifests meaning through names, such as "man" or "woman.
"Life-force" (jīva) refers to longevity, meaning the non-disintegration of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Question:
What is the difference between the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and the formations of life-span (*jīvita-saṃskāra*)? Answer:
Some say there is no difference between them.
Others say that the fruit of past karma is called "life-span" (*āyus*), while the fruit of cultivation is called "vitality" (*jīvita*).
Question:
Why did the World-Honored One relinquish the fifth portion of his lifespan? Answer:
Because he had brought the Buddha-activities to perfect completion, whereas other matters were already brought to completion by the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, because one abides in the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), both existence and its requisites are exhausted without remainder.
"To obtain" means to obtain all dharmas; "obtaining" and "accomplishing" have the same meaning, as will be explained in detail later.

That which is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), as well as the four characteristics of all phenomena, are non-material and dissociated [from consciousness]; they are taught to be conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
The "nature of an ordinary person" refers to the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
The four characteristics are birth, duration, aging, and impermanence, as already explained in the Chapter on Formations (*saṃskāra-varga*).
Regarding their non-material nature: these dharmas do not possess the nature of matter (*rūpa*), because the four primary elements and derived matter are not part of their constitution.
They are non-associated because they lack an object-condition (*ālambana*).
They are said to be conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) because they act for the sake of others and exist for the sake of others.
Question:
Among these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate? Answer:
Two are wholesome, five are of three kinds, and one should know that seven are indeterminate.
Two are within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and one is in the formless stage (*ārūpyabhūmi*).

Regarding the two that are wholesome: the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are wholesome because their nature is that of cultivated virtue.

The five kinds [of characteristics] consist of three types: acquisition (*prāpti*), arising (*jāti*), and duration (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*). Among these, they are wholesome within the wholesome, unwholesome within the unwholesome, and indeterminate within the indeterminate. This is because arising and the others share a single fruit with the phenomenon (*dharma*) itself, and because acquisition is not non-distinct from its own basis.

It should be known that the seven indeterminate factors (*avyākṛta*) are: non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), genus (*nikāya-sabhāga*), phrases (*pada*), syllables (*vyañjana*), names (*nāman*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Question:

Among these dharmas, how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer:

Two are situated within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); namely, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), both of which are bound to the realm of form. This is because the Heaven of Non-conception is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna, and the meditative attainment of non-conception is subsumed under the fourth dhyāna.
One exists in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is bound to the formless realm, as it is comprised within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Two realms are said to have three [types]; the remainder exist in all three realms.
Five are both outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*); the remainder are entirely outflow-tainted.

Regarding the statement that three [factors] exist in two realms: the phrase (*pada*), the flavor (*rasa*), and the name-body (*nāmakāya*) exist in the desire realm and the form realm, but not in the formless realm, because speech is not a constituent part there.

As for the others existing in all three realms: the generic character (*jāti*), acquisition (*prāpti*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), as well as the characteristics of acquisition (*prāptilakṣaṇa*), exist throughout the three realms because they are universal.
Question:
How many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)? Answer:

There are five [factors] that are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), namely the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa). When these exist within phenomena that are without-outflows, they are without-outflows; when they exist within phenomena that are with-outflows, they are with-outflows, because they share the same fruit as those phenomena.
Regarding "attainment" (*prāpti*): if it is the attainment of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is likewise [bound].

If it is the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it may be either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), because it is shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

If it is the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is with outflows, because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is precisely according to this principle that "being bound" (*baddha*) and "not being bound" (*abaddha*) are explained.

As for the remainder, which are entirely with-outflows (sāsrava): the Heaven of Non-conception, the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, the category of sentient beings, the life-faculty, phrases, and phonemes—these are termed the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva); they are exclusively with-outflows because they are included [within the realm of outflows].
Question:
Being separated from the noble dharmas is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
How is it relinquished? How is it severed?
Answer: In the first untainted mind, one should know that [the fetters] are abandoned but not yet attained [as destroyed];
for ordinary beings wandering through the realms, they are extinguished at the time of detachment from desire.

Regarding the statement that one should know what is abandoned and not acquired within the initial untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*): when the first untainted mind arises in a noble one (*ārya*), they abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

This initial untainted mind refers to that which is associated with the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); at the moment it arises, one abandons the nature of an ordinary person.

If it were said that [the path] is abandoned once it has arisen, then at the time of abiding in the patience toward the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), one would not be a noble one (*ārya*), because one has not yet abandoned the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, it is said to arise at that very moment.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that when two factors arise, they bring their respective tasks to completion: the internal factor refers to the retinue of the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma of suffering), while the external factor refers to the various radiances.

When ordinary persons transmigrate through the realms, at the time of transmigration, if they die in this realm, they immediately relinquish this realm; if they are born in that realm, they immediately acquire that realm. This is because [the factors involved] are not obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
yet it is not a definitive relinquishment, because they have not yet attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).

Regarding "extinguished at the time of detachment from desire": when one becomes detached from the desire of a particular stage, whether they be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or an noble one (*ārya*), at that moment they sever the state of being an ordinary person belonging to that stage, because it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Question:
What are the characteristics of the three unconditioned phenomena? Answer:
The severance of afflictions and their dissociation is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
that which is characterized by the absence of all obstructions is called space (*ākāśa*).

Regarding "the severance of afflictions and their dissociation is called analytical cessation": through wisdom, one severs the afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) along with their attendants; having attained this and attained dissociation from them, these various dissociations are termed "analytical cessation. This is because they correspond to the specific categories of medicines and diseases.
Some say that although the object of cessation is unique because it lacks internal differentiation (*svabhāga*), there are numerous acquisitions (*prāpti*).
If this acquisition is the realization of the cessation-acquisition, then it is precisely *nirvāṇa*; therefore, *nirvāṇa* is not shared.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The matter of bondage here is identical to the matter of dissociation here.

If they were different, then when the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are severed, the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) would also have to be severed, because they constitute a single realized fact."
If that were so, the subsequent remedies would be useless;
however, because they have not yet reached ultimate completion, the respective functions of the dharmas remain distinct.
Since there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is said that there is no homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*).

This [state] lacks its own specific cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) and does not bestow the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) upon others along with its retinue; although it lacks its own specific cause, it bestows its own specific cause upon others.
Because that category is not its own portion, it is said to be "non-category" (*apakṣa*).

Because afflictions have been extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa*; because it is beyond verbal description, it is said to be "not described"; because it surpasses all phenomena, it is called "supreme"; because it is the fruit of wisdom, it is called "wisdom"; because it is immovable, it is called "non-arising"; because it lies at the limit of the path of liberation, it is called a "limit"; because it transcends all phenomena, it is called "transcendence"; and because it is free from faults such as impermanence, it is called "sublime."
That which is characterized by the absence of all obstructions is called space; this means that because it does not obstruct various forms and allows for coming and going, it is designated as space.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Space is neither form nor non-form; the term 'space' is spoken merely in conformity with worldly convention. Others say:
"It is not that space does not exist, for there is room [for things] within it."
If space did not exist, there would be no room for things to exist.
Because there is room for existence, the reality of space exists.
Depending upon various conditioned phenomena, there are supports and objects.
If the conditions are not complete, it does not arise; this cessation is not [due to] clarity.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through the power of conditions and objects, for they are weak and inferior;
when their constituent parts are absent, they do not arise.

Just as visual consciousness arises through the conjunction of the eye, visible forms, light, space, and their corresponding mental attention—failing to arise if even one of these is absent—so too, when other consciousnesses manifest, the eye ceases and a new eye arises in every moment; because the requisite conditions are not fully assembled, visual consciousness cannot arise.
If visual consciousness were to arise depending on that eye, it would not arise; because the basis and so forth have already ceased, it ultimately does not arise.
Since it ceases without prior application, it is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with all groups of consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the untainted, one who follows the path by faith (śraddhānusārin) subsequently attains the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the path of following the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
All paths are likewise; one should understand them according to their respective meanings as fully as possible.
Question:
If this is attained through the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), why is it not subsumed under the fruits of the path (*mārgaphala*)?
Answer:

Because it is for the sake of other matters, because it severs afflictions, and because its diligent application is not for the sake of non-analytical cessation, it is therefore not subsumed under the fruit of the path.
Question:
Regarding the statement that all conditioned phenomena have causes: what serves as the cause for what? Answer:
The preceding cause is similar and increasing, or they arise together in mutual dependence.
"Two causes and one condition are said to apply exclusively to that which has already arisen.
Regarding "the preceding cause being similar and augmenting": the preceding dharma serves as the cause and the augmenting cause for the subsequent similar dharma, but it is not a weak cause.
This means that when practicing the Dharma, [the factors] either remain as they are or increase, rather than decreasing.
Or, those that arise in mutual dependence are the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Regarding the statement that two causes and one condition are said to be "exclusively already arisen," this refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) being described as already arisen, not as yet unarisen.
The former is the cause of the latter; for that which has not yet arisen, there is no distinction of before or after.
The same applies to the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
The condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is also explained in terms of what has already arisen.
The meaning of causes and conditions has already been explained in the Chapter on Practice (*Caryā-varga*).
Question:
Should retribution (*vipāka*) be said to belong to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*) or to the category of non-sentient beings (*asattva-saṃkhyāta*)?
Answer: Retribution refers to that which is included within the category of sentient beings; it consists of conditioned phenomena and the fruits of liberation.
It is said to function in association with objects and to operate upon the characteristics of others.

Regarding the statement "retribution refers to that which is included within the category of sentient beings": retribution is said to be included within the category of sentient beings because it is not shared; thus, it is not seen by the eyes of others, nor is it accomplished [by them].
The same principle applies to the meaning of other forms of retribution as well.

One should know that various requisites such as clothing and food are the fruition of effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruition (*adhipati-phala*), and not part of the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*), because they are common [to all].
Question:
What is fruition?
Answer: There is the fruit of conditioned liberation; all conditioned phenomena are said to have causes from which they arise, as well as cessation through deliberation.
It also speaks of the fruit of the path.
The meaning of "fruit" has already been explained in the Chapter on Karma (Karmavarga).
Question:
How do the mind and mental factors operate with respect to their objects? Answer:
They are said to operate together because they possess objects; if the dharmas that possess objects operate together within an object, it is because they accomplish a single task.
Question:
By what conditions does it arise? Answer:
This means that they operate with respect to other characteristics; the mind and mental factors take other phenomena as their objects, not their own nature. Why is this?

Because there is no duality [of subject and object], because they do not act upon themselves, because they do not take associated factors as their objects—since they share a single mode of activity and a single object—and because they do not take co-existent factors as their objects—since they share the same fruit.
This meaning shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-prakaraṇa*.
Question:
Do the mind and mental factors have a spatial location (*deśa*), or are they without a spatial location?
Answer: Because the universal cause has no fixed location, at the moment of arising the mind is liberated.
While the afflictions remain within the path-consciousness, they are relinquished even until the moment of cessation.

Regarding "the universal cause having no spatial location": the mind and mental factors arise from a universal cause; that is to say, two eyes serve as the cause for the arising of a single consciousness, and it is the same for the auditory and olfactory consciousnesses.
If they possessed a specific spatial location, [the consciousness] would have to function within only one eye.
If that were the case, one would see forms with only one eye and not see them simultaneously.
This point has already been explained in the "Chapter on Elements" (Dhātunirdeśa).
Furthermore, it is not the case that two consciousnesses arise simultaneously.
Why is this? Because the second [condition], the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), is not applicable.
It is not the case that one consciousness abides while two eyes see forms, for there is no such division.
If a single consciousness were to abide within both eyes, it would necessarily have parts.
If it abides in the left eye, it is not present in the right, because their locations are distinct.
This, however, does not apply to formless [consciousness], as it lacks spatial parts.
If, moreover, a single consciousness were to abide in both eyes, it would also have to arise within the body-faculty (kāyendriya) between those two eyes.
If that were the case, then visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) would be identical to body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna).
If it were not produced in the interim, it would have to be severed into two parts.
It has already been stated that [the mind] is not one, because two consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Question:
In which lifetime is the mind liberated?
Answer: At the time of birth, the mind is liberated.
The time when the Path arises is the time when the afflictions cease; therefore, at the moment the Path arises, the mind is liberated.
It is like a dam with a leak: water emerges first from the spot nearest the breach. This is exactly the same.
Furthermore, it is said that all future liberation of the mind does not occur solely at the moment of its arising; rather, it is spoken of as "arising" because of its initial liberation.
Question:
When the Path arises, are the afflictions abandoned?
Answer: Defilements exist within the mind of the Path and are abandoned until the moment of its cessation.
They cease when the Path ceases, because the objective basis for the defilements has been fully exhausted.
If that which is arising is the future, how can a future path bring about the ultimate result?
Therefore, it is said that afflictions are abandoned at the moment the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) ceases.
Question:
How many kinds of craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) are there? Answer:
Craving for existence is of five kinds; craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) has but a single characteristic.
Craving, objects, and the remaining afflictions—when these are extinguished, this is the cessation of the three realms.

Regarding "craving for existence has five types": craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) has five types, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through the path of cultivation; this is because there is craving for existence in five modes.
That which lacks even a single characteristic is the absence of craving, which is said to be abandoned through seeing.
That which has already produced a joyful attachment toward its own retribution is abandoned through cultivation. Why is this so?
Craving for views (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*); this craving follows along with its retribution (*vipāka*).
That which arises as retribution due to impermanence (*anityatā*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*), because it is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The same applies to impermanence itself as retribution; because it shares the same fruit (*eka-phala*) as the retribution, it is not abandoned through the path of seeing.
Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*).
This craving for non-existence is not abandoned by the *srotāpanna* or *sakṛdāgāmin*, yet they do not manifest it, because it is nourished by the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Just as [the mind] is nourished by remorse and doubt, the *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* likewise do not engage in them.
Question:

The World-Honored One has spoken of the realm of the three worlds (*traidhātuka*), the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
What does this mean? Answer:
Craving, objects, and other afflictions—their cessation constitutes the three realms.

The exhaustion of craving is the realm of dispassion (*virāga-dhātu*); the exhaustion of things is the realm of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*); and the exhaustion of remaining afflictions is the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇa-dhātu*), because it serves as the immediate antidote.
The commentator explains thus:
In the Sūtra, the Blessed One stated that the exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called the realm of abandonment; the realms of dispassion and cessation are likewise.
Question:
Regarding the twelve dharmas—wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and non-obscured-neutral in the desire realm;
and three in the form realm, excluding the unwholesome—
The three [categories] of the formless realm are likewise;
as are those of the learner (śaikṣa) and the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
Regarding these twelve factors, how many are obtained within a defiled mind, how many within a wholesome mind, and how many within a neutral mind?
Answer: If nine kinds of factors are obtained, one should know that it is a defiled mind.
A wholesome mind attains six types; an indeterminate [mind] is itself indeterminate.

If one attains nine types of dharmas, it should be known that this refers to a defiled mind. Regarding the realms and stages from which one returns: when one dies in the higher realms and is reborn in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), one attains the indeterminate mind of transformation belonging to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the three minds of the Form Realm, and the wholesome mind of the Desire Realm.
At the time when the roots of goodness are reconnected and at the time when one falls away from them, one acquires the defiled minds of the three realms as well as the mind of a learner (śaikṣa).
As for those not acquired: these refer to the wholesome minds of the formless realm, the non-obscured neutral minds, and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Although wholesome states of the formless realm are few and there is no attainment through falling away—meaning there is no "falling-away portion" (hānabhāgīya) therein—it is nevertheless stated here that one attains them while being entirely non-possessed of them.
This is a general statement; it does not mean that a single person, within a single moment of mind, attains nine dharmas.

Regarding "the wholesome mind attains six kinds": within a wholesome mind, one attains six minds—namely, the non-obscured neutral of the desire realm, the wholesome and non-obscured neutral of the form realm, the wholesome of the formless realm, as well as the learner's and the non-learner's minds. Furthermore, this is a general statement regarding their attainment, not that they are attained simultaneously.
Regarding "the indeterminate is itself indeterminate": the non-obscured indeterminate is itself indeterminate and nothing else, because it is weak and inferior.
Question:
Among the ten factors of the path-limbs (mārga-aṅga), how many are of the nature of faculties (indriya) and how many are not of the nature of faculties?
Answer: The factors of the path consist of six dharmas; one should know these as being of the nature of faculties.
If various dharmas are associated with them, these are said to be of the nature of others.

Regarding the statement that "among the factors of the path, there are six dharmas that should be known as having the nature of faculties": one should know that the five faculties beginning with faith and the factor of joy within the awakening factors have the nature of faculties, because they possess the characteristics of faculties.
The others are not of the nature of faculties (*indriya*).
Question:
Is that which is associated (the *samprayukta*) of the same nature as itself, or of a different nature?
Answer: When dharmas are associated, they are said to be of "other-nature" (parabhāva).

Dharmas are associated with other-natures, not with their own-nature (svabhāva), because there is no single nature that arises simultaneously with two moments, because the preceding and succeeding moments do not coincide, and because a self-nature does not act upon itself.
This meaning has already been explained at length in the Chapter on Practice (Caryā-paṭala).
Question:
From what is one liberated?
Answer: Liberation is attained through conditions; this is what the Great Sage has taught.
There is also bondage through cessation, occurring on both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

Regarding that which was spoken by the Great Sage concerning liberation through conditions: one should know that liberation through conditions does not constitute liberation through dissociation, because it occurs in a single moment and because the mind arises simultaneously with the afflictions.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding conditions; liberation arises from the cessation of those very afflictions of non-delusion.
Question:
Is liberation simply the severance [of afflictions]?
Answer: If liberation were identical to abandonment, there would be cases where something is abandoned yet one remains bound, and cases where there is a partial abandonment that is not liberation.
This refers to when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, such that the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering have been abandoned.
There is the binding of all pervasive latent proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), because their objects have not yet been severed;
as well as the binding of one grade to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), up to the binding of the ninth grade, because there remains only one latent proclivity.

Regarding those eight categories, there is first abandonment and subsequently liberation; for the ninth category, there is both abandonment and liberation simultaneously. It is the same for all others.
Question:
How does one attain indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*) through the vision of the truths?
Answer: Two types of understanding regarding the three truths, and four through seeing the right path, result in the attainment of indestructible purity; these are cultivated in two lifetimes.

Regarding the second explanation—that one attains the four kinds of indestructible confidence (*aveccappasāda*) through the vision of the True Path: by means of the immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one attains indestructible confidence in the Dharma and in the noble precepts; by means of the immediate realization of the Path, one attains the four kinds of indestructible confidence.
This meaning shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga* (Chapter on Analysis).
Question:
What is cultivation in the three periods of time?
Answer: They are cultivated in two time periods.

Those of the present are cultivated through practice because they manifest before one; those of the future are cultivated through attainment because they do not manifest and because they follow in succession upon attainment.
The past is not cultivated, because the present cause is not its constituent part.
Question:
Which dharmas revolve together with the mind?
Answer: All mental factors are said to arise simultaneously with the mind;
they are also the various characteristics of this mind, as well as its other characteristics and its activities.

Regarding the statement that all mental factors (*citta-dharma*) arise simultaneously with the mind: all mental factors arise simultaneously with the mind because they share the same fruit as the mind.

Furthermore, regarding the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of this mind: the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) of this mind also arise simultaneously with the mind, for they likewise share the same fruit as the mind.
Regarding the remaining characteristics: these mental factors also arise simultaneously with the mind.

As for their "activity," this refers to the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*); because it arises through the mind, it also arises simultaneously with the mind, as it shares the same fruit as the mind.
Question:
What is the dharma of abandonment? Answer:
The dharmas to be abandoned are those with outflows; the knower is likewise stainless.
That which is yet to arise is said to be distant; the rest are said to be near.
"The dharmas to be abandoned are those with outflows" because they possess faults.
Just as one washes clothes that have stains, but not those that are stainless, so it is in this case as well.
Question: What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: That which knows is also without defilement.
All phenomena, whether contaminated or uncontaminated, are said to be known according to their respective natures.
Why is this? Because it eliminates ignorance.
Question:
What is the distant dharma?
Answer: That which is in the future is said to be distant.
Past and future dharmas are said to be distant because they are remote from present consciousness; this refers to distance in terms of time.
The meaning of the four types of distance has already been explained in the *Caryāpāda* (Chapter on Practice).
As for the others, they are said to be near: the present is called near because it coexists with the body of consciousness.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is said to be "near" because it is not bound to any location;
it is attained in whichever direction one may be by means of the Path.
It is not analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because that requires diligent seeking.
The meaning of "world" has already been explained in detail in the Chapter on Elements (*Dhātuvarga*).
Question: What is the nature of fixed phenomena (*niyata-dharma*)?
Answer: What are called the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and the various untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are designated by the wise as "concentration" (*samādhi*);
that which is the locus of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) is said to be tainted (*sāsrava*).

Regarding the statement that "the so-called ānantarya karmas and the wisdom of the various untainted paths are called 'fixed' (niyata)": the ānantarya karmas are said to be "wrongly fixed" because they lead inevitably to rebirth in hell.
Untainted (anāsrava) formations are said to be "rightly fixed" (samyaktva-niyata), because they are definitely destined for the fruit of liberation.
Others are not so fixed.
Question:
When the World-Honored One established the three categories of sentient beings beneath the Bodhi tree, was this for the sake of establishing a limit for sentient beings,
or was it for the sake of establishing a limit for dharmas?
If it pertains to the limits of sentient beings, why do you say that the limit of sentient beings cannot be reached and that sentient beings are infinite?
If it pertains to the limits of dharmas, then the Śrāvakas should also establish them; why then do you say they are the unique qualities (āveṇika) of the Tathāgata?

Answer: Some say that the "limitation of sentient beings" refers to their general characteristics rather than their specific characteristics; that is to say, when one speaks of the four modes of birth (*yoni*), there are no sentient beings other than these.
Question:
If that were so, the Śrāvakas should also be established [as such].
What, then, is the difference between a Tathāgata and a Śrāvaka? Answer:
There is a distinction.
The Tathāgata establishes [the teachings] by his own power, whereas the Śrāvakas hear them from the Buddha; this is the distinction.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata establishes the limits of sentient beings, while the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas establish the limits of dharmas.

Having established the three categories of sentient beings, the World-Honored One continues even now to bring peace and happiness to them; out of great compassion, he observes sentient beings with his Buddha-eye three times during the day and night.
Question:
What is the locus of views? Answer:
The "sphere of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*) refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). All phenomena with outflows are the sphere of views, being defiled by views and associated with them.
If a phenomenon is defiled by views through either being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for those views or being associated (*samprayukta*) with them, it is called the sphere of views.

Furthermore, it is said that because they are conditioned by the power of views within their own realm (*svadhātu*), tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) receive the designation "locus of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*).
This is not the case for other underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), as they do not belong to that category.
Such being the case, the former explanation is considered superior.
Question:
If a sentient being possesses faculties, how many faculties does he possess? Answer:
It is said that there are nineteen faculties; this refers to the maximum number achieved.
The minimum is eight, as understood by those who clearly comprehend what is taught regarding the faculties.

Regarding the statement "it is said that there are nineteen faculties, which refers to the maximum number achieved": a noble person (ārya) achieves a maximum of nineteen faculties, namely one who has not yet abandoned desire but possesses all the faculties.

If one abides in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of "no more to be known" (*ajñātāvīndriya*), as well as one gender organ, are excluded;

if one abides in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the faculty of "not yet known" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "no more to be known," as well as one gender organ, are excluded.
Ordinary worldlings do not sever their roots of goodness; they possess all the faculties as well as both sexual organs, with the exception of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

Regarding the statement that the minimum number of faculties one can possess is eight: this refers to the minimum of eight faculties. This means that when the roots of goodness are severed and one gradually passes away, being reborn in the Avīci Hell and pressed by the great mountains, one possesses only the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind faculty (*manendriya*), and the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*). As for the remainder, it refers to those who die gradually while still possessing the body faculty.
If one is an ordinary person born in the formless realm, they possess the faculties of mind, life, equanimity, and the five beginning with faith.
Question:
How many kinds of contact are there?
Answer: Because it possesses many names, it is called "designation" (adhivacana) and "with resistance" (sapratigha).
Regarding the spheres of clarity and ignorance, that which is termed "attaining the fruit" constitutes the matter of the twofold path.

Regarding "designation, the resistant, and that which is intermediate between clarity and ignorance": as for "designation," it refers to contact associated with the group of mental consciousness; because it takes all phenomena as its object, it is called designation.
Furthermore, it is called "designation" (*adhivacana*) because it takes multiple names as its object.

Although the fifth type of contact (*sparśa*) also takes multiple names as its object, there is no fault [in calling it designation], because that [designation] first receives its name in relation to the five consciousnesses.
If the contact associated with the group of the five consciousnesses relies upon a resistant faculty (*sapratighendriya*), it is therefore called "resistant" (*sapratigha*).
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "contact associated with knowledge" (*vidyā-saṃprayukta-sparśa*), because it is associated with knowledge.
Regarding the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because ignorance arises from it.
Regarding the non-defiled tainted (*akliṣṭa-sāsrava*), it is called "neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance contact" (*naivavidyānāvidyā-sparśa*), because it is associated with neither.
These five contacts are said to be of sixteen kinds based on their conformity, non-conformity, association, support, and discrimination.

Regarding the establishment of conformity and non-conformity: it means that because of the association with contact linked to craving and aversion, there are the contacts of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Based on conceptual differentiation, one speaks of the contacts of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Question:
Is that which attains the fruit the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) or the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
Answer: That which is called "attaining the fruit" refers to the function of the two paths.
Both paths together attain the fruit: the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) attains the abandonment of afflictions, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes liberation.
Furthermore, it is said that the path of non-obstruction attains the fruit, because the path of liberation protects the work accomplished by the former, ensuring it is not lost.
Thus it was said.
Question:
The Blessed One has stated that through disenchantment one becomes free from desire.
What is revulsion?
What is detachment from desire? Answer:

If wisdom resides in the cause of suffering, and patience is likewise described as "disgust," they are said to constitute the four [foundations] of detachment because they are able to abandon craving.

Regarding the statement that "if wisdom resides in the cause of suffering, and patience is likewise described as disgust": wisdom and patience directed toward the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) are called "disgust" because they take as their object that which is to be reviled.
Because the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination are the bases for unwholesome conduct and afflictions, they are described as "objects of aversion.

Because one is able to abandon sensual desire through them, the four truths are said to be "for the sake of detachment"; when patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) operate toward the four truths until their exhaustion, this is called "detachment," because it destroys sensual desire.
Although one is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*), desire (*rāga*) is the very foundation of those afflictions; therefore, it is said that one must "leave desire.
That which is aversion, displeasure, and turning away from evil—this is the distinction of "disgust" (*nirveda*).
"Detachment, cessation, liberation, and total exhaustion"—these are the distinctions of detachment.
Question:
In what state of mind does an Arhat abide when entering parinirvāṇa?
Answer: The Arhat dwells in the mind born of retribution (*vipākaja*) and the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*);
because these minds cease in accordance with the flow [of the path], he proceeds toward parinirvāṇa.
An Arhat enters parinirvāṇa while abiding in a mind born of retribution or in a mind of deportment.
Why is this? Because it accords with the cessation of the mind.
A wholesome mind is firmly established and does not conform to the cessation of the mind.
An indeterminate mind is weak; because it is weak, it conforms to the cessation of the mind.
Furthermore, this is because its faults are few.
A wholesome mind possesses the fruit of dependence (*niśraya-phala*) because it transcends birth through the gateway of fruition.
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) possesses only the fruit of dependence and lacks the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Furthermore, this is because it turns its back on the various realms of existence (*gati*).
If one were to head toward the various realms of existence, one would necessarily bring forth a virtuous mind with diligence, thinking, "May I not be born within the evil destinies.
Therefore, because such a person turns away from all destinies, they abide in a mind of constant nature.

At times, within that constituent part, the wholesome mind is empty as if its roots of goodness were severed; the unwholesome mind is also empty as if one had abandoned the desires of the desire realm.
Furthermore, it is because of the gradual departure from birth and death.

That is to say: in the desire realm, one is separated from the mind of desire and the unwholesome mind; in the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), one is separated from the defiled mind; when the indeterminate mind manifests, one is separated from the wholesome mind; and when the death-moment mind manifests, one is separated from the indeterminate mind.
The Venerable said: "This Dharmatrāta refers to the ancient Dharmatrāta as 'the Venerable.
For one whose diligence is continuous, the virtuous mind does not fail to follow upon at the time of death."

Some say that those who wish to maintain that there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution in the lower stages claim that in the desire realm, up to the fourth dhyāna, there is the arising of retribution-born mind and deportment mind, as well as parinirvāṇa.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only birth as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*); there is no deportment (*airyāpathika*), because matter (*rūpa*) is not a constituent part [of that realm].

Some maintain that there is no experience of neither-painful-nor-pleasant maturation in the lower realms; they assert that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the third dhyāna, one attains parinirvāṇa while abiding solely in a mind of deportment.
The rest is as explained above.
Question: How many kinds of existence (bhava) are there?
Answer: Birth-existence (upapatti-bhava) and death-existence (bhaṅga-bhava), as well as fundamental existence (mūla-bhava) and intermediate existence (antarā-bhava)—
one should know that these two existences each consist of two moments, while one [existence] is defiled and three existences are twofold.

Regarding "birth-existence (jāti-bhava), death-existence (maraṇa-bhava), fundamental existence (mūla-bhava), and likewise intermediate existence (antara-bhava)": birth-existence refers to the constituent of birth; because the five aggregates arise simultaneously with birth, it is called birth-existence, in the sense that the mind of continuity arises together [with them].

The "existence at death" (*cyuty-bhava*) refers to the limit of death; because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) coexist with death, it is called the existence at death, in the sense that it arises simultaneously with the mind of passing away.
