It is the fool who falls into the evil realms, not the wise person; it is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who falls into the evil realms, not the noble one (*ārya*); it is the transgressor of the precepts who falls into the evil realms, not the upholder of the precepts; it is the one with an evil mind who falls into the evil realms, not the one with a virtuous mind, as stated in the *Sūtra-pāda*.
The Chapter on the Selection of Food shall now be explained.
There are four types of nutriment in the desire realm, and the same is true for the four modes of birth and the five destinies.
In the two upper realms, there are three types of nutriment; there, the nutriment of physical morsels does not exist.
Regarding the four nutriments existing in the desire realm: there are four nutriments in the desire realm.

As it is with the four modes of birth and the five destinies, these also possess the four nutriments; even though the iron balls and molten copper in the hells increase suffering and destruction, they are called "nutriments" because they satisfy hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, even the touch of cool wind upon the body is called nutriment.

Regarding the statement that "among the three nutriments, the first two do not exist in the upper two realms": in the Form and Formless Realms, there is no solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), because the bodies are subtle and because there is no physical form.
Question:
Among the various realms of existence (*gati*), which food predominates in each individual realm? Answer:
In that realm of hungry ghosts, mental nutriment (*manomaya-āhāra*) is predominant;
the same is true for those born from eggs and for those in the three formless realms (*ārūpya*).

Regarding the statement "in that realm of hungry ghosts, mental nutriment is predominant": in the realm of hungry ghosts, mental nutriment is predominant because of the abundance of their mental activities (*manas-karma*).

As for those born from eggs, they too have an increase in mental nutriment (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*); because those born from eggs in that state constantly think of their mother, they do not rot or decay.

The same applies to the three formless realms: with the exception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the remaining three formless realms also have an increase in mental nutriment, because of the abundance of mental formations (*manosaṃskāra*).
In the womb-born, edible food increases; it is said that among those in the human realm, consciousness-food increases in the hells, and the same is true for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Regarding "in the womb-born, edible food increases; it is said that among those in the human realm": for those born from a womb, edible food increases within the human realm, because the body is sustained by edible food.

Regarding the statement that "in the hells the nutriment of consciousness increases, and so it is in the Peak of Existence": in the hells, the nutriment of consciousness increases because consciousness sustains name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as well, the nutriment of consciousness increases because consciousness sustains name (*nāman*).

The desire-realm devas are like those in the human realm; In the form realm, the nutriment of contact increases, As does that of the animal realm, And likewise for those born from moisture. Regarding "the desire-realm devas are like those in the human realm":
among the devas of the desire realm, the nutriment of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) increases.

Regarding the increase of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): for the devas of the realm of form, the nutriment of contact increases because they practice meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, it is likewise for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*); for those born from moisture among the animals, the nutriment of contact increases. "Holding" (*dhṛti*) has the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*), just as a support (*dhṛti*) holds a jar so that it remains stable and does not break.
In this way, by sustaining the body with food, the body does not perish; because it draws forth existence (*bhava*), it is called "food.
Question:
If that is so, then all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are food, because they draw forth existence.
Answer: They are called "powers" (*bala*) because they are predominant; they are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*) because they are able to draw forth existence.
There are two reasons for calling them "nutriments": namely, drawing forth through preliminary application, and further nourishing once they have been drawn forth.
Question:
For what reason are four said to be nutriments? Answer:
This should not be questioned, for all [objections] would arise.
However, because it corresponds to the appropriate measure, only four are taught.
As for that "edible food" (*kavalīkārāhāra*), it is called "food" because it nourishes the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Contact is called nutriment because it nourishes the mind and mental factors.
Volition is called nutriment because it nourishes future existence.
Consciousness is called nutriment because it nourishes name-and-form.
Therefore, the four nutriments are taught.
Question:

Regarding those who take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—since in the Sanskrit language the names of the Three Jewels (*triratna*) carry the sense of "protection," and since the meaning of taking refuge is "to turn toward" or "to approach," it should be called "taking refuge in [the sense of] turning toward."
The Buddha provides protection, and the Dharma and Sangha do likewise; to what, then, does one take refuge?
The Three Jewels each have two aspects: the Buddha has two kinds of bodies, namely the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Dharma is also of two kinds: namely, the Dharma of ultimate nirvana and the Dharma of universal selflessness.
The Sangha is also of two kinds: namely, the ultimate Sangha and the conventional Sangha.
To what does one take refuge? Answer:
One takes refuge in those Buddhas and the dharmas of no-more-learning (aśaikṣadharma) they have attained.
The unsurpassed Dharma of Nirvāṇa, and the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training within the Saṅgha.
The dharmas beyond training accomplished by all Buddhas are called "Buddha.
To take refuge means to take refuge in the dharmas beyond training attained by the Buddha; this is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
They do not return to the Buddha because they have accomplished various contaminated dharmas such as the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*), and because their intrinsic nature is not liberated.
For this reason, one should know that the birth-body (*janmakāya*) is also excluded.

If it is claimed that one who gives rise to an evil mind toward the Tathāgata and wounds his foot so that it bleeds does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), this is not so. Why?
Because they gave rise to an evil mind.

This means that because he gave rise to an evil mind toward the dharmas of no-more-learning attained by the Buddha and thereby injured his foot, he incurred an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).

Furthermore, it is because he destroyed the basis upon which the Buddha’s dharmas of no-more-learning depend; since the basis is destroyed, that which depends upon it is also destroyed, just as when a jar is broken, the milk within is also lost.
Taking refuge in the exhaustion of craving is called taking refuge in the Dharma, because it is wholesome and permanent.
One should know that this excludes other dharmas, as other dharmas lack both wholesomeness and permanence.
Taking refuge in the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) attained by the Saṃgha is called taking refuge in the Saṃgha.

One does not take refuge in the qualities that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) accomplished by the Saṃgha, nor in the physical body, because they are tainted (*sāsrava*) and because they cannot be destroyed even by the destruction of the Saṃgha.
Question:
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of taking refuge?
Answer: Some say its intrinsic nature is that of vocal action (*vākkarman*), because it is a conventional designation for the conjunction of speech.
Others say it is also the intrinsic nature of both bodily and vocal action, because it is the intrinsic nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Question:
What is the meaning of taking refuge? Answer:
The meaning of protection is the meaning of reliance; the meaning of consolation is the meaning of reliance. For these reasons, taking refuge is the gateway for receiving the vows (*saṃvara*).
Although the four types of indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*) were mentioned in the *Sūtra-varga*, they shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-varga*; they will now be discussed here.
The path of the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the three True Realities—
faith that is stainless toward these is the indestructible purity regarding the Dharma (*dhammappasāda*).

The three faculties and their attendants attained by the Pratyekabuddhas, the path practiced by all Bodhisattvas, and the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation— arising from untainted faith (*anāsava-saddhā*) directed toward these various phenomena is called the indestructible purity regarding the Dharma.
The destruction of the indestructible purities will be explained later.
Following the arising of pure ethical discipline, the Buddha and the Saṅgha are spoken of as "refuges.
This matter is of two kinds, and its names are said to be fourfold.

"Pure precepts that arise accordingly" refers to the untainted bodily and vocal actions that arise accordingly; these are the precepts esteemed by the noble ones, and are called "unshakable purity of virtue."

Regarding the statement "the Buddha and the Sangha are as explained in the refuge formula": one should understand that the Buddha and the Sangha are as previously described in the explanation of taking refuge.
That untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) which takes the Buddha and the Dharma as its object is the unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*) directed toward the Buddha.
The untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) regarding the Sangha is the indestructible clarity of faith (*aveccappasāda*) in the Sangha.

If one takes as an object the untainted dharmas attained by the Buddha and the dharmas of training (*śaikṣadharma*) attained by Bodhisattvas, this is called the indestructible clarity of faith in the dharma that takes conditioned objects (*saṃskṛtālambana*).

Thus, taking as objects the teachings of the Buddha, the *pratyekabuddhas*, and the *śrāvakas*, up to all the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training—this is also called the unshakable confidence in the dharma that takes things as its object (*dharme 'vetyaprasāda*).
Question:
How many factors are there in the indestructible purities? Answer:
This matter consists of two kinds, namely faith and precepts.
Faith is the purity of the mind; the precepts are the purity of the four great elements.
As for the explanation that there are four names, they are established based on the conditions of the phenomena; because the conditions of faith are distinct, they are categorized into three types.
"Knowing purity" means knowing, attaining, or maintaining purity.
Question:
What is it that is known?
Answer: The Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, some say they are called "unshakable purities," as in the case of the householder Śūra.
Furthermore, because of their valor, they do not cease.

Some say these are called "unshakable purities" (aveccappasāda). Just as it was said regarding the elder, both of these elders attained the first path; Māra cannot destroy them nor can he sever them, and each is named according to what they themselves proclaimed.
Question:
What is the sequence? Answer:
The Buddha knows that purity precedes [all else], for the Buddha is the root because he teaches it.
Question:
What is the Buddha capable of?
Answer: It is the awakening to phenomena (*dharmas*).
Question:
Who upholds the Dharma? Answer:
The Sangha.
Question:
How does that Saṃgha attain a single flavor? Answer:
The noble precepts.
Furthermore, the one who can speak is the Buddha;
what is it that he speaks?
It refers to the Dharma.
For whom was it taught?
It refers to the Sangha.
Who upholds the Dharma?
It is the precepts.
Furthermore, the Buddha is the skilled physician, the Dharma is the treatment for the disease, the Saṅgha is the nurse, and the noble precepts are the medicine.
This is called the sequential explanation.

Regarding the truths of suffering and its origin, as well as the truth of the path for those of dull faculties, one attains indestructible purity through a single causal condition, namely faith. For those of the three [higher] faculties, faith and wearying revulsion arise toward suffering and its origin; however, those of dull faculties have not yet attained love and delight for the path, possessing only faith.

Regarding the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path for those of medium and superior faculties, they attain unshakable purity through two causes and conditions: namely, faith and aspiration. Those of the three faculties all delight in cessation, while those of medium and superior faculties are able to delight in the path; both [delight] and faith coexist therein.
The *Sūtra-pāda* has spoken of the fruits of śrāmaṇya; they shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-pāda*, which will now be discussed.
These so-called fruits of śrāmaṇya are both unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The conditioned fruits of those in training (*śaikṣa*) are three; the fruit of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the fourth.
There are two kinds of fruits of śrāmaṇya: conditioned and unconditioned.
The conditioned fruits of training (śaikṣa) are three; the conditioned fruit of no-more-training (aśaikṣa) is the fourth.
All unconditioned [fruits] are neither of training nor of no-more-training.
The eighty-nine noble ones, the fruits of the śramaṇa’s unconditioned state, and that which is also called the conditioned—all these are the paths of the śramaṇa.
Among them, the eight patiences of the path of seeing constitute the eight knowledges of the śramaṇa; these are the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa.
The abandonment of the eight types of afflictions is the unconditioned fruit of the śramaṇa.

The nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the separation from desire through the cultivation path (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of the desire realm, and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the śramaṇa, are the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa.
The abandonment of the nine types of afflictions is the unconditioned fruit of the śramaṇa.
In this manner, one should understand that this extends up to the exhaustion of desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Because they are clearly manifested, the World-Honored One taught four [fruits]. This is because five conditions are complete in these stages: namely, abandoning the previously traversed path and attaining the previously unattained path; the exhaustion of fetters and the attainment of the single-flavored liberation; the simultaneous acquisition of the eight knowledges; and the simultaneous cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Because the path in this state is certain and its culmination is certain;
if it is abandoned, that which was to be done has been accomplished and its culmination reached.
Question:
Is it possible that, in a single moment of thought, a single cognition knows all phenomena? Answer: No.
Why is this? Although one knows all things are empty, it is not that one knows everything;
setting aside their mutual association, their intrinsic nature is likewise so.

If this wisdom arises, it knows that all phenomena are empty and selfless, yet it does not know itself; its own nature does not look back upon itself, just as a fingertip cannot touch itself—this is likewise the case here.

Furthermore, because there is no determination of two [objects], there is no single cognition that determines two things; for it knows itself and knows another, yet it does not know them as corresponding factors together, since they share a single mode of activity and a single object-condition.

All dharmas associated with a single category share the same activity and the same object; they do not know one another as co-existent dharmas because they have a single fruit and turn together with fixed determination.
This wisdom consists of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), but not the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Why is this? Because the cultivation of wisdom takes discrete segments as its object.
Therefore, it speaks of the desire realm and the form realm, for in the formless realm, hearing and reflection are not applicable.
Question:
How many kinds of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are there? Answer:
What are called the antidotes of abandonment, the antidote of destruction, the antidote of maintenance, and the antidote of distancing— these four should be known as the types of antidotes.
There are four kinds of antidotes: namely, the antidote of abandonment, the antidote of destruction, the antidote of maintenance, and the antidote of distancing.
The antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) is so called because it abandons the acquisition of afflictions through the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).

The antidote of destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*) is so called because it performs an analysis of faults regarding the objects of perception, such as [contemplating them as] impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and so forth.

The antidote of retention (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*) is that which is conjoined with the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions; this refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and all subsequent paths that are conjoined with the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions.

The antidote of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*) begins with the path of liberation; for example, the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is [the antidote] to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing suffering.
The counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) and the counteractive of destruction (*vidūṣaṇapratipakṣa*) apply to other phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for the counteractive of destruction, it is also the counteractive of distancing (*dūrabhāgapratipakṣa*) when one has exhausted craving for the desire realm and attained the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) that transcends and rises above [the world].
All such paths should be understood according to their respective meanings as fully as possible.
While the meaning of cultivation was explained in the *Sūtra-varga*, it shall now be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-varga*.

Initial attainment, cultivation through practice, cultivation as an antidote, and cultivation through abandonment— one should know that these four kinds are what is meant by the meaning of "cultivation. The four kinds of cultivation are:

cultivation through attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation as an antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), and cultivation through abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) refers to the initial attainment of previously unattained conditioned virtues.
Cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*) refers to the continuous arising of wholesome dharmas that have already been attained.

Cultivation as antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation of the four types of antidotes, which is called cultivation as antidote; it is the path that acts as the adversary to contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas.

Regarding "cultivation through abandonment" (*prahāṇabhāvanā*): this refers to the cultivation of the path for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*). While the term "abandonment" primarily signifies the attainment of the state where afflictions have been abandoned, here we take that which is to be countered and that which is to be abandoned as the object of "cultivation. This can be understood by referring to the four preceding propositions.

Regarding those dharmas that are cultivated by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), but are neither cultivated as antidotes (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) nor cultivated for abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhāvanā*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation consists of untainted conditioned dharmas (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The second permutation consists of unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) and neutral conditioned dharmas (*avyākṛta-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The third phrase refers to wholesome conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
The fourth phrase refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Some say there are six kinds of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): the first four, plus analytical cultivation (*vibhāvana-bhāvanā*) and protective cultivation (*ārakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation through discernment is as taught in the sūtras, namely: "This body consists of hair, body hair, nails, teeth," and so forth.
Cultivation through protection refers to the sense faculties, as it is said: "One should properly restrain the six sense faculties," and so on, as explained at length.
Such excellence refers to the four kinds of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as previously explained;
these two types of cultivation are subsumed under the cultivation of abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).

Having already explained the definitive characteristics of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the meaning of their distinctions shall now be explained.

Afflictions pertain to all three realms; if they are abandoned through seeing, there are two types, and if abandoned through both [seeing and cultivation], there are three types. Both occur prior to the path of seeing.
If afflictions are bound to the three realms and are abandoned through the path of seeing, these refer to the five views and doubt.

Regarding these two sets of five views that precede the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), doubt is definitely severed prior to the path of seeing; craving, pride, and ignorance perish simultaneously with the views. Although they have not actually been exhausted, they are said to be "fully subsumed. Because they receive their names according to the views they follow, they are termed "preliminary" (*pūrvamgama*).

The path of cultivation does not depend upon the path of seeing; therefore, it precedes the path of seeing. [Defilements] are either abandoned by the path of seeing, or abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
What is abandoned by the path of seeing?

If the fetters are bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are abandoned by the patience of uninterrupted realization (ānantarya-kṣānti) for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) or follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
These are said to be "bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" because of the determination of their level (bhūmi).
The "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin) and the "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārin) are spoken of here in terms of the certainty of the person.
"Uninterrupted patience" (ānantarya-kṣānti) is spoken of here in terms of the certainty of the antidote.
"Abandonment" (prahāṇa) is spoken of here in terms of the certainty of what has been accomplished.
What is abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation?
It refers to the eight stages.
If abandoned by ordinary persons, it is abandoned through the path of cultivation; if abandoned by noble ones, it is abandoned through the path of seeing.
Question:
For what reason do ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) sever the afflictions (kleśa) exclusively through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)? Answer:
Ordinary persons cannot abandon afflictions partially, such that some are abandoned through seeing and others through cultivation.
Furthermore, ordinary persons cannot abandon nine types [of afflictions] by means of a single path.

If there are five types within the three realms—namely craving, pride, and ignorance—these three, which are the precursors to the path of seeing, are either abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

If those afflictions are bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and are abandoned by the patience of uninterrupted realization (*anantarya-kṣānti*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), they are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If they are abandoned by those who have seen the tracks of training (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) across the nine stages, they are abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Regarding the remaining eight stages: if abandoned by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); if abandoned by noble ones (*ārya*), they are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
As for the afflictions of the desire realm, there are two types of fivefold [categories];
because their cultivation has a fixed limit, it is said that the path of cultivation precedes them.

Regarding the five types of factors in the desire realm, those that precede the path of cultivation are of two kinds: either abandoned by the path of cultivation, or abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Those which are abandoned by the path of cultivation for one who has entered the stream and trains in the path of cultivation are "abandoned by the path of cultivation."

As for the others: if they are abandoned by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); if they are abandoned by noble ones (*ārya*), they are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Since those [abandonments] are necessarily preceded [by this], it is therefore called "preceding.
Question:
Regarding the conditions previously mentioned, at what time do these conditions perform their functions?
Answer: The function performed by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is said to occur at the moment that [the subsequent] dharma arises.
The activity performed by the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is said to occur when that dharma ceases.

As for the activity of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is said to occur when that dharma arises; this is because "the time of arising" refers to the future, as it occurs simultaneously with the transition [to the present].
It should also be said that at the time of transition and when those dharmas arise, the sequential condition (samanantara-pratyaya) performs its function.
It is called a sequential condition in the sense of providing a place, because those arising dharmas obtain a place [for their occurrence].

If it is argued that form (*rūpa*) and all formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) also arise by obtaining a locus (*sthāna*), and thus should be described as having the condition of immediate antecedent (*samanantarapratyaya*), this is not so; for that matter has already been explained in the *Saṃskāra-skandha*.

Regarding the statement that "the activity performed by the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) occurs when that dharma ceases": at the time the dharma ceases, the object-condition performs its activity. This is because the time of the dharma's cessation is the present, which is capable of apprehending the objective sphere (*viṣaya*); it is not the future, because [future dharmas] have not yet arisen;
nor is it the past, because [past dharmas] have already ceased.
The activity performed by three causes refers to when those phenomena arise;
it is the activity of two causes that should be understood as occurring at the time of cessation.

Regarding "the activity performed by three causes refers to when those phenomena arise": at the time of arising, three causes perform their activity—namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Due to the power of its own cause (*svabhāva-hetu*), phenomena arise as a similar continuity; therefore, when a phenomenon arises, its own-cause performs its function.

Because the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) establish the arising of phenomena in accordance with them, they perform their functions when those phenomena arise.
Speaking in general terms, it is said that when a dharma arises, three causes perform their functions:
excluding the first moment of untainted (anāsrava) dharmas, the remaining wholesome (kuśala) ones;
and excluding those arising from retribution (vipāka), the remaining non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) ones.

Regarding "the functioning of the self-nature cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) as defilement": this refers to the functioning of the self-nature cause and the pervasive cause. Regarding "the functioning of the retribution cause (*vipāka-hetu*) as retribution":

this refers to the functioning of the self-nature cause and the retribution cause. It should be understood that when it is said "the functioning of these two causes occurs at the time of cessation," this means that at the time of the cessation of a conditioned phenomenon (*sappaccaya-dhamma*), the associated cause (*sampayutta-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*) function; this is because their activity is identical and they share a single fruit, whereas for non-associated phenomena (*vippayutta-dhamma*), the co-existent cause lacks an object (*anālambana*).
The dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) exists at all times without obstruction; therefore, it is not mentioned, as there is no need to mention it.
The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is also like this.
Question:
How is it that the minds of all sentient beings arise equally, abide equally, and cease equally, such that they are not crooked?
The reason for asking this is: among sentient beings, some bodies are large and some are small; does a large body entail a large mind, and a small body entail a small mind?
Are they equal for all?
Furthermore, since the movements and pauses of sentient beings differ in their slowness or speed, is it that a slow movement corresponds to a slow mind and a fast movement to a fast mind?
Or are they all equal?

Furthermore, among sentient beings, some possess a tranquil awareness as stable as a mountain, while others are restless, moving like drifting dust. Is it that the mind of the tranquil one is slow, whereas the mind of the restless one is fast?
Are they all equal? Answer:
For all classes of sentient beings, the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind are equal.
Associated with greed and so forth, as well as dissociated from them, it is likewise so.

Regarding the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the minds of all classes of sentient beings: the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the minds of all sentient beings occur simultaneously, without any difference in duration.
Why is this? Because it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Furthermore, it has neither magnitude nor minuteness, because it is not material form (*arūpa*).
Due to the differences among the four great elements, bodies vary in size; those with lighter bodies move swiftly, while those with heavier bodies move slowly.
Because the mind turns toward many objects, it feels flickering and restless; when the mind rests upon a single object, mindfulness becomes calm and still.

Regarding the statement that "the same applies to association with and dissociation from greed and so forth": whether a mind possesses greed or is free from greed, all such minds arise together, abide together, and cease together, because they are momentary.
Because an unwholesome mind does not perform [virtuous] action, it appears heavy; because a wholesome mind performs action, it appears light.
This should be understood to apply to everything up to liberation and non-liberation.
The presence or absence of greed is as explained in the *Dhātuvarga*.
Question:
It has already been stated that for all sentient beings, the mind arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with its mental factors (*caitasika*).
What, furthermore, is meant by the "mindless state"?

It refers to when those who have entered the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) have their minds extinguished, while the minds of other sentient beings arise.
When they emerge from that concentration, this mind arises again, while the minds of other sentient beings cease.
What is meant by "how"? Answer:
It should be understood that this teaching applies to those with a mind, and likewise to those without a mind.

That is to say, when one enters the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), while the minds of other sentient beings arise, this initial moment of attainment also arises.
Upon awakening from the concentration, when the minds of other sentient beings cease, this subsequent attainment also ceases.

When one abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the minds of other sentient beings both arise and cease, and this state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) likewise both arises and ceases.
Furthermore, some say that the arising of all minds is not necessarily uniform; there may be instances where a mind arises but does not cease.
This forms four propositions.
The first proposition refers to arising from the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The second proposition refers to the moment of entering those meditative attainments.
The third phrase refers to those who possess a mind.
The fourth phrase refers to the time of abiding in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
This [emptiness] has no smallness or greatness, because it is formless.
Having already explained the arising and ceasing of all minds, the extensive meaning of "mind" shall now be explained.

There are four [minds] in the desire realm, three each in the form and formless realms, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training; these are said to arise in this sequential order.

Regarding the statement that there are four minds in the desire realm, three each in the form and formless realms, and the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), making twelve minds in total: these are the wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm; the same for the formless realm; and the mind of one in training and the mind of one beyond training.
Question:
How are the twelve types of consciousness established? Answer:
The establishment of the bound and unbound realms and their seeds is as follows:

two types of mind are established based on the bound and the unbound. Regarding the bound, ten types of mind are established through the differentiation of the realms and their seeds; regarding the unbound, two types of mind are established through the differentiation of the seeds. Therefore, twelve types of mind are taught.
Regarding the statement that these arise in succession: these various minds arise one after another in sequence.
Now, the various minds shall be explained.
A wholesome mind of the desire realm gives rise to nine, and it likewise arises from eight.
The two defiled [minds] give rise to four, and they also arise from ten minds.

Regarding "the wholesome mind of the desire realm gives rise to nine": the wholesome mind of the desire realm arises in succession from nine minds—four belonging to the desire realm itself and five belonging to its own level.
The wholesome mind of the form realm refers to the time when one first applies effort to enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), because it is conducive to that state.
This is a general statement;
it does not apply to all minds of the form realm.
Some say it is comprised within the preparatory stage (anāgamya-dhyāna) and not the others;
others say it is comprised within the preparatory stage and the first dhyāna;
and yet others say it is comprised within the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
It extends up to the second dhyāna.

Just as in the case of the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*), one arises from the first dhyāna, leaps over the second dhyāna and its attendants, and the third dhyāna becomes manifest; this is also the same here.
The defiled mind of the form realm refers to when one dies with this wholesome mind and is born with that defiled mind continuing in succession.
The same applies to the defiled mind of the formless realm.

Furthermore, because they are also concordant with the minds of those in training and those beyond training, the non-obscured neutral minds of the form and formless realms do not arise immediately in succession; this is because the mind is bound to its own respective level.
Wholesome states of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also do not manifest [there], because they are extremely remote.

As for the statement "this also arises from eight," the wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) likewise arises in succession from eight minds: four from the desire realm and four from its own level.
The wholesome and defiled wholesome minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are as previously explained.

Regarding the "defiled," this refers to being afflicted by the afflictions of the first dhyāna stage; because one relies on the wholesome mind of the desire realm for protection, the wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests immediately after arising from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the second point, "the two defiled [minds] give rise to four": from an unwholesome mind of the desire realm and a concealed-neutral mind, four minds of their own realm arise in succession, but not those of higher stages, because they are incompatible.

Regarding "also arising from ten minds": those two types of defiled minds in the desire realm arise in succession from ten minds—four from their own realm and six from the form and formless realms, namely at the time of rebirth.
The indeterminate [mind] gives rise to seven immediately after;
it also arises from five. The wholesome mind of the form realm consists of eleven; it also arises from nine minds.
Regarding "the indeterminate gives rise to seven immediately after": following the non-obscured indeterminate mind of the desire realm, seven minds arise in succession: four from its own realm;

The wholesome mind of the form realm refers to the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*); from it, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind arises in succession, which occurs at the time of taking birth;
the same applies to the obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm.

Regarding "also arising from five": in the desire realm, the non-obscured neutral mind arises in succession from five minds—four from its own realm and the wholesome mind of the form realm, namely the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
Regarding "the eleven wholesome [minds] of the form realm": eleven minds arise in succession from a wholesome mind of the form realm, excluding the non-obscured neutral mind of the formless realm.

Regarding "also arising from nine minds": a wholesome mind of the form realm arises in succession from nine minds, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the non-obscured neutral mind of the formless realm.
The defiled [minds] of the form realm are six; they also arise from eight minds.
The neutral [minds] give rise to six in succession, and from three, they arise in sequence.

Regarding "the defiled [minds] of the form realm are six": following a concealed-neutral mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the form realm, six minds arise in succession—three from its own realm and three from the desire realm, excluding the non-concealed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the desire realm.

Regarding "also arising from eight minds": the obscured-neutral mind of the form realm arises in succession from eight minds, excluding the two defiled minds and the two untainted minds of the desire realm.

Regarding "the indeterminate is followed by six": following a non-obscured indeterminate mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), six minds arise in succession: three of its own realm, two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and one defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding those arising from the three [types of minds] in succession: they arise in succession from the three minds of their own realm.
A wholesome mind of the formless realm gives rise to nine; it also arises from six minds.
An afflicted mind gives rise to seven; it also arises from seven.

Regarding "the wholesome [minds] of the formless realm give rise to nine": following a wholesome mind of the formless realm, nine minds arise in succession, excluding the wholesome mind of the desire realm, the non-obscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, and the non-obscured-neutral mind of the form realm.

Regarding "also arising from six minds": wholesome minds of the formless realm also arise in succession from six minds—namely, the three of its own realm, the wholesome mind of the form realm, and the two untainted minds.

Regarding "the defiled mind gives rise to seven": following a concealed-indeterminate mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), seven minds arise in succession: three from its own realm, the wholesome mind and the defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding those that also arise from seven: the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the formless realm also arises in succession from seven minds—namely, the three of its own realm, and the wholesome and non-obscured-unspecified minds of the desire and form realms.
The indeterminate mind gives rise to six, and likewise arises from three;
the mind of one in training gives rise to five, and likewise arises from four minds.

Regarding "the indeterminate mind gives rise to six": following the non-obscured indeterminate mind of the formless realm, six minds arise in succession—three of its own realm and three defiled minds of the lower realms.

Regarding "arising again from three": in the formless realm, the non-obscured neutral mind arises in succession from three minds of its own realm, and not from others, because it is a result of maturation (*vipāka*).

Regarding the statement that "the mind of training arises from five": the mind of training arises in succession from five types of minds—namely, two untainted minds and the wholesome minds of the three realms.
It does not arise from defiled minds because their natures are mutually contradictory; nor does it arise from non-obscured neutral minds because their nature is not swift.

Regarding "also arising from four minds": the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) also arises in succession from four minds, namely, the mind of one in training itself and the wholesome minds of the three realms.
It does not arise from the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because that is its cause; nor does it arise from others, as previously explained.
The mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) gives rise to four minds, and it also arises from five minds.
Having already explained the twelve minds, the twenty should now be explained.

Regarding "the mind of one beyond training gives rise to four": the mind of one beyond training arises in succession from four minds, namely, the mind of one beyond training itself and the wholesome minds of the three realms.
It is not the state of training (*śaikṣa*), because it is a fruit;
it is not the others, as previously stated.

Furthermore, regarding "it also arises from five minds": the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises in succession from five minds—namely, the two untainted minds and the wholesome minds of the three realms.

Regarding the statement "The twelve minds have already been explained; the twenty [minds] should now be explained": the sequential arising of the twelve minds has already been explained; these twelve minds shall now be analyzed into twenty and explained.
Two are wholesome, two are defiled; they are born of retribution, of deportment, of craftsmanship, and the fruits of dhyāna—these are the eight minds within the desire realm.

The eight minds of the desire realm refer to: the wholesome mind produced through effort, the wholesome mind acquired at birth, the unwholesome mind, and the obscured-unspecified and non-obscured-unspecified minds.

The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds are of four kinds: those born of retribution (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those of transformation (*nairmāṇika*).
Excluding the unwholesome (*akuśala*) minds of craftsmanship, the remaining types exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
excluding the fruits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-phala*) that are of deportment, the remaining four exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

"Excluding unwholesome [minds] and those of craftsmanship, the rest exist in the form realm": there are six minds in the form realm; excluding the unwholesome and those of craftsmanship, the rest are as previously described.

Regarding the statement that, apart from the fruits of dhyāna and the *airyāpathika* mind, the remaining four exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): there are four types of mind in the formless realm, excluding the *airyāpathika* and the *nairmāṇika* (transformative) minds.
In both the form and formless realms, the *śailpasthānika* (artisanal) mind is excluded because there is no engagement in worldly work or craft.
Unwholesome states are excluded because of the absence of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).
States of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are excluded from the [meditative] deportments (*airyāpathika*), because coming and going are not part of their nature.
The mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) is excluded, because the [meditative] branches (*aṅga*) are subsumed therein and dhyāna is not part of its nature.
The minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), these constitute twenty;
those minds arise in succession, each explained according to its respective meaning.

Regarding "the minds of those in training and those beyond training, these constitute twenty": the minds of those in training and those beyond training, together with the preceding eighteen, make up the twenty minds.
The distinctions between the bound, the unbound, and the realms have been explained in general terms previously;
now, the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral [factors] are also distinguished according to their types.
Regarding the statement that those minds arise in succession, each explained according to its specific meaning: this refers to how these minds arise in successive order, which shall now be explained.
The mind of desire (*kāmāvacara*) arises from ten [minds] and also arises from eight minds;
the mind of acquisition (*upapattilābhika*) arises next from nine [minds] and also arises from eleven [minds].

Regarding "the ten [minds] arising from the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the desire realm": following the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm, ten minds arise in succession: seven of its own realm—excluding the transformation mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), because that arises in succession to the pure dhyāna—and the preparatory wholesome minds of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "also arising from eight minds": those skillful preparatory (*prayoga*) minds of the desire realm arise in succession from eight minds—namely, the two skillful and two defiled minds of its own realm, the preparatory skillful and defiled minds of the form realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "the innate [wholesome mind] gives rise to nine in the subsequent birth": following the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm, nine minds arise in succession—seven of its own realm (excluding the mind of transformation), and the defiled minds of the form and formless realms.
Regarding "also arising from eleven": the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm arises in succession from eleven minds: seven from its own realm as previously stated;
the preparatory wholesome mind, the defiled mind, and the minds of those in training and those beyond training of the form realm.
The two defiled [minds] give rise to seven; they also arise from fourteen.
The retributive and the formal [minds] are eight; these also arise from seven.

Regarding "the two defiled give rise to seven": the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm arise in succession from seven minds of their own realm, excluding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
Regarding "also arising from fourteen": these two defiled minds arise in succession from fourteen minds— seven from their own realm (excluding the mind of transformation),
four from the form realm (excluding the wholesome mind of application and the mind of transformation),
and three from the formless realm (excluding the wholesome mind of application).

Regarding the eight minds produced by retribution and those of deportment: from the retribution-born and deportment minds of the desire realm, eight minds arise in succession—namely, six minds of its own realm (excluding the wholesome mind of preparation and the mind of transformation), as well as the defiled minds of the form and formless realms.

Regarding "these also arise from seven": these minds of retribution and deportment in the desire realm also arise in succession from seven minds of their own realm, excluding the mind of transformation.
The *śailpasthānika-citta* (artistic/technical mind) gives rise to six; it also arises from seven.
The *nirmāṇa-citta* (transformation mind) gives rise to two; it also arises from two.

Regarding "the *śailpasthānika-citta* gives rise to six": the *śailpasthānika-citta* of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) successively gives rise to the six minds of its own realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) and the transformation mind.
Regarding "it also arises from seven": those [seven] also arise in succession from seven minds within their own realm, excluding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).

Regarding "the mind of transformation arises from two": the mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm arises in succession from two minds—the mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm itself and the wholesome mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) belonging to the form realm.
That which arises from two likewise arises in succession from these two minds.
The twelve preparatory stages of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-prayoga*) likewise arise from ten;
those born of attainment (*upapatti-lābhika*) subsequently give rise to eight, and they also arise from five minds.

Regarding the twelve [minds] arising from the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): following the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, twelve minds arise in succession—six from its own realm;
three from the desire realm, namely the preparatory wholesome mind, the innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*), and the transformation mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*);
and the preparatory wholesome mind of the formless realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "this also arises from ten": the skillful mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-kuśala*) in the form realm arises in succession from ten minds: four from its own realm—excluding those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and those born of retribution (*vipākaja*);
two from the desire realm—the skillful mind of preparatory effort and the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika*);
and three from the formless realm—the skillful mind of preparatory effort, the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa*), and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the eight minds that arise in succession from those acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*): from a wholesome mind acquired at birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), eight minds arise in succession—namely, five of its own realm (excluding the mind of transformation), two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding those that also arise from five minds: the innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) of the form realm arises in succession from five minds of its own realm, excluding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
Nine minds arise from a defiled (*kliṣṭa*) mind of the form realm; it also arises from eleven.
Seven minds arise from a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*); they arise in succession from five.

Regarding "the defiled mind of the form realm gives rise to nine": following a defiled mind of the form realm, nine minds arise in succession—five from its own realm (excluding the mind of transformation), and four from the desire realm (two wholesome and two defiled minds).
Regarding "also arising from eleven": a defiled mind of the form realm arises in succession from eleven minds—five from its own realm, excluding the mind of transformation;
three from the desire realm, namely the innate wholesome, the deportment, and the resultant;
and three from the formless realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome mind.

Regarding "the seven minds arising from the deportment mind": following a deportment mind (*airyāpathika-citta*) of the form realm, seven minds arise in succession: four of its own realm—excluding the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the transformation mind (*nairmāṇika*);
two defiled minds (*kliṣṭa*) of the desire realm; and one defiled mind of the formless realm.

Regarding those arising from the fivefold sequence: the deportment-mind (*airyāpathika*) of the form realm arises in succession from the five minds of its own realm, excluding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
It should be known that the mind born of karmic maturation (*vipākaja*) in the form realm is also explained like the deportment-mind;
namely, those various fruits of dhyāna should be understood as being like those in the desire realm.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that the mind born of retribution in the realm of form is also as explained for the mind of deportment": the mind born of retribution in the realm of form arises in succession from seven minds and also arises from five minds, just as was explained for the mind of deportment.

It should be understood that the fruits of those dhyānas are like those of the desire realm: from the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the form realm, two minds arise in succession—the wholesome mind of skillful means (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) of the form realm and the transformative mind; likewise, these two minds also arise in succession from those same two minds.
The first [mind] of the formless realm arises from seven; these also arise from six.
That which is acquired at birth also gives rise to seven; it should be known that these arise from four.

Regarding "the first [mind] of the formless realm arises from seven": following the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) of the formless realm, seven minds arise in succession: the four [minds] of its own realm, the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "this also arises from six": the skillful mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-kuśala*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) arises in succession from six minds: three from its own realm—excluding those born of retribution (*vipākaja*)—as well as the skillful mind of preparatory effort in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "the innate also gives rise to seven": the innate wholesome [minds] of the formless realm also give rise to seven minds in succession—four of its own realm and three defiled [minds] of the lower realms.
It should be known that as for those arising from four: they arise in succession from the four minds of their own realm.
The defiled arises from eight minds, and it arises from ten minds.
The retributive mind arises from six, and it also arises from four.

Regarding the "defiled mind giving rise to eight minds": following a defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), eight minds arise in succession: four from its own realm, two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) and the defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding those that arise from ten types of mind: the defiled minds of the formless realm arise in succession from ten minds—four from their own realm;
three from the desire realm, namely the innate wholesome, the deportment, and the resultant;
and likewise for the form realm.

Regarding "the retribution-born mind arises from six": the retribution-born mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) arises in succession from six minds—three from its own realm (excluding the wholesome mind of preparation), and three defiled (*kliṣṭa*) minds from the lower stages.
Regarding "these also arise from four": that mind born of retribution arises in succession from the four minds of its own realm.
The mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) gives rise to six in succession; it arises from four.
The mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) gives rise to five; this also arises from five.

Regarding "the learner’s mind successively gives rise to six": the learner’s mind successively gives rise to six types of minds: the preparatory wholesome minds (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the three realms; the innate wholesome minds (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) of the desire realm—which are strong and sharp—while those of the two higher realms are weak and dull; and the learner’s and non-learner’s minds (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa-citta*).

Regarding those arising from the fourfold sequence: the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) arises in succession from four minds—the preparatory wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one in training.

Regarding the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) giving rise to five: the mind of one beyond training arises in succession from five minds—the preparatory wholesome minds of the three realms, the innate wholesome minds of the desire realm, and the mind of one beyond training.

"Also arising from five types of mind" refers to the preparatory wholesome minds (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) of the three realms, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Question:
For what reason does the preparatory wholesome mind arise in immediate succession?

Regarding the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those born of retribution (*vipākaja*), why do these various minds not arise in succession from a wholesome mind of application (*prayogika*)?

Answer: Because the minds of deportment and craftsmanship are produced through one’s own spontaneous delight in their respective activities; because the mind born of retribution is weak and inferior; and because it is devoid of volitional effort.
This means that because the mind of deportment delights in practicing deportment, the skillful mind of application does not arise immediately following it;
however, because the mind of emergence does not exert effort in application, the skillful mind of application arises immediately after it.
The same applies to the mind of majestic deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
The mind born of retribution (*vipākaja*) is weak and inferior because it performs no intentional action and is merely the result of seeds planted by past karma.
Therefore, one who enters such a state of mind cannot emerge from it, as they lack diligence in skillful means (*upāya*); thus, it arises in succession from a wholesome mind of skillful means.

If it is argued that because a defiled mind is attached to its objects and is weak and inferior, a skillful mind of expedient means should not arise immediately after the object of a defiled mind, this is not so.
Why is this? Because the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is not different [from the mind], because one perceives its faults, and because it is not weak or inferior.

When the faults and evils within that objective sphere are transformed, virtues arise from that very same sphere; therefore, that objective sphere is not different from that practice. This is because of the exhaustion and weariness caused by the afflictions (*kleśa*), and because one observes that very objective sphere as the long night’s habituation to the afflictions.
Because the defiled mind is not weak or inferior, one should therefore give rise to a wholesome mind of skillful means (upāya) in succession.
Although the innate wholesome mind (upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta) of the desire realm is swift, it is not a mind of skillful means.

Because it is swift, it arises in succession from those wholesome minds of skillful means in the form realm, as well as from the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because it is not a mind of skillful means, it cannot arise in succession from those various [other] minds.
The innate wholesome mind of the form realm is neither swift nor produced through application.

Because it is not swift, it does not arise in immediate succession from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), nor from the applied wholesome mind of the formless realm.
Because it is not an appropriate means (*anupāya*), those various minds do not arise in succession from it.
The same applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

A defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) of the form realm can give rise in succession to a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala-citta*) of the desire realm, because of its swiftness.
A defiled mind of the formless realm does not arise immediately after [a mind of] the wholesome state acquired at birth in the form realm, because it is not swift.
Question:
What is the True Dharma?
Answer: The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are called the conventional true Dharma;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are said to be the ultimate truth.

Regarding the statement that "the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are called the conventional true Dharma": the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are the true Dharma of verbal expression; this is because they arise based on names and designations, as has already been explained previously.
The Buddha’s speech has the nature of speech itself, yet speech functions by relying on names.
Because it functions through other [conventional] means, it is therefore called a conventional designation (*saṃvṛti-saṃketa*).
It is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*) because it reveals the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*); for it reveals the meaning by means of names.

Regarding the statement that "the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)," the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the true dharma of the ultimate truth because they arise apart from names.

Although the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) also functions apart from names, it is not called the true dharma of the ultimate truth because it is accompanied by defilements (*sa-mala*).
Just as there are two kinds of True Dharma, there are likewise two kinds of practitioners of the Dharma:
those who cultivate the Dharma and those who cultivate meditation. Cultivating the Dharma refers to recitation and study; cultivating meditation refers to the practice of dhyāna.
Regarding those conventional designations, "Right Dharma" (saddharma) refers to practice, and "Dharma" carries the sense of upholding.
From the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), Right Dharma is practice.
Therefore, it is said that when those who practice the Dharma abide, the Right Dharma abides; when those who practice the Dharma cease to exist, the Right Dharma ceases to exist.
Because the World-Honored One encourages practitioners to engage in cultivation, he does not specify the limits [of the practice], as previously stated.
The "Chapter on the Selection of the Vajra Samādhi" shall be explained in detail; it shall now be expounded.
Fifty-two and more, and again eighty are taught;
some say there are thirteen—these are the vajra-samādhis.
Some say there are fifty-two vajra-samādhis, which are subsumed within the preparatory stage of dhyāna (anāgamya).

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship by means of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) based on the dhyāna of the future [realm], one contemplates the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. If one attains it by means of the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna), one contemplates each of the four aspects of the truth of origin individually.

If it is the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), one contemplates the four aspects of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) regarding the cessation of formations bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), one contemplates the four aspects of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) regarding the path that severs formations bound to the desire realm.

If it is the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), one contemplates the cessation of formations associated with the level of the first dhyāna, or even up to the cessation of formations associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If it is the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one attains the fruit of arhatship by contemplating the four aspects of the path within the category of subsequent knowledge across those nine levels.

Thus, because the objects of this wisdom-practice involve the differentiation of aspects, there are fifty-two distinct cessations due to the diversity of sufferings; because their emotional dispositions are separated, the contemplations are distinct. Therefore, in the cessation of the eighth stage, there are thirty-two [aspects]. The practice of the path is likewise: by penetrating the different stages while sharing the same nature of emotional disposition, the contemplation is comprehensive. This comprehensive contemplation of the nine stages involves only four practices; combined with the sixteen practices of the four truths previously mentioned, they total fifty-two.
As it is for the preliminary stage of the first dhyāna, so it is for the stages up to the fourth dhyāna.

In the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana), there are twenty-eight: eight aspects of the Truths of Suffering and Origin belonging to its own level, four aspects of the Truth of Cessation, sixteen aspects of the Truth of Cessation belonging to the nine levels of the Path, and four aspects of Cessation belonging to the higher levels. Thus, as the number of cessations gradually decreases in the higher realms, there are twenty-four aspects in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) and twenty in the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).

Because there is no knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) within the formless realm (*ārūpya*), and because *dharmajñāna* takes the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object, it does not belong to the formless realm.

This is because the cessation practiced in a lower stage is not the objective domain of the suffering of that lower stage, and because the objects of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) of the lower stages function as successive causes.
Some say there are eighty diamond-like samādhis (vajra-samādhi) in the future [of the dhyānas].

Regarding the distinctions therein: it is said that the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) also consists of the subsequent knowledge of the path cultivated in each stage as an antidote to its respective objects; since one contemplates the seven stages of the path to Arhatship, and each stage has four aspects, there are twenty-eight. Combined with the previous fifty-two, this makes eighty.
As it is for the preliminary stage of dhyāna, so it is up to the fourth dhyāna.
In the sphere of infinite space there are forty; in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thirty-two; and in the sphere of nothingness, twenty-four.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:

There are thirteen diamond-like samādhis (vajropama-samādhi) subsumed under the future stage of dhyāna; four samādhis associated with the four types of subsequent patience (anvaya-kṣānti) during the path of seeing (darśana-mārga); and nine samādhis associated with the nine paths of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) during the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) for the sake of detachment from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
All of these are the supreme antidotes to existence, for they are not the domain of the mundane path of the vajra-samādhi.
This applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna; it is the same for the nine stages from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness.
This is a general statement.

If one speaks in terms of the distinctions of patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), practice (*caryā*), types (*prakāra*), and conditions (*pratyaya*) within the future [state] subsumed under dhyāna, there are then one thousand four hundred and ninety-two vajra-samādhis.

The same applies up to the fourth dhyāna: there are four hundred and sixty-eight in the sphere of infinite space, three hundred and twenty-four in the sphere of infinite consciousness, and two hundred and sixteen in the sphere of nothingness.
Question:
Regarding the supernormal powers (abhijñā) described in the Chapter on Knowledge (jñāna-varga), are those supernormal powers entirely wholesome (kuśala), or are they not? Answer:
The three supernormal powers (abhijñā) are said to be wholesome; the other two are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
One should know that they rely upon the realms of desire and form, and the World-Honored One has declared their nature to be wisdom (prajñā).

Regarding "the three supernormal powers are said to be wholesome": the power of psychic transformation (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna), the power of knowing the minds of others (paracitta-jñāna), and the power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna)—these three supernormal powers are said to be wholesome.

Why is this? Because it is the fruit of affection; because it arises from extreme skillful means; because it subdues others; and because it causes those who lack faith and delight to gain faith and delight.
These three [qualities] cause others to attain supreme subduing, whereby they rejoice; the wisdom associated with this joyful mind is wholesome, as it is associated with faith and confidence.
The other two are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely the divine eye and the divine ear.
These two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are indeterminate because they are not conducive to the fruits of craving nor to the ultimate application of effort.
Furthermore, it arises from the reception of forms and sounds; therefore, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question: Where does it manifest?
What is its nature? Answer:
It should be known that, based on the desire and form realms, the Blessed One spoke of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This supernormal power manifests in the realms of desire and form, and not elsewhere, because it relies upon form.
Since it first arose in the realm of desire, it is subsequently able to manifest in the realm of form.
That is not capable for a beginner, as it is not within their scope.

Because this nature of wisdom arises from conceptualization and because the basis gives rise to that which depends upon it, this explanation establishes that it is designated by the name "eye" due to its arising from the eye.

As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, at that time the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) formed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) is complete, and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is purified.
Regarding the matters of the faculties (*indriya*) as explained in the *Sūtra-varga*, it was said they would be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-varga*; this shall now be explained.
One should know that those faculties are well-distinguished by the wise:
there are twenty-two in name, but seventeen in substance.
The Buddha taught that the faculties have twenty-two names, yet their actual entities number seventeen.

The male and female faculties, as well as the three untainted faculties, do not establish a separate category of "thing" (*vastu*) because they lack distinct entities; they are subsumed within other faculties.
Since the male and female faculties are nothing other than the body faculty, this is why it is so stated.
What is the male faculty?
It is a portion of the body faculty.
The female faculty is likewise.
Furthermore, because of the basis of a single consciousness:

if consciousness arises based on the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it necessarily arises based on the male or female faculties (*strī- or puruṣendriya*), as there are no faculties that arise together without distinct characteristics.
A single consciousness consists of three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), for it is composed of nine faculties.

The nine faculties are the mental faculty (manas), the faculty of pleasure (sukha), the faculty of joy (saumanasya), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā), and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
These nine faculties are established as three faculties based on the distinctions of the path and the person.

Regarding the distinction of the paths: the path of seeing is said to be the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya); the path of cultivation is said to be the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya); and the path of no-more-learning is said to be the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya). Regarding the distinction of persons:

those practicing in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin) and those practicing in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin) are said to possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and those who have realized the body (kāyasākṣin) are said to possess the faculty of "knowing"; and those liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) are said to possess the faculty of "one who has known."
Question:
What are the characteristics of the conventional and the ultimate truth? Answer:
When analyzing a thing, if one discards its name, it is then called "equal" (*sama*) and so forth;
when analyzing it, there is nothing to be discarded—this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "when analyzing a thing, if one discards its name, it is then called 'equal' and so forth": if, upon analyzing a thing, one discards its name, this refers to things that are equal to other things. In the Sanskrit language these are called *samnipāta*, which is translated as "equal collection" (*dengji*), or also "equal accumulation. There are three types of such assemblies, and that which is non-existent is termed an "equal collection."
These are not determinate entities in the ultimate sense, because they cannot be apprehended.

For example, when one analyzes a jar in terms of its color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility, the name "jar" is relinquished; yet, apart from color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility, there is no separate entity named "jar. Therefore, names and such are [mere designations].

"In all such cases, that which is not discarded during conceptual differentiation is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This means that if, when things are being conceptually differentiated, their names are not discarded, that is the ultimate truth.
Just as the five aggregates of clinging are called the Truth of Suffering, even when analyzed into five stages, they do not lose the name "suffering," because form is suffering.
This applies likewise up to consciousness.

That form is further of eleven kinds; each individual base (*āyatana*) is entirely suffering, such that even when analyzed down to moments (*kṣaṇa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*), it does not lose its designation as suffering, because it possesses those characteristics.
All such [matters] are as explained regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the *Prakaraṇapāda*; they shall be explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-pāda*.
Question:
Is it determinate or indeterminate?
Answer: The realms, destinies, and stages are determinate; the intermediate state (antarābhava) is unimpeded in five respects.
It is called "fragrance-food" (*gandharva*). Those who seek existence proceed by means of mental formations.

Regarding those who are certain as to their realm, destination, and stage: in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the realm, destination, and stage do not change; one in the intermediate state of the desire realm will necessarily be born in the desire realm, and one in the intermediate state of the form realm will be born in the form realm.

In this way, those born into the hell realm are born in hell, and so on up to those born into the human realm being born as humans; likewise for those born among the Four Great Kings being born among the Four Great Kings, and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Regarding the five aspects of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): the nature of the intermediate state consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), because it possesses coming and going.

Since there is no coming or going apart from form (*rūpa*), the intermediate state exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but not in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because form is not present therein.
