It is wisdom not separated from desire, because it is associated with the desire realm. Therefore, this is
There is. That is to say, when a noble one has abandoned the desires of the desire realm but has not yet abandoned the desires of the first dhyāna,
the transformation-mind that is the fruit of the desire realm and the first dhyāna is free from desire, because craving for the desire realm has been exhausted.
The wisdom of the first dhyāna has not yet abandoned desire, because craving for it has not been exhausted.
All transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) are likewise; according to their respective meanings, they exclude the fruits of their own level.
Is it that one who abides in the path of non-obstruction attains the various cessations?
Is this contrary to the afflictions, yet not [the result of] that untainted vision? Answer:

There is. That is to say, when an ordinary person cultivates supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they attain various cessations (*nirodha*) by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are contrary to those powers through the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*); it is not [the cessation] of those contrary to the outflow-free vision (*anāsrava-darśana*).

Why is this? Because when a noble one (ārya) becomes free from desire, the patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti) manifests before them, whereby the afflictions (kleśa) that are incompatible with that patience are extinguished.
Is it possible that there are afflictions which are extinguished and obtained by one who is free from desire?
Is it possible to attain the stainless exhaustion [of suffering] without severing the afflictions? Answer: Yes.

This means that when one dies in a higher realm and is reborn in the Brahma Heaven, one attains the cessation of afflictions belonging to the desire realm, yet does not sever those [higher] afflictions, because they have already been severed previously.
This is likewise for all other stages.
Is there a stainless pure stage that one has never before attained but now attains,
which is neither the abandonment of desire nor a falling back, and does not depend upon the path of vision? Answer:

There is. That is to say, when one has become detached from desire through the first dhyāna, and by relying on the first dhyāna and its attendants, transcends and rises above the state of ordinary birth, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) arises, whereby one achieves the fruit of *anāgāmin* across three stages.
Emerging from that concentration, one enters the second dhyāna and attains the untainted (anāsrava) second dhyāna.
At the moment of attaining that untainted state, it is not a case of becoming free from desire, because one was already free from desire previously.
It is not a case of regression, because there is superior progress;
it is not the path of seeing, because the path of seeing has been brought to completion.
It should be understood that the same applies to the higher stages and to the enhancement of the faculties.
"Has anyone attained what was never before attained, and yet attained nirvāṇa?
Is it not by not abandoning that which is not attained?
If you can know this, please speak."
Answer: Yes.

That is to say, with the exception of the acquisition [attained] through the retinue of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), it is acquired by other untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).
That initial untainted equanimity (*anāsrava-upekṣā*) cannot be attained by any ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The others are not relinquished, because they have already been relinquished previously.
If one accomplishes the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), one also accomplishes the seven knowledges (*jñāna*).
Regarding these various untainted views (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*), what is it that they do not see?
Answer: There is.

This means that when this person abides in the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), they accomplish all wisdom of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-prajñā*) and perceive all cessations and all paths, with the sole exception of the retinue of the subsequent patience regarding the path itself.

That patience does not perceive an intrinsic nature because it is not self-observed and because it lacks duality; nor does it perceive association because it consists of a single practice and a single object-condition.
It does not perceive coexistence because it has a single fruit and a single determination.
Is there any phenomenon never before attained, which is within the sphere of the outflows and the limits [of existence], such that only one who is immovable can strike it as a wholesome dharma?
Answer: No.

There is. That is to say, the signless-signless (animittānimitta) has never before been attained throughout the infinite cycle of birth and death; yet, because it attains the noble path of emptiness (śūnyatā-āryamārga), it is said to have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana).
Because it is not analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it is said to have a limited sphere (prāntakoṭika-viṣaya).
Since the others are not of that category, it is said they are "only immovable.
Because it is the noble path of emptiness, it is called the "striking" of wholesome dharmas.
Having already given rise to untainted wisdom, [one acts] toward those [dharmas] not yet arisen.
Is it that what was produced in a previous life is not the cause for what follows? If you can know this, please explain. Answer:
There is. That is to say, what was previously superior is not the cause for what is subsequently weak, because its fruit is similar and increased.
Is it possible that one who has abandoned desire for the six stages, even if they are a noble one (ārya), might also accomplish that fruit?
Is it not established as untainted dhyāna?
If you can know this, please explain. Answer:

There is. That is to say, having become free from desire for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one relies on the preparatory stage of dhyāna (*anāgamya*) to transcend and emerge from the state of ordinary birth; at this point, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen. Because there are eighty-nine fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇya-phala*), it is said that he has accomplished those fruits.

Because the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is the fruit of support (*niśraya-phala*) and the fruit of effort (*prayoga-phala*) of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), and because the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering is the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) and the fruit of effort, yet it does not constitute untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), as it has not yet been attained.
Are there any untainted (anāsrava) dharmas that are subsumed within the realms (dhātu), yet those which produce such dharmas do not enter into those realms?
Answer: [Yes].
There is. That is to say, untainted (anāsrava) precepts are subsumed under that realm, not subsumed under the outflows (āsrava).
Precepts are produced from the four great elements (mahābhūta), for they are their fruit.
The four great elements are subsumed within the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), as they are the objective domain of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Is it possible that one great element ceases while two other great elements remain present, without arising in the stages of meditative absorption (*dhyānabhūmi*)?
"If one can know it, please explain.
Answer: "There is."
This refers to a noble being born in the desire realm, for whom the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna is immediately followed by the manifestation of the tainted (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna.

One type of the four great elements ceases, namely the four great elements of the desire realm; because they are accompanied by the untainted, when that [untainted state] arises and manifests, it is produced by the four great elements of that very stage.

Regarding the two kinds of the four great elements that manifest before one: this refers to the four great elements of the desire realm and the stage of the first dhyāna that accompany the path of untainted precepts (*anāsrava-anuvartaka*). If one is born in that desire realm, they are produced by the four great elements of that very desire realm; therefore, these four great elements arise and cease simultaneously with the untainted state.
Are there any dharmas that take the three paths as their cause, yet possess these three kinds of self-nature—namely, being of three kinds in one stage and also existing in three stages?
Answer: [Yes].

There is. It refers to the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*). Taking the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) as its causes, it has the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is said to be of three types based on the distinctions of weak, medium, and superior; it is said to be of one stage because it is subsumed within the stage of one beyond training; and it exists in three stages based on the distinctions of being with vitarka and vicāra, and so forth.

Is there any tainted feeling (*sāsrava-vedanā*) such that two [factors] are established while one is not, and two faculties (*indriya*) are established in two ways? This is what is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*). Answer: Yes, there is. When one is in the state of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) is not yet established, while the other two are established. Furthermore, when one is in the state of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is established in two ways—both as a faculty and as the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—while the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" is not established. This is what is called "bodily realization."

There is. That is to say, a person who has attained realization through bodily witness (kāyasākṣin), relying on the first dhyāna and its attendants, as well as the second dhyāna, and having further developed their faculties, does not bring the higher stages into manifestation, yet accomplishes the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the contaminated faculty of pleasure (sāsrava-sukhendriya).

This person had previously attained the untainted bliss of the third dhyāna stage; because of the transformation of their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), they relinquished it and have not yet reacquired it. Since they are advancing their faculties by relying on a lower stage, they do not cultivate the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) belonging to a higher stage.
Just as one who has attained the fruit of training does not possess the single faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) because they have abandoned desire,

they fully possess both the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), each of which is of two kinds— namely, contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Because the dhyānas of the threshold (anāgamya) and the intermediate (dhyānāntara) stages include the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), one thereby acquires the faculty of equanimity.
Because the first and second dhyānas include the faculty of joy (prītīndriya), one thereby acquires the faculty of joy.

The afflictions of the ninth stage are extinguished, and one attains the various dhyānas; yet one does not attain the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti). Should it be said that one might nonetheless attain them? Answer: [The afflictions] of the ninth stage are extinguished, and one attains the various dhyānas; one does not attain the formless absorptions. Or rather, should it be said that one might attain them? Answer: [One does not.]

There is. That is to say, an Arhat is able to attain dhyāna-concentration but not the formless attainments; he both attains and manifests the various dhyānas, whereas he accomplishes the formless attainments but does not practice them.
A single dharma has a manifold nature; it may be one, three, existent, or non-existent.
That which is the dharma of one beyond training—is it nurtured by the power of causes? Answer:
There is. It refers to the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown.
Because it establishes a single faculty, it is said to be one.
Because of the conjunction of the nine faculties, they are said to be manifold; because they are manifold, they are said to be not one.

Because it is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), it is said to be a single stage; because of initial and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and discrimination, it is said to be three stages.
"Existence" refers to having a name; "non-existence" means there is no distinct entity.
They are called "dharmas of one beyond training" because they are attained by one beyond training, and they are called "nourished by causes" because they are established through three causes.
Are there any phenomena that possess parts, which— along with other phenomena possessing parts—
arise, abide, and perish in a similar manner?
If you can know this, please explain.
Answer: There is.

That is to say, the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is a "part of another existence" (bhavāṅga); its characteristics arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with that sphere, because they share a single fruit.

The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is called "other-dependent" (parabhāga) because it does not perform an action; its characteristic (lakṣaṇa), however, is included within the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and is therefore "self-dependent" (svabhāga).
Are there any associated mental factors (saṃprayuktadharma) that are either called "other-dependent" or called "self-dependent"?
"If one can know it, please explain.
He replied:
"There is."
That is to say, the future mental base (*manāyatana*) consisting of non-arising phenomena is "with remainder" (*sabhāga*), because it does not perform its function.
Other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are also "with remainder," because they are subsumed within the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Is it possible for two *anāgāmins* to be born together in the same stage (*bhūmi*), such that when one achieves the first dharma (*ānantarya-mārga*), both simultaneously obtain the fruit of that stage?
Answer: Yes.

There are. Specifically, one *anāgāmin* who, relying on the second dhyāna, transcends to the state beyond birth (*abhisamaya-nyāma*), and a second *anāgāmin* who relies on the third dhyāna; both, at the end of their lives, are reborn together in the third dhyāna.
When one transcends and rises above the state of birth by relying on the second dhyāna, it is because of the advancement of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
When one abandons the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) and relies immediately upon the third dhyāna, one achieves non-abandonment.
The same applies to the higher stages.
One who attains the fruit of a single stage is said to possess the dhyāna that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Is there not one of immovable nature who, together with others, experiences a single existence?
Question: Is there a case where one achieves nine stages, yet possesses neither wholesome nor tainted states? Answer: Yes.
This refers to one who is born once in the desire realm and once in the first dhyāna.
Regarding birth in the desire realm, one accomplishes the impure dharmas (*sāsravadharma*) of nine stages.
Regarding birth in the first dhyāna, one accomplishes those of eight stages, excluding the stage of the desire realm.
Because one experiences both increase and abandonment within a single existence (*bhava*), it is called "a single existence.
As for "with outflows" (*sāsrava*): since one born in a higher realm through the untainted (*anāsrava*) state still accomplishes the lower [realms], it is said to be "with outflows."
Is it possible that, abiding for even a single kṣaṇa, one attains the abandonment of three gates of liberation,
or perhaps abandons two, or abandons one and then regains it? Answer:
There is. This refers to one born in the formless realm who is about to attain arhatship while abiding in the vajra-samādhi.

Having attained the samādhi-gate of the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa), they relinquish the gate of liberation of the stage of training (śaikṣa); they relinquish the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodha-samāpatti) as well as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and they relinquish all factors conducive to decline while attaining all superior factors. Since both relinquishing and attaining occur within a single thought-moment, it is called "one thought-moment."

Through the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) and the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one is said to abandon two [factors] and achieve the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Because one abandons [inferior states], falls back [from them], and attains the superior, one thus abandons one and acquires another.
Is it possible to accomplish the fruits of śramaṇaship while simultaneously accomplishing both the noble (*ārya*) and the non-noble (*anārya*)?
"And yet one cannot attain the knowledge of cessation?
If you can know it, then speak.
He replied:

There is. That is to say, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen through immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, at that time one possesses eighty-nine factors of the fruits of śrāmaṇya, but does not possess the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, nor has one attained the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
To cross that unsurpassed ocean is a task beyond the capacity of those with little strength;
now, according to my own ability, I shall proclaim this profound meaning.
As for those who are impoverished in this world, they may suddenly be made wealthy.
Without wisdom, it is not so; one must employ great skillful means.
Worldly treasures are easy to obtain, but the treasure of wisdom is exceedingly difficult to acquire.
Therefore, one should study diligently and gradually enter into profound knowledge.
Right understanding is the path to Nirvana; False delusions are the track of birth and death.
Wisdom can extinguish the darkness of ignorance, Just as the sun dispels the deep gloom.
For the sake of seeking liberation, One should diligently cultivate wisdom.
The Bhikṣu Saṃghabhadra has composed these verses to adorn the Abhidharma; may all sentient beings have their wisdom gradually increase and swiftly attain liberation.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven.
